| Outlook  || Temperature || Humidity || Windy || Play |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|   || *Yes* || *No* ||   || *Yes* || *No* ||   || *Yes* || *No* ||   || *Yes* || *No* || *Yes* || *No* |
| Sunny || 2 || 3 || Hot || 2 || 2 || High || 3 || 4 || False || 6 || 2 || 9 || 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Overcast || 4 || 0 || Mild || 4 || 2 || Normal || 6 || 1 || True || 3 || 3 ||   ||   |
| Rainy || 3 || 2 || Cool || 3 || 1 ||   ||   ||   ||   ||   ||   ||   ||   |
| Sunny || 2/9 || 3/5 || Hot || 2/9 || 2/5 || High || 3/9 || 4/5 || False || 6/9 || 2/5 || 9/14 || 5/14 |
| Overcast || 4/9 || 0/5 || Mild || 4/9 || 2/5 || Normal || 6/9 || 1/5 || True || 3/9 || 3/5 ||   ||   |
| Rainy || 3/9 || 2/5 || Cool || 3/9 || 1/5 ||   ||   ||   ||   ||   ||   ||   ||   |

![Image](images/T000054tabt0015.png)

Now suppose we encounter a new example with the values that are shown in [Table 4.3](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#t0020). We treat the five features in [Table 4.2](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#t0015)—*outlook*, *temperature*, *humidity*, *windy*, and the overall likelihood that *play* is *yes* or *no*—as equally important, independent pieces of evidence and multiply the corresponding fractions. Looking at the outcome *yes* gives

*L**i**k**e**l**i**h**o**o**d* *o**f* *y**e**s*\=2/9×3/9×3/9×3/9×9/14=0.0053.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Likelihood of</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0053</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si2.png)

Table 4.3

A New Day

 
| Outlook || Temperature || Humidity || Windy || Play |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sunny || Cool || High || True || ? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

![Image](images/T000054tabt0020.png)

The fractions are taken from the *yes* entries in the table according to the values of the attributes for the new day, and the final 9/14<mml:math><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>/</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si3.png) is the overall fraction representing the proportion of days on which *play* is *yes*. A similar calculation for the outcome *no* leads to

*L**i**k**e**l**i**h**o**o**d* *o**f* *n**o*\=3/5×1/5×4/5×3/5×5/14=0.0206.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Likelihood of</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">no</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0206</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si4.png)

This indicates that for the new day, *no* is more likely than *yes*—four times more likely. The numbers can be turned into probabilities by normalizing them so that they sum to 1:

${Probability\\ of}\\ \\mathit{yes} = \\frac{0.0053}{0.0053 + 0.0206} = 20.5\\%,$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Probability of</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.0053</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.0053</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0206</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>20.5</mml:mn><mml:mo>%</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si5.png)

${Probability\\ of}\\ \\mathit{no} = \\frac{0.0206}{0.0053 + 0.0206} = 79.5\\%.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Probability of</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">no</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.0206</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.0053</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0206</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>79.5</mml:mn><mml:mo>%</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si6.png)

This simple and intuitive method is based on Bayes’ rule of conditional probability. Bayes’ rule says that if you have a hypothesis *H* and evidence *E* that bears on that hypothesis, then

$P(H\\text{∣}E) = \\frac{P(E\\text{∣}H)P(H)}{P(E)}$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mtext mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mtext><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mtext mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mtext><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math> (4.1)

![Equation](images/F000054si7.png)(4.1) 

We use the notation that *P*(*A*) denotes the probability of an event *A* and *P*(*A**⃒**B*)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">A</mml:mi><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">&#8402;</mml:mtext><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si8.png) denotes the probability of *A* conditional on another event *B*. The hypothesis *H* is that *play* will be, say, *yes*, and *P*(*H**⃒**E*)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">H</mml:mi><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">&#8402;</mml:mtext><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si9.png) is going to turn out to be 20.5%, just as determined previously. The evidence *E* is the particular combination of attribute values for the new day, *outlook* = *sunny*, *temperature* = *cool*, *humidity* = *high*, and *windy* = *true*. Let’s call these four pieces of evidence *E*[1], *E*[2], *E*[3], and *E*[4], respectively. Assuming that these pieces of evidence are independent (given the class), their combined probability is obtained by multiplying the probabilities:

$P(\\mathit{yes}\\textit{⃒}E) = \\frac{P\\left( {E\_{1},\\mathit{⃒},\\mathit{yes}} \\right) \\times P\\left( {E\_{2},\\mathit{⃒},\\mathit{yes}} \\right) \\times P\\left( {E\_{3},\\mathit{⃒},\\mathit{yes}} \\right) \\times P\\left( {E\_{4},\\mathit{⃒},\\mathit{yes}} \\right) \\times P\\left( \\mathit{yes} \\right)}{P\\left( E \\right)}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">&#8402;</mml:mtext><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">&#8402;</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">&#8402;</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">&#8402;</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">&#8402;</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (4.2)

![Equation](images/F000054si10.png)(4.2) 

Don’t worry about the denominator; we will ignore it and eliminate it in the final normalizing step when we make the probabilities of *yes* and *no* sum to 1, just as we did previously. The *P*(*yes*) at the end is the probability of a yes outcome without knowing any of the evidence E, without knowing anything about the particular day in question—it’s called the prior probability of the hypothesis *H*. In this case, it’s 9/14, because 9 of the 14 training examples had a *yes* value for play. Substituting the fractions in [Table 4.2](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#t0015) for the appropriate evidence probabilities leads to

$P(\\mathit{yes}\\mathit{⃒}E) = \\frac{\\left. 2\\slash 9 \\times 3\\slash 9 \\times 3\\slash 9 \\times 3\\slash 9 \\times 9\\slash 14 \\right.}{P\\left( E \\right)},$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">&#8402;</mml:mi><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si11.png)

as we calculated previously. Again, the *P*(*E*)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si12.png) in the denominator will disappear when we normalize.

This method goes by the name of Naïve Bayes, because it’s based on Bayes’ rule and “naïvely” assumes independence—it is only valid to multiply probabilities when the events are independent. The assumption that attributes are independent (given the class) in real life certainly is a simplistic one. But despite the disparaging name, Naïve Bayes works very well when tested on actual datasets, particularly when combined with some of the attribute selection procedures introduced in [Chapter 6](#Ch006_209-259_B9780443158889000078.xhtml#Ch006_209-259_B9780443158889000078), “Preparation: data preprocessing and exploratory data analysis,” that eliminate redundant, and hence non-independent, attributes.

Things go badly awry in Naïve Bayes if a particular attribute value does not occur in the training set in conjunction with *every* class value. Suppose that in the training data the attribute value *outlook* = *sunny* was always associated with the outcome *no*. Then the probability of *outlook* = *sunny* given a *yes*, *P*(*o**u**t**l**o**o**k* = *s**u**n**n**y**|**y**e**s*),<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">outlook</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">sunny|yes</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si13.png) would be zero, and because the other probabilities are multiplied by this the final probability of *yes* in the earlier example would be zero no matter how large they were. Probabilities that are zero hold a veto over the other ones. This is not a good idea. But the bug is easily fixed by minor adjustments to the method of calculating probabilities from frequencies.

For example, the upper part of [Table 4.2](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#t0015) shows that for *play = yes*, *outlook* is *sunny* for two examples, *overcast* for four, and *rainy* for three, and the lower part gives these events probabilities of 2/9, 4/9, and 3/9, respectively. Instead, we could add 1 to each numerator, and compensate by adding 3 to the denominator, giving probabilities of 3/12, 5/12, and 4/12, respectively. This will ensure that an attribute value that occurs zero times receives a probability which is nonzero, albeit small. The strategy of adding 1 to each count is a standard technique called the *Laplace estimator* after the great 18th-century French mathematician Pierre Laplace. Although it works well in practice, there is no particular reason for adding 1 to the counts; we could instead choose a small constant μ and use

$\\frac{\\left. 2 + \\mu\\slash 3 \\right.}{9 + \\mu},\\frac{\\left. 4 + \\mu\\slash 3 \\right.}{9 + \\mu},{and}\\frac{\\left. 3 + \\mu\\slash 3 \\right.}{9 + \\mu}.$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">and</mml:mi><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si14.png)

The value of μ, which was set to 3 in the formula shown, effectively provides a weight that determines how influential the a priori values of 1/3, 1/3, and 1/3 are for each of the three possible attribute values. A large μ says that these priors are very important compared with the new evidence coming in from the training set, whereas a small one gives them less influence. Finally, there is no particular reason for dividing μ into three *equal* parts in the numerators. We could use

$\\frac{2 + \\mu p\_{1}}{9 + \\mu},\\frac{4 + \\mu p\_{2}}{9 + \\mu},{and}\\frac{3 + \\mu p\_{3}}{9 + \\mu}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">and</mml:mi><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si15.png)

instead, where *p*[1], *p*[2], and *p*[3] sum to 1. Effectively, these three numbers are a priori probabilities of the values of the *outlook* attribute being *sunny*, *overcast*, and *rainy*, respectively.

This technique of smoothing parameters using pseudo counts for imaginary data can be rigorously justified using a probabilistic framework. Think of each parameter—in this case, the three numbers—as having an associated probability distribution. This is called a Bayesian formulation, to which we will return in greater detail in [Chapter 13](#Ch014_485-514_B9780443158889000145.xhtml#Ch014_485-514_B9780443158889000145), “Probabilistic methods: fundamentals,” and [Chapter 14](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157), “Advanced probabilistic methods.” The initial “prior” distributions dictate how important the prior information is, and when new evidence comes in from the training set they can be updated to “posterior” distributions, which take that information into account. If the prior distributions have a particular form, namely “Dirichlet” distributions, then the posterior distributions have the same form. Dirichlet distributions are defined in [Appendix A.2](#TableA1_617-636_B9780443158889000212.xhtml#s0050), which contains a more detailed theoretical explanation.

The upshot is that the mean values for the posterior distribution are computed from the prior distribution in a way that generalizes the previous example. Thus this heuristic smoothing technique can be justified theoretically as corresponding to the use of a Dirichlet prior with a nonzero mean for the parameter, then taking the value of the posterior mean as the updated estimate for the parameter.

This Bayesian formulation has the advantage of deriving from a rigorous theoretical framework. However, from a practical point of view it does not really help in determining just how to assign the prior probabilities. In practice, as long as zero values are avoided in the parameter estimates, the prior probabilities make little difference given a sufficient number of training instances, and people typically estimate frequencies using the Laplace estimator by initializing all counts to one instead of zero.

 

### Missing Values and Numeric Attributes

One of the really nice things about Naïve Bayes is that missing values are no problem at all. For example, if the value of *outlook* were missing in the example of [Table 4.3](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#t0020), the calculation would simply omit this attribute, yielding

$\\begin{matrix} \\left. {Likelihood\\ of}\\mathit{yes} = 3\\slash 9 \\times 3\\slash 9 \\times 3\\slash 9 \\times 9\\slash 14 = 0.0238 \\right. \\\\ \\left. {Likelihood\\ of}\\mathit{no} = 1\\slash 5 \\times 4\\slash 5 \\times 3\\slash 5 \\times 5\\slash 14 = 0.0343. \\right. \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Likelihood of</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0238</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Likelihood of</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">no</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0343</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si16.png)

These two numbers are individually a lot higher than they were before, because one of the fractions is missing. But that’s not a problem because a fraction is missing in both cases, and these likelihoods are subject to a further normalization process. This yields probabilities for *yes* and *no* of 41% and 59%, respectively.

If a value is missing in a training instance, it is simply not included in the frequency counts, and the probability ratios are based on the number of values that actually occur rather than on the total number of instances.

Numeric values are usually handled by assuming that they have a “normal” or “Gaussian” probability distribution. [Table 4.4](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#t0025) gives a summary of the weather data with numeric features from [Table 1.3.](#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029.xhtml#t0020) For nominal attributes, we calculate counts as before, while for numeric ones we simply list the values that occur. Then, instead of normalizing counts into probabilities as we do for nominal attributes, we calculate the mean and standard deviation for each class and each numeric attribute. The mean value of *temperature* over the *yes* instances is 73, and its standard deviation is 6.2. The mean is simply the average of the values—the sum divided by the number of values. The standard deviation is the square root of the sample variance, which we calculate as follows: subtract the mean from each value, square the result, sum them together, and then divide by one less than the number of values. After we have found this “sample variance,” take its square root to yield the standard deviation. This is the standard way of calculating mean and standard deviation of a set of numbers (the “one less than” is to do with the number of degrees of freedom in the sample, a statistical notion that we don’t want to get into here).

The probability density function for a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ is given by the rather formidable expression

$f\\left( x \\right) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}\\sigma}e^{- \\frac{{(x - \\mu)}^{2}}{2\\sigma^{2}}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>&#960;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si17.png)

But fear not! All this means is that if we are considering a *yes* outcome when *temperature* has a value, say, of 66; we just need to plug *x* = 66, μ = 73, and σ = 6.2 into the formula. So the value of the probability density function is

$f(\\mathit{temperature} = 66\\text{∣}\\mathit{yes}) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi} \\cdot 6.2}e^{- \\frac{{(66 - 73)}^{2}}{2 \\cdot 6.2^{2}}} = 0.0340.$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">temperature</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>66</mml:mn><mml:mtext mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mtext><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>&#960;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo>&#8901;</mml:mo><mml:mn>6.2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mn>66</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>73</mml:mn><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8901;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>6.2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0340</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si18.png)

And by the same token, the probability density of a *yes* outcome when *humidity* has a value, say, of 90 is calculated in the same way:

*f*(*h**u**m**i**d**i**t**y*\=90∣*y**e**s*) = 0.0221.<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">humidity</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>90</mml:mn><mml:mtext mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mtext><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0221</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si19.png)

The probability density function for an event is very closely related to its probability. However, it is not quite the same thing. If temperature is a continuous scale, the probability of the temperature being *exactly* 66—or *exactly* any other value, such as 63.14159262—is zero. The real meaning of the density function *f*(*x*) is that the probability that the quantity lies within a small region around *x*, say,between *x*−*ε*/2<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#949;</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si20.png) and *x*+*ε*/2<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#949;</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si21.png), is *ε* ⋅ *f*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>&#949;</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8901;</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si22.png). You might think we ought to factor in the accuracy figure ε when using these density values, but that’s not necessary. The same *ε* would appear in both the *yes* and *no* likelihoods that follow and cancel out when the probabilities were calculated.

Using these probabilities for the new day in [Table 4.5](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#t0030) yields

$\\begin{matrix} \\left. {Likelihood\\ of}\\mathit{yes} = 2\\slash 9 \\times 0.0340 \\times 0.0221 \\times 3\\slash 9 \\times 9\\slash 14 = 0.000036, \\right. \\\\ \\left. {Likelihood\\ of}\\mathit{no} = 3\\slash 5 \\times 0.0279 \\times 0.0381 \\times 3\\slash 5 \\times 5\\slash 14 = 0.000137; \\right. \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable width="336pt"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Likelihood of</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0340</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0221</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.000036</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Likelihood of</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">no</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0279</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0381</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.000137</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si23.png)

which leads to probabilities

${Probability\\ of}\\mathit{yes} = \\frac{0.000036}{0.000036 + 0.000137} = 20.8\\%,$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Probability of</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.000036</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.000036</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.000137</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>20.8</mml:mn><mml:mo>%</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si24.png)

${Probability\\ of}\\mathit{no} = \\frac{0.000137}{0.000036 + 0.000137} = 79.2\\%.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Probability of</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">no</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.000137</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.000036</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.000137</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>79.2</mml:mn><mml:mo>%</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si25.png)

These figures are very close to the probabilities calculated earlier for the new day in [Table 4.3](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#t0020), because the *temperature* and *humidity* values of 66 and 90 yield similar probabilities to the *cool* and *high* values used before.

The normal-distribution assumption makes it easy to extend the Naïve Bayes classifier to deal with numeric attributes. If the values of any numeric attributes are missing, the mean and standard deviation calculations are based only on the ones that are present.

 

### Naïve Bayes for Document Classification

An important domain for machine learning is document classification, in which each instance represents a document and the instance’s class is the document’s topic. Documents might be news items and the classes might be domestic news, overseas news, financial news, and sport. Documents are characterized by the words that appear in them, and one way to apply machine learning to document classification is to treat the presence or absence of each word as a Boolean attribute. Naïve Bayes is a popular technique for this application because it is very fast and quite accurate.

However, this does not take into account the number of occurrences of each word, which is potentially useful information when determining the category of a document. Instead, a document can viewed as a *bag of words*—a set that contains all the words in the document, with multiple occurrences of a word appearing numerous times (technically, a *set* includes each of its members just once, whereas a *bag* can have repeated elements). Word frequencies can be accommodated by applying a modified form of Naïve Bayes called *multinominal* Naïve Bayes.

Suppose *n*[1], *n*[2], …, *n[k]* is the number of times word *i* occurs in the document, and *P*[1], *P*[2], …, *P[k]* is the probability of obtaining word *i* when sampling from all the documents in category *H*. Assume that the probability is independent of the word’s context and position in the document. These assumptions lead to a *multinomial distribution* for document probabilities. For this distribution, the probability of a document *E* given its class *H*—in other words, the formula for computing the probability *P*(*E*|*H*) in Bayes’ rule—is

$P(E\\text{∣}H) = N! \\times \\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{k}\\frac{{P\_{i}}^{n\_{i}}}{n\_{i}!}$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mtext mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mtext><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>!</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>!</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si26.png)

where *N* = *n*[1] + *n*[2] + ⋯<mml:math><mml:mo>&#8943;</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si27.png) + *n[k]* is the number of words in the document. The reason for the factorials is to account for the fact that the ordering of the occurrences of each word is immaterial according to the bag-of-words model. *P[i]* is estimated by computing the relative frequency of word *i* in the text of all training documents pertaining to category *H*. In reality there could be another term that gives the probability that the model for category *H* generates a document whose length is the same as the length of *E*, but it is common to assume that this is the same for all classes and hence can be dropped.

For example, suppose there are only two words, *yellow* and *blue*, in the vocabulary, and a particular document class *H* has *P*(*yellow* | *H*) = 75% and *P*(*blue* | *H*) = 25% (you might call *H* the class of *yellowish green* documents). Suppose *E* is the document *blue yellow blue* with a length of *N* = 3 words. There are four possible bags of three words. One is {*yellow yellow yellow*}, and its probability according to the preceding formula is

$P(\\left\\{ \\mathit{yellow\\ yellow\\ yellow} \\right\\}\\text{∣}H) = 3! \\times \\frac{0.75^{3}}{3!} \\times \\frac{0.25^{0}}{0!} = \\frac{27}{64}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yellow yellow yellow</mml:mi><mml:mo>}</mml:mo><mml:mtext mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mtext><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>!</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.75</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>!</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.25</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>!</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>27</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>64</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si28.png)

The other three, with their probabilities, are

$P(\\left\\{ \\mathit{blue\\ blue\\ blue} \\right\\}\\text{∣}H) = \\frac{1}{64}$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">blue blue blue</mml:mi><mml:mo>}</mml:mo><mml:mtext mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mtext><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>64</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si29.png)

$P(\\left\\{ \\mathit{yellow\\ yellow\\ blue} \\right\\}\\text{∣}H) = \\frac{27}{64}$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yellow yellow blue</mml:mi><mml:mo>}</mml:mo><mml:mtext mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mtext><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>27</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>64</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si30.png)

$P(\\left\\{ \\mathit{yellow\\ blue\\ blue} \\right\\}\\text{∣}H) = \\frac{9}{64}$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yellow blue blue</mml:mi><mml:mo>}</mml:mo><mml:mtext mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mtext><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>9</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>64</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si31.png)

*E* corresponds to the last case (recall that in a bag of words the order is immaterial); thus its probability of being generated by the *yellowish green* document model is 9/64, or 14%. Suppose another class, *very bluish green* documents (call it *H*′<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo accent="false">&#8242;</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si32.png)), has *P*(*yellow* |*H*′<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo accent="false">&#8242;</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si33.png)) = 10% and *P*(*blue* |*H*′<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo accent="false">&#8242;</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si34.png)) = 90%. The probability that *E* is generated by this model is 24%.

If these are the only two classes, does that mean that *E* is in the *very bluish green* document class? Not necessarily. Bayes’ rule, given earlier, says that you have to take into account the prior probability of each hypothesis. If you know that in fact *very bluish green* documents are twice as rare as *yellowish green* ones, this would be sufficient to outweigh the 14%–24% disparity and tip the balance in favor of the *yellowish green* class.

The factorials in the probability formula don’t actually need to be computed because—being the same for every class—they drop out in the normalization process anyway. However, the formula still involves multiplying together many small probabilities, which soon yields extremely small numbers that cause underflow on large documents. The problem can be avoided by using logarithms of the probabilities instead of the probabilities themselves.

In the multinomial Naïve Bayes formulation, a document’s class is determined not just by the words that occur in it but also by the number of times they occur. In general it performs better than the ordinary Naïve Bayes model for document classification, particularly for large dictionary sizes.

 

#### Remarks

Naïve Bayes gives a simple approach, with clear semantics, to representing, using, and learning probabilistic knowledge. It can achieve impressive results. People often find that Naïve Bayes rivals, and indeed outperforms, more sophisticated classifiers on many datasets. The moral is, always try the simple things first. Repeatedly, people have eventually, after an extended struggle, managed to obtain good results using sophisticated learning schemes, only to discover later that simple methods such as 1 R and Naïve Bayes do just as well, or even better. The primary reason for its effectiveness in classification problems is that maximizing classification accuracy does not require particularly accurate probability estimates; it is sufficient for the correct class to receive the greatest probability.

There are many datasets for which Naïve Bayes does not do well, however, and it is easy to see why. Because attributes are treated as though they were independent given the class, the addition of redundant ones skews the learning process. As an extreme example, if you were to include a new attribute with the same values as *temperature* to the weather data, the effect of the *temperature* attribute would be multiplied; all of its probabilities would be squared, giving it a great deal more influence in the decision. If you were to add 10 such attributes, the decisions would effectively be made on *temperature* alone. Dependencies between attributes inevitably reduce the power of Naïve Bayes to discern what is going on. They can, however, be ameliorated by using a subset of the attributes in the decision procedure, making a careful selection of which ones to use. [Chapter 6](#Ch006_209-259_B9780443158889000078.xhtml#Ch006_209-259_B9780443158889000078), “Preparation: data preprocessing and exploratory data analysis,” shows how.

The normal-distribution assumption for numeric attributes is another restriction on Naïve Bayes as we have formulated it here. Many features simply aren’t normally distributed. However, there is nothing to prevent us from using other distributions; there is nothing magic about the normal distribution. If you know that a particular attribute is likely to follow some other distribution, standard estimation procedures for that distribution can be used instead. If you suspect it isn’t normal but don’t know the actual distribution, there are procedures for “kernel density estimation” that do not assume any particular distribution for the attribute values. Another possibility is simply to discretize the data first.

Naïve Bayes is a very simple probabilistic model, and we examine far more sophisticated ones in [Chapter 13](#Ch014_485-514_B9780443158889000145.xhtml#Ch014_485-514_B9780443158889000145), “Probabilistic methods: fundamentals,” and [Chapter 14](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157), “Advanced probabilistic methods.”

 

## 4.3 Divide-and-Conquer: Constructing Decision Trees

The problem of constructing a decision tree can be expressed recursively. First, select an attribute to place at the root node, and make one branch for each possible value. This splits up the example set into subsets, one for every value of the attribute. Now the process can be repeated recursively for each branch, using only those instances that actually reach the branch. If at any time all instances at a node have the same classification, stop developing that part of the tree.

The only thing left is how to determine which attribute to split on, given a set of examples with different classes. Consider (again!) the weather data. There are four possibilities for each split, and at the top level they produce the trees in [Fig. 4.2](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#f0015) Which is the best choice? The number of *yes* and *no* classes are shown at the leaves. Any leaf with only one class—*yes* or *no*—will not have to be split further, and the recursive process down that branch will terminate. Because we seek small trees, we would like this to happen as soon as possible. If we had a measure of the purity of each node, we could choose the attribute that produces the purest daughter nodes. Take a moment to look at [Fig. 4.2](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#f0015) and ponder which attribute you think is the best choice.

![Fig. 4.2 Tree stumps for the weather data.](images/F000054f04-02-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. 4.2 Tree stumps for the weather data.

The measure of purity that we will use is called the *information* and is measured in units called *bits*. Associated with a node of the tree, it represents the expected amount of information that would be needed to specify whether a new instance should be classified *yes* or *no*, given that the example reached that node. Unlike the bits in computer memory, the expected amount of information usually involves fractions of a bit—and is often less than one! It is calculated based on the number of *yes* and *no* classes at the node; we will look at the details of the calculation shortly. But first let’s see how it’s used. When evaluating the first tree in [Fig. 4.2](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#f0015), the number of *yes* and *no* classes at the leaf nodes are \[2, 3\], \[4, 0\], and \[3, 2\], respectively, and the information values of these nodes are:

$\\begin{matrix} {{Info}\\left( \\left\\lbrack 2,3 \\right\\rbrack \\right) = 0.971{bits}} \\\\ {{Info}\\left( \\left\\lbrack 4,0 \\right\\rbrack \\right) = 0.0{bits}} \\\\ {{Info}\\left( \\left\\lbrack 3,2 \\right\\rbrack \\right) = 0.971{bits}} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2,3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.971</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">bits</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4,0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">bits</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3,2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.971</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">bits</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si35.png)

We calculate the average information value of these, taking into account the number of instances that go down each branch—five down the first and third and four down the second:

$\\begin{matrix} \\left. {Info}(\\left\\lbrack 2,3 \\right\\rbrack,\\left\\lbrack 4,0 \\right\\rbrack,\\left\\lbrack 3,2 \\right\\rbrack) = (5\\slash 14) \\times 0.971 + (4\\slash 14) \\times 0 + (5\\slash 14) \\times 0.971 = 0.693{bits}. \\right. \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable width="336pt"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2,3</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>4,0</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>3,2</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="nobreak">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.971</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.971</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.693</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">bits</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si36.png)

This average represents the amount of information that we expect would be necessary to specify the class of a new instance, given the tree structure in [Fig. 4.2A](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#f0015).

Before any of the nascent tree structures in [Fig. 4.2](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#f0015) were created, the training examples at the root comprised nine *yes* and five *no* nodes, corresponding to an information value of

*I**n**f**o*(\[9,5\]) = 0.940*b**i**t**s*.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>9,5</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.940</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">bits</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si37.png)

Thus the tree in [Fig. 4.2A](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#f0015) is responsible for an information gain of

$\\begin{matrix} {\\text{Gain}\\left( \\mathit{outlook} \\right) = {info}(\\lbrack 9,5\\rbrack) - {info}(\\left\\lbrack 2,3 \\right\\rbrack,\\left\\lbrack 4,0 \\right\\rbrack,\\left\\lbrack 3,2 \\right\\rbrack) = 0.940 - 0.693 = 0.247\\text{bits},} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable width="336pt"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mtext>Gain</mml:mtext><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">outlook</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>9,5</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2,3</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>4,0</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>3,2</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="nobreak">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.940</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.693</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.247</mml:mn><mml:mtext>bits</mml:mtext><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si38.png)

which can be interpreted as the informational value of creating a branch on the *outlook* attribute.

The way forward is clear. We calculate the information gain for each attribute and split on the one that gains the most information. In the situation of [Fig. 4.2](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#f0015),

$\\begin{matrix} {{Gain}\\left( \\mathit{outlook} \\right) = 0.247{bits}} \\\\ {{Gain}\\left( \\mathit{temperature} \\right) = 0.029{bits}} \\\\ {{Gain}\\left( \\mathit{humidity} \\right) = 0.152{bits}} \\\\ {{Gain}\\left( \\mathit{windy} \\right) = 0.048{bits,}} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable width="336pt"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Gain</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">outlook</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.247</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">bits</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Gain</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">temperature</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.029</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">bits</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Gain</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">humidity</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.152</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">bits</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Gain</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">windy</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.048</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">bits,</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si39.png)

so we select *outlook* as the splitting attribute at the root of the tree. Hopefully this accords with your intuition as the best one to select. It is the only choice for which one daughter node is completely pure, and this gives it a considerable advantage over the other attributes. *Humidity* is the next best choice because it produces a larger daughter node that is almost completely pure.

Then we continue, recursively. [Fig. 4.3](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#f0020) shows the possibilities for a further branch at the node reached when *outlook* is *sunny*. Clearly, a further split on *outlook* will produce nothing new, so we only consider the other three attributes. The information gain for each turns out to be

$\\begin{matrix} {{Gain}\\left( \\mathit{temperature} \\right) = 0.571{bits}} \\\\ {{Gain}\\left( \\mathit{humidity} \\right) = 0.971{bits}} \\\\ {{Gain}\\left( \\mathit{windy} \\right) = 0.020\\text{bits},} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable width="336pt"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Gain</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">temperature</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.571</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">bits</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Gain</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">humidity</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.971</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">bits</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Gain</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">windy</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.020</mml:mn><mml:mtext>bits</mml:mtext><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si40.png)![Fig. 4.3 Expanded tree stumps for the weather data.](images/F000054f04-03-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 4.3](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#Bf0020) Expanded tree stumps for the weather data.

so we select *humidity* as the splitting attribute at this point. There is no need to split these nodes any further, so this branch is finished.

Continued application of the same idea leads to the decision tree of [Fig. 4.4](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#f0025) for the weather data. Ideally the process terminates when all leaf nodes are pure, that is, when they contain instances that all have the same classification. However, it might not be possible to reach this happy situation because there is nothing to stop the training set containing two examples with identical sets of attributes but different classes. Consequently, we stop when the data cannot be split any further. Alternatively, one could stop if the information gain is zero. This is slightly more conservative, because it is possible to encounter cases where the data can be split into subsets exhibiting identical class distributions, which would make the information gain zero.

![Fig. 4.4 Decision tree for the weather data.](images/F000054f04-04-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 4.4](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#Bf0025) Decision tree for the weather data.

 

### Calculating Information

Now it is time to explain how to calculate the information measure that is used as a basis for evaluating different splits. We describe the basic idea in this section, then in the next we examine a correction that is usually made to counter a bias toward selecting splits on attributes with large numbers of possible values.

Before examining the detailed formula for calculating the amount of information required to specify the class of an example given that it reaches a tree node with a certain number of *yes*’s and *no*’s, consider first the kind of properties we would expect this quantity to have:

*   • When the number of either *yes*’s or *no*’s is zero, the information is zero;
*   • When the number of *yes*’s and *no*’s is equal, the information reaches a maximum.

Moreover, the measure should be applicable to multiclass situations, not just to two-class ones.

The information measure relates to the amount of information obtained by making a decision, and a more subtle property of information can be derived by considering the nature of decisions. Decisions can be made in a single stage, or they can be made in several stages, and the amount of information involved is the same in both cases. For example, the decision involved in

*I**n**f**o*(\[2,3,4\])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2,3,4</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si41.png)

can be made in two stages. First decide whether it’s the first case or one of the other two cases:

*I**n**f**o*(\[2,7\])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2,7</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si42.png)

and then decide which of the other two cases it is:

*I**n**f**o*(\[3,4\])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>3,4</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si43.png)

In some cases the second decision will not need to be made, namely, when the decision turns out to be the first one. Taking this into account leads to the equation

*I**n**f**o*(\[2,3,4\])=*i**n**f**o*(\[2,7\])+(7/9)×*i**n**f**o*(\[3,4\]).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2,3,4</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2,7</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>7</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>3,4</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si44.png)

Of course, there is nothing special about these particular numbers, and a similar relationship should hold regardless of the actual values. Thus we could add a further criterion to the list shown earlier:

*   • The information should obey the multistage property that we have illustrated.

Remarkably, it turns out that there is only one function that satisfies all these properties, and it is known as the *information value* or *entropy*:

*E**n**t**r**o**p**y*(*p*[1], *p*[2], …, *p*[*n*]) =  − *p*[1]log *p*[1] − *p*[2]log *p*[2]… − *p*[*n*]log *p*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Entropy</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si45.png)

The reason for the minus signs is that logarithms of the fractions *p*[1], *p*[2], …, *p*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si46.png) are negative, so the entropy is actually positive. Usually the logarithms are expressed in base 2, and then the entropy is in units called *bits*—just the usual kind of bits used with computers.

The arguments *p*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si47.png), *p*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si48.png),… of the entropy formula are expressed as fractions that add up to one, so that,

*I**n**f**o*(\[2,3,4\])=*e**n**t**r**o**p**y*(2/9,3/9,4/9).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2,3,4</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">entropy</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9,3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9,4</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si49.png)

Thus the multistage decision property can be written in general as

${Entropy}(p,q,r) = {entropy}(p,q + r) + (q + r) \\cdot {entropy}\\left( \\frac{q}{q + r},\\frac{r}{q + r} \\right)$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Entropy</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">entropy</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8901;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">entropy</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si50.png)

where *p* + *q* + *r* = 1

Because of the way the log function works, you can calculate the information measure without having to work out the individual fractions:

$\\begin{matrix} \\left. {Info}(\\left\\lbrack 2,3,4 \\right\\rbrack) = - 2\\slash 9 \\times \\log 2\\slash 9 - 3\\slash 9 \\times \\log 3\\slash 9 - 4\\slash 9 \\times \\log 4\\slash 9 = \\lbrack - 2\\log 2 - 3\\log 3 - 4\\log 4 + 9\\log 9\\rbrack\\slash 9. \\right. \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable width="336pt"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2,3,4</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si52.png)

This is the way that the information measure is usually calculated in practice. So the information value for the first node of the first tree in [Fig. 4.2](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#f0015) is

*I**n**f**o*(\[2,3\])=−2/5×log2/5−3/5×log3/5=0.971bits,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2,3</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.971</mml:mn><mml:mtext>bits</mml:mtext><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si53.png)

as stated earlier.

 

### Highly Branching Attributes

When some attributes have a large number of possible values, giving rise to a multiway branch with many child nodes, a problem arises with the information gain calculation. The problem can best be appreciated in the extreme case when an attribute has a different value for each instance in the dataset, as an identification code attribute might.

[Table 4.6](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054_a.xhtml#t0035) gives the weather data with this extra attribute. Branching on *ID code* produces the tree stump in [Fig. 4.5](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054_a.xhtml#f0030). The expected information required to specify the class given the value of this attribute is

$\\frac{1}{14}({info}(\\left\\lbrack 0,1 \\right\\rbrack) + {info}(\\left\\lbrack 0,1 \\right\\rbrack) + {info}(\\left\\lbrack 1,0 \\right\\rbrack) + \\cdots + {info}(\\left\\lbrack 1,0 \\right\\rbrack) + {info}(\\left\\lbrack 0,1 \\right\\rbrack)),$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>14</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0,1</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0,1</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1,0</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8943;</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1,0</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0,1</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si54.png)

Table 4.6

The Weather Data with Identification Codes

 
| ID Code || Outlook || Temperature || Humidity || Windy || Play |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a || Sunny || Hot || High || False || No |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| b || Sunny || Hot || High || True || No |
| c || Overcast || Hot || High || False || Yes |
| d || Rainy || Mild || High || False || Yes |
| e || Rainy || Cool || Normal || False || Yes |
| f || Rainy || Cool || Normal || True || No |
| g || Overcast || Cool || Normal || True || Yes |
| h || Sunny || Mild || High || False || No |

![Fig. 4.5 Tree stump for the ID code attribute.](images/F000054f04-05-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. 4.5 Tree stump for the *ID code* attribute.

which is zero because each of the 14 terms is zero. This is not surprising; the *ID code* attribute identifies the instance, which determines the class without any ambiguity, just as [Table 4.6](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054_a.xhtml#t0035) shows. Consequently, the information gain of this attribute is merely the information at the root, info(\[9,5\]) = 0.940 bits. This is greater than the information gain of any other attribute, and so *ID code* will inevitably be chosen as the splitting attribute. But branching on the identification code is no good for predicting the class of unknown instances.

The overall effect is that the information gain measure tends to prefer attributes with large numbers of possible values. To compensate for this, a modification of the measure called the *gain ratio* is widely used. The gain ratio is derived by taking into account the number and size of daughter nodes into which an attribute splits the dataset, disregarding any information about the class. In the situation shown in [Fig. 4.5](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054_a.xhtml#f0030), all counts have a value of 1, so the information value of the split is

*I**n**f**o*(\[1,1,…,1\])=−1/14×log1/14×14<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1,1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si55.png)

because the same fraction, 1/14, appears 14 times. This amounts to log 14, or 3.807 bits, which is a very high value. This is because the information value of a split is the number of bits needed to determine to which branch each instance is assigned, and the more branches there are, the greater this value is. The gain ratio is calculated by dividing the original information gain, 0.940 in this case, by the information value of the attribute, 3.807, yielding a gain ratio value of 0.247 for the *ID code* attribute.

Returning to the tree stumps for the weather data in [Fig. 4.2](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#f0015), *outlook* splits the dataset into three subsets of size 5, 4, and 5 and thus has an intrinsic information value of

*I**n**f**o*(\[5,4,5\]) = 1.577<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Info</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>5,4,5</mml:mn><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.577</mml:mn></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000054si56.png)

without paying any attention to the classes involved in the subsets. As we have seen, this intrinsic information value is greater for a more highly branching attribute such as the hypothesized *ID code*. Again, we can correct the information gain by dividing by the intrinsic information value to get the gain ratio.

The results of these calculations for the tree stumps of [Fig. 4.2](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#f0015) are summarized in [Table 4.7](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054_a.xhtml#t0040). *Outlook* still comes out on top, but *humidity* is now a much closer contender because it splits the data into two subsets instead of three. In this example, the hypothetical *ID code* attribute, with a gain ratio of 0.247, would still be preferred to any of these four. However, its advantage is greatly reduced. In practical implementations, we can use an ad hoc test to guard against splitting on such a useless attribute.

Table 4.7

 Gain Ratio Calculations for the Tree Stumps of 

| Outlook  || Temperature || Humidity || Windy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Info: || 0.693 || Info: || 0.911 || Info: || 0.788 || Info: || 0.892 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gain: 0.940–0.693 || 0.247 || Gain: 0.940–0.911 || 0.029 || Gain: 0.940–0.788 || 0.152 || Gain: 0.940–0.892 || 0.048 |
| Split info: info(\[5,4,5\]) || 1.577 || Split info: info(\[4,6,4\]) || 1.557 || Split info: info(\[7,7\]) || 1.000 || Split info: info(\[8,6\]) || 0.985 |
| Gain ratio: 0.247/1.577 || 0.156 || Gain ratio: 0.029/1.557 || 0.019 || Gain ratio: 0.152/1 || 0.152 || Gain ratio: 0.048/0.985 || 0.049 |

Unfortunately, in some situations the gain ratio modification overcompensates and can lead to preferring an attribute simply because its intrinsic information is much lower than for the other attributes. A standard fix is to choose the attribute that maximizes the gain ratio, provided that the information gain for that attribute is at least as great as the average information gain for all the attributes examined.

The basic information-gain algorithm we have described is called ID3. A series of improvements to ID3, including the gain ratio criterion, culminated in a practical and influential system for decision tree induction called C4.5. Further improvements include methods for dealing with numeric attributes, missing values, noisy data, and generating rules from trees. They are described in [Appendix C](#FigC1_655-685_B9780443158889000236.xhtml#FigC1_655-685_B9780443158889000236), Implementation details of trees and rules.

 

## 4.4 Covering Algorithms: Constructing Rules

As we have seen, decision tree algorithms are based on a divide-and-conquer approach to the classification problem. They work top-down, seeking at each stage an attribute to split on that best separates the classes and then recursively processing the subproblems that result from the split. This strategy generates a decision tree, which can if necessary be converted into a set of classification rules—although if it is to produce effective rules, the conversion is not trivial.

An alternative approach is to take each class in turn and seek a way of covering all instances in it, at the same time excluding instances not in the class. This is called a *covering* approach because at each stage you identify a rule that “covers” some of the instances. By its very nature, this covering approach leads to a set of rules rather than to a decision tree.

The covering method can readily be visualized in a two-dimensional space of instances as shown in [Fig. 4.6A](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054_a.xhtml#f0035). We first make a rule covering the *a*’s. For the first test in the rule, split the space vertically as shown in the center picture. This gives the beginnings of a rule:

![Fig. 4.6 Covering algorithm. (A) Covering the instances. (B) Decision tree for the same problem.](images/F000054f04-06-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. 4.6 Covering algorithm. (A) Covering the instances. (B) Decision tree for the same problem.

 

```
If x > 1.2 then class = a
```

However, the rule covers many *b*’s as well as *a*’s, so a new test is added to the rule by further splitting the space horizontally as shown in the third diagram:

If x > 1.2 and y > 2.6 then class = a

This gives a rule covering all but one of the *a*’s. It’s probably appropriate to leave it at that, but if it were necessary to cover the final *a*, another rule would be necessary—perhaps.

 

```
If x > 1.4 and y < 2.4 then class = a
```

The same procedure leads to two rules covering the *b*’s:

 

```
If x ≤ 1.2 then class = b
```

 

```
If x > 1.2 and y ≤ 2.6 then class = b
```

Again, one *a* is erroneously covered by these rules. If it were necessary to exclude it, more tests would have to be added to the second rule, and additional rules would be needed to cover the *b*’s that these new tests exclude.

 

### Rules Vs. Trees

A top-down divide-and-conquer algorithm operates on the same data in a manner, at least superficially, quite similar to a covering algorithm. It might first split the dataset using the *x* attribute and would probably end up splitting it at the same place, *x* = 1.2<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si57.png). However, whereas the covering algorithm is concerned only with covering a single class, the division would take both classes into account, because divide-and-conquer algorithms create a single concept description that applies to all classes. The second split might also be at the same place, *y* = 2.6<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.6</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000054si58.png), leading to the decision tree in [Fig. 4.6B](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054_a.xhtml#f0035). This tree corresponds exactly to the set of rules, and in this case there is no difference in effect between the covering and the divide-and-conquer algorithms.

But in many situations there *is* a difference between rules and trees in terms of the perspicuity of the representation. For example, when we described the replicated subtree problem in [Section 3.4](#Ch003_67-89_B9780443158889000042.xhtml#s0025), we noted that rules can be symmetric whereas trees must select one attribute to split on first, and this can lead to trees that are much larger than an equivalent set of rules. Another difference is that, in the multiclass case, a decision tree split takes all classes into account, trying to maximize the purity of the split, whereas the rule-generating method concentrates on one class at a time, disregarding what happens to the other classes.

 

### A Simple Covering Algorithm

Covering algorithms operate by adding tests to the rule that is under construction, always striving to create a rule with maximum accuracy. In contrast, divide-and-conquer algorithms operate by adding tests to the tree that is under construction, always striving to maximize the separation between the classes. Each of these involves finding an attribute to split on. But the criterion for the best attribute is different in each case. Whereas divide-and-conquer algorithms such as ID3 choose an attribute to maximize the information gain, the covering algorithm we will describe chooses an attribute–value pair to maximize the probability of the desired classification.

[Fig. 4.7](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054_a.xhtml#f0040) gives a picture of the situation, showing the space containing all the instances, a partially constructed rule, and the same rule after a new term has been added. The new term restricts the coverage of the rule; the idea is to include as many instances of the desired class as possible and exclude as many instances of other classes as possible. Suppose the new rule will cover a total of *t* instances, of which *p* are positive examples of the class and *t*–*p* are examples in other classes—they are errors made by the rule. Then choose the new term to maximize the ratio *p*/*t*.

![Fig. 4.7 The instance space during operation of a covering algorithm.](images/F000054f04-07-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 4.7](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054_a.xhtml#Bf0040) The instance space during operation of a covering algorithm.

An example will help. For a change, we use the contact lens problem of [Table 1.1](#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029.xhtml#t0010). We will form rules that cover each of the three classes, *hard*, *soft*, and *none*, in turn. To begin, we seek a rule.

 

```
If? then recommendation = hard.
```

For the unknown term “?,” we have nine choices:

| age = young || 2/8 |
| --- | --- |
| age = prepresbyopic || 1/8 |
| age = presbyopic || 1/8 |
| spectacle prescription = myope || 3/12 |
| spectacle prescription = hypermetrope || 1/12 |
| astigmatism = no || 0/12 |
| astigmatism = yes || 4/12 |
| tear production rate = reduced || 0/12 |
| tear production rate = normal || 4/12 |

The numbers on the right show the fraction of “correct” instances in the set singled out by that choice. In this case, *correct* means that the recommendation is *hard*. For instance, *age = young* selects eight instances, two of which recommend hard contact lenses, so the first fraction is 2/8. (To follow this, you will need to look back at the contact lens data in [Table 1.1](#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029.xhtml#t0010) and count the entries in the table.) We select the largest fraction, 4/12, arbitrarily choosing between the seventh and the last choice in the list, and create the rule:

 

```
If astigmatism = yes then recommendation = hard
```

This rule is quite inaccurate, getting only 4 instances correct out of the 12 that it covers, shown in [Table 4.8](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054_a.xhtml#t0045). So we refine it further:

Table 4.8
