The data consists of estimated probabilities and 0/1 values; assume it has been sorted according to the estimated probabilities. The basic PAV algorithm iteratively merges pairs of neighboring data points that violate the monotonicity constraint by computing their weighted mean—initially this will be the mean of 0/1 values—and using it to replace the original data points. This is repeated until all conflicts have been resolved. It can be shown that the order in which data points are merged does not affect the outcome of the process. The result is a function that increases monotonically in a stepwise fashion. This naïve algorithm is quadratic in the number of data points but there is a clever variant that operates in linear time.

Another popular calibration method, which also presupposes a monotonic relationship, is to assume a linear relation between the log-odds of the estimated class probabilities and the target class probabilities. Here the logistic function is appropriate, and logistic regression can be used to estimate the calibration function, with the caveat that it is important to use log-odds of the estimated class probabilities rather than the raw values as the input for logistic regression.

Given that logistic regression, with only two parameters, uses a simpler model than the PAV approach, it can be more appropriate when little data is available for calibration, but with a large volume of data PAV-based calibration is generally preferable. Logistic regression has the advantage that it can easily be applied to calibrate probabilities for multiclass problems because multiclass versions of logistic regression exist. In the case of isotonic regression it is common to use the one-vs-rest method for problems with more than two classes, but pairwise coupling or ensembles of nested dichotomies—discussed in [Section 6.6](#Ch006_209-259_B9780443158889000078.xhtml#s0155)—offer an alternative.

Note that situations exist in which the relationship between the estimated and true probabilities is not monotonic. However, rather than switching to a more complex calibration method—or using discretization-based calibration, which does not assume monotonicity—this should perhaps be taken as an indication that the underlying class probability estimation method is not powerful enough for the problem at hand.

 

## 6.8 Exploratory Data Analysis

As we emphasized in [Chapter 2](#Ch002_43-66_B9780443158889000030.xhtml#Ch002_43-66_B9780443158889000030), “Input: Concepts, instances, attributes,” in the initial stages of data mining it is crucial to gain an understanding of what is going on in your dataset. The process of exploring and visualizing a dataset for this purpose is called *exploratory data analysis* (EDA). This process may help you make better decisions about how to preprocess the data using the techniques described in this chapter. At this juncture, it bears reiterating that plotting your data (e.g., using histograms of individual attributes and scatter plots of pairs of attributes) is always a good idea. It is worth spending the time to open your data file and examine the first few rows by hand, which may reveal errors, or your own incorrect assumptions about how the data were obtained and encoded.

Other useful tools and measurements include summary statistics such as the mean, standard deviation, and the five number summary: the minimum, *Q*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000078si47.png) (the first quartile, i.e., the 25th percentile), the median, *Q*[3]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000078si48.png) (the third quartile, i.e., the 75th percentile), and the maximum. Boxplots visually show the information in the five number summary at a glance. Based on the five number summary we can easily obtain the interquartile range *I**Q**R* = *Q*[3] − *Q*[1]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">IQR</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000078si49.png), which is useful as a measure of spread that is robust to outliers.

It is also valuable to analyze the relationships between attributes. Pearson’s correlation coefficient measures the linear correlation between two attributes as a number between –1 and +1, while the covariance of two attributes measures the extent to which they tend to be above or below their respective means at the same time. These measurements can be used to identify redundant attributes, which can occur when merging data from several data sources via data integration. Association rule mining, which we discussed in [Section 4.5](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054_a.xhtml#s0075), is another useful strategy for identifying relationships between the attributes in your dataset in the form of rules.

 

### Visualizing Data in Two Dimensions With t-SNE and UMAP

To understand the high-level structure of a dataset, it can be instructive to visualize it by projecting down to two dimensions. Non-linear *manifold learning* projection methods like *t*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000078si50.png)\-*Stochastic Neighbor Embedding* (*t*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000078si51.png)\-SNE) are generally a better option than linear projection methods such as PCA, since they do not assume that the surface that most of the points occupy (a manifold) is linear. The *t*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000078si52.png)\-SNE method tries to keep points that were close together in the original embedding space close together in the projected two-dimensional space. It also tries to preserve the relationships between more distant points, but it is more relaxed about those relationships and is willing to let those drift if necessary for better preserving the relationships between closer points.

More recently, Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) has arisen as a reliable and accurate alternative to *t*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000078si53.png)\-SNE, which often performs better in practice. UMAP is based on mathematical theory from Riemannian geometry and algebraic topology. Although the theoretical underpinnings of UMAP are complex, in practice UMAP constructs its low-dimensional projections using a *force-directed graph layout* method, in which attractive forces and repulsive forces compete to place the projected data points at the ideal distances from other points. Edges in an appropriately chosen graph have attractive forces between points, while the nodes (corresponding to the embedded data points) repel each other. The first phase of the algorithm is to construct a particular weighted *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000078si54.png)\-neighbor graph. Then a process reminiscent of simulated annealing—in which the attractive and repulsive forces are gradually decreased—is used to place the points in the low-dimensional embedding space while ensuring convergence to a local optimum in the algorithm’s objective function.

 

## 6.9 Further Reading and Bibliographic Notes

Attribute selection, under the term *feature selection*, has been investigated in the field of pattern recognition for decades. Backward elimination was introduced in the early 1960s ([Marill and Green, 1963](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur376)). [Kittler (1978)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur313) surveys the feature selection algorithms that have been developed for pattern recognition. Best-first search and genetic algorithms are standard artificial intelligence techniques ([Goldberg, 1989](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur223); [Winston, 1992](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur568)).

The experiments that show the performance of decision tree learners deteriorating when new attributes are added are reported by [John (1997)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur293), who gives a nice explanation of attribute selection. [Langley and Sage (1997)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur347) showed that for an instance-based learner to reach a given performance level, the number of training instances must grow exponentially with the number of attributes. The idea of finding the smallest attribute set that carves up the instances uniquely is from [Almuallin and Dietterich (1991](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur10), [1992](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur11)) and was further developed by [Liu and Setiono (1996)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur368). [Kibler and Aha (1987)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur83) and [Cardie (1993)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur83) investigated the use of decision tree algorithms to identify features for nearest-neighbor learning; [Holmes and Nevill-Manning (1995)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur273) used 1 R to order features for selection. [Kira and Rendell (1992)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur311) used instance-based methods to select features, leading to a scheme called *RELIEF* for *Recursive Elimination of Features*. [Gilad-Bachrach, Navot, and Tishby (2004)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur217) show how this scheme can be modified to work better with redundant attributes. The correlation-based feature selection method was developed by [Hall (2000)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur242).

The use of wrapper methods for feature selection is due to [John, Kohavi, and Pfleger (1994)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur294) and Kohavi and [John (1997)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur293), and genetic algorithms have been applied within a wrapper framework by [Vafaie and DeJong (1992)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur539) and [Cherkauer and Shavlik (1996)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur95). The selective Naïve Bayes learning scheme is due to [Langley and Sage (1994)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur346). [Guyon, Weston, Barnhill, and Vapnik (2002)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur241) present and evaluate the recursive feature elimination scheme in conjunction with support vector machines. The method of raced search was developed by [Moore and Lee (1994)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur402). [Gütlein, Frank, Hall, and Karwath (2009)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur240) investigate how to speed up scheme-specific selection for datasets with many attributes using simple ranking-based methods.

[Dougherty, Kohavi, and Sahami (1995)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur144) give a brief account of supervised and unsupervised discretization, along with experimental results comparing the entropy-based method with equal-width binning and the 1 R method. [Frank and Witten (1999)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur183) describe the effect of using the ordering information in discretized attributes. Proportional *k*\-interval discretization for Naïve Bayes was proposed by [Yang and Webb (2001)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur582). The entropy-based method for discretization, including the use of the MDL stopping criterion, was developed by [Fayyad and Irani (1993)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur163). The bottom-up statistical method using the χ² test is due to [Kerber (1992)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur304), and its extension to an automatically determined significance level is described by [Liu and Setiono (1997)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur368). [Fulton, Kasif, and Salzberg (1995)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur200) investigate the use of dynamic programming for discretization and derive the quadratic time bound for a general impurity function (e.g., entropy) and the linear one for error-based discretization. The example used for showing the weakness of error-based discretization is adapted from [Kohavi and Sahami (1996)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur320), who were the first to clearly identify this phenomenon.

Principal component analysis is a standard technique that can be found in most statistics textbooks. [Fradkin and Madigan (2003)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur177) analyze the performance of random projections. The algorithm for partial least squares regression is from [Hastie et al. (2009)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur253). The *T**F* × *I**D**F*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">TF</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">IDF</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000078si55.png) metric is described by Witten et al. (1999b).

[Hyvärinen and Oja (2000)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur281) created the fast ICA method. [Duda et al. (2001)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur149) and [Murphy (2012)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur407) explain the algebra underlying solutions to Fisher’s linear discriminant analysis. [Sugiyama (2007)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur512) has extended it in two ways in a variant called “local Fisher discriminant analysis.” First, instead of means in the scatter matrix computations he uses computations between datapoints themselves, which allows the dimensionality of the reduced representation to be increased. Second, he applies Scholköpf and Smola’s (2002) kernel trick to obtain nonlinear projections.

There are many alternatives to the type of linear data projections discussed earlier. For example, multilayer perceptrons provide a way to learn data projections because their hidden layers can be treated as projections of the data. [Chapter 10](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X), “Deep learning: fundamentals,” examines deep neural networks, including an approach for unsupervised dimensionality reduction based on a type of neural network known as an “autoencoder.”

The experiments on using C4.5 to filter its own training data were reported by [John (1995)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur292). The more conservative approach of a consensus filter involving several different learning algorithms has been investigated by [Brodley and Fried (1996)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur71). [Rousseeuw and Leroy (1987)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur463) describe the detection of outliers in statistical regression, including the least median of squares method; they also present the telephone data of [Fig. 6.7](#Ch006_209-259_B9780443158889000078.xhtml#f0040). It was [Quinlan (1986)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur441) who noticed that removing noise from the training instance’s attributes can decrease a classifier’s performance on similarly noisy test instances, particularly at higher noise levels.

[Barnett and Lewis (1994)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur24) address the general topic of outliers in statistical data, while [Pearson (2005)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur430) describes the statistical approach of fitting a distribution to the target data. [Schölkopf, Williamson, Smola, Shawe-Taylor, and Platt (2000)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur480) describe the use of support vector machines for novelty detection, while [Abe, Zadrozny, and Langford (2006)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur3), among others, use artificial data as a second class. Combining density estimation and class probability estimation using artificial data is suggested as a generic approach to unsupervised learning by [Hastie et al. (2009)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur253), and [Hempstalk, Frank, and Witten (2008)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur261) describe it in the context of one-class classification. [Hempstalk and Frank (2008)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur260) discuss the fair comparison of one-class and multiclass classification when several classes are available at training time and we want to discriminate against an entirely new class at prediction time.

[Vitter (1985)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur548) explored the idea of reservoir sampling; he called the method we described algorithm *R*. Its computational complexity is *O*(*N*), where *N* is the number of instances in the stream because a random number must be generated for every instance to determine whether to place it in the reservoir, and where. Vitter describes several other algorithms that improve upon *R* by reducing the number of random numbers that must be generated to produce the sample.

[Rifkin and Klautau (2004)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur456) show that the one-vs-rest method for multiclass classification can work well if appropriate parameter tuning is applied. [Friedman (1996)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur194) describes the technique of pairwise classification, [Fürnkranz (2002)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur201) further analyzes it, and [Hastie and Tibshirani (1998)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur252) extend it to estimate probabilities using pairwise coupling. [Fürnkranz (2003)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur202) evaluates pairwise classification as a technique for ensemble learning. The idea of using error-correcting output codes for classification gained wide acceptance after a paper by [Dietterich and Bakiri (1995)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur134); [Ricci and Aha (1998)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur452) showed how to apply such codes to nearest-neighbor classifiers. [Frank and Kramer (2004)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur182) introduce ensembles of nested dichotomies for multiclass problems. [Dong, Frank, and Kramer (2005)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur142) considered using balanced nested dichotomies rather than unrestricted random hierarchies to reduce training time.

The importance of methods for calibrating class probability estimates is now well-established. [Zadrozny and Elkan (2002)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur585) applied the PAV approach and logistic regression to calibration and also investigated how to deal with multiclass problems. [Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur415) compared a variant of logistic regression and the PAV-based method in conjunction with a large set of underlying class probability estimators and found that the latter is preferable for sufficiently large calibration sets. They also found that multilayer perceptrons and bagged decision trees produce well-calibrated probabilities and do not require an extra calibration step. [Stout (2008)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur510) describes a linear-time algorithm for isotonic regression based on minimizing the squared error.

The *t*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000078si56.png)\-SNE method for visualizing high-dimensional data via manifold learning is due to [van der Maaten and Hinton (2008)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur542). The UMAP method of [McInnes et al. (2018)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur385) aims to improve on this method leveraging topological theory, and it consequently tends to be more reliable than *t*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000078si57.png)\-SNE.

 

## 6.10 Weka Implementations

Attribute selection

*   • *CfsSubsetEval* (correlation-based attribute subset evaluator)
*   • *ConsistencySubsetEval* (measures class consistency for a given set of attributes, in the *consistencySubsetEval* package)
*   • *ClassifierSubsetEval* (uses a classifier for evaluating subsets of attributes, in the *classifierBasedAttributeSelection* package)
*   • *SVMAttributeEval* (ranks attributes according to the magnitude of the coefficients learned by a support vector machine, in the *SVMAttributeEval* package)
*   • *ReliefF* (instance-based approach for ranking attributes)
*   • *WrapperSubsetEval* (uses a classifier plus cross-validation)
*   • *GreedyStepwise* (forward selection and backward elimination search)
*   • *LinearForwardSelection* (forward selection with a sliding window of attribute choices at each step of the search, in the *linearForwardSelection* package)
*   • *BestFirst* (search method that uses greedy hill-climbing with backtracking)
*   • *RaceSearch* (uses the race search methodology, in the *raceSearch* package)
*   • *Ranker* (ranks individual attributes according to their evaluation) 
    *   Learning decision tables: *DecisionTable*
    *   Discretization
*   • *Discretize* (unsupervised and supervised versions)
*   • *PKIDiscretize* (proportional *k*\-interval discretization) 
    *   Discriminant analysis for classification
*   • *LDA, FLDA*, and *QDA* (in the *discriminantAnalysis* package) 
    *   Discriminant analysis for dimensionality reduction
*   • *MultiClassFLDA* (in the *discriminantAnalysis* package) 
    *   Other pre- and postprocessing operations
*   • *PrincipalComponents* and *RandomProjection*
*   • Arithmetic operations; time-series operations; obfuscation; generating cluster membership values; adding noise; various conversions between numeric, binary, and nominal attributes; and various data cleansing operations
*   • *PLSFilter* (partial least squares transformation)
*   • Resampling and reservoir sampling
*   • *MultiClassClassifier* (includes many ways of handling multiclass problems with two-class classifiers, including error-correcting output codes)
*   • *FastICA* (independent component analysis, in the *StudentFilters* package)
*   • *StringToWordVector* (text to attribute vectors)
*   • *END* (ensembles of nested dichotomies, in the *ensemblesOfNestedDichotomies* package)

 

## 6.11 Exercises

 

*   6.1 Which is not a benefit of attribute selection? 
    1.  A. May allow learning algorithms to operate faster
    2.  B. May improve classification accuracy in some cases
    3.  C. Increases discriminating power
    4.  D. Produces a more compact, easily interpreted representation of the target concept
*   6.2 Outliers correspond to bad data and should always be excluded from the dataset. 
    1.  A. True
    2.  B. False
*   6.3 **List** at least three reasons why data may be noisy.
*   6.4 **Compare and contrast** attribute selection and principal component analysis.
*   6.5 **Identify** an advantage of random projections over principal component analysis.
*   6.6 Consider the Student Performance Data Set from the UCI Repository, available at [http://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Student+Performance](http://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Student+Performance). The task is to predict student achievement (grades) in math and Portuguese, based on demographic-, social-, and school-related features. **Identify** as many preprocessing steps as you can that might be useful for this dataset, and **explain** why they might be useful.

# Chapter 7 Ethics: what are the impacts of what’s been learned?

 

## Abstract

This chapter discusses ethical issues arising from artificial intelligence and data mining technologies, and the responsible AI practices that may help to address these issues. We overview the issue of privacy in the context of data mining and technologies that can help address it, such as *k*\-anonymity, differential privacy, and federated learning. We then tackle fairness and bias issues in machine learning, including the sources of bias and both technical and nontechnical interventions to mitigate them. Finally, we explain how AI alignment problems can potentially lead to harmful, or even catastrophic, results.

 

### Key Words

AI ethics; responsible AI; fairness and bias in AI; privacy; deepfakes; AI safety; AI and society

The development of machine learning and data mining technologies has happened alongside the rise of the internet, social media, and the large technology companies that aim to profit from these technologies. This is not a coincidence. The “Big Tech” industry has quickly realized that it might be able to profit from any and all data it can obtain about its users or its potential future users. Given the decreasing cost of data storage, technology companies are incentivized to store all the data that they can on the people that interact with their platforms, right down to the level of clicks or individual keystrokes. Even if they do not have a plan for its use, they might say to themselves that they had better hang onto it just in case they need it later.

The catch, as you might have realized, is that all this data is not just a pile of numbers lying idly in a database somewhere. Frequently, it comes from real people. Myriad ethical issues can arise whenever personal data is stored or is used.

The potential impacts increase further as the use of data mining techniques spreads beyond commercial applications. Today, data-driven algorithms are being used to determine whether people—such as yourself—will be offered a job interview, awarded a loan, be admitted to college, receive healthcare services such as Medicaid, or even be given bail or parole. In large-scale applications the impacts can be at the scale of entire societies, such as influencing the outcomes of national elections or perpetuating patterns of racism and sexism.

A growing awareness of ethical issues around artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and data mining technologies has led companies and organizations to develop guidelines, standards, and principles for responsible AI best practices. For example, the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM)’s Statement on Principles for Responsible Algorithmic Systems provides the following set of principles for designing algorithmic systems, including those based on AI:

*   • *Legitimacy and competency*: The developers of such systems (and their managers) should have the competence, expertise, and scientific and legal bases to build and deploy them, and the systems should have social legitimacy from impacted stakeholders.
*   • *Minimizing harm*: Developers and stakeholders should be aware of possible harms from a system and take appropriate steps to mitigate the harms.
*   • *Security and privacy*: It is important to keep sensitive data secure from intruders and to protect the privacy of those whose data are used.
*   • *Transparency*: Developers should ensure that design decisions are appropriately documented, uncertainty in algorithmic decisions is communicated, and that potential unfair biases in the system can be scrutinized externally.
*   • *Interpretability and explainability*: It should be possible to understand the process that an algorithmic system uses to make its decisions (*interpretability*) and to understand each decision itself (*explainability*). Rationalizations of the decisions, made after the fact without reference to the actual decision-making process, are generally insufficient.
*   • *Maintainability*: The proper performance of the system should be maintained throughout its life cycle, and this should be documented.
*   • *Contestability and auditability*: It should be possible to contest decisions made or informed by algorithmic systems and to seek redress for harmful decisions. Developers should store and preserve the information necessary to ensure that it is possible to audit the models, algorithms, data, etc. that the system uses to make its decisions.
*   • *Accountability and responsibility*: Organizations (and government agencies, etc.) that create and/or use algorithmic systems should be held accountable for their systems’ decisions and should be responsible for the systems, including correcting issues that arise and stopping the systems when it is necessary to do so.
*   • *Limiting environmental impacts*: The negative impact on the environment by algorithmic systems, for example, due to carbon emissions or energy consumption, should be monitored and restricted.

These ethical concerns are important enough that we emphasized them as early as [Chapter 1](#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029.xhtml#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029), “What’s it all about?” In this chapter, we will go deeper into these issues and their potential solutions. We’ll consider privacy concerns that arise from AI, machine learning, and data mining, as well as issues of fairness and bias in the behavior of algorithms. We’ll then discuss AI safety issues including the possible risk of catastrophic consequences of advanced AI. We will return to the topic of the ethics and impacts of these systems in [Chapter 15](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169), “Moving on: applications and their consequences,” where we consider certain application areas of concern and the impacts of AI on our society at large.

 

## 7.1 Privacy

In [Chapter 1](#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029.xhtml#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029), “What’s it all about?” (and later, in [Chapter 4](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054), “Algorithms: the basic methods”), we learned how supermarkets analyze their shoppers’ purchases to find patterns such as an association between buying diapers and beer (market basket analysis) and to personalize special offerings and coupons for specific customers. While customers may often enjoy receiving personalized discounts, some of these offers can be a bit *too* personal. In 2012, Andrew Pole, a statistician working for the retail firm Target, admitted to *New York Times* journalist and author Charles Duhigg that the company was attempting to identify customers who are pregnant. The goal, the statistician told Duhigg, was to convince its customers to go to Target for all their baby-related items such as diapers and bottles. In turn, this could lead busy and exhausted new parents to purchase other nonbaby-related items at Target while in the store, potentially changing their purchasing habits for years to come.

Duhigg recounted an anecdote, told to him by a Target employee, in which a father complained to a store manager that Target was inappropriately sending his teenage daughter coupons for cribs and baby clothes, which he felt might encourage her to get pregnant. Later, on the phone to the manager, the father gave an embarrassed apology. As it turned out, his daughter was already pregnant. Target had learned of her pregnancy before her father did!

Realizing that these personalized pregnancy-related coupons could be seen to be creepy, Target began to obfuscate them by mixing them together with ads for things that pregnant women would be unlikely to buy, such as lawnmowers and wine glasses. It found that its customers would use the coupons as long as they believed that they were not being targeted at them. The ad campaign was a huge success. Target’s Mom and Baby division sales increased dramatically. Its overall sales went up substantially in this time period as well, and the company’s president specifically mentioned this product category when speaking to investors. The statistician, Pole, got promoted.

It should be noted that Target is far from the only retailer to employ data mining, and it is likely that other firms have employed similar tactics. The retailer Walmart has built what is, as of 2023, one of the largest private cloud platforms in the world. It uses this for real-time analysis at its analytics hub, which it calls its “Data Café.” The Data Café helps to, for example, diagnose the reasons for sales declines for particular items in a particular store such as stocking mistakes and pricing errors.

 

### Data Breaches

Even when not used for dubious purposes, the storage of detailed large-scale customer data incentivizes hackers to attempt to steal it, putting customers at risk. Data breaches at large tech companies have exposed personal data from hundreds of millions—or even billions—of accounts. A data breach at the US company Yahoo in 2013, revealed in 2016, was later revealed to have impacted three billion accounts, while breaches at the Indian company Aadhar (2018) and the Chinese company Alibaba (2019) each impacted around one billion users. Data leaked in these breaches included answers to security questions (Yahoo), biometric data and bank account numbers (Aadhar), criminal records (Alibaba), and phone numbers and email or physical addresses (all three of the earlier mentioned breaches). A 2016 data breach at The FriendFinder Network, home of several adult-oriented social networks and hookup sites such as Adult Friend Finder, included names, email addresses, and phone numbers, with potentially embarrassing consequences, and doubtless marital implications. Similarly, Ashley Madison, a “dating site” for people to cheat on their spouses and partners, had a data breach in 2015 that revealed 32 million accounts’ personally identifiable information and stated sexual desires, thus exposing infidelity and affairs. Several of the affected members committed suicide after the breach.

 

### Government Surveillance

Of course, companies are not the only entities that collect potentially invasive information. Edward Snowden’s 2013 leaks revealed secret US National Security Agency (*NSA*) programs that were being used to spy on people both in the United States and abroad. The leaks revealed the Planning Tool for Resource Integration, Synchronization, and Management (*PRISM*) program, which collects data from US internet companies, was monitoring as much data as the entire Library of Congress every 14.4 seconds, even as early as 2006. The XKeyscore program allows the NSA to search and analyze such data. According to Snowden, XKeyscore could be used to read anyone’s email, watch traffic to and from any website, watch any computer, and track any laptop as it moves around throughout the world.

 

### Defining Privacy

The examples we’ve discussed show that privacy is a serious issue. But what is privacy, exactly? We should first note that *computer security*, which protects computer systems against unauthorized access and disruptive attacks, is not privacy, or at least, it is not sufficient by itself to ensure privacy. The most sophisticated security system in the world won’t help protect your data if an organization decides to share your data with the world. Alternatively, a simplistic definition of privacy might be: “privacy means keeping our secrets and revealing as little information on us as possible.” Since we are all being constantly tracked online, by this definition, our privacy is reducing rapidly. So then, is privacy already over for us, and should we simply give up on it?

According to some who subscribe to this definition, we may have already met the *death of privacy*. Back in 1999, Scott McNealy, the CEO of the company that created the Java programming language, Sun Microsystems, controversially said, “You have zero privacy anyway … Get over it.” According to Vint Cerf in 2013, one of the leading figures in the creation of the internet, “Privacy may be an anomaly” and “It will be increasingly difficult for us to achieve it.” Cerf said that this is largely our fault: “Our social behavior is quite damaging to privacy. Technology has outraced our social intellect.” Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg put it even more bluntly: “The age of privacy is over.”

Fortunately, if we are willing to scale back our view of privacy to a more realistic conception for the big data era, we shall realize that all is not lost. A more useful definition of privacy, due to legal scholars and privacy experts Neil M. Richards and Jonathan H. King, from their 2014 paper “Big Data Ethics,” is as follows:

“Privacy should not be thought of merely as how much is secret, but rather about *what rules are in place (legal, social, or otherwise) to govern the use of information as well as its disclosure*.” (Emphasis mine.)

If we adopt this definition, in which we seek to appropriately *control the flow of information*, privacy is still alive and thriving, aided by laws that ensure privacy protections on information flows. For example, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) is a US law, established in 1996, that protects patients’ healthcare information by regulating the flow of such information. Under HIPAA, covered entities, which include physicians, healthcare providers, hospitals, etc., may not disclose protected health information (PHI) without patients’ consent.

Although it was originally considered overcomplicated, HIPAA has largely succeeded in making patients feel safe in sharing their health information with physicians and clinicians while still allowing the flow of information that facilitates treatment, research, and public health. Under certain restrictions, it can even enable the release of medical data that can be analyzed via machine learning. HIPAA allows researchers to obtain PHI without patient consent if an institutional review board (IRB) or a privacy board determines that there is minimal risk from the research and obtaining consent would be impractical. Under HIPAA, datasets for which a designated set of 18 types of personally identifiable information (PII) have been removed, to anonymize the data, can be shared for research or commercial purposes.

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the European Union’s (EU’s) 2018 landmark privacy regulation law, is another important law that protects privacy in terms of information flows. The GDPR applies to any organization that collects data on people living in the European Economic Area, which includes the EU, Iceland, Liechtenstein, and Norway. It also impacts non-EU companies that do business with the EU. As such it has impacted privacy policies well beyond the EU. It may be difficult to enforce outside of the EU, however. The GDPR aims to give users control over their personal information, and it states that personal data may not be processed without a legal basis for doing so. The key principles of the GDPR are:

*   • Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
*   • Accountability
*   • Purpose limitation
*   • Data minimization
*   • Accuracy
*   • Storage limitation
*   • Security.

Some legal scholars have argued that the GDPR mandates a right to explanation, that is, an explanation of a decision made by an AI or machine learning algorithm. This has motivated much research on explainable AI techniques. However, this view has been disputed by other scholars, and its legal status is currently unclear.

 

### Anonymization and Linkage Attacks

A natural approach to try to achieve privacy is to *anonymize* the data, so that each record is not associated with the name of the individual in question. For example, as previously mentioned, HIPAA allows the release of data if a specified set of 18 types of PII have been excised. However, as was discussed in [Chapter 1](#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029.xhtml#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029), “What’s it all about?,” this approach is unsatisfactory because individuals can often be re-identified when enough information is available. The crux of the problem is a *curse of dimensionality*—for every additional attribute that is measured, in the worst case there are exponentially fewer data points corresponding to each possible feature vector. Like snowflakes, everyone is unique and special so if you know enough about someone you can pick them out of a crowd.

A key strategy for re-identifying individuals is the *linkage attack*, in which an anonymized dataset is combined with additional auxiliary data from another dataset. For example, if an anonymized record can be “linked” to a corresponding identified record from another dataset its identity would be revealed. A famous example of this is the Netflix Prize dataset, which we discussed in [Chapter 1](#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029.xhtml#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029), “What’s it all about?” The online movie rental service Netflix released an anonymized dataset to be used as the training dataset for its contest to improve its recommendation algorithm, which had a million-dollar prize. However, using a linkage attack strategy, security researchers were able to re-identify some of the dataset by connecting it to public movie ratings data from IMDb, another website that is a source of information on film and television media. Although movie ratings data might appear to be innocuous, when associated with a timestamp, it reveals what the users were doing in their own home on a particular evening, which could be rather personal. This privacy vulnerability led to a class-action lawsuit that resulted in Netflix having to scrap its follow-up data mining contest.

 

### *k*\-Anonymity

The simplest linkage attack is to simply look for a match between the anonymized dataset and the background knowledge dataset when looking at the potentially relevant features that remain after removing *explicit identifiers*; for example, the attributes that uniquely identify individuals. These attributes are called *quasiidentifiers*—a set of attributes that, in combination, can uniquely identify individuals. The approach used on the Netflix Prize was slightly more sophisticated and does not require knowing which attributes are quasiidentifiers, but it was along these same lines.

An early and relatively direct attempt to prevent linkage attacks is a methodology due to privacy researcher Latanya Sweeney, called *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi1.png)*\-anonymity*. The goal of this approach is to release a version of a dataset that is safe from the harms of re-identification while still being useful for analysis. Note, however, that this approach does not actually guarantee this is achieved. The definition is as follows:

*A release of a dataset is said to satisfy* *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi2.png)*\-anonymity if and only if each sequence of quasiidentifier values occurs at least* *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi3.png) *times in the release*.

The idea here is that if an adversary matches their background knowledge to a sequence of quasiidentifier values, they won’t know which of the *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi4.png) or more individuals with those same quasiidentifier values that it refers to. So, in theory, individuals can’t be uniquely identified via linkage attacks. For example, [Table 7.1](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#t0010) shows a version of the Contact Lens Data that satisfies 2<mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi5.png)\-anonymity, that is, *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi6.png)\-anonymity where *k* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi7.png).

Table 7.1

A Version of the Contact Lens Data that Satisfies 2<mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi195.png)\-Anonymity. (Here, all attributes are assumed to be quasi-identifiers.)

 
| Age || Spectacle Prescription || Astigmatism || Tear Production Rate || Recommended Lenses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Young || Myope || No || Reduced || None |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Young || Myope || No || Reduced || None |
| Young || Myope || No || Normal || Soft |
| Young || Myope || No || Normal || Soft |
| Young || Hypermetrope || No || Reduced || None |
| Young || Hypermetrope || No || Reduced || None |
| Prepresbyopic || Myope || No || Reduced || None |
| Prepresbyopic || Myope || No || Reduced || None |
| Presbyopic || Myope || No || Reduced || None |
| Presbyopic || Myope || No || Reduced || None |

Credit: James Foulds

The first step in achieving *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi8.png)\-anonymity is to partition the attributes into explicit identifiers, quasiidentifiers, and nonidentifiers. Explicit identifiers are *suppressed* (removed from the release) while *nonidentifiers* (which we suppose do not help with identifying individuals) are ignored. The key challenge is to process the quasiidentifiers to achieve the desired value of *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi9.png). We can do this using the strategies of *suppression* (replacing one or more values of attributes with a dummy value, \*<mml:math><mml:mo>\*</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi10.png)) and *generalization* (coarsening the granularity of an attribute by binning it into certain ranges).

While the method looks nice on paper, unfortunately, *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi11.png)\-anonymity has several severe limitations that hamper it in practice. First, if you don’t correctly determine the quasiidentifiers, or the adversary knows more than the designated set of quasiidentifiers, the method will fail completely. Second, it’s difficult to achieve in high dimensions since we may need to process the data to have *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi12.png) copies of an exponentially large number of feature vectors.

Even more seriously, *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi13.png)\-anonymity is vulnerable to several attacks. Suppose *S* is a *sensitive attribute* that an adversary is trying to learn via a linkage attack. The *homogeneity attack* exploits a lack of diversity in the sensitive attribute. Consider a case where all *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi14.png) values of *S* for the data instances with a particular quasiidentifier *Q*<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi15.png) have the same value *v*. Then if an individual, Alice (who is in the dataset), has quasiidentifier *Q*<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi16.png), the adversary can infer that *S* = *v*<mml:math><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi17.png) for Alice, even though they cannot determine which of the *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi18.png) instances matching *Q*<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi19.png) corresponds to Alice. An example is given in [Table 7.2](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#t0015), where an adversary can determine that Alice has *Medical Condition* = *Eye Disease* based on her quasiidentifiers, even though they cannot determine which row her record belongs to.

| --- | --- | --- |
| Name || Spectacle Prescription || Astigmatism || Tear Production Rate || Medical Condition |
| Alice || Myope || No || Reduced || Eye Disease |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bob || Myope || No || Reduced || Eye Disease |
| Claire || Myope || No || Reduced || Eye Disease |

Credit: James Foulds

Another related attack, the *background knowledge attack*, exploits background knowledge on the sensitive attributes to narrow down the possibilities. For instance, suppose that Bob (who is in the dataset) matches quasiidentifiers with *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi20.png) individuals whose sensitive attribute, a medical condition, is either chest pain or obesity. Let’s say that the adversary happens to know that Bob is a personal fitness trainer, so it is extremely unlikely that Bob is obese. Then the adversary could infer that Bob has chest pain. We illustrate this scenario in [Table 7.3](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#t0020).

Table 7.3

 Example of the Background Knowledge Attack. 

 
| Explicit Identifier  || Quasiidentifiers || Sensitive Attribute |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name || Spectacle Prescription || Astigmatism || Tear Production Rate || Medical Condition |
| Alice || Myope || No || Reduced || Obesity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bob || Myope || No || Reduced || Chest pain |
| Claire || Myope || No || Reduced || Obesity |

### Differential Privacy

We have seen that *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi21.png)\-anonymity has serious flaws, and it cannot ensure protection against linkage attacks, as was its goal. We’d like to instead have a methodology that has more rigorous guarantees of protection against such attacks. To do so, ideally we would like to set up our database’s security system so that *if someone obtains access to it, they cannot learn anything about an individual that they could not otherwise know*, even in the presence of auxiliary information. For example, in this ideal setting one could not learn which movies a person has rated unless one could already learn those ratings without having access to the movie rating database. Thus the database would not reveal any unknown private data. This ideal “nothing learned” notion of privacy has been compared to the property of public key encryption schemes such as Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (*RSA*), called *semantic security*, in which access to the encrypted data (“*cyphertext*”) reveals no information about the decrypted data (“*cleartext*”).

However, it turns out that this idealized notion of privacy is impossible to achieve in general. This is because auxiliary information is so pernicious that it can even expose the data of someone who is not in the dataset! Suppose, for example, we know that user Alice rates the movie “Titanic” one star lower than the average US user does. To determine Alice’s rating, we could simply compute the average star rating that US users give to “Titanic” and subtract one star from this figure. As we can see from this example, if an adversary has access to arbitrary side information it may not be possible to prevent them from making new inferences about a person based on information gleaned from our database. In this case, the inference could be made even if Alice’s data is not in our database. Our goal for privacy must therefore retreat to something more attainable.

In this example, it did not matter whether Alice’s data is in the database or not—it was exposed either way. While we could not control the risk of a privacy-breaching disclosure in an *absolute* sense, as it turns out, the way forward is to instead control the *relative* risk of a privacy-breaching disclosure *for an individual who contributes their data to the database* compared to if they were to leave their data out of the database. *Differential privacy* is a mathematical definition of privacy that takes this approach (hence the name, which refers to this difference between these two scenarios).

Differential privacy is a promise—“*If you add your data to the database you will not be affected too much*.” This promise holds even in the presence of auxiliary data, such as the linkage attack used against the Netflix Prize dataset. Suppose that the database is stored on a secure server, owned by someone trustworthy, called the *data curator*. The data curator’s goal is to make available information about the overall population, without revealing too much about any one person’s data. The data curator entertains queries from untrusted users, and they only return answers that protect the individuals’ private information. We illustrate the scenario assumed by differential privacy in [Fig. 7.1](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#f0010).

![Fig. 7.1 A schematic of the scenario assumed by differential privacy. Credit: James Foulds](images/F00008Xf07-01-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 7.1](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#Bf0010) A schematic of the scenario assumed by differential privacy. Credit: James Foulds

More formally, let *M*(*D*)<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi22.png) be a privacy mechanism that returns the answer to a query on database *D*<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi23.png). Then *M*(*D*)<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi24.png) is *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi25.png)\-differentially private if for all pairs of datasets *D*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi26.png) and *D*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi27.png) differing in a single element and all *S* ⊆ *R**a**n**g**e*(*M*)<mml:math><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8838;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">Range</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi28.png),

Pr (*M*(*D*[1])∈*S*) ≤ *e*^(*ϵ*) × Pr (*M*(*D*[2])∈*S*).<mml:math><mml:mi>Pr</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8804;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>Pr</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math> (7.1)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi29.png)(7.1) 

In other words, if one instance in the dataset was changed, the probability of any output of the algorithm would be almost the same, up to a small multiplicative constant *e*^(*ϵ*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi30.png). Here, *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi31.png) is the degree to which the mechanism is differentially private (lower is better).

 

### Techniques for Achieving Differential Privacy

Differential privacy is typically achieved by injecting random noise to the answers to the queries, with the amount of noise being calibrated to ensure that very little can be learned about any one person’s data. For example, suppose we are interested in learning the proportion of the population that engages in an embarrassing or illegal activity. You can no doubt think of a few of those. Pick your favorite one! For no particular reason, we will refer to this activity as XXX.

If the participants of our study are to contribute their data, they would like reassurance that the study will not reveal whether they engage in XXX. To help keep their secret safe, the participants are asked to flip a coin. If the coin comes up tails, they will answer the question truthfully, “yes” or “no.” If the coin comes up heads, they will instead answer randomly by flipping the coin again and responding “yes” if it is heads and “no” if it is tails. This gives them plausible deniability as a “yes” answer could have come from the coin flips instead of from their honest answer. If the coin comes up heads both times the participant would respond “yes” regardless of their data, and this happens one-quarter of the time. We then count the number of “yes” responses across the population.

Finally, we must correct for the randomness of the coin flips to estimate the true proportion of the population that engages in XXX. The expected number of “yes” votes is one-quarter of the participants who do not engage in XXX and voted “yes” due to flipping two heads, plus three-quarters of the participants who do engage in XXX since we expect one-quarter of them to respond “no” due to flipping a heads then a tails. So we calculate the expected proportion of “yes” votes *p*[*y*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi32.png) as $p\_{y} = \\frac{1}{4}\\left( {1 - p} \\right) + \\frac{3}{4}p = \\frac{1}{4} + \\frac{p}{2}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi33.png). Solving for *p*<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi34.png), we estimate *p*<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi35.png) as $p \\approx 2p\_{y} - \\frac{1}{2}$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8776;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi36.png). This technique is called *randomized response* in the social science literature. As it turns out, randomized response is *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi37.png)\-differentially private, where *ϵ* = ln ⁡(3)<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>ln</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#8289;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi38.png), as we will now show. In calculating the expected proportion of “yes” votes, we have already worked out that $P\\left( {{\\mathit{response} = \\text{yes}},|,{\\mathit{XXX} = \\mathit{true}}} \\right) = \\frac{3}{4}$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">response</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>yes</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">XXX</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">true</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi39.png) and $P\\left( {{\\mathit{response} = \\mathit{yes}},|,{\\mathit{XXX} = \\mathit{false}}} \\right) = \\frac{1}{4}$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">response</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">yes</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">XXX</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">false</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi40.png). Then we have

$\\frac{P\\left( response = yes \\middle| XXX = true \\right)}{P\\left( response = yes \\middle| XXX = false \\right)} = \\frac{\\frac{3}{4}}{\\frac{1}{4}} = 3.$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac bevelled="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi41.png)

By a similar argument, we have

$\\frac{P\\left( response = no \\middle| XXX = false \\right)}{P\\left( response = no \\middle| XXX = true \\right)} = \\frac{\\frac{3}{4}}{\\frac{1}{4}} = 3.$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msp1/><mml:mfrac bevelled="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi42.png)

The probability of each of the outcomes differs by at most a multiplicative factor of 3 = *e*^(ln ⁡(3))<mml:math><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ln</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#8289;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi43.png) when we change one data point, and so ln (3)<mml:math><mml:mi>ln</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi44.png)\-differential privacy is achieved.

Randomized response is applicable to discrete data. In practice, we frequently want to privatize numeric data. For example, a common use-case of differential privacy is to privatize a machine learning model’s parameters so the model can be disclosed without risk of it being reverse-engineered to expose any information about the individuals who contributed their data for training the system. The trick to doing this is to add just enough noise to the data to obscure any one person’s data point.

The *Laplace mechanism* is a commonly used approach to achieve this. This method makes use of the Laplace distribution, which is essentially two exponential distributions, back-to-back. Its probability density function is:

$Lap\\left( x \\middle| b \\right) = \\frac{1}{2b}\\exp\\left( {- \\frac{\\left| x \\right|}{b}} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>exp</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.2)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi45.png)(7.2) 

As input, it requires a quantity called the *l*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi46.png)\-*sensitivity*, the maximum possible amount that the answer to our query *f*<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi47.png)(D) about the data can be changed by one person’s data:

*Δ**f* = *max* *f*(*D*[1]) − *f*(*D*[2)])[1].<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">max</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mrow/><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.3)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi48.png)(7.3) 

The Laplace mechanism adds noise to the query, with the amount of noise being determined by the *l*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi49.png)\-sensitivity:

*M*[*L**a**p**l**a**c**e*](*D*,*f*(⋅),*ϵ*) = *f*(*D*) + \[*Y*[1],*Y*[2],…,*Y*[*k*]\],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">Laplace</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8901;</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.4)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi50.png)(7.4) 

where each *Y*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi51.png) is independently drawn from a Laplace distribution *L**a**p*(*Δ**f*/*ϵ*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">Lap</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8725;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi52.png).

The Laplace mechanism is *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi53.png)\-differentially private. We can choose a target value of *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi54.png), and the previous equation will tell us how much noise to add to achieve that level of privacy. Of course, if the sensitivity is too high, we must add too much noise to achieve a reasonable degree of differential privacy, ruining any information we might glean from the output of our privatized query.

Another option is to add noise from a normal distribution, in a method called the *Gaussian mechanism*. The amount of noise to add depends on the *l*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi55.png)\-sensitivity, which is defined similarly to the *l*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi56.png)\-sensitivity but is computed based on the *L*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi57.png)\-norm (Euclidean distance). Compared to the Laplace mechanism, the Gaussian mechanism allows less noise to be added, and the noise requirements scale more gracefully in the number of queries performed. However, it comes at a cost. The definition of differential privacy must be relaxed to allow a “fudge factor” *δ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#948;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi58.png) that represents a small probability that the privacy guarantee can be violated and information be released, potentially “in the clear.” This relaxed privacy definition is sometimes called (![ent](images/epsi_1013.png),δ)-differential privacy, which is pronounced as “*epsilon-delta differential privacy*,” and it is also sometimes referred to as *approximate differential privacy*, or simply “*differential privacy*,” thus expanding the definition to include this fudge factor.

A privacy mechanism *M*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi59.png) is (*ϵ*, *δ*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#948;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi60.png)\-differentially private if for all pairs of datasets *D*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi61.png) and *D*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi62.png) differing in a single element, and all *S* ⊆ *R**a**n**g**e*(*M*)<mml:math><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8838;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">Range</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi63.png),

Pr (*M*(*D*[1])∈*S*) ≤ *e*^(*ϵ*) × Pr ⁡(*M*(*D*[2])∈*S*) + *δ*.<mml:math><mml:mi>Pr</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8804;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>Pr</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#8289;</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#948;</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.5)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi64.png)(7.5) 

If *δ* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>&#948;</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi65.png) the definition corresponds to *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi66.png)\-differential privacy. For the definition to offer meaningful privacy guarantees, *δ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#948;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi67.png) must be very small, as it only ensures that the guarantees of *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi68.png)\-differential privacy will be enforced with probability 1 − *δ*<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#948;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi69.png).

Stated informally, these guarantees and other useful properties include:

*   • *Neutralization of linkage attacks*. No matter what auxiliary data is available, an adversary cannot undo the obfuscation of the query due to noise to increase its privacy parameters *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi70.png) and *δ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#948;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi71.png).
*   • *Closure under postprocessing*. Without access to the private database, no further computation can make the algorithm *M*<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi72.png) less differentially private.
*   • *Economic guarantees for those who contribute their data*. For any utility function, a user’s utility value will not be changed by more than a multiplicative factor of *e*^(*ϵ*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi73.png), which approximately equals 1 + *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi74.png) for small values of *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi75.png), due to their decision to contribute their data to the dataset.
*   • *Group privacy*. It is possible to calculate the quantification of differential privacy as it extends to a group of individuals, to an entire family.
*   • *Composition*. When performing multiple differentially private computations, the privacy parameters of the overall process increase gracefully and in a measurable way. If an *ϵ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi76.png)\-differentially private operation is performed followed by an *ϵ*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi77.png)\-differentially private operation, then the overall procedure is (*ϵ*[1] + *ϵ*[2])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi78.png)\-differentially private.

This type of composition calculation is much more complicated in the case of (*ϵ*, *δ*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#948;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi79.png)\-differential privacy but with some sophisticated mathematical wizardry, which can be outsourced to software libraries, it can be done. For a fixed value of *δ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#948;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi80.png), we can view *ϵ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi81.png) of the *i*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi82.png)th query as its “*privacy cost*,” which accumulates toward using up an overall target “*privacy budget*” *ϵ*[*o**v**e**r**a**l**l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">overall</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi83.png).

 

### Differentially Private Machine Learning

In practice, the art of differentially private machine learning is to carefully design a privacy-preserving learning scheme so that the target level of differential privacy is achieved while retaining satisfactory performance. We can see from the equation for the Laplace mechanism that the more private we want to make it (smaller *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi84.png)), the more noise we need to add, garbling the results. In general, there is a trade-off between differential privacy and the accuracy or usefulness of the output, often referred to as “utility.” We must engineer our privacy-preserving learning algorithm to manage this *privacy-utility trade-off*.

Suppose that we want to achieve differential privacy to ensure that the parameters of a machine learning algorithm can be released without risk of reverse-engineering the data of any individual in the dataset. It is not generally feasible to compute the sensitivity of an entire machine learning algorithm, so we cannot usually apply the Laplace mechanism or the Gaussian mechanism directly to the output of the learning algorithm. Furthermore, the algorithms typically work on individual data points, not aggregate data, so we cannot just privatize the data ahead of time. Instead, the typical strategy for privatizing a machine learning algorithm is to add noise to each iteration of the machine learning algorithm, to a minibatch gradient descent (or Adam, etc.) update. Typically, we compute the sensitivity of the individual updates in each iteration, then privatize them by adding appropriate noise.
