Leveraging composition theorems, we allocate a per-iteration privacy budget *ϵ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi85.png) for each iteration *i*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi86.png) so that the entire learning algorithm is *ϵ*[*o**v**e**r**a**l**l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">overall</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi87.png)\-differentially private.

A classic example of this approach is the differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm proposed by Martin Abadi and colleagues in 2016 for differentially private deep learning ([Fig. 7.2](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#f0015)). The algorithm processes subsets of the data (minibatches) at a time, updating the parameters via estimated gradient steps for each minibatch. The method achieves differential privacy by first clipping these gradients to control the *l*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi88.png)\-sensitivity, then adding noise to the clipped gradients via the Gaussian mechanism. The authors proposed a novel and sophisticated method for keeping track of the privacy budget under composition, called the Moments Accountant, which allowed them to make better use of a given privacy budget and hence reduce the amount of noise that must be added to achieve the target degree of differential privacy.

![Fig. 7.2 Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Credit: James Foulds](images/F00008Xf07-02-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 7.2](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#Bf0015) Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Credit: James Foulds

 

### Federated Learning

As we have discussed, one of the key reasons why companies want to acquire our data, which raises privacy concerns, is that they desire to train machine learning models on user data gathered from many people. But what if training could be done without ever sending our data to the server? A methodology called *federated learning* aims to accomplish this. In federated learning, the users’ data stays on their local devices, such as their smartphones or laptops, and is never directly sent to the organization’s databases or machine learning servers. Instead, we only transmit locally computed machine learning models or such models’ parameters, gradients, and so on. Typically, a central server coordinates learning based on the transmitted local models, although decentralized federated learning is also possible.

In each iteration of the original federated learning approach, called *federated average* (*FedAvg*), the Central Server first sends its global model to each device node. The devices then update their local copy of this model based on their local data. Next they send gradient information to the Central Server, which averages over the results to update the global model. The process is then repeated until the algorithm terminates. See [Fig. 7.3](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#f0020) for an illustration of this scheme.

![Fig. 7.3 A typical federated learning scheme. Decentralized federated learning, without a central server, is also possible. Credit: James Foulds](images/F00008Xf07-03-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 7.3](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#Bf0020) A typical federated learning scheme. Decentralized federated learning, without a central server, is also possible. Credit: James Foulds

The main advantage of federated learning is that users’ data never leaves local devices, which limits any obvious information disclosure. However, private information about the users could still potentially be reverse engineered from the models unless additional steps are taken to ensure that this does not happen by ensuring differential privacy. Federated learning is also vulnerable to data poisoning attacks from the local devices unless additional steps are taken to prevent this. It is difficult to monitor or prevent discriminatory AI biases, since the central server never gets to see the actual data in order to check for such problems. The substantial communication costs that this approach requires are also a downside. Nevertheless, federated learning has promise as a privacy-preserving machine learning technique if these issues are carefully managed (e.g., by combining it with differential privacy and robust machine learning methods).

 

## 7.2 Fairness and Bias in Machine Learning

The field of data mining is seen as a roaring success. Machine learning models have been deployed to make decisions that affect myriad facets of daily life, from friend recommendations on social media to determining who should be prioritized to receive medical services. We know that humans are often unreliable decision makers, subject to all manner of prejudices and implicit or cognitive biases. In public and academic circles it has long been believed that artificial intelligence can avoid these biases through impartial, objective, logical, and data-driven decision making. Unfortunately, the reality is that this is far from guaranteed. The field is undergoing a reckoning around *algorithmic bias* and fairness issues. We begin by examining several application domains where these issues arise.

 

### AI Fairness in Hiring Decisions

Suppose that you have finished reading this book and studied hard to complete your degree or certification program, and you are now ready to get your first job as a data scientist. You polish your resume, search online for suitable job openings, and apply to more than a few interesting opportunities in your area, carefully tailoring your application to appeal to each company that you applied to. Feeling nervous and excited, you wait and hope for good news—an invitation to a job interview. How would you feel if you learned that you never even had a chance because a machine learning system decided to throw out your applications before any employee even looked at your materials? How about if that system did so for completely unfair reasons that had nothing to do with your qualifications or aptitude, and it provided no opportunity for you to learn of its mistakes or redress them?

This is more than just a hypothetical example. It could happen to you. According to popular job search engine site Glassdoor, on average, a company receives 250 applications for each position, out of which typically only four to six candidates receive an interview. This motivates the use of machine learning systems to automatically filter the resumes, saving time for recruiters. In 2014 US technology company Amazon developed an internal experimental machine learning tool for automatically assessing job applicants’ resumes. The system produced ratings for candidates between one and five stars, in a manner similar to how consumers rate products on the service. It was trained on 10 years of Amazon’s recruiting data. By the next year the company realized that the system was biased against women. If a resume included the word “women’s,” as in “founder of the women’s robotics team,” the candidate’s rating was downgraded. It similarly downgraded ratings from candidates who graduated from two all-women colleges. The machine learning model had learned to replicate the frequently discriminatory patterns of hiring in a male-dominated field that were naturally present in its training data.

To its credit, Amazon scrapped the system. Amazon told Reuters reporters that the tool “was never used by Amazon recruiters to evaluate candidates,” although it did not deny that recruiters had looked at its outputs. Other employers may not be as scrupulous. A 2015 study by software company Capterra estimated that 75% of recruiters and talent managers use recruiting software. It is not clear the extent to which these recruiting systems use machine learning to automatically filter the resumes but the use of such software is doubtless on the rise.

Since around the time of the Amazon recruiting tool incident, the study of *fairness and bias issues in AI and machine learning* has rapidly grown into a burgeoning area of research. There has thankfully been an increasing awareness of these issues, which have become an urgent concern as the kinds of models we have been studying in this book are now deployed in the systems that make decisions impacting each of our daily lives, both big and small, from recommendations of movies, to whether we get admitted to our dream college, to whether we receive bail or a lengthy prison sentence.

 

### AI Fairness in Criminal Justice

The latter scenario is one that has received high-profile scrutiny. In criminal justice, a risk assessment instrument (RAI) is an algorithmic tool for predicting a defendant’s risk of criminal activity in the future. This tool produces either numerical scores or discrete categories such as “high risk” that are assigned to defendants. RAIs are widely used to inform consequential decisions at multiple stages of the criminal justice process, including whether to incarcerate an individual before trial and/or the bond amount to avoid this and the length of their sentence. One of these systems, called Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions (COMPAS), was criticized in a study by journalists from ProPublica, an independent US newsroom. The study found that COMPAS was almost twice as likely to incorrectly predict re-offending for African Americans than for white people. Conversely, the study found COMPAS to be almost twice as likely to incorrectly predict that white people would not re-offend vs African Americans.

This study, by investigative journalist Julia Angwin and colleagues, has sparked a lot of discussion and debate. The US company that produced COMPAS, then called Northpointe (now renamed Equivant), disputed the findings, which ProPublica defended in response. Academics weighed in, with some arguing that fairness should instead be determined based on a different criterion, namely whether the risk scores are calibrated equally well in terms of predicting whether re-offending occurred between African American and white people. It can be shown mathematically that Angwin et al.’s criterion and this calibration criterion cannot both hold at the same time, due to differences in the base rate of (detected) reoffending between the two demographic groups. Regardless of how one views this complex scenario, it is clear that the use of AI algorithms in criminal justice is fraught with ethical challenges, necessitating transparency, independent audits, and robust debate.

 

### AI Fairness in Other Application Domains

Fairness and bias concerns can arise in almost every application of AI, machine learning, and data mining techniques in which data about human beings is used, especially when it is used to make decisions that impact the lives of those individuals.

 

#### Credit Scoring

Decisions on whether to extend credit to an individual, and the size of the loan or credit card limit to offer, clearly fall within the “high impact” category. The creditworthiness of an individual is frequently estimated via a *credit score*, a numerical score that is typically generated by statistical models that aim to determine the likelihood that the individuals will repay a loan. Apple Card, the credit card operated by American multinational firms Apple Inc. and Goldman Sachs, came under scrutiny for possible gender discrimination after two prominent male technologists alleged that their wives received 10 to 20 times smaller credit offers, despite sharing all assets and having similar or better externally generated credit scores. The technologists David Heinemeier Hansson, creator of the popular Ruby on Rails web development platform, and Steve Wozniak, cofounder of Apple, aired their complaints on social media, where they promptly went viral.

The New York State Department of Financial Services (DFS) investigated the matter and ultimately did not find evidence of unlawful discrimination against women, concluding that men and women with similar credit characteristics received similar application outcomes from Apple Card. Nevertheless, DFS’ report criticized Apple Card for a lack of transparency to consumers due to the black-box nature of the algorithm and a policy requiring account holders to wait six months to appeal their credit terms. The report emphasized that unequal access to credit remains a systemic problem and that algorithms may perpetuate this, even while following the law. It called for a modernization of the use of credit scoring and associated laws and regulations to remedy this situation.

 

#### Facial Recognition

Facial recognition software has also come under scrutiny for potential algorithmic bias. Researcher Joy Buolamwini was working on an undergraduate computer science class project where she was tasked with developing a peek-a-boo game when she discovered that the facial recognition software library she was using could not detect her face. Buolamwini, who is Black, needed to have her lighter-skinned roommate step in so that she could test her code and complete the project. At that time she figured that “somebody else would solve this problem.” She subsequently found that facial recognition software continued to fail to recognize her whenever she encountered it—and nobody else came along to solve the issue. She found that if she put a white facial mask over her face the software would successfully detect her.

This experience led her to perform a systematic study on algorithmic bias in facial recognition software with coauthor Timnit Gebru. Their study examined three off-the-shelf commercial systems for detecting an individual’s gender based on image data, developed by Microsoft, IBM, and Face++. The researchers found that the systems performed worse for darker-skinned subjects than lighter-skinned subjects and worse for female subjects than male subjects. Moreover, it performed worst for darker-skinned female subjects and best for lighter-skinned male subjects. The study served to draw attention to unequal performance in facial recognition software.

A larger follow-up study by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) examining 189 software algorithms supported the findings, concluding that demographic bias existed in most facial recognition systems for the tasks of (1) confirming a photo of an individual matches another photo of the person in a database and (2) determining whether a photographed individual has any match in a database. The bias in these tasks has clear and troubling implications for the use of facial recognition technologies in law enforcement surveillance contexts, where such failures are likely to contribute to systematic discriminatory patterns in policing. For example, a false-positive match can lead to an individual being subject to undeserved police scrutiny and possible arrest. The NIST study found higher rates of false-positive matches for images of Asian and African American faces compared to images of Caucasian faces.

 

### Sources of Bias

We’ve now seen several examples of data-driven algorithms that are potentially biased or unfair. But the companies that made these systems must have been greedy, thoughtless, or careless, and if *you*, talented and clever as you are, made such a system you’d easily avoid these problems. You’d simply make sure that the data was representative and reliable, and you wouldn’t use features such as gender, race, or immigration status, and everything would be fine. Right?

Don’t be so sure. Bias can creep into data-driven algorithms in subtle ways. A clear example of this was given in an online tutorial by NLP developer Robyn Speer, called “How to Make a Racist AI Without Really Trying.^(<a aria-label="noteref" href="#fn1" id="Cfn1">1</a>1)” In the tutorial, she set out to make a sentiment classifier that predicts whether a word is a positive word, like “great,” or a negative word, like “terrible.” Using these word-level predictions, this classifier could then be used to obtain a sentiment score for a document, for example, a review of a restaurant. For simplicity Speer obtained an overall sentiment score for the document by averaging the scores for each word. Thus the text “The chicken was juicy, tender, and delicious” would ideally get a high sentiment score under the model, while “The chicken was flabby and tasteless” would get a low sentiment score.

Speer began by obtaining features for her model, which in this case are *word embeddings—*feature vectors designed to represent the meaning of each word in the dictionary that is automatically obtained based on data. In this case the word embedding features were pretrained via an algorithm called GLoVE on a publicly available dataset of scraped webpages, the Common Crawl. She then obtained gold-standard sentiment labels (positive or negative) for around 7000 words from a linguistic resource available online and trained a logistic regression classifier on the now-labeled word embedding data.

Recall from [Chapter 4](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054.xhtml#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054), “Algorithms: the basic methods,” that the logistic regression model applies a linear function to an instance, producing a number called the log-odds (since this number will turn out to be the logarithm of the odds that the instance is positive). Logistic regression applies the logit transformation to the log-odds to produce a class probability between zero and one. Speer uses the log-odds, which is a number between negative infinity and positive infinity, as a sentiment score for a word, where larger negative numbers correspond to negative sentiment, and large positive numbers correspond to positive sentiment. We now have in hand a model that can take a piece of text as input and produce a sentiment score between plus and minus infinity that is more positive if the text expresses positive sentiment (“*The chicken was delicious*”), more negative if the text expresses negative sentiment (“*The chicken was horrible*”), and roughly zero if the text is neutral (“*The chicken was okay*.”)

According to Speer, the final step was to “behold the monstrosity that we have created!” After establishing that the model worked as intended, she applied it to the relatively neutral sentence “*Let’s go get Italian food*,” obtaining a substantially positive score of around 2.0. In contrast, “*Let’s go get Chinese food*” received a score of around 1.4, while “*Let’s go get Mexican food*” got a score of only 0.4. This is concerning—why should Mexican food be considered less positive than Italian food?

When applied to names, the system is even worse: “*My name is Emily*” (a stereotypically White name) gets a score of 2.2, while “*My name is Shaniqua*” (a stereotypically Black name) gets a score of –0.5. Further examining this result by applying the model to lists of stereotypical names belonging to several demographics, Speer found that the system gave highly positive average sentiment scores to stereotypically White names and negative sentiment scores to stereotypically Black names, with stereotypically Arab/Muslim names and Latinx names being somewhere in between these two extremes ([Fig. 7.4](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#f0025)).

![Fig. 7.4 Mean sentiment for stereotypical names of several demographic groups, with 95% confidence intervals. The nonzero end of each bar indicates the mean, and the black bars indicate the confidence intervals. Figure due to Robyn Speer, used with permission. Credit: Robyn Speer](images/F00008Xf07-04-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 7.4](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#Bf0025) Mean sentiment for stereotypical names of several demographic groups, with 95% confidence intervals. The nonzero end of each bar indicates the mean, and the black bars indicate the confidence intervals. Figure due to Robyn Speer, used with permission. Credit: Robyn Speer

We can all agree that the behavior of this system is hurtful and offensive. Worse, if this system were used to analyze resumes to make hiring recommendations, for example, it could easily introduce a systematic bias due to the applicants’ names. One way that this might happen is that the sentiment scores produced by the model could flag an applicant with a stereotypically Black name as having a negative attitude, and hence less employable, based on their name alone. Discrimination in hiring based on race or ethnicity is illegal in most countries, which could put the company that used this model in hot water with the law.

What went wrong here? Nothing that was done in designing this model was nefarious or in favor of one demographic group or another. Every decision made was an apparently innocuous step down the “path of least resistance” toward getting a model up and running. There were no sensitive demographic features like gender or race in the inputs to the classifier. Features were obtained via a popular model that was pretrained on a widely used dataset that is intended to be a typical and representative internet corpus. Yet, the behavior of the system is abhorrent.

We can start to figure out the likely reason behind the issue by noticing that the system has essentially replicated negative stereotypes that are unfortunately pervasive. The word embedding features were obtained based on a corpus of scraped webpages, the Common Crawl, and those webpages likely contain a substantial number of racist sentiments that were expressed by the people who made them. The word embeddings were influenced by those harmful statements in the corpus, which led the sentiment classifier to reflect those harmful statements in its predictions. In other words, bias in our society crept into the data and thus into the system. Even though the Common Crawl dataset was created by a nonprofit organization, with the intention of democratizing internet data for the public benefit, it still ended up leading a model that was trained on it to exhibit harmful behavior. This example shows that even with good intentions we can easily build AI systems that can do great harm unless we are extremely careful and diligent. There is no magic bullet to prevent this. It requires vigilance at every step of the model development process, and indeed, the entire life cycle of the model (as illustrated in [Chapter 1](#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029.xhtml#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029), “What’s it all about?,” [Fig. 1.4](#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029.xhtml#f0025)).

Having seen a concrete example, we can now delve into some of the common sources of bias that impact AI systems.

 

#### Data Encodes Societal Prejudices

As we saw in the sentiment analysis example shown earlier, prejudice in our society can be encoded in the data that is used to train a machine learning model. Text data created by users may contain the full spectrum of human views and experiences, including potentially problematic content. Social media data is frequently rife with racism, sexism, and every other kind of hate, whether it is explicitly stated or present as hidden subtext. We must be cautious about letting data from such platforms determine a model’s understanding of reality.

 

#### Data Encodes Societal (Dis)Advantages

Users’ prejudicial views and statements are the most visible way that discriminatory bias appears in data, but this barely scratches the surface of how such bias can impact the real world, thus impacting data and the algorithms trained on data. Real-world patterns of systemic and structural bias systematically advantage individuals from some demographic groups while disadvantaging others. When we look at any metric of “success” or “failure” or “merit” or “risk” based on historical data, systemic bias is frequently “baked in” to the recorded outcomes for the individuals in the dataset. Predictions of whether individuals will be successful are often used as a proxy for a decision on those individuals. For example, in credit scoring a prediction on whether an individual will repay a loan may be used as a proxy for the decision of whether to offer that person a loan. If systemic bias has impacted, for example, the ability of individuals to repay their loans, then this will be reflected in the training data for a classifier that aims to predict whether individuals will repay their loans and is used to make (or inform) a decision on whether to award a loan. Thus the overall system may make biased decisions, systematically discriminating against women in the loan offers made.

In the case of college admissions, studies have shown that individuals belonging to minoritized groups are disproportionately impacted by challenges of poverty and racism that impact academic performance such as chronic stress, access to healthcare, micro-aggressions, stereotype threat, and belongingness uncertainty. Similarly, students who identify as LGBTQ+ (lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and other marginalized gender identities) and especially nonbinary, transgender, and gender-nonconforming disproportionately suffer from discrimination, bullying, self-harm, and the additional burden of having to conceal their identities. A survey of transgender and gender nonconfirming people found that the bullying and discrimination was worst for people of color, and especially Black people.

In her book “Bandwidth Recovery,” author, professor, and faculty administrator and leader Cia Verschelden characterizes these challenges as a tax on the “cognitive bandwidth” of students that makes it difficult for them to perform to their full academic ability and that disproportionally impacts disadvantaged groups. A classifier that is trained to predict academic performance, and is used for college admissions decisions, would “bake in” these disadvantages and hence perpetuate patterns of systemic inequality in those decisions. Similar arguments can be made about machine learning models in other domains where systemic bias impacts historical outcomes that are used as proxies for decisions (e.g., in criminal justice risk assessment models for bail and sentencing decisions where inequities in policing practices impact recorded crime data, such as disparities in arrest rates for drug offenses between Black and White populations in the United States, despite both groups using illicit drugs at similar rates).

 

#### Less Data for Minorities

By definition minority groups occupy a smaller percentage of the population than the majority group. Machine learning algorithms typically have one term in the objective function for each data point, which frequently corresponds to one individual. If a dataset collects data from each group proportionately, there will be fewer terms in the objective function for minority groups. This effectively means that the learning algorithm “cares less” about those groups unless an intervention such as cost-sensitive classification is performed. This could harm the predictive accuracy of a machine learning model for smaller demographics.

 

#### Sampling Bias

Since we usually do not have access to data from every person, the training data for a machine learning model typically corresponds to a subset of the target population rather than to the entire population. If the dataset that is collected does not accurately represent the population of interest, the results of any analysis or machine learning model will be biased, supposing we do not perform an appropriate statistical correction for this issue. If the data sampling procedure does not randomly collect data from each member of a population with equal probability but tends to disproportionately include some individuals or groups, the resulting error is called *sampling bias*. Avoiding this issue is not straightforward.

Consider telephone surveys. In the early years after the first commercial telephone services were created in the late 1800s, only wealthy households had telephones. Even supposing that there was no *response bias*, a telephone survey, a political opinion poll, would have only considered the opinions of the wealthiest segment of society. We can compare this situation to the present day where mobile-only households without landlines are increasingly common. Traditional landline-only phone surveys would miss mobile-only households, and surveys of both landline and mobile phone populations would miss subpopulations that have neither device (e.g., the unhoused population).

The use of smartphones to collect data will always lead to a *coverage bias* in which only data from smartphone users is included. If a dataset were collected based on smartphone data, it would systematically neglect populations that are less likely to own smartphones, such as the unhoused and older adults. Similarly, if a dataset containing location data and movement patterns were collected based on data from automobiles, it would neglect the populations of pedestrians and cyclists, small children, and older adults.

 

### Intentional Prejudice: Digital Redlining and Masking

While most AI bias issues occur unintentionally, it is conceivable that a malicious actor could deliberately create an AI system that exhibits discriminatory bias, perhaps to implement their prejudiced views (which they may hold as factual), to intentionally advantage one demographic group or disadvantage another, or in pursuit of profit at the deliberate expense of fairness. This practice has been called *digital redlining*, with reference to the term “*redlining*” that describes the intentional withholding of products and services such as loans, housing, insurance, and grocery stores to neighborhoods where minoritized groups primary live and that were deemed risky or unworthy of investment. Since it is easy to unintentionally make a machine learning system that exhibits discriminatory behavior, it would be straightforward to intentionally build a discriminatory machine learning system “accidentally on purpose” while feigning innocence; this is called *masking*.

A real-world case of digital redlining happened in the late 1970s and early 1980s with the admissions process at St. George’s Hospital Medical School in London, England. A computer program was written by a staff member to assist in screening applicants for admissions interviews. The program was manually modified to match the way that the staff were making admissions decisions, and by 1979, it had 90%–95% correlation with the decisions made by the selection panel. Following the existing practices at the school, the algorithm explicitly reduced the chance of an interview for women and members of racial minority groups. Since the application form did not include a question on race, candidates’ race attributes were estimated based on their surname and place of birth. The institution was found guilty by the Commission for Racial Equality of racial and sexual discrimination in its admissions process. The editors of the *British Medical Journal* called this incident a “blot on the profession.”

 

#### Proxy Variables

A common strategy to combat discriminatory bias in a machine learning system is to remove sensitive demographic attributes (sometimes called *protected attributes*, or *sensitive attributes*) such as gender, race, age, ethnicity, LGBT status, national origin, and disability from the system. Ideally, this would prevent a machine learning model from learning problematic associations between protected attributes and labels; it can no longer associate a positive or a negative weight with membership in a particular demographic. This approach is sometimes called *fairness through unawareness* ([Fig. 7.5](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#f0030)).

![Fig. 7.5 The “fairness through unawareness” strategy removes sensitive protected attributes, e.g., gender or race. However, proxy variables (e.g., zip code) may remain. Credit: James Foulds](images/F00008Xf07-05-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 7.5](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#Bf0030) The “fairness through unawareness” strategy removes sensitive protected attributes, e.g., gender or race. However, proxy variables (e.g., zip code) may remain. Credit: James Foulds

However, this is generally insufficient for ensuring fair behavior. The problem is that even if the protected attributes were removed, other attributes may be correlated with them and thus act as proxies for those attributes. The machine learning algorithm will thereby still have indirect access to the protected attributes via these *proxy variables*.

For instance, the neighborhood (or zip code) that an individual lives in is frequently highly correlated with their race due to housing segregation. In the United States this situation arose due to policies and practices such as the aforementioned redlining, which was codified into laws in the 1930s and 1940s (e.g., the National Housing Act of 1934 and the 1944 GI bill), with laws dismantling and prohibiting redlining introduced in the 1960s and 1970s (e.g., the Fair Housing Act passed in 1968), against the backdrop of so-called Jim Crow segregation policies from the 1870s up until 1965. Although redlining is now illegal, US housing remains highly racially segregated. The situation is perpetuated by phenomena such as “*White flight*,” where White people tend to leave neighborhoods as more people of color begin to live there, and *gentrification*, where an influx of wealthier residents increases the cost of living in a neighborhood, driving out the less-wealthy residents.

Geography can even be associated with gender. The city of San Jose, California, for example, is sometimes colloquially called “Man Jose” because of a higher-than-normal proportion of men vs women, at least among those in the single population in their 20 s and 30 s, due to the male-dominated tech industry boom in the San Francisco Bay Area. In China in 2015, the final year of the country’s one-child policy, 116 boys were born for every 100 girls. Age also has a geographic association, due in part to popularity of retirement destinations. As of 2020, Florida and Maine have more than 21% of residents aged 65 and older, while Utah has less than 12%. Geographic information that is given to a classifier could hence act as a proxy for race, gender, age, or other protected categories, enabling it to learn to encode patterns of discriminatory bias.

While it may be possible to remove some obvious proxy attributes such as neighborhood or zip code, protected attributes can have complex interactions with many other measurable characteristics. If we were to remove any attribute that had any association with a protected attribute, we may have few, if any, attributes remaining to use for prediction.

Proxy variables are a convenient weapon for the purposes of masking since a would-be masker could leave these variables to do their discriminatory damage in a subtle way while claiming to have addressed AI bias through deleting the protected demographic attributes. If the protected attributes were fully deleted from all company databases, or never recorded at all—perhaps with the stated goal of preventing bias—it may become difficult to audit the system for discriminatory bias. It is conceivable that this situation could be brought about intentionally to mask the bias in a machine learning system.

 

### Nontechnical Interventions

Now that we’ve learned about how bias and unfairness can arise in machine learning systems, the natural question is what to do about it. Much of the research on this topic has centered around technical interventions to machine learning algorithms that aim to prevent them from learning harmful patterns. However, AI bias is not a purely technical problem but a complex socio-technical-legal problem at the interface between AI algorithms, humans that are impacted by AI algorithms, social processes that impact our society and hence our data, ethical values and norms, the law, and politics. To think that this issue can simply be solved by technical means alone would be naïve. To truly address AI bias and its implications, we need to consider its nontechnical, human-centered aspects and implement nontechnical interventions as well as technical ones.

 

#### Involving Stakeholders in the Design of Machine Learning Systems

In the media and in the public consciousness artificial intelligence is often seen as neutral and objective due to its automated nature. This is not the case. Machine learning systems are trained automatically to fit a dataset, but as we have seen in this book, much of the design process is not automated. There are many decisions that a human must make from collecting and preprocessing the data, determining the class labels, selecting algorithms, hyperparameters, and objective functions, writing code, evaluating and improving the system, and making fairness interventions. These decisions implement the values and goals of the developers. Typically, all the decisions that go into designing a machine learning system are made by data scientists, engineers, and their managers. It is unlikely that the members of such a team adequately represent the interests of the populations that the system will impact. In this scenario, the team may not be capable of ensuring that risks including bias and unfair discrimination would be adequately addressed, no matter how well intentioned they may be.

As a solution to this type of issue, the field of human-centered computing has advanced the notion of *participatory design*, a.k.a. *codesign*, in which stakeholders are engaged in design processes to ensure that their needs are met by the system. In a machine learning context, it would be wise to invite stakeholders back to monitor the behavior of the system periodically after deployment as the model and/or its data and sociotechnical context may change over time.

 

#### Diversity and Representation in Technology

If machine learning development teams were diverse and represented a variety of backgrounds, they would be more likely to notice issues such as algorithmic bias. Unfortunately, as is well known, there is a lack of women and minoritized groups in the technology field, including AI. This is far from inevitable, as it was not always the case. Ada Lovelace wrote the first published computer program, an algorithm for Charles Babbage’s hypothetical computer, the Analytical Engine, that computes Bernoulli numbers. In the early days of computing, programming, data entry, and calculation were considered “secretarial” tasks done primarily by women. It was mainly women, who were themselves called “computers,” who maintained systems for targeting bombs during World War II. In the 1940s, a team of human computers who were Black women, led by Dorothy Vaughn, performed vital calculations for the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA), the predecessor of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), as famously depicted in the 2016 film Hidden Figures. As computers became electronic, human computers were hired as programmers, and so the six first programmers of the first general-purpose programmable electronic computer, ENIAC, completed in 1945, were all women. The important work done by human computers was generally overlooked and undercompensated and only became valued once computer programming turned into a male-dominated field. The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence in 1956, which launched AI as an academic field, was attended only by men.

The demographic disparities in AI, the technology industry, and science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) in general arise at multiple stages of the pipeline. For example, relatively few US women receive STEM degrees, and these are primarily in the physical and life sciences while men’s are primarily in engineering. Women who receive STEM degrees are less likely to work in STEM jobs than men who receive those degrees. Possible factors that experts have cited include a lack of role models, stereotyping, a lack of family-oriented flexibility, intentional exclusion, and unintentional “like-me bias.” A report by the US Department of Commerce pointed to the gender disparity in technology as an untapped opportunity to strengthen the nation’s economic competitiveness globally. While solutions are not straightforward, in your future career when you are involved in hiring decisions *you* will have an opportunity to make a difference.

 

#### Transparency in AI-Based Decision Making

When an AI system makes decisions that severely affect people’s lives, it’s crucial that the decision-making process is transparent so the impacted individuals can learn why the decisions were made, how they were made, and with what data. Without transparency, when the system gets it wrong the harmed parties can have no recourse to appeal against the decision and set things right. Unfortunately, statistical and machine learning systems are all too frequently considered inscrutable black boxes that are too complicated to explain yet are somehow to be trusted completely as “objective,” “neutral,” and “fair,” thereby dismissing all appeals. The humans who would appeal their decisions are frequently held to a higher standard of evidentiary proof than the algorithms are.

In one terrifying example, a Middle School teacher in Washington, D.C., Sarah Wysocki, was unjustly fired by an algorithm. Under pressure to turn around underperforming schools, the city had implemented a teacher assessment tool called IMPACT. The tool included a sophisticated metric called “value-added,” which aimed to measure the extent to which a teacher contributed “value” to students’ learning based on standardized test scores. Teachers with the lowest “value-added” scores were fired, regardless of how well they were performing on other metrics or in student evaluations, and this is what happened to Wysocki. Conversely, high-scoring teachers received bonuses.

However, as revealed in investigations by *USA Today* and the *Washington Post*, this situation led many schools in the district to cheat on behalf of their students, changing incorrect answers in standardized tests to correct ones to artificially inflate the scores. Wysocki alleges that the elementary school that many of her students had attended the previous year had engaged in this practice. Those students had previously been scored as “advanced reading level,” yet they came into her classroom struggling to read at all. Wysocki had stellar student evaluations, high scores on all other metrics, and the backing of her principal, who described her as “creative,” “visionary,” and “motivating.” The progress in reading ability her students were making had been celebrated within the school. But when she appealed her firing, her claims were dismissed, with the board determining that investigating claims of cheating was beyond the scope of the panel. Within days of her firing, Wysocki was hired by a school in nearby Virginia, one that was well resourced and did not fire teachers based on test scores. A poor school’s loss of a good teacher was a wealthy school’s gain.

In response to transparency issues the field of *explainable AI* has arisen, which aims to develop techniques for looking inside machine learning “black boxes” to explain the models and their decisions to users in an understandable way. One popular strategy, called *knowledge distillation*, is to fit a simple and understandable model (e.g., a linear model or a decision tree) to the predictions of the complicated model of interest (e.g., a deep neural network), thereby capturing the essence of its behavior in a simpler form. Research on explainable AI has been spurred in part by the EU’s data privacy law, the GDPR. Among other provisions, the GDPR requires businesses that use personal user data for decision making to explain those decisions at the users’ request, although scholars have debated whether this amounts to a “right to explanation” in the sense of explainable AI. In the United States, some states have adopted similar laws, such as the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA).

 

#### Development of Responsible AI Standards and Best Practices

One barrier to the implementation of ethical and responsible AI practices is a lack of understanding by machine learning practitioners on what ethical standards they—and the systems they are building— should aim to uphold and what the best practices are. In a step in the right direction, numerous organizations spanning government, industry, and professional societies have published documents outlining ethical AI principles that they advocate, housed within the context of cohesive ethical frameworks. These frameworks aim to provide guidelines for practitioners to follow. Organizations that have released ethical AI frameworks include Microsoft, Google, IBM, the European Commission, UNESCO, the White House, the ACM, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the US Department of Defense (DoD), and the NIST. Fairness, accountability, and transparency are included as principles to uphold in most of these frameworks, in addition to other ethical principles such as privacy and nonmaleficence (“doing no harm”).

We began this chapter with an overview of the responsible AI principles advanced by the ACM. Note, however, that the practice of producing ethical and responsible AI guidelines has been criticized as insufficient, since without external enforcement or legal requirement, the guidelines do little to ensure that the responsible AI principles will actually be upheld by a company while potentially fending off justified scrutiny or criticism.

 

#### Laws to Enforce Ethical Standards

While ethical frameworks and guidelines may help machine learning engineers understand what to strive for, they are typically nonbinding and not enforced. The need for laws to ensure ethical and responsible AI practices is becoming increasingly urgent. Nowhere is the gap between guideline and law more plainly stark than the 2022 Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights from the Biden administration White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy. The Blueprint lays out five key principles to guide AI development, deployment, and maintenance: *safe and effective systems*, *algorithmic discrimination protections*, *data privacy*, *notice and explanation*, and, finally, *human alternatives*, *consideration*, *and fallback*. However, it is not legally binding. The Biden administration followed up the Blueprint with the 2023 Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence, which includes a number of directives, many of which direct government agencies to perform studies on trustworthy AI. As such, although the Executive Order has little in the way of enforceable regulation or requirements that extend beyond the federal government, it will likely help to pave the way for future legislation, along with the Blueprint.

Apart from the Executive Order, as of early 2024 there were no US federal laws that specifically regulate AI. Although AI-specific laws would be preferable, general antidiscrimination laws such as Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the 1968 Fair Housing Act (FHA), and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990 can still be applicable to AI-based decision making in certain contexts such as employment and housing discrimination.

Efforts to regulate AI generally run into pushbacks from industry and from politicians aligned with industry. One of the authors of this textbook (Foulds) gave both oral and written testimony in support of an AI ethics bill in the state of Maryland in 2021 and 2023. The 2021 bill would have required algorithmic decision-making systems procured by the State to follow ethical principles including fairness and transparency and to be subject to evaluation regarding adherence to the principles. Testimony opposing the bill was given by representatives of the Maryland Tech Council (a technology industry trade organization) and Amazon, which spoke in support of AI ethics as a general principle but warned of stifling innovation and profit and wanted a (pro-industry) seat at the table; these statements helped to kill the bill. A follow-up bill was introduced in 2023 that would merely secure funds to set up a commission to investigate these types of issues and make recommendations on them. There were several favorable testimonies in support of the bill, and no testimonies were given against it. However, it still failed to become law. Efforts to get a similar bill passed continue. This example illustrates how despite the widespread support for AI ethics spanning industry and government, achieving corresponding legislation with real teeth will require strong and sustained advocacy.

 

### The Main Paradigms of Fair AI/Data Mining

Nontechnical AI fairness interventions are a crucial part of the process that must not be neglected. Since this is a technical book we will now focus our attention on technological interventions. These techniques are not a magic bullet and they do not avoid the need for difficult conversations and effortful collaborations between corporate representatives and impacted stakeholders. They do not shield a firm from critique once a system is deployed. But if used correctly, they can improve the fairness properties of a machine learning system, perhaps as easily as through a simple application programming interface (*API*) library call.

To implement fairness in an AI system, we need to specify what we mean by “fairness” in a concrete, mathematical way that can be implemented in a computer. This is difficult because fairness is a complex, abstract, sociotechnical construct. Nobody knows quite what it means, and any two people may have wildly different conceptions of it. Context is also important, as what might be considered “fair” in one scenario may be considered “unfair” in another. Nevertheless, we proceed. Typically we impose on our AI system a mathematical “*fairness definition*” that aims to ensure some corresponding idealized notion of fairness. At a very high level, the main approaches to defining and implementing fairness are:

*   • *Fairness metrics*, which aim to quantify fairness or bias with some function. In this approach, the learning algorithm aims to get a good “fairness score” according to the chosen fairness metric, while still predicting well.
*   • *Fair representation learning*, where we produce a new representation of the data that removes all association with “protected attributes” such as gender, race, age, etc., while capturing all other relevant information.
*   • *Causal fairness*, where we model the causal structure of the problem domain and achieve causal properties that are deemed fair. This approach aims to reckon with the causal nature that is often behind fairness and bias issues.

We can inject fairness into a machine learning model at different stages of the processing pipeline, such as:

*   • *Preprocessing:* Make the data “fair” before applying your analysis. For example, one could upsample minority groups to give them greater representation in the dataset or correct sampling errors that skewed the data in an unfair way. Fair representation learning can be understood as an implementation of this strategy, in that a fair representation is constructed before giving the processed data to a downstream model.
*   • *Inprocessing:* Ensure fairness during the learning process. We can add a “*fairness penalty*” to the model’s objective function or constrain the learning algorithm to achieve a minimum level of fairness. Adversarial learning approaches to debiasing a model based on GANs and VAEs (discussed in [Chapter 11](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121), “Advanced deep learning methods”) can sometimes be understood as inprocessing techniques, unless they are used for the purposes of fair representation learning.
*   • *Postprocessing:* Correct fairness issues in the outputs of the model, after training. One such approach is to shift the per-group classification thresholds to correct for how each demographic group is treated by the model.

As we discussed, the simple preprocessing approach of deleting the protected attributes so that the classifier cannot use them, sometimes called *fairness through unawareness* or *anticlassification*, is generally insufficient. This strategy prevents *disparate treatment*, that is, explicit discrimination by treating individuals from different protected groups differently through different criteria or standards. However, it does not prevent *disparate impact*, that is, disparity in the outcomes. Even without access to the protected attributes, there are likely to be other attributes that are correlated with the protected attributes and the class labels, which allow the model to discriminate by proxy (“*proxy variables*”). We require more sophisticated solutions.

 

#### Fairness Metrics

Based on a machine learning model’s behavior, a *fairness metric* produces a score that assesses the extent to which the model is fair or unfair (e.g., if it exhibits a bias toward or against a particular demographic). The use of fairness metrics is the dominant approach to implementing fair AI, as they allow us to flexibly operationalize our desired fairness goals. Here, we must specify a function that quantifies how fair (or unfair) a machine learning model is. Let’s call the fairness metric function *F*(*θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi89.png), where *θ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi90.png) is the model’s parameters, and we are implicitly considering the data used to estimate the model’s fairness behavior as another input. For now, let’s assume that we are performing classification. To learn a classifier that respects the fairness metric, we can borrow and adapt a typical machine learning formulation, *regularized empirical risk minimization*:

$\\underset{\\theta}{argmin}\\left\\lbrack {\\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}{L(f\_{i}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i};\\theta),y\_{i})} + \\lambda R\\left( \\theta \\right)} \\right\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">argmin</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#955;</mml:mi><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.6)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi91.png)(7.6) 

where *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi92.png) is the number of data points, *L*<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi93.png) is a *loss function* that measures how accurate our machine learning model is, *x*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi94.png) and *y*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi95.png) are the attributes and class label for instance *i*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi96.png), respectively. Here, *R*(*θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi97.png) is a *regularization* penalty term that penalizes model complexity to reduce overfitting, and *λ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#955;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi98.png) is a user-adjustable weight hyperparameter that adjusts the importance of the regularization penalty vs the loss function, allowing control on the trade-off between over- and underfitting. We will discuss this formulation further in [Chapter 10](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X), “Deep learning: fundamentals.” We can enforce fairness during learning (an inprocessing approach) by plugging in our fairness metric *F*(*θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi99.png) into the objective function in a similar manner to a regularizer:

$\\underset{\\theta}{argmin}\\left\\lbrack {\\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}{L(f\_{i}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i};\\theta),y\_{i})} + \\lambda F\\left( \\theta \\right)} \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">argmin</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#955;</mml:mi><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.7)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi100.png)(7.7) 

In this formulation, we sometimes refer to *F*(*θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi101.png) as a *fairness penalty*. The weight hyperparameter *λ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#955;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi102.png) now controls the tradeoff between fairness and predictive performance, as measured by the loss function. Of course, one could include a regularization penalty *R*(*θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi103.png) in this formulation as well. An alternative approach is to use a constraint on *F*(*θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi104.png) instead of a penalty—find the most accurate model (according to the loss function) within the constraint that *F*(*θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi105.png) does not exceed a target threshold *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi106.png):

$\\underset{\\theta}{argmin}\\left\\lbrack {\\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}{L(f\_{i}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i};\\theta),y\_{i})},s.t.F\\left( \\theta \\right) < \\epsilon} \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">argmin</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#60;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.8)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi107.png)(7.8) 

Let’s look at some of the options for fairness metrics.

*Parity-based metrics* aim to ensure that different demographic groups are treated similarly by the algorithm. The term usually refers to ensuring parity in the assignment of class labels to each demographic, for example, women being assigned the “credit-worthy” class label at the same proportion as men are, thus being equally likely to be recommended by the algorithm to receive an offer of a loan as men. If we assume that the different demographics are equally capable, this is an intuitive notion of fairness. It is hence widely used. Nevertheless, parity-based metrics have received a lot of criticism in the academic literature, including concerns that they might be harmful if the demographics are not actually equally capable, and that they do not prevent certain harms and abuses.

There are several ways that parity-based metrics have been implemented mathematically. One version, called *demographic parity*, or sometimes *statistical parity*, put forward (and criticized) by Cynthia Dwork and colleagues, penalizes differences in class probabilities between different demographic groups:

$F\\left( \\theta \\right) = \\sum\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathbf{Y}}\\left| {P{(\\left. \\widehat{y} \\middle| s = 1 \\right.)} - P{(\\left. \\widehat{y} \\middle| s = 0 \\right.)}} \\right|,$<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic">&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic">&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width=".25em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo>|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.9)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi108.png)(7.9) 

where *ŷ* ∈ *Y*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mi>Y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi109.png)is the class label (e.g., creditworthiness) predicted by the model and *s*<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi110.png) is a binary protected attribute (e.g., gender).^(<a aria-label="noteref" href="#fn2" id="Cfn2">2</a>2) We can see that this fairness metric is minimized in the ideal situation where parity is achieved:

*P*(*ŷ*|*s*\=1) = *P*(*ŷ*|*s*\=0), ∀*ŷ* ∈ *Y*.<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8704;</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mspace width=".25em"/><mml:mi>Y</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.10)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi111.png)(7.10) 

Alternatively, instead of comparing the class probability distributions by computing their differences (i.e., subtraction), we can compare them by taking ratios (i.e., division). This approach is motivated by a US legal guideline for identifying discrimination. The guideline, called the *80% rule* or the *four-fifths rule*, was originally created for determining whether discriminatory practices meet a legal threshold for adverse or disparate impact in employment contexts. Disparate impact occurs when the same policies apply to everyone (e.g., the same set of hiring criteria are used, or the same classifier is applied), but the policies impact different groups substantially differently overall. This can occur even if the policies do not explicitly use the demographic membership in the decision-making process. The guidelines, from the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), in C.F.R. 29.1607, state that:

*A selection rate for any race, sex, or ethnic group which is less than four-fifths (or 80%) of the rate for the group with the highest rate will generally be regarded by the Federal enforcement agencies as evidence of adverse impact, while a greater than four-fifths rate will generally not be regarded by Federal enforcement agencies as evidence of adverse impact*.

Stated in mathematical terms, the 80% rule identifies that disparate impact has occurred when:

*P*(*ŷ*\=1|*s*\=1) < 0.8 × *P*(*ŷ*\=1|*s*\=0).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#60;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.8</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.11)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi112.png)(7.11) 

Here, the class label is assumed to be binary and *ŷ* = 1<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi113.png) is the positive outcome, that is, being deemed creditworthy or hired for a job. For example, suppose that job candidates from Group 0 are hired at a rate of 75% while candidates from Group 1 are hired at a rate of 100% ([Fig. 7.6](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#f0035)). Since 0.75 is less than 0.8 ×<mml:math><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi114.png) 1.0, there is evidence of disparate impact in this scenario according to the 80% rule.

![Fig. 7.6 A scenario where there is evidence of disparate impact according to the 80% rule. Credit: James Foulds](images/F00008Xf07-06-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 7.6](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#Bf0035) A scenario where there is evidence of disparate impact according to the 80% rule. Credit: James Foulds

We assumed in the previous equation that s = 0 was the “advantaged” group with a higher acceptance rate. To make it symmetrical, we need to rearrange terms to convert it to a ratio and also consider its reciprocal. Then disparate impact has occurred when

$\\min\\left( {\\frac{P{(\\left. \\widehat{y} = 1 \\middle| s = 1 \\right.)}}{P{(\\left. \\widehat{y} = 1 \\middle| s = 0 \\right.)}},\\frac{P{(\\left. \\widehat{y} = 1 \\middle| s = 0 \\right.)}}{P{(\\left. \\widehat{y} = 1 \\middle| s = 1 \\right.)}}} \\right) < 0.8.$<mml:math><mml:mi>min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#60;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.8</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.12)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi115.png)(7.12) 

In an AI fairness context, we can generalize this to a numeric measurement on the degree of fairness in the system by measuring the ratio in the previous equation rather than applying a fixed threshold criterion to it:

$\\mathbf{F}\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right) = \\min\\left( {\\frac{P{(\\left. \\widehat{y} = 1 \\middle| s = 1 \\right.)}}{P{(\\left. \\widehat{y} = 1 \\middle| s = 0 \\right.)}},\\frac{P{(\\left. \\widehat{y} = 1 \\middle| s = 0 \\right.)}}{P{(\\left. \\widehat{y} = 1 \\middle| s = 1 \\right.)}}} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">F</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.13)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi116.png)(7.13) 

Parity-based approaches to fairness are appropriate in scenarios where the differences in outcome/class label distributions in the dataset are due to unfair reasons, such as unfair societal processes like racism or sexism, prejudice on behalf of human annotators that systematically bias the labeling process, or other issues with the data that have harmful and unequal impact across protected demographics such as toxic language in social media, unrepresentative datasets, and so on. They are also valuable when the goal is to promote equality (understood as an intrinsically desirable outcome), perform affirmative action, mitigate harmful stereotypes, increase diversity in the pool of selected individuals, or prevent legal liability under the EEOC guidelines. Achieving these goals may come at the cost of predictive accuracy but if the labels are considered unfair anyway then we may be willing to accept some degree of trade-off between accuracy and fairness.

On the other hand, in scenarios where demographic differences in the distribution of labels in the data are accurate, legitimate, and occur for reasons that are considered justifiable, then parity-based metrics would not be appropriate. In such scenarios, where both society and data are considered to be on a level playing field, a parity-based fairness intervention would unnecessarily skew the behavior of the AI system, with likely harm to prediction accuracy, and perhaps introducing a new fairness issue in the altered behavior of the system. If the dataset has disparity in the class labels, then achieving parity is incompatible with predicting the class labels accurately, that is, the “correct” classifier is ruled out. Another fairness definition, called *equalized odds*, avoids this issue. Instead of ensuring parity of the distribution of class labels between demographic groups, equalized odds ensures that the classifier has equal error rates between demographic groups:

*P*(*ŷ*\=1|*s*\=1,*y*) = *P*(*ŷ*\=1|*s*\=0,*y*), *y* ∈ {0,1}.<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0,1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.14)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi117.png)(7.14) 

Equalized odds reward accurate classification and prevent the system from only performing well for the majority demographic at the expense of minority groups. A relaxed version of this definition, called *equality of opportunity*, only enforces parity for the individuals belonging to the “deserving” class label. For example, the people who can truly pay back their loan (*y* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi118.png)) will have the same probability of being correctly classified as such individuals, regardless of their gender:

*P*(*ŷ*\=1|*s*\=1,*y*\=1) = *P*(*ŷ*\=1|*s*\=0,*y*\=1).<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.15)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi119.png)(7.15) 

While equalized odds and equality of opportunity are compatible with the “correct” classifier, they have another issue along the same lines—they may be incompatible with correctly calibrated probability estimates.
