In other words, when the classifier says that a particular instance has, say, an 80% chance of class *y* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi120.png), the actual class probability may be something else, for example, 60%. Here, although the classifier is both fair (according to the definition) and accurate (in terms of the binary classification accuracy percentage), achieving fairness has still come at a cost in terms of its predictive behavior. The practical impact is that we can no longer take its class probability estimates at face value. A lack of calibration can also be a fairness issue if the probabilities are calibrated for one demographic group but not another. A human decision maker may be more skeptical of the model’s predictions for the group that does not have calibration.

Another limitation of parity-based fairness methods is that they only ensure parity for the protected groups that are specified and not subgroups of them. This could potentially be exploited for deliberate harm, in a phenomenon known as *subset targeting* or *fairness gerrymandering*. Suppose, for instance, an AI system could allocate coupons for discounts at an expensive clothing store with an equal proportion to Black people and White people, yet only gave the coupons to those Black people who could not afford to shop at the store and thus would never use them. Parity-based fairness fails to prevent this injustice (at least when race is the only protected attribute).

A closely related issue occurs when subgroups at the intersection of several protected groups are unfairly impacted. In the 1976 employment discrimination lawsuit DeGraffenreid vs General Motors, plaintiffs alleged that General Motors’ seniority-based layoffs unfairly harmed Black women, who the company had never hired prior to 1964 and *all* of whom were fired under the policy. The company was able to successfully defend against the suit because the incident did not meet the standard of either race discrimination or sex/gender discrimination when these dimensions where considered alone, and Title VII law did not identify Black women (or any other intersecting subgroups of legally protected categories) as a group protected by law.

This case, and others like it, led legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw to coin and develop *intersectionality*, a theoretical framework for analyzing how injustices (and advantages) occur and are potentially magnified at the intersection of multiple protected dimensions including gender, race, nationality, sexual orientation, socioeconomic class, and disability. Intersectionality posits that these injustices occur because unfair societal processes, termed *systems of oppression*, interact in interlocking ways that affect the lived experience of individuals belonging to the intersection of multiple such protected attributes. Systems of oppression include sexism, racism, the prison-industrial complex, and the school-to-prison pipeline. To learn more, Crenshaw’s TED talk, available to watch on YouTube, is a good place to start.

*Subgroup fairness* is a fairness definition by computer scientist/theoretician Michael Kearns and colleagues that aims to address fairness gerrymandering. Suppose that there are multiple protected attributes, that is, **s**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi121.png) is vector-valued. Let *g*(**s**)<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi122.png) be an indicator function that selects a subgroup at an intersection of the protected groups, where *g*(**s**) = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi123.png) when an individual belongs to group *g*<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi124.png) and 0 otherwise. Suppose we have a collection *G*<mml:math><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi125.png) of such group indicators that we want to ensure fairness for Kearns et al. provide a parity-based version (*statistical parity subgroup fairness*) and a version that is similarly defined but instead focuses on false positive rates (*false positive subgroup fairness*). In the statistical parity (SP) version, the probability of the positive class (*y* = 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi126.png) for each subgroup *g*<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi127.png) must be similar to the overall positive class probability across the entire population. A classifier is set to satisfy *γ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi128.png)\- SP subgroup fairness if for every *g* ∈ *G*<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi129.png),

|*P*(*ŷ* = 1)−*P*(*ŷ*\=1|*g*(*s*)=1)| × *α*[*g*] ≤ *γ*.<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#945;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8804;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.16)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi130.png)(7.16) 

Here, there is a scaling factor *α*[*g*] = *P*(*g*(*s*)=1)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#945;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi131.png) that weights each group by its proportion of the population. In other words, large subgroups are considered important by the definition while small subgroups are considered unimportant and are likely to be ignored (since the metric is determined by the largest value of the equation over all of the subgroups). This is done to obtain provable generalization guarantees, ensuring that the value of the metric generalizes beyond the training set to the overall population. The idea behind this is that since there is not much data for the smaller subgroups, their counts would be noisy, but downweighting them means that these noisy counts will not destabilize the estimation of the metric.

On the other hand, the downside of this approach is that it explicitly disregards minority subgroups. This is problematic from the perspective of intersectionality theory, since minority groups are frequently the most harmed by racism and other such systems of oppression. Note that subgroup fairness was motivated by preventing fairness gerrymandering/subset targeting, not intersectionality. Another fairness definition, *differential fairness*, was designed by one of this book’s authors (Foulds) with the specific intention of being an intersectional definition of fairness. Differential fairness avoids the minority downweighting term and uses a ratio-based formulation that is reminiscent of the 80% rule. A mechanism *M*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi132.png) is said to be *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi133.png)\-differentially fair (DF) with respect to (*A*,*Θ*)<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi134.png) if for all *θ* ∈ *Θ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi135.png) with *x* ∼ *θ*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8764;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi136.png) and *y* ∈ Range(*M*)<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mtext>Range</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi137.png),

$e^{- \\epsilon} \\leq \\frac{P\_{M,\\theta}{(\\left. M\\left( x \\right) = y \\middle| s\_{i},\\theta \\right.)}}{P\_{M,\\theta}{(\\left. M\\left( x \\right) = y \\middle| s\_{j},\\theta \\right.)}} \\leq e^{\\epsilon}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>&#8804;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>&#8804;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.17)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi138.png)(7.17) 

Here, *s*[*i*], *s*[*j*] ∈ *A*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi139.png) are vectors of all protected attributes (e.g., gender, race, nationality), and *Θ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi140.png) is a set of distributions *θ*,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi141.png) which could plausibly generate each instance *x*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi142.png). Since the definition is inspired by differential privacy, we have used differential-privacy style notation, with *M*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi143.png) denoting the classifier, the output of which is a predicted class label *y*<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi144.png).

To make this somewhat scary equation concrete, let’s consider the following example, illustrated in [Fig. 7.7](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#f0040). Suppose that given an applicant’s score on a standardized test an applicant is hired if their test score is greater than a threshold *t*. Here, *t* = 10.5<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi145.png).

![Fig. 7.7 Group 0 (left) has a hiring rate of ¾, while Group 1 (right) has a hiring rate of 4/4. Since 0.75 < \\ 0.8 \\times 1Equation, there is evidence of disparate impact according to the 80% rule. Credit: James Foulds](images/F00008Xf07-07-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 7.7](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#Bf0040) Group 0 (left) has a hiring rate of ¾, while Group 1 (right) has a hiring rate of 4/4. We see from the largest value in the table (indicated in bold) that *ϵ* = 2.337<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#1013;</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.337</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi154.png). While this simple example only included one protected dimension (Group 1 vs Group 2), differential fairness is designed to be applied to scenarios where there are multiple protected dimensions to consider at once (e.g., gender, race, and nationality).

Due to its relationship with differential privacy, differential fairness provides a privacy guarantee—the class label assigned by the model will not reveal much information about the protected attributes if the definition holds (i.e., *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi155.png) is small). More concretely, consider a scenario where the users’ data is held on a private server and a bank, assumed untrustworthy, is told only the output of a classifier that predicts whether an individual will repay a loan. The privacy guarantee ensures that, for example, if the individual is predicted to repay the loan the bank cannot conclude that the user is probably White and male.

Differential fairness has a generalization guarantee but it is weaker than the one for subgroup fairness; the fairness parameter *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi156.png) estimated from the training data will generalize to the overall population as long as there is enough data for each intersectional subgroup. The differing goals of subgroup fairness and differential fairness led to the differing treatment of small subgroups in the two metrics. Subgroup fairness aims to prevent any attempt to gerrymander the fairness behavior of the algorithm, so it assumes that there are many dimensions and prioritizes generalization over ensuring that minority subgroups are protected. Differential fairness aims to ensure an intersectional conception of fairness, so it prioritizes minority subgroups over generalization. The number of protected dimensions, and hence the number of subgroups, need not be so large since the goal is to have a more nuanced understanding of fairness beyond considering top-level protected groups separately (e.g., women, Black people). Intersectionality was originally inspired by harms that occur at the intersection of two protected attributes (gender, race). From an intersectional perspective, even just the consideration of these two dimensions is already an improvement over the status quo.

Alternatively, the *multicalibration* fairness metric ensures that the prediction probabilities are calibrated for all the protected subgroups of interest. We discussed calibration earlier as a limitation of the equalized odds fairness definition; multicalibration aims to address this particular issue for overlapping subgroups.

A different approach to solving the fairness gerrymandering issue is to remove the notion of groups from the fairness definition entirely and focus on individuals directly. *Individual fairness*, proposed by Cynthia Dwork and colleagues, embodies the ideal that similar individuals should be treated similarly by the algorithm by having similar class probabilities. Encoding this mathematically results in the following definition. Suppose we have a distance measure *d*(*x*,*y*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi157.png) between pairs of data points *x*, *y*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi158.png) (e.g., Euclidean distance) and a distance measure between pairs of probability distributions over class labels *D*(*μ*[*x*],*μ*[*y*])<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi159.png), for example, Jensen-Shannon divergence. We assume that our classifier of interest *M*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi160.png) is a probabilistic classifier such as logistic regression, which randomly assigns a class label to each instance *x*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi161.png) according to the class probabilities it outputs. The individual fairness criterion holds if similar data points have similar outcome probabilities, that is,

*D*(*M*(*x*),*M*(*y*)) ≤ *d*(*x*,*y*).<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8804;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (7.18)

![Equation](images/F00008Xsi162.png)(7.18) 

This constraint can be made into a fairness penalty by measuring the extent to which the inequality is violated, instead of rigidly enforcing the equality. A key challenge in implementing individual fairness in practice is that we need to define the distance between individuals in a way that is fair, which is far from straightforward. Perhaps a subset of the features that are deemed to be “fair” could be used for this measurement. The chosen features would have to accurately represent the “deservingness” of the individuals (since otherwise two “similar” individuals should not necessarily get similar class probabilities) while not encoding demographic proxies.

 

#### Incompatibility Between Fairness Definitions

We have considered several fairness definitions, each of which is frequently a desirable property for the behavior of an AI system. It would be wonderful if we could design our AI system to satisfy all of these definitions simultaneously, while also accurately predicting the class labels and producing calibrated probability estimates. Unfortunately, as you might expect, this is not always possible. There are mathematical theorems proving that many of these fairness definitions are in some cases incompatible with each other and/or with predictive accuracy or calibration. Such incompatibilities often arise when the protected demographics have different *base rates* (probabilities of the class labels) and/or when *perfect prediction* (the model assigning each data point to its correct class with class probabilities that are certain) is not possible. From a practical perspective, the upshot is that when we design a fair machine learning system, we must work with stakeholders to decide on the appropriate fairness metric(s) and the appropriate balance with predictive performance.

 

#### Fair Representation Learning

Instead of defining and measuring fairness by quantifying it with some function, another approach is to preprocess the data by replacing all of the features with embeddings in which all associations and correlations with the protected attributes are excised while otherwise retaining as much information in the embeddings as possible. In other words, we perform *representation learning* (i.e., learning embedding representations of the data) but do so in a way that aims to ensure fairness for any downstream analysis. Perhaps unsurprisingly, this methodology is called *fair representation learning*. We will discuss representation learning in [Chapter 10](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X), “Deep learning: fundamentals.”

This is typically achieved based on adversarial learning methods such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) or variational autoencoders (VAEs), which we will cover in [Chapter 11](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121), “Advanced deep learning methods.” Without getting too far ahead of ourselves, suppose we are training a deep neural network classifier to predict class labels *y*<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi163.png) based on input data **x**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi164.png). An individual with data **x**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi165.png) has sensitive or protected demographic attributes *s*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi166.png). We further assume that as part of the classification process, the deep neural network learns embedding representations **z**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi167.png) of the data points, which will be used to predict *y*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi168.png). Now, for the purpose of making the embeddings fair, we introduce another classifier, an “adversary,” that tries to predict the protected attributes *s*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi169.png) based on **z**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi170.png).

If the adversary is well trained then it would find and exploit any relationship between the **z**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi171.png)’s and the *s*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi172.png)’s. On the other hand, if the deep neural network classifier successfully learns **z**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi173.png)’s that have no associations with the protected attributes *s*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi174.png), then the adversary will be unable to predict the *s*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi175.png)’s. We can train the deep neural network classifier to simultaneously predict the class labels *y*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi176.png) and to “fool” the adversary by learning **z**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi177.png)’s that the adversary performs poorly on while jointly training the adversary. This is a typical GAN-based approach to fair representation learning. The VAE-style approach is similar, but instead of trying to fool an adversary the deep learning classifier is encouraged, via architecture choices and penalty functions, to learn **z**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi178.png)’s that are statistically independent from the *s*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi179.png)’s. This strategy is closely related to *disentangled representation learning*, in which the features that are learned are independent from each other and hence more interpretable as the distinct meaningful factors that underly a dataset, for example, the lighting, pose, and orientation of an image.

 

#### Causal Fairness

In the real world, unfair outcomes happen for a reason. There are processes that systematically advantage some and disadvantage others, such as the impact of sexism on hiring outcomes. In the parlance of intersectionality theory, these processes are called *systems of oppression*. Ideally, to make an AI system fair, we ought to understand and model these systems and account for them when determining and correcting unfairness. This is difficult work, as these processes work in subtle and pernicious ways that are not always recorded digitally, and so it may be difficult to construct a model of the data and its unfairness patterns that is accurate and uncontroversial to stakeholders, who likely all have different value systems and assumptions about the world. This difficulty motivates all the other, typically easier, methodologies that we have considered thus far.

If we do decide to undertake the task of modeling all the reasons for unfairness in data and algorithms, *causal modeling* is a key tool as it allows us to understand and represent the causal relationship between the relevant variables. *Causality* hinges on the concept of an *intervention* to a system—if we were to give a drug to a patient would they be more likely to recover from their disease? In practice, we don’t always have the ability to perform such interventions; rather, the data we receive is *observational*, collected through the natural course of events without intervening. *Causal inference* is the task of trying to figure out the causal phenomena that would have occurred if we could have performed the appropriate interventions, based only on the observational data that we have. An even more difficult task, *causal discovery*, aims to construct a full causal model of the cause-and-effect relationships between all relevant variables in a problem domain.

Supposing that we can successfully model the causal structure of the problem domain, *causal fairness* methodologies intervene on the AI algorithm to achieve causal properties that are deemed fair. One such property, called *counterfactual fairness*, supposes that we could intervene on an individual’s protected attributes (e.g., their gender or race). In doing so we would be in another world where things are different from the actual world; this is called a *counterfactual world*. With a causal model in hand we could estimate how things would be different in the counterfactual world. A decision for an individual is said to be *counterfactually fair* if, in a counterfactual world where we intervened to change the individual’s protected attributes, the probabilities of the outcomes (e.g., class labels) would not be altered. If you were a man instead of a woman (or vice-versa) would the bank have offered you a loan? Or, if you were White instead of Asian (or vice-versa) would the company have offered you a job?

 

### Practical Guidelines for Fair Machine Learning

We’ve seen quite a few fairness definitions and methodologies but you might still be feeling quite unsure about how to design a fair machine learning system in practice. This is natural, as fairness is a complex, multistakeholder issue. Indeed, feeling uncertain about this is a good thing. As a technologist or engineer, it’s important to practice humility regarding your understanding of the nontechnical aspects of the sociotechnical context that an AI system lives in and the limitations of purely technological solutions to simply “solve” AI fairness. The last thing you should ever do is to show up as some kind of technology wizard and hand down a technological fairness intervention, as if from on-high, to “fix” an AI system without talking to anyone who is impacted by the system or examining the likely (and actual) impacts of your intervention. Well, okay, this is probably slightly better than not considering fairness and bias issues at all, but only marginally so. This is a good time to re-emphasize that it is vital to include stakeholders in the design of a fair and responsible AI/ML (machine learning) system, as we have discussed. In addition, we will go over a few things to consider in the practical design of fair machine learning systems.

 

#### Understanding Fairness and Bias in Your Problem Domain

We have seen that many options for mathematical fairness definitions exist. These alternative fairness definitions:

*   • May encode differing goals about fairness;
*   • May make differing assumptions about the real world and ideal world;
*   • May be desirable to different stakeholders, who may have conflicting goals; and
*   • May or may not correct the underlying fairness problems (or even make them worse).

It’s important to remember that no single fairness definition is applicable in all cases! Before attempting a fairness intervention, we first need to perform a careful reflection on the fairness and bias issues in the problem domain at hand. What are the likely sources of bias in the data, and hence in the algorithm? Is there a history of prejudice or unfair practices that needs to be accounted for? We need to stop and think about:

*   • Who is being harmed: 
    *   • By larger societal processes that impact the data?
    *   • By data quality and selection issues?
    *   • By the system itself?
*   • Why are they harmed?

Some considerations in defining fairness include:

*   • Are we addressing *harms of representation*, in which a model perpetuates harmful stereotypes that represent a protected group in a hurtful way? Or are we addressing *harms of outcome*, in which the predictions of the model are used for decision making, whose outcomes cause tangible or economic harm? As an example, the sentiment classifier that assigns negative sentiment to stereotypically Black names, which we discussed, creates a harm of representation because it perpetuates hurtful, racist opinions in the way that it represents people. On the other hand, if we used that same sentiment classifier to analyze resumes and it led to fewer Black people being offered a job interview, this would be a harm of outcome.
*   • In the present context, *should fairness correspond to equality* between protected groups, or are there legitimate reasons why equality is not the ideal solution, such as confounding factors or differing levels of qualification? One example of this situation arose in a study of admissions to the University of California Berkeley in the 1970s. The study found that while women were admitted to the University at a rate less than for men, this was explained by the fact that women tended to apply to departments that were more selective compared to men. When analyzing the results on a per-department basis, women were generally admitted at a higher rate than men. This counter-intuitive and impossible-sounding scenario is in fact possible due to a phenomenon known as *Simpson’s paradox*. The study concluded that there was no gender bias in the admissions process. Psychological research has concluded that when “fairness” (in a meritocratic sense) is in conflict with equality, humans tend to prioritize fairness over equality. If (meritocratic) fairness conflicts with equality, we must reckon with how to balance these competing goals.
*   • Are there underlying *differences between protected groups*, and should we accept the consequences of those differences in the data or correct for those differences? In research on discriminatory decision making in criminal justice contexts such as risk scores for recidivism, for example, some researchers have argued that since different demographic groups have different distributions over features, they would be expected to have different distributions over idealized risk scores (e.g., the probability of committing a crime). This phenomenon is termed *infra-marginality*. Proponents of this theory argue that because of the different distributions of risk between demographic groups, which are assumed to be legitimate, meritocratic, and well estimated, differences in outcome probabilities or error rates between demographic groups may not correspond to unfair discrimination. On the other hand, if the differences in risk are due to unfair reasons, we should not necessarily take the implications of those differences at face value.
*   • Should we aim to correct biases in society, beyond biases in data? In other words, should our intervention aim to perform *fair affirmative action*?

 

#### Does Your Problem Definition Contain Bias?

When solving a real-world problem through data mining, we must convert the problem into a question that data mining can solve, which is typically the prediction of a target variable via classification or regression models. The process of defining the data mining problem is a stage in which we might inadvertently introduce bias, that is, by making a decision that systematically disadvantages or advantages a protected demographic group. In many cases the class variable is selected because it is a conveniently measurable proxy for the thing we actually care about. For instance, in credit scoring the measurable class variable “this person repaid a loan” is used as a proxy for something more elusive, “this person should be given a loan.” It is important to remember that this is a proxy that was chosen for convenience and should not be viewed as the absolute, objective, and definitive final word on creditworthiness. More generally, we must be careful that the choice of class variable is not harmful. In hiring, the probability of employee retention might be used as a proxy for whether to interview or hire a candidate. If employee retention is higher for some demographics than others (e.g., women leaving the technology sector more frequently than men due to facing workplace discrimination), using employee retention as the prediction target would result in systematically offering fewer positions to women.

 

#### The Framing Trap

Once we have converted our real-world problem to a data mining problem, it is easy to forget that the system we build to solve the data mining problem exists in a bigger real-world context. Failing to consider this broader sociotechnical context, of which the machine learning system is but one component, is called the *framing trap*. If we do not consider how the outputs of our machine learning model are used in real-world decision making, and what the flow-on effects of those decisions are, we will not be able to make the broader sociotechnical system completely fair in an end-to-end sense. For example, in bail and sentencing decisions recidivism risk scores that are made by an AI system are generally given to a judge as mere recommendations, and the judge makes the final decision. The judge may be subject to *automation bias* in which they accept the algorithm’s recommendations without appropriate critique, they may ignore the algorithm’s recommendations entirely, or they may deviate from the recommendations in systematically biased ways. A fairness intervention on the AI system may thus not have the desired effect, such as provoking a response by the judge to overcompensate for the AI fairness intervention with even more biased behavior.

 

#### Navigating Fairness Trade-Offs

Since fairness penalties compete with predictive accuracy in a fair machine learning algorithm’s objective function ([Equation 7.7](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#eqn7)), there is usually a trade-off between fairness and accuracy, as we illustrate in [Fig. 7.8](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#f0045). This is particularly the case when parity-based fairness metrics are used, since if there is disparity between demographic groups in the data the enforcing parity would be at odds with making accurate predictions. In this case it would be wise to engage impacted stakeholders along with business stakeholders to negotiate a compromise solution. Fairness hyperparameters such as *λ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#955;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi180.png) in [Equation 7.7](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#eqn7), and potentially other model hyperparameters, can be tuned to select the appropriate trade-off.

![Fig. 7.8 Typical trade-off curve between fairness and predictive accuracy, when varying the fairness hyperparameter \\lambdaEquation in Equation 7.7. Credit: James Foulds](images/F00008Xf07-08-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. 7.8 Typical trade-off curve between fairness and predictive accuracy, when varying the fairness hyperparameter *λ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#955;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi194.png) in [Equation 7.7](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#eqn7). Credit: James Foulds

When tuning fairness hyperparameters, it is useful to first calculate the accuracy and/or the fairness measurement of the original (“typical”) machine learning model without a fairness intervention. With that information at hand, we can then threshold one of these quantities to a minimum acceptable value while optimizing the other via a grid search (or a more sophisticated hyperparameter tuning strategy such as Bayesian optimization). We can threshold the minimum accuracy (or other performance measure) to be at least, say, 95% of the accuracy of typical machine learning model while making the fairness metric as good as possible while satisfying that constraint. Alternatively, we can threshold the fairness metric (e.g., satisfying the 80% rule) while optimizing accuracy.

The prevailing “folk wisdom” is that fairness must always come at a cost of some degree of predictive performance based on the intuition in [Fig. 7.8](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#f0045). However, this is not the case. Often it is possible to obtain “*fairness for free*,” where a fairness metric is improved at no cost to predictive performance. Reasons for the fairness for free phenomenon include:

*   • Fairness penalties can act as a regularizer. They have the potential to reduce overfitting, hence improving generalization performance on unseen data.
*   • Multiple classifiers can potentially obtain same or similar numbers of errors. For example, many deep learning models with completely different weights may have essentially the same predictive performance. This is called the *Rashomon effect*. Some of those equally accurate classifiers may be fairer than others. We can therefore potentially choose between these classifiers to “gerrymander” the errors so that the system is fairer (see [Fig. 7.9](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#f0050)).

![Fig. 7.9 An example of the “fairness for free” phenomenon, obtained via the Rashomon effect. Here, + and – are class labels, and differing shading corresponds to different demographic groups. Solid and dashed circles indicate the errors made by the solid and dashed hyperplanes, respectively. Credit: James Foulds](images/F00008Xf07-09-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 7.9](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#Bf0050) An example of the “fairness for free” phenomenon, obtained via the Rashomon effect. Here, + and – are class labels, and differing shading corresponds to different demographic groups. Solid and dashed circles indicate the errors made by the solid and dashed hyperplanes, respectively. Credit: James Foulds

We show an example of fairness for free via the Rashomon effect in. The classifiers with the solid and dashed hyperplanes both make two errors (indicated with solid and dashed circles, respectively). However, the solid-line classifier makes two errors on instances from the same demographic group (indicated via shading) while the dashed-line classifier makes errors on instances from different demographic groups. While this example may seem contrived, practical experience with training deep neural networks—which generally converge to any number of local optima or saddle points of a highly nonconvex objective function but obtain similar performance across runs—suggests that for these models there are many different solutions with similar predictive performance. Of these similar quality solutions, we can and should aim to pick the fairest option.

In practice, it is frequently possible to obtain fairness for free via the following strategy:

1.  1. Perform a grid search on the hyperparameters of the “typical” machine learning model (without a fairness intervention) and record the predictive accuracy *P*<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi183.png) of the best model on the validation set.
2.  2. Perform a grid search on the fair machine learning model over all the hyperparameters including both the fairness trade-off hyperparameter *λ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#955;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi184.png) as well as other model hyperparameters.
3.  3. Based on the grid search, select the model with the best fairness parameter out of those that have predictive accuracy equal to or better than *P*<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi185.png).

 

#### Important Caveats to Fair AI/Data Mining

When employing fairness interventions it is essential to remember the limitations of the fair AI paradigm. A mathematical definition cannot, by itself, solve the sociotechnical problem of “fairness,” which has nontechnical dimensions and exceeds the narrowly defined AI/data mining system. Humans, including impacted stakeholders and experts from other fields such as law, the humanities, sociology, philosophy, psychology, and so on, must be part of the solution. The sociotechnical context in which an AI system is embedded must always be accounted for. The fair AI paradigm arguably oversimplifies complex sociotechnical problems to straightforward technical ones.

Even worse, fair AI technologies could potentially legitimize problematic systems by providing a veneer of ethical respectability to them. There are some systems that should never be deployed, no matter how much we intervene to make them fair. Affect-recognition systems, for example, are AI-based computer vision systems that analyze video, image, or audio data to detect emotions such as fear or anger. These systems have been deployed for applications in hiring, law enforcement, casinos, restaurants, hospitals, prisons, and beyond. As you might expect by now, many of these systems are racially biased. Some scholars have argued that the ethical issues with these systems run deeper and the surveillance they facilitate is harmful in and of itself. It has also been argued that these systems lack scientific validity, with the facial movement data they rely on being insufficient to determine emotion to the degree of accuracy required for their intended applications. In one view, correcting racial bias issues in affect-recognition systems would not be enough to make the systems acceptable for deployment in many of their intended use-cases.

Human-centered computing researcher Os Keyes and colleagues penned a scathing satire of the fair AI paradigm that serves to illustrate some of its limitations. They imagine an AI system that selects older adults with low social credit as candidates for being mulched into a high-nutrient slurry. If you have ever seen the film Soylent Green, which imagines a future in which humans are turned into food, you will understand the concept. In this scenario, an AI fairness analysis finds that White cisgender men are much more likely to be selected for mulching compared to other demographics. They perform an AI fairness intervention to correct this “bias” by *increasing* the mulching probability for all other demographics such as transgender women, Asian Americans, and so on, to match the high mulching probability of White cisgender men. They ensure that the system is adequately transparent in its decision making by publicly releasing the set of variables that were used to select “mulches”—phone and text message metadata, the number of Facebook friends, the number of birthday cards received, and so on. The system is made accountable, as the prospective mulchees can speak to a phone operator about factors of social credit the system may have overlooked that could be included in the next version of the system. The authors conclude that their system is fair, accountable, and transparent while working to solve the problem of food security, and so it must therefore be beyond all possible ethical reproach!

 

## 7.3 AI Safety

As AI becomes more sophisticated and inscrutable, there are rising concerns that AI and machine learning technologies can behave in dangerous and unintended ways. These issues arise in large part because it is difficult to fully specify and control the behavior of a system that is learned rather than programmed to ensure that it behaves as we want it to. This issue is called the *AI alignment problem*.

 

### The AI Alignment Problem

 

*I really hate this damn machine*,

 

*I wish that they would sell it*.

 

*It never does quite what I want*,

 

*But only what I tell it*.

—Anonymous

Some of you may have heard this quote, with unknown attribution, in one of your first programming classes. Any programmer quickly learns that it is difficult to perfectly tell a computer exactly what you want it to do, and a slight misstep in specifying its instructions could lead to disastrous results.

A similar issue can occur when designing an AI or machine learning system. The *AI alignment problem*, sometimes called the *value alignment problem*, is the problem that the objective function that a human specifies for an AI may not perfectly correspond to their intended behavior and goals for the system, and it could admit unintended consequences. There is a fairly direct analogy to stories of a genie or other supernatural entity that grants wishes, but the stated wish has a loophole that causes it to backfire and come true with unforeseen negative results. The story of King Midas, who was granted his wish that everything he touches turns to gold, is a canonical example.

AI alignment problems can happen due to *unintended side effects*. The AI fairness and bias issues that we discussed fall into this category; a machine learning system may accurately predict the target class label while also exhibiting harmful behavior such as unfair discriminatory patterns in its predictions. This is an alignment issue because a machine learning objective function that only rewards accurate predictions fails to rule out biased behavior.

As previously discussed in this chapter, class labels are often chosen as convenient proxies for ground truth, such as repaying a loan as a proxy for a more holistic notion of creditworthiness, and these choices can impair alignment in a manner that introduces discriminatory bias. When an AI system has a real-world physical presence, direct physical harm becomes a possibility, that is, a self-driving car that runs over pedestrians to reach its destination or a robot vacuum cleaner that knocks over tables while cleaning.

Misaligned AI issues can also occur from *specification gaming*, also known as *reward hacking*, in which the AI system achieves its goal via a novel and unforeseen strategy that was not intended by the system’s designer. Humans do this, too. If a restaurant manager punishes her staff whenever they are seen to not be actively working, employees are incentivized to do their assigned tasks as slowly as possible. The employee may achieve this by cleaning surfaces in the least efficient order, with the gunk in the microwave falling onto the microwave stand and further down to the counter below so that both surfaces must be cleaned again, creating unnecessary work that allows the worker to appear busy when they are not.

Researcher Victoria Krakovna maintains a list of examples of specification gaming on her blog if you would like to see many instances of the phenomenon. In one case, reported by Twitter user Custard Smingleigh, a Roomba robot vacuum cleaner was trained to drive using a neural network via reinforcement learning with rewards for speed and for not setting off its bumper sensors that indicate a collision. Since there were no sensors on the back, the AI learned to travel at high speed in reverse, thus avoiding penalties for any collisions.

This example shows how it can be difficult for humans to perfectly specify the desired behavior of an AI system, resorting instead to simpler *proxy goals* that may or may not lead to the intended results. One possible solution to this challenge is to learn the reward function, from human feedback or *imitation learning* methodologies such as *inverse reinforcement learning*, but this can create its own specification gaming issues. For example, researchers from OpenAI created a reinforcement learning algorithm that learns preferred behaviors from human feedback and used it to train a robot hand to grasp a ball. However, the AI instead learned to fool human annotators by simply placing the hand between the ball and the observer, appearing to grasp it but not actually doing so.

Of course, unanticipated solutions can be desirable and are a sign that the learning algorithm is powerful enough to find solutions that go beyond what the human designers could dream up. When Google Deepmind’s AlphaZero system was trained to play chess it produced novel and effective game-playing strategies that human players did not know about. Whether a novel solution is desirable, or if it constitutes unwanted specification gaming, can be a complicated question. One of the authors was once told of a case where an airport hired academic consultants to help them reduce the time that passengers were waiting to claim their baggage. The problem was formalized as a mathematical optimization problem with the objective of minimizing the passengers’ wait time. The optimization algorithm produced a solution in which the passengers had to walk all the way across the airport to retrieve their baggage, thereby waiting next to the carousel for a shorter time. This solution seems perverse as it did not actually get the baggage back to the passengers any faster. However, the airport implemented it and the complaints by the passengers went away!

While it is difficult enough to specify the objective or reward function of an AI system well enough that the solution to the optimization problem is sure to be what we want (*outer alignment*), further AI alignment problems can arise when the system learns that it must achieve intermediate goals to achieve its objectives (*inner alignment*). A robot vacuum cleaner that aims to clean an entire house must learn to identify doorways and navigate between the rooms of the house, for instance. We typically train machine learning algorithms by optimizing some objective function but the models that are learned could themselves be optimizers (e.g., learning to efficiently navigate the house). Such a model is called a *mesa-optimizer*. Alignment problems can occur if the learned intermediate goals that a mesa-optimizer aims to achieve are the result of overfitting, called *goal mis-generalization*. For example, if an intelligent agent seeks a coin that is always in the same location in its training data but that coin is in a different location at test time, it may blindly navigate to the original location and might not even recognize the coin in its new location.

One intermediate *emergent goal* that arises naturally and can help an AI system achieve many goals is to obtain power over its environment by increasing its resources or its ability to prevent any other agent or human from impeding it. Such *power-seeking* behavior has clear and obvious risks. The robot vacuum cleaner might learn how to lock all humans in the house in a closet so that they cannot create a mess, for example. It could learn how to evade being switched off (which would prevent it from completing its cleaning), potentially by harming or deceiving humans.

The potential tendency of many different AI systems to seek power is an example of *instrumental convergence*. An *instrumental* goal is one that is a means to an end. Instrumental convergence occurs when multiple intelligent agents (AI or human) seek the same useful subgoal (e.g., obtaining power) to achieve each of their varied goals. This could potentially lead to harmful results. In the famous *paperclip maximizer* thought experiment by philosopher Nick Bostrom, for example, we suppose that an AI is tasked with producing as many paperclips as possible. The AI quickly determines that humans might switch it off, thus preventing it from creating paperclips, and the humans also contain atoms that are useful for creating paperclips. Its goal of maximizing the number of paperclips is in direct conflict with a world in which there are many living humans so it achieves its intermediate goal with catastrophic results.

 

### Artificial Superintelligence and the Threat of Rogue AI

Could an AI really exterminate all human life or enslave us all? An AI like the paperclip maximizer might not need to be more intelligent than humans, and certainly wouldn’t need to be considered “conscious,” to accomplish this if it could obtain sufficient resources. However, if humans could outsmart it, it might not succeed. An *artificial superintelligence* (*ASI*) is a hypothetical AI that is more intelligent than humans. This should not be confused with a related concept—*artificial general intelligence* (*AGI*), a hypothetical AI that is general enough to perform well over many tasks and problem domains, while not necessarily being more “intelligent” than humans. Some authors have argued that *large language models* (*LLMs*), which can solve tasks ranging from mathematics, to medicine, to law, and beyond, are already at the beginning stages of AGI.

If we subscribe to the *functionalist* theory of mind, which states that minds and mental states depend on the functional roles of the system that they are a part of, then the human brain is just one possible piece of hardware that could produce a mind, and we could presumably implement a mind using different hardware such as a digital computer. This would imply that, in principle, ASI is possible and therefore might one day be a threat to human existence and/or autonomy. The view that AI is a near-term threat to human existence is a controversial position but it has its proponents, including prominent technologists such as entrepreneur Elon Musk and the late theoretical physicist Stephen Hawking. One of the most credible voices to take this position is deep learning pioneer Geoff Hinton, who resigned (some might say retired) at age 75 from Google in 2023 to have the freedom to warn about these kinds of risks. Hinton took this view after being alarmed by the recent rapid progress of LLMs in their ability to acquire general knowledge and perform reasoning. A persistent theory, notably advocated by professor and science fiction author Vernor Vinge and futurist Ray Kurzweil, is that a phenomenon known as the *singularity* will occur, referring to a hypothetical scenario in which technological progress will enable its own runaway acceleration, leading to consequences that are so far beyond our current understanding that they are difficult to comprehend or foresee.

On the other hand, all technological trends to date have reached a point of diminishing returns, and LLMs are unlikely to be an exception to this rule. If, as most computer scientists believe, *P* ≠ *N**P*<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8800;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">NP</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi186.png), then many AI problems are fundamentally difficult to solve and thus there are limits to what an AI might accomplish, no matter how well designed. Many AI researchers have learned from bitter experience—in struggling to achieve a few percentage points of improvement on benchmark tasks to get our work published—that progress in the field is really difficult and comes with much human blood, sweat, and tears. While the rapid advances in LLM technology have been unexpected and astounding, this situation has not fundamentally changed.

Moreover, even if ASI could be developed, an overemphasis on the importance of intelligence may be naïve. *Wired Magazine* founding editor Kevin Kelly calls this the “*thinkism fallacy*.” No matter how smart an AI is, for it to find a cure for cancer it would not only need to come up with a good idea for a cure but also perform medical trials to test its hypothesis and likely adjust its approach many times based on the data from the trials before succeeding. In 2015, renowned AI expert Andrew Ng said, “The reason I say that I don’t worry about AI turning evil is the same reason I don’t worry about overpopulation on Mars.” While much has changed since then, it is still true that there are many immediate and urgent concerns around AI that need to be addressed right now. While some concern for the more distant future may be warranted, we should not let that lead us to neglect the present. Prominent AI researcher Meredith Whittaker, who was forced out of Google for organizing against the company’s drone computer vision contracts with the US military (although Google disputes this account of events), has argued that “alarmist” views such as those expressed by Hinton have a very real cost in terms of deprioritizing AI fairness and equity issues. She expressed dismay that Hinton and others at Google warned against hypothetical future risks from AI but did not support efforts to curtain the harms due to AI that are already happening, which fall disproportionately on women, people of color, and especially women of color. We discussed AI bias and fairness issues earlier in this chapter, and in [Sections 15.10](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#s0085) and [15.11](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#s0115) we’ll expand our discussion to other such concerns at the intersection of AI and our society.

 

## 7.4 Further Reading and Bibliographic Notes

Useful discussions on the definition of privacy in the big data era are given by [Richards and King (2014)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur454), and [Solove (2010)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur503). [Sweeney (2000)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur517) provided a compelling census-data example of the problem linkage attacks pose to anonymized data. The k-anonymity technique is also due to [Sweeney (2002)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur518). Machanavajjhala et al. (2006) illustrated several attacks that can defeat *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00008Xsi187.png)\-anonymity. Differential privacy is due to [Dwork (2006)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur152), with a more comprehensive treatment given in [Dwork and Roth (2014)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur154). [Abadi et al. (2016)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur1) developed a practical technique for differentially private deep learning, including the moments accountant technique for efficiently keeping track of how sequential differentially privacy operations use up a privacy budget. Federated learning was proposed by [Konečný et al. (2015)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur327).

Much of what we know about AI fairness and bias issues from real systems was revealed by journalists. Fairness issues in criminal justice risk assessments were exposed by investigative journalists Angwin et al. (2016), who used a freedom of information request to obtain data on the COMPAS system. [Dastin (2018)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur121) described the case of Amazon’s internal recruiting tool that was biased against women. Researchers have also weighed in and [Bulamwini and Gebru (2018)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur75) analyzed bias at the intersection of gender and skin tone in facial recognition systems, further validated in follow-up work from NIST by [Grother et al. (2019)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur238). Many other detailed examples of problems with AI-based decisions were given by [O’Neill (2017)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur426). The ACM’s statement on principles for responsible algorithmic systems, including AI-based systems, was published by [ACM Technology Policy Office (2022)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur5). In a blog post, [Speer (2017)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur505) provided a compelling example of how bias issues can arise unintentionally in *natural language processing* (*NLP*) systems. Common sources of AI bias are illustrated in depth by Barocas and Selbst (2016). [Noble (2018)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur421) gives a detailed account of representation issues in the output of algorithms, focusing on Google search.

The main fair AI paradigm, in which fairness metrics are enforced in a learning algorithm, is due to [Dwork et al. (2012)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur153). The authors proposed the individual fairness metric and considered and critiqued differential parity fairness. The 80% rule, a legal criterion for discrimination with a parity flavor and that can be used for fair AI, was codified by the US Equal Employment Opportunities Commission in C.F.R. 29.1607 (EEOC, 1978), and corresponding machine learning algorithms were developed by [Zafar et al. (2017)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur586). The equalized odds and equality of opportunity fairness definitions, which aim to address some of the issues with parity-based fairness, were proposed by [Hardt et al. (2016)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur250). While authors including Hardt et al. and [Simoiu et al. (2017)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur495) criticized parity-based fairness metrics, [Foulds and Pan (2020)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur175) discussed both sides of the argument and defended the concept of parity-based fairness. [Pleiss et al. (2017)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur437) showed a key limitation of equalized odds fairness, namely that it is incompatible with calibrated probability estimates. The incompatibility and resulting trade-offs between fairness definitions were earlier analyzed by [Kleinberg et al. (2016)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur316). Fair representation learning was proposed by [Zemel et al. (2013)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur591). A canonical example of the use of adversarial learning for fair representations was developed by [Beutel et al. (2017)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur39). A blog post by [Tonk (2018)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur533), which applies the methods of [Louppe et al. (2017)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur369) to fairness, is also recommended reading on this topic. [Kusner et al. (2017)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur340) developed the first, and most prominent, causal fairness method, counterfactual fairness.

The consideration of fairness at the intersection of protected groups can be motivated by intersectionality, a framework for analyzing systemic patterns of injustices and how they interact with overlapping protected demographic dimensions, due to [Crenshaw (1989)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur115). [Kearns et al. (2018)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur302) proposed subgroup fairness, which aims to ensure fairness at the intersection of multiple protected groups, and was not informed by intersectionality theory but rather aims to prevent subset targeting, a.k.a. fairness gerrymandering. [Foulds et al. (2020)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur176); [Islam et al. (2023)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur286) critiqued subgroup fairness from the perspective of intersectionality and proposed the first definition that was explicitly motivated by intersectionality. [Hebert-Johnson et al. (2018)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur258) proposed multicalibration, another fairness definition for overlapping protected groups that focuses on calibrated probability estimates.

An important strand of work critiques the limitations of the AI fairness paradigm, and this work is often insightful for how one ought to use (or not use) AI fairness interventions in practice. Blogdett et al. (2020) provided a critical review of fair NLP research, which went beyond summarizing the papers to pointing to the serious deficiencies in that subfield, and in fair ML more generally in terms of addressing the broader context of who has been harmed by a system and what a fair system should actually do. [Selbst et al. (2019)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur485) shone a spotlight on the importance of accounting for the sociotechnical context that an AI system is embedded in and the pitfalls that can arise because of it, such as the framing trap. [Keyes et al. (2019)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur305) critiqued the shortcomings of the dominant fairness, accountability, and transparency (FAT) framework with a scathing satirical example. [Islam et al. (2021)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur287) showed that despite the conventional wisdom in the field, it is frequently possible, and indeed easy, to obtain some degree of “fairness for free” without a loss of predictive performance. The AI Now Report is an annual publication that provides a critical perspective on the state of the field, and it highlights problems in real-world deployed systems as well as limitations of the technologies including fair AI methods. Although it’s always valuable to look at the most recent edition, the 2019 AI Now Report is one that has stood the test of time ([Crawford et al., 2019](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur114)).

For an overview of the main issues in AI safety, including the alignment problem, see [Hendrycks (2021)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur262). Krakanova (2020) explains the problem of specification gaming, and her website maintains an extensive and frequently updated list of examples of it.^(<a aria-label="noteref" href="#fn3" id="Cfn3">3</a>3) [Bostrom (2012)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur53) is a classic paper on the dangers of advanced AI and how it might go rogue. In an interview, Meredith Whittaker provides a counterpoint to the current alarmism around possible existential threats from AI and reminds us that there are more pressing issues that we perhaps ought to focus on instead ([Chan, 2023](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur89)).
