stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F00011Xsi21.png)

Each *preactivation function* **a**^((*l*))(**x**)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi22.png) is typically a linear operation with matrix **W**^((*l*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi23.png) and bias **b**^((*l*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi24.png), which can be combined into a parameter **θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi25.png):

$\\begin{matrix} {\\mathbf{a}^{(l)}\\left( \\mathbf{x} \\right) = \\mathbf{W}^{(l)}\\mathbf{x} + \\mathbf{b}^{(l)},} \\\\ {\\mathbf{a}^{(l)}\\left( \\widehat{\\mathbf{x}} \\right) = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(l)}\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}},l = 1} \\\\ {\\mathbf{a}^{(l)}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{h}}}^{(l - 1)}) = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(l)}{\\widehat{\\mathbf{h}}}^{(l - 1)},l > 1.} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#62;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mi>.</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F00011Xsi26.png)

The “hat” notation $\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi27.png) indicates that 1 has been appended to the vector **x**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi28.png). Hidden-layer activation functions **h**^((*l*))(**x**)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi29.png) often have the same form at each level but this is not a requirement.

[Fig. 10.1](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#f0010) shows an example network. In contrast to graphical models such as Bayesian networks, where hidden variables are random variables, the hidden units here are intermediate deterministic computations, which is why they are not represented as circles. However, the output variables *y*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi30.png) are drawn as circles because they can be formulated probabilistically.

![Fig. 10.1 A feedforward neural network. Credit: Christopher J. Pal](images/F00011Xf10-01-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 10.1](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#Bf0010) A feedforward neural network. Credit: Christopher J. Pal

 

### Activation Functions

Activation functions generally operate on the preactivation vectors in an elementwise fashion. [Table 10.3](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#t0020) depicts common hidden-layer activation functions, along with their functional forms and derivatives.

| ![image](images/F00011Xu10-01-9780443158889.jpg) || $h(x) = \\frac{1}{1 + \\exp( - x)}$<mml:math><mml:mstyle displaystyle="true"><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>exp</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mstyle></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi173.png) || $h\\prime(x) = h(x)\\lbrack 1 - h(x)\\rbrack\\begin{matrix} \\quad \\\\ \\quad \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo accent="false">&#8242;</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mspace width="1em"/></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mspace width="1em"/></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi174.png) |

| ![image](images/F00011Xu10-04-9780443158889.jpg) || $h(x) = \\max(0,x)\\begin{matrix} \\quad \\\\ \\quad \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>max</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mspace width="1em"/></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mspace width="1em"/></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi179.png) || $h\\prime(x) = \\left\\{ \\begin{matrix} 1 \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\end{matrix}\\begin{matrix} {{if}x \\geq 0} \\\\ {{if}x < 0} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right.$<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo accent="false">&#8242;</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">if</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8805;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">if</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#60;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi180.png) |
| ![image](images/F00011Xu10-05-9780443158889.jpg) || $h(x) = \\left\\{ \\begin{matrix} {x{if}x \\geq 0} \\\\ {\\mathit{ax}{if}x < 0} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right.$<mml:math><mml:mstyle displaystyle="true"><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">if</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8805;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ax</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">if</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#60;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mstyle></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi181.png) || $\\left. h\\prime(x \\right) = \\left\\{ \\begin{matrix} {1{if}x \\geq 0} \\\\ {a{if}x < 0} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right.$<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo accent="false">&#8242;</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">if</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8805;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">if</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#60;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi182.png) |

![Image](images/T00011Xtabt0020.png)

Credit: Christopher J. Pal

While sigmoid functions have been popular, the hyperbolic tangent function (*tanh*) is sometimes preferred, partly because it has a steady state at 0. However, more recently the *rectify*() function or *rectified linear units* (*ReLUs*) have been found to yield superior results in many different settings. Since this function is 0 for negative argument values, some units in the model will yield activations that are 0, giving a “sparseness” property that is useful in many contexts. Moreover, the gradient is particularly simple—either 0 or 1. The fact that when activated the activation function has a gradient of exactly 1 helps address the *vanishing or exploding gradient problem*—we discuss this in more detail later, under recurrent networks. ReLUs are a popular choice for **h**^((*l*))(**x**)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi31.png), while piecewise linear functions (the last entry of [Table 10.3](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#t0020)) have also grown in popularity for deep learning systems. Like ReLUs these are not differentiable at 0 but gradient descent can be applied by using a subgradient instead, which means that *h*′(0)<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo accent="false">&#8242;</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi32.png) can be set to *a*<mml:math><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi33.png).

Many deep learning software packages make it easy to use a variety of activation functions, including piecewise-linear ones. Some determine the gradients needed for the backpropagation algorithm automatically, using symbolic computations built into the software.

[Fig. 10.2](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#f0015) is a computation graph that shows the general form of a canonical deep network architecture with several hidden layers. It illustrates how predictions are computed, how the loss *L*<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi34.png) is obtained, and how the forward pass of the backpropagation algorithm is computed. Hidden-layer activation functions are given by act(**a**^((*l*)))<mml:math><mml:mtext>act</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi35.png), and the final layer activation function is given by out(**a**^((*L* + 1)))<mml:math><mml:mtext>out</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi36.png). We previously discussed backpropagation in [Section 9.2](#Ch010_347-389_B9780443158889000108.xhtml#s0050). A more detailed treatment is given in [Appendix D.1](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#s0010).

![Fig. 10.2 Computation graph showing forward propagation in a deep network. Credit: Christopher J. Pal](images/F00011Xf10-02-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 10.2](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#Bf0015) Computation graph showing forward propagation in a deep network. Credit: Christopher J. Pal

 

### Computation Graphs and Complex Network Structures

For a simple feedforward network learning takes place in two phases: a forward pass and a backward pass. Furthermore, using vector notation, as shown in [Appendix D.1](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#s0010), the gradient computations decompose into a simple chain of matrix products.

But what if the graph does not have a simple layered structure? It turns out that more complex computations consisting of applying functions to intermediate results can also be represented by computation graphs. The *Computation Graphs and Backpropagation* subsection of [Appendix D.1](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#s0010) gives an example of a more advanced computation for which finding the gradients needed for backpropagation can be understood and visualized using a computation graph.

Implementing general mechanisms for backpropagation efficiently can become quite complex. Using the concept of a computation graph, gradient information “simply” needs to be propagated along the path found by reversing the arrows in the graph used to define the steps of the forward-propagation of information. Many software packages use interleaved forward propagation and backward propagation phases within computation graphs. Some allow users to define complex network structures in such a way that the system can obtain the required derivatives automatically and perform computations efficiently using libraries that call graphics processing units.

In principle learning in a deep network could be by gradient descent or more sophisticated methods that exploit higher-order derivatives. However, in practice, a variation of stochastic gradient descent based on “mini-batches” is by far the most popular method, such that software packages and implementations are often optimized assuming that this will be used. We discuss this method and its more advanced extensions such as Adam, and other key practical aspects of training deep networks, in [Section 10.2](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#s0040).

 

## 10.2 Training and Evaluating Deep Networks

When working with deep learning, it is vital to have separate training, test, and validation sets. The validation set is used to tune a model’s hyperparameters for model selection.

 

### Validation, Cross-Validation, and Hyperparameter Tuning

Hyperparameters are tuned by identifying what settings lead to best performance on the validation set with early stopping. Common hyperparameters include the strength of parameter regularization, model complexity in terms of the number of hidden units and layers and their connectivity, the form of activation functions, and parameters of the learning algorithm itself. Because of the many choices involved, performance monitoring on validation sets assumes an even more central role than it does with traditional ML methods.

As usual, the test set should be set aside for a truly final evaluation because repeated rounds of experiments using test-set data would give misleading estimates of performance on fresh data. For this reason the research community has come to favor public challenges with hidden test-set labels, a development that has undoubtedly helped gauge progress in the field. However, controversy arises when participants submit multiple entries, and some favor a model where participants submit code to a competition server so that the test data itself is hidden.

The use of a validation set is different from using *k*\-fold cross-validation to evaluate a learning technique or to select hyperparameters. As [Section 5.3](#Ch005_165-207_B9780443158889000066.xhtml#s0020) explained, cross-validation involves creating multiple training and testing partitions. But data sets for deep learning tend to be so massive that a single large test set adequately represents a model’s performance, reducing the need for cross-validation. Since training often takes days or weeks, even using graphics processing units, cross-validation is impractical anyway.

To obtain the best possible results, one needs to tune hyperparameters, usually with a single validation set extracted from the training set. However, there is a dilemma—omitting the validation set from final training can reduce performance in the test. It is advantageous to train on the combined training and validation data but this risks overfitting. One solution is to stop training after the same number of epochs that led to the best validation set performance; another is to monitor the average loss over the combined training set and stop when it reaches the level it was at when early stopping was performed using the validation set.

Hyperparameters in deep learning are often tuned heuristically by hand, or using grid search. An alternative is random search, where instead of placing a regular grid over hyperparameter space, probability distributions are specified from which samples are taken. Another approach is to use ML and Bayesian techniques to infer the next hyperparameter configuration to try in a sequence of experimental runs, a methodology called Bayesian optimization.

We have been talking about tuning model hyperparameters, such as the weight used for the regularization term. However, many of the parameters and choices that arise later can be viewed as learning algorithm hyperparameters that could also be tuned. In practice they are often chosen during informal manual trials but they could be determined by automated searching using validation sets as a guide.

 

### Mini-Batch-Based Stochastic Gradient Descent

[Section 9.2](#Ch010_347-389_B9780443158889000108.xhtml#s0050) introduced the method of stochastic gradient descent. For convex functions such as the one used in logistic regression with *L*[2] regularization, and a learning rate that decays over time *t*, it can be shown that the approximate gradients converge at a rate that is of the order 1/*t*. Earlier in this chapter, we remarked on the fact that deep learning architectures are often optimized using mini-batch-based stochastic gradient descent. We now explain this technique.

Stochastic gradient descent updates the model parameters according to the gradient computed from one example. The mini-batch variant uses a small subset of the data and bases updates to parameters on the average gradient over the examples in the batch. This operates just like the regular procedure—initialize the parameters, enter a parameter update loop, and terminate by monitoring a validation set. However, in contrast to standard stochastic gradient descent the main loop iterates over mini-batches that have been obtained from the training set and updates the parameters after processing each batch. Normally these batches are randomly selected disjoint subsets of the training set, perhaps shuffled after each epoch, depending on the time required to do so.

Each pass through a set of mini-batches that represent the complete training set is an epoch. Using the empirical risk plus a regularization term as the objective function, after processing a mini-batch the parameters are updated by

$\\left. \\mathbf{\\theta}^{\\mathit{new}}\\leftarrow\\mathbf{\\theta} - \\eta\_{t}\\left\\lbrack \\frac{1}{B\_{k}}\\sum\\limits\_{i \\in I}\\left\\lbrack \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}}L(f(\\mathbf{x}\_{i};\\mathbf{\\theta}),\\mathbf{y}\_{i}) \\right\\rbrack + \\frac{B\_{k}}{N}\\lambda\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}}R\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right) \\right\\rbrack, \\right.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">new</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>&#8592;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#951;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8706;</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8706;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>&#955;</mml:mi><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8706;</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8706;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F00011Xsi37.png)

where *η*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#951;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi38.png) is the learning rate (which may depend on the epoch *t*); the *k*th batch has *B[k]* examples and is represented by a set *I* = *I*(*t*, *k*)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi39.png) of indices into the original data; *N* is the size of the training set; *L*(*f*(**x**[*i*]; **θ**), **y**[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi40.png) is the loss for example ***x****[i]*, label ***y****[i]* and parameters **θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi41.png); and *R*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi42.png) is the regularizer, with weight *λ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#955;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi43.png). At one extreme, where a single mini-batch contains the entire training set, is the standard update for batch gradient descent, while at the other, with a batch size of 1, is the standard single-example stochastic gradient descent update.

Mini-batches typically contain two to several hundred examples, although for large models the choice may be constrained by computational resources. The batch size often influences the stability and speed of learning; some sizes work particularly well for a given model and data set. Sometimes a search is performed over a set of potential batch sizes to find one that works well before launching a lengthy optimization.

The mix of class labels in the batches can influence the result. For unbalanced data there may be an advantage in pretraining the model using mini-batches in which the labels are balanced and then fine-tuning the upper layer or layers using the unbalanced label statistics. This can involve implementing a sampling scheme that ensures that as one cycles through examples they are presented to the learning procedure in an unbiased way.

 

### Pseudocode for Mini-Batch Based Stochastic Gradient Descent

Given data **x**[*i*], **y**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi44.png), *I* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi45.png), …, *N*, loss function *L*\[*f*(**x**[*i*]; **θ**), **y**[*i*]\]<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi46.png) with parameters **θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi47.png), and a parameter regularization term *R*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi48.png) weighted by *λ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#955;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi49.png), we wish to optimize the empirical risk plus regularization term, that is,

${1/N}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}{L\\left\\lbrack {f\\left( {\\mathbf{x}\_{i};\\mathbf{\\theta}} \\right),\\mathbf{y}\_{i}} \\right)\\rbrack + \\lambda R\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right)}.$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo>/</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#955;</mml:mi><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F00011Xsi50.png)

The pseudocode in [Fig. 10.3](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#f0020) accomplishes this. It uses *K* mini-batches indexed by the sets *I[k]*, each of which contains B*[k]* examples. The learning rate *η*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#951;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi51.png) may depend on time *t*. The gradient vector is **g**, and the update *Δ***θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi52.png) incorporates a momentum term. Mini-batches are often created before entering the *while* loop; however, in some cases shuffling within the loop yields an improvement.

![Fig. 10.3 Pseudocode for mini‑batch–based stochastic gradient descent. Credit: Christopher J. Pal](images/F00011Xf10-03-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 10.3](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#Bf0020) Pseudocode for mini‑batch–based stochastic gradient descent. Credit: Christopher J. Pal

 

### Learning Rates and Schedules

The learning rate *η*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#951;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi53.png) is a critical choice when using mini-batch–based stochastic gradient descent. Small values such as 0.001 often work well but it is common to perform a logarithmically spaced search, say in the interval \[10^(−8), 1\], followed by a finer grid or binary search.

The learning rate may be adapted over epochs *t* to give a learning rate schedule *η*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#951;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi54.png). A fixed learning rate is often used in the first few epochs, followed by a decreasing schedule such as

$\\eta\_{t} = \\frac{\\eta\_{0}}{1 + \\varepsilon t},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#951;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#951;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#949;</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F00011Xsi55.png)

or

$\\eta\_{t} = \\frac{\\eta\_{0}}{t^{\\varepsilon}},(0.5 < \\varepsilon \\leq 1).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#951;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#951;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#949;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#60;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#949;</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8804;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F00011Xsi190.png)

There are, however, many heuristics for adapting learning rates by hand during training. For example, the AlexNet model that won the ImageNet 2012 challenge divides the rate by 10 when the validation error rate ceases to improve. The intuition is that a model may make good progress with a given learning rate but eventually become stuck, jumping around a local minimum in the loss function because the parameter steps are too large. Monitoring performance on the validation set is a good guide as to when the learning rate should be changed.

Second-order analysis based on a Taylor expansion of the loss to higher-order terms can also help explain why smaller rates may be desirable in the final stages of learning. If stochastic gradient descent is used it can be shown that the learning rate must be reduced for the approach to yield results consistent with batch gradient descent.

 

### Advanced Learning Algorithms

SGD is the workhorse of deep learning. Performing updates after every mini-batch, instead of after processing an entire dataset, is what makes it possible to scale deep learning to the massive datasets that it needs to achieve excellent performance. However, “scalable” (i.e., able to process a large number of data points) is not the same thing as “fast” (rapid in running time, both per-iteration and overall time to convergence). There is therefore a strong motivation to improve over it. Several variations on SGD have been proposed, and these have made a big impact on the application of deep learning methods.

There are two main limitations of SGD that these sophisticated learning methods aim to address. First, SGD is myopic, in the sense that it does not look ahead in any way. It just takes a step downhill in the direction of the stochastic estimate of the gradient. Each step can be noisy (potentially taking the model’s parameters in a bad direction). It could get stuck in a small local optimum or plateau. And the now steepest downhill direction may not actually always be the best direction to go in. Second, the learning rate (a.k.a. the step size, how far to “step” in the chosen direction) is the same for all dimensions, and this may not be ideal. Some dimensions may not need to be changed much at all, while others may need to change a lot, and this could vary during the learning process.

 

#### SGD With Momentum

As a metaphor for the dynamics of SGD, imagine a ball rolling down a hill. If the hill is bumpy the ball might get stuck in a hole (i.e., a local minimum), or it could stop partway down on a plateau. If the ball is not too heavy it could also go off in many arbitrary, inefficient directions, since it would tend to follow the downhill directions, which are determined by the little bumps and not by the overall shape of the hill. Now suppose that the ball is much heavier. It will build momentum as it falls, and the momentum would carry it through the holes and keep it going more directly downhill rather than sliding side to side on the bumps. As we discussed in [Section 9.2](#Ch010_347-389_B9780443158889000108.xhtml#s0050), there is a version of regular (i.e., batch) gradient descent that aims to model this process, called *gradient descent with momentum*. This is sometimes referred to as the *heavy ball method*.

As with regular gradient descent, invoking momentum in SGD—sometimes called the *stochastic heavy ball method*—can help the optimization escape local optima and plateaus in the loss function. If the current gradient of the loss is ∇[**θ**]*L*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8711;</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi56.png), momentum is implemented by computing a moving average of the gradients and adding this moving average to the SGD updates. It updates the parameters by adding *Δ***θ** =  − *η*∇[**θ**]*L*(**θ**) + *α**Δ***θ**^(*o**l**d*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#951;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8711;</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">old</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi57.png), where *α* ∈ \[0, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mi>&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0,1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi58.png). Since the mini-batch approach operates on a small subset of the data, this averaging can allow information from other recently seen mini-batches to contribute to the current parameter update. A momentum value of 0.9 is often used as a starting point but it is common to hand-tune it, the learning rate, and the schedule used to modify the learning rate during the training process.

A variant of this method, called *Nesterov momentum*, uses the moving average of the gradients to “look ahead.” Instead of stepping to that point, the algorithm calculates the gradient at that look-ahead point and then uses this new gradient to take a step from the original position. Essentially the method is able to anticipate how the gradients would change and use that information to update its position instead.

 

#### Adaptive Gradient Methods

As we mentioned earlier, SGD uses a single learning rate for all parameters. Intuitively, some parameters might be relatively settled during training while others might need to change a lot, so some parameters could require different learning rates than others to converge quickly. If we could have a different learning rate for each parameter, the ones that have already converged could slow down their learning rates, while the ones that are still far off could move more quickly. If some of the features are sparse and occur rarely, we also want to move faster on their corresponding parameters when we do see them. The *AdaGrad (Adaptive Gradient)* algorithm aims to adaptively set learning rates for each parameter. In its practical implementation AdaGrad maintains a sum of the (elementwise) squares of past gradients and divides the learning rate of each dimension by the square root of the corresponding sum.

An advantage of AdaGrad is that it is relatively robust to the overall learning rate *η*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#951;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi59.png). However, it has a flaw in that its per-parameter learning rates get divided by larger and larger values, eventually slowing learning to a crawl. The *AdaDelta* algorithm is a variant of AdaGrad, which addresses this by instead using a moving average of the elementwise squares of the previous gradients so that the values to divide each dimension’s learning rate by don’t keep getting larger. AdaDelta also removes the learning rate hyperparameter *η*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#951;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi60.png), relieving the analyst of the burden of setting it. If the analyst prefers to have control over the learning rate, *RMSProp* is similar to AdaDelta (and was invented independently of it at around the same time) but it has a settable learning rate.

At the time of writing, the most popular optimizer for deep learning is *Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation)*, a variant of RMSProp that uses a moving average of past gradients for each parameter for the updates instead of the current gradients. (It also includes some terms to correct for a bias toward zero due to how it is initialized.)

When choosing between these learning algorithms, it is worth noting that some studies have found that SGD (with or without momentum) can have better generalization properties than these more sophisticated adaptive gradient methods in some cases. While the precise reasons for this are not well understood, there is a complex relationship between the learning algorithm and the local optima that it tends to find—in the ability (or inability) of the learning algorithm to escape certain local optima—and differences in this regard likely play a role. Intuitively, overfitting could also be part of the reason for this gap, perhaps the adaptive gradient methods fit *too* well to the training data. Nevertheless, the faster convergence of adaptive gradient methods makes them the method of choice in many deep learning applications. AdaGrad, AdaDelta, and RMSProp are precursors to Adam and may perform as well as it in some cases. They can be used fairly interchangeably. Adam typically performs as well as those methods, though there could be exceptions. It is a good default choice of optimizer. If feasible, a grid search over learning algorithms and their hyperparameters, measuring performance on a validation set, will reveal the best choice for the specific problem at hand.

 

### Regularization With Priors on Parameters

Many standard techniques for parameter regularization are applicable to deep networks. We mentioned earlier that *L*[2] regularization corresponding to a Gaussian prior on parameters has been used for neural networks under the name “weight decay.” As with logistic regression, such regularization is usually applied just to the weights in a network, not to the biases. Alternatively, a weighted combination of *L*[2] and *L*[1] regularization, *λ*[2]*R*[*L*[2]](**θ**) + *λ*[1]*R*[*L*[1]](**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#955;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#955;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi61.png), can be applied to the weights in a network, as in the elastic net model discussed in [Section 14.4](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#s0160). Although the loss functions used in deep learning may not generally be convex, such regularizers can nevertheless be implemented.

 

### Dropout

Dropout is a form of regularization that randomly deletes units and their connections during training, with the intention of reducing the degree to which hidden units coadapt and thus combat overfitting. It has been argued that this corresponds to sampling from an exponential number of networks with shared parameters from which some connections are missing. One then averages over them at test time by using the original network without any dropped-out connections but with scaled-down weights. If a unit is retained with probability *p* during training, its outgoing weights are rescaled or multiplied by a factor of *p* at test time. In effect, by performing dropout a neural network with *n* units can be made to behave like an ensemble of 2*^n* smaller networks.

One way to implement dropout is with a binary mask vector **m**^((*l*)) for each hidden layer *l* in the network; the dropped out version of **h**^((*l*)) masks out units from the original version using elementwise multiplication, **h**[*d*]^((*l*)) = **h**^((*l*)) ⊙ **m**^((*l*))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>&#8857;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi62.png). If the activation functions lead to diagonal gradient matrices, the backpropagation update is *Δ*^((*l*)) = **d**^((*l*)) ⊙ **m**^((*l*)) ⊙ (**W**^((*l* + 1))*Δ*^((*l* + 1)))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>&#8857;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>&#8857;</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi63.png).

 

### Batch Normalization

Batch normalization is a way of accelerating training and many studies have found it to be important to use to obtain state-of-the-art results on benchmark problems. With batch normalization each element of a layer in a neural network is normalized to zero mean and unit variance, based on its statistics within a mini-batch. This can change the network’s representational power, so each activation is given a learned scaling and shifting parameter. Mini-batch-based stochastic gradient descent is modified by calculating the mean *μ*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi64.png) and variance *σ*[*j*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi65.png) over the batch for each hidden unit *h[j]* in each layer and then normalizing the units, scaling them using the learned scaling parameter *γ*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#947;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi66.png) and shifting them by the learned shifting parameter *β*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#946;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi67.png):

$\\left. {\\widehat{h}}\_{j}\\leftarrow\\gamma\_{j}\\frac{h\_{j} - \\mu\_{j}}{\\sqrt{\\sigma\_{j}^{2} + \\varepsilon}} + \\beta\_{j}. \\right.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8592;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#947;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#956;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#949;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#946;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F00011Xsi68.png)

Of course, to update the scaling and shifting parameters one needs to backpropagate the gradient of the loss through these additional parameters.

 

### Parameter Initialization

The strategy used to initialize parameters before training commences can be deceptively important. Bias terms are often initialized to 0 but initializing the weight matrices can be tricky. For example, if they are initialized to all 0 s it can be shown that the tanh activation function will yield zero gradients. If the weights are all the same the hidden units will produce the same gradients and behave the same as each other, wasting the model’s capacity.

One solution is to initialize all elements of the weight matrix from a uniform distribution over the interval \[−*b*, *b*\]. Different methods have been proposed for selecting the value of *b*, often motivated by the idea that units with more inputs should have smaller weights. For example, for a given layer *l* one might scale *b* by the inverse of the square root of the dimensionality of **h**^((*l* − 1))(**x**)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi69.png), known as the “fan-in size.” Or one might incorporate the fan-out size as well.

The weight matrices of ReLUs have been successfully initialized using a zero-mean isotropic Gaussian distribution with standard deviation of 0.01.

 

### Early Stopping

[Chapter 9](#Ch010_347-389_B9780443158889000108.xhtml#Ch010_347-389_B9780443158889000108), “Extending instance-based and linear models,” mentioned that “early stopping” is a simple way of alleviating overfitting during training. Deep learning utilizes high-capacity architectures, which are susceptible to overfitting even when data is plentiful, and early stopping is standard practice even when other methods to reduce overfitting are employed, such as regularization and dropout. This is done by monitoring learning curves that plot the *average* loss for the training and validation sets as a function of epoch. The key is to find the point at which the validation set average loss begins to deteriorate.

[Fig. 10.4](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#f0025) plots a pair of training set and validation set curves, although with mini-batch–based stochastic gradient descent they are usually noisier. To combat this, model parameters can be retained over a window of recent updates to select the final version to be applied to the test set.

![Fig. 10.4 Typical learning curves for the training and validation sets. Credit: Christopher J. Pal](images/F00011Xf10-04-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 10.4](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#Bf0025) Typical learning curves for the training and validation sets. Credit: Christopher J. Pal

People often use one of the standard loss function formulations for neural network outputs simply because it is already integrated into software tools. However, the underlying goal of learning may be different—to minimize the classification error, or perhaps to optimize some combination of precision and recall. In these cases it is important to monitor the true evaluation metric as well as the average loss, to gain a clearer idea as to whether the model is overfitting the training set. Furthermore, it can be instructive to determine whether the model can classify the data perfectly by adding more capacity and stopping at the appropriate point.

While early stopping is an effective tool for preventing overfitting, a downside is that it muddies the relationship between the capacity of the model and the tendency of the system to overfit. If the model is trained to convergence then increasing model capacity (e.g., increasing the number of layers, or number of neurons per layer) increases the propensity to overfit and reduces the propensity to underfit. In contrast, with early stopping we can no longer be sure that these interventions will have the desired effect on mitigating over- or underfitting, complicating the hyperparameter selection process. Some experts eschew this technique for that reason.

 

### Unsupervised Pretraining

Unsupervised pretraining can be an effective way to both initialize and regularize a feedforward network, especially when the volume of labeled data is small relative to the model’s capacity. The general idea is to model the distribution of unlabeled data using a method that allows the parameters of the learned model to be somehow transferred to the network, or used to initialize or regularize it. We will return to the subject of unsupervised learning in [Section 10.4](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#s0140) and [Appendix D.3](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#s0040), and we will discuss an important variation of it, *self-supervised learning*, in [Section 11.2](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#s0030). However, the use of activation functions such as ReLUs that improve gradient flow in deep networks, along with good parameter initialization techniques, mitigates the need for sophisticated pretraining methods.

 

### Data Augmentation and Synthetic Transformations

Data augmentation can be critical for best results. As [Table 10.1](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#t0010) illustrates, augmenting even a large data set with transformed training data can increase performance significantly—and not just for deep architectures. A simple transformation for visual problems is simply to jiggle the image. If the object to be classified can be cropped out of a larger image, random bounding boxes can be placed around it, adding small translations in the vertical and horizontal directions. By reducing the cropped image larger displacements can be applied. Other translations such as rotation, scale change, and shearing are appropriate as well. In fact, there is a hierarchy of rigid transformations that increase in complexity as parameters are added. One augmentation strategy is to apply them to the original image and then crop a patch of given size out of the distorted result.

 

### Residual Connections

The trend toward deeper and deeper neural networks brings challenges in training. As we backpropagate the gradients in a very deep network, going backward through the layers from the output toward the input, the layers are further removed from the output and have smaller direct impacts on the loss. Consequently, their gradients typically get smaller, making it harder to learn them efficiently. This is called the *vanishing gradient* problem.

In an ideal world adding more layers would do no harm to training set performance. If some of the layers were unnecessary for prediction the model could simply make those extraneous layers be *identity mappings*; the output they produce is the same as the input; thus the network mimics a shallower one. However, in practice additional layers may hurt performance, even on the training set, since vanishing gradients make the model harder to train. It may well fail to learn even the simple identity mappings that would resolve this issue. Since the power and promise of neural networks is in deep models trained on big data, this impediment to training deep networks is particularly painful.

*Residual networks* (*ResNets*) are an architectural strategy that aims to address vanishing gradients and make it easier to learn identity mappings; they have been crucial to progress in fitting deeper networks than were previously feasible. They enabled the authors of the research, Kaiming He and colleagues from Microsoft Research, to win multiple computer vision contests in 2015. The key idea in residual networks is the *residual connection*—a connection between neurons that skips over a block of layers and outputs the identity mapping. This makes it easier to learn identity mappings, since it is already there by default and can be easily obtained by setting the weights of other (direct) connections to zero. Residual connections are an instance of the more general class of *skip connections*, a.k.a. *shortcut connections*, that skip over one or more layers and may or may not output the identity. Skip connections, including residual connections, also create shortened paths to the output layer, thereby mitigating vanishing gradients.

A block of layers with a residual connection around it is called a *residual module*. A *deep residual network* stacks multiple residual modules on each other to build the overall network. Following the original ResNet model in 2015, it is common for CNN models in computer vision (discussed later) to stack residual modules that each contain one or more of the typical sequences of layers in CNNs: convolution, followed by batch normalization, followed by a ReLU layer. Residual connections are also used in the transformer architecture (discussed in the next chapter).

 

## 10.3 Convolutional Neural Networks

CNNs are a special kind of feedforward network that has proven extremely successful for image analysis. When classifying images, filtering them—by applying a filter for edge detection—can provide a useful set of spatially organized features. Imagine now if one could learn many such filters jointly, along with the other parameters of the neural network. Each filter can be implemented by multiplying a relatively small spatial zone of the image by a set of weights and feeding the result to an activation function like those discussed earlier for vanilla feedforward networks. Because this filtering operation is simply repeated around the image using the same weights it can be implemented using so-called convolution operations. The result is a CNN, for which it is possible to learn both the filters and the classifier using gradient descent and the backpropagation algorithm.

In a CNN once an image has been filtered by several learnable filters each filter bank’s output is often aggregated across a small spatial region, using the average or maximum value. Aggregation can be performed within nonoverlapping regions, or using subsampling, yielding a lower-resolution layer of spatially organized features—a process that is sometimes referred to as “decimation.” This gives the model a degree of invariance to small differences as to exactly where a feature has been detected. For example, if aggregation uses the max operation, a feature is activated if it is detected anywhere in the pooling zone.

We have seen how synthetic transformations allowed deep feedforward networks to yield state-of-the-art performance in the MNIST evaluation, and that cropping small regions of an image can be a useful, easy-to-implement transformation. Although this can be applied to any classification technique, it is particularly effective for training CNNs. Random cropping positions can be used, or deterministic strategies such as cropping from the corners and center of the image can be. The same strategy can be used at test time, where the model’s predictions are averaged over crops from the test image. These networks are designed to have a certain degree of translational invariance but augmenting data through such global transformations can increase performance significantly.

[Fig. 10.5](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#f0030) shows a typical network structure. A smaller part of the original image is subjected to repeated phases of convolutional filtering, pooling, and decimation before being passed to a fully connected, nonconvolutional multilayer perceptron, which may have a number of hidden layers prior to making a final prediction.

![Fig. 10.5 Typical convolutional neural network architecture. Credit: Christopher J. Pal](images/F00011Xf10-05-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 10.5](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#Bf0030) Typical convolutional neural network architecture. Credit: Christopher J. Pal

CNNs are usually optimized using mini-batch–based stochastic gradient descent, and the practical discussion earlier about learning deep networks applies here as well. Resource issues related to the amount of central processing unit (CPU) vs. graphics processing unit (GPU) memory available are often important to consider, particularly when processing videos.

 

### The ImageNet Evaluation and Very Deep Convolutional Networks

The ImageNet challenge has been crucial in demonstrating the effectiveness of deep CNNs. The problem is to recognize object categories in typical imagery that one might find on the Internet. The 2012 ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) classification task was to classify imagery obtained from Flickr and other search engines into the correct one of 1000 possible object category classes. This task served as a standard benchmark for deep learning. The imagery was hand-labeled based on the presence or absence of an object belonging to these categories. There were 1.2 *million* images in the training set, with 732-1300 training images available per class. A random subset of 50,000 images was used as the validation set and 100,000 images were used for the test set, with 50 and 100 images per class, respectively.

Visual recognition methods not based on deep CNNs hit a plateau in performance on this benchmark. The “top-5 error” is the percentage of times that the target label does not appear among the five highest-probability predictions, and many methods cannot get below 25%. [Table 10.4](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#t0025) summarizes the performance of different CNN architectures as a function of network depth for the ImageNet challenge. Note that CNNs dramatically outperform the 25% plateau, and that increasing network depth can further improve performance. Smaller filters have been found to lead to superior results in deep networks; the ones with 19 and 152 layers use filters of size 3 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi70.png). The performance for human agreement has been measured at 5.1% top-5 error for ImageNet so deep CNNs are able to outperform people on this task.
