### Other Recurrent Network Architectures

A wide variety of other recurrent network architectures has been proposed. For example, the network given by [Eq. (10.1)](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#eqn1) can be used with rectified linear activation functions, using scaled versions of the identity matrix to initialize the recurrent weight matrix, and initializing biases to zero. The identity initialization means that error derivatives flow through the network unmodified. Initializing with smaller, scaled versions of the identity matrix has the effect of causing the model to forget longer range dependencies. This approach is known as an identity recurrent neural network (*IRNN*). Another possibility is to simplify LSTM networks by dispensing with separate memory cells and using gated recurrent units (*GRUs*). For some problems GRUs can provide performance comparable with LSTMs but with a lower memory requirement.

Recurrent networks can be made bidirectional, propagating information in both directions; [Fig. 10.14A](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#f0075) shows the general structure. Bidirectional networks have been used for a wide variety of applications, including protein secondary structure prediction and handwriting recognition. Modern software tools determine the gradients required for learning via backpropagation automatically by manipulating computation graphs.

![Fig. 10.14 Recurrent neural networks: (A) bidirectional, (B) encoder-decoder. Credit: Christopher J. Pal](images/F00011Xf10-14-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. 10.14 Recurrent neural networks: (A) bidirectional, (B) encoder-decoder. Credit: Christopher J. Pal

[Fig. 10.14B](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#f0075) shows an “encoder-decoder” network. Such networks allow the creation of fixed-length vector representations for variable-length inputs and can use the fixed-length encoding to generate another variable-length sequence as the output. This is particularly useful for machine translation, where the input is a string in one language and the output is the corresponding string in another language. Given enough data, a deep encoder-decoder architecture such as that of [Fig. 10.15](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#f0080) can yield results that compete with those of systems that have been hand-engineered over decades of research. The connectivity structure means that partial computations in the model can flow through the graph in a wave, illustrated by the darker nodes in the figure. We discuss machine translation further in [Sections 11.2](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#s0030) and [11.4](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#s0090).

![Fig. 10.15 A deep encoder-decoder recurrent network. Credit: Christopher J. Pal](images/F00011Xf10-15-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 10.15](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#Bf0080) A deep encoder-decoder recurrent network. Credit: Christopher J. Pal

 

## 10.6 Further Reading and Bibliographic Notes

The backpropagation algorithm has been known in close to its current form since Werbos’ (1974) PhD thesis; in his extensive literature review of deep learning, [Schmidhuber (2015)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur476) traces key elements of the algorithm back even further. He also traces the idea of “deep networks” back to the work of [Ivakhnenko and Lapa (1965)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur288). Modern CNNs are widely acknowledged as having their roots with the “neocognitron” proposed by [Fukushima (1980)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur199). However, the work of [LeCun, Bottou, Bengio, and Haffner (1998)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur358) on the LeNet convolutional network architecture has been extremely influential.

The popularity of neural network techniques has gone through several cycles. While some factors are social, there are important technical reasons behind the trends. A single-layer neural network cannot solve the XOR problem, a failing that was derided by [Minsky and Papert (1969)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur396) which, as mentioned in [Section 4.10](#Ch004_91-164_B9780443158889000054_a.xhtml#s0200), stymied neural network development until the mid-1980s. However, it is well known that networks with one additional layer can approximate any function ([Cybenko, 1989](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur117); [Hornik, 1991](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur276)), and Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams’ (1986) influential work repopularized neural network methods for a while. However, by the early 2000s they had fallen out of favor again. Indeed, the organizers of NeurIPS, the *Neural Information Processing Systems* conference, which was (and still is) widely considered to be the premier forum for neural network research, found that the presence of the term “neural networks” in the title was highly correlated with the paper’s rejection!—a fact that is underscored by citation analysis of key neural network papers during this period. The recent resurgence of interest in deep learning really does feel like a “revolution.”

It is known that most complex Boolean functions require an exponential number of two-step logic gates for their representation ([Wegener, 1987](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur557)). The solution appears to be greater depth. According to [Bengio (2009)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur30), the evidence strongly suggests that “functions that can be compactly represented with a depth-*k* architecture could require a very large number of elements to be represented by a shallower architecture.”

Stochastic gradient descent methods go back at least as far as [Robbins and Monro (1951)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur459). [Bottou (2012)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur54) is an excellent source of tips and tricks for learning with stochastic gradient descent, while [Bengio (2012)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur31) gives further practical recommendations for training deep networks. Adaptive gradient methods, which adapt the learning rates for each parameter separately, have improved and accelerated DNN training for many models. These include AdaGrad ([Duchi et al., 2011](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur147)), AdaDelta ([Zeiler, 2012](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur589)), and RMSProp ([Tieleman and Hinton, 2012](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur526)), culminating in Adam ([Kingma and Ba, 2012](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur309)). On the other hand, [Zhou et al. (2020)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur597) provided a theoretical explanation of why SGD frequently generalizes better than Adam.

Bergstra and [Bengio (2012)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur31) give empirical and theoretical justification for the use of random search for hyperparameter settings. [Snoek, Larochelle, and Adams (2012)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur500) propose the use of Bayesian learning methods to infer the next hyperparameter setting to explore, and their Spearmint software package performs Bayesian optimizations of both deep network hyperparameters and general ML algorithm hyperparameters.

Good parameter initialization can be critical for the success of neural networks, as discussed in LeCun et al.’s (1998) classic work and the more recent work of [Glorot and Bengio (2010)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur220). Krizhevsky et al.’s (2012) convolutional network of ReLUs initialized weights using 0-mean isotropic Gaussian distributions with a standard deviation of 0.01, and initialized the biases to 1 for most hidden convolutional layers as well as the model’s hidden fully connected layers. They observed that this initialization accelerated the early phase of learning by providing ReLUs with positive inputs.

The origins of dropout and more details about it can be found in [Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, and Salakhutdinov (2014)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur507). [Ioffe and Szegedy (2015)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur285) proposed batch normalization and give more details on its implementation. [Glorot and Bengio (2010)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur220) cover various weight matrix initialization heuristics and how the concepts of fan-in and fan-out can be used to justify them for networks with different kinds of activation functions.

The MNIST data set containing 28 × 28<mml:math><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>28</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi151.png)\-pixel images of handwritten digits has been popular for exploring ideas in the deep learning research community. However, it was the ImageNet challenge, with a variety of much higher resolutions, that catapulted deep learning into the spotlight in 2012 ([Russakovsky et al., 2015](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur466)). The winning entry from the University of Toronto processed the images at a resolution of 256 × 256<mml:math><mml:mn>256</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>256</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi152.png) pixels. Up till then, CNNs were simply incapable of processing such large volumes of imagery at such high resolutions in a reasonable amount of time. Krizhevsky et al.’s (2012) dramatic win used GPU-accelerated CNNs. This spurred a great deal of development, reflected in rapid subsequent advances in visual recognition performance on the ImageNet benchmark.

In the 2014 challenge the Oxford Visual Geometry Group and a team from Google pushed performance even further using much deeper architectures—16 to 19 weight layers for the Oxford group, using tiny 3 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi153.png) convolutional filters ([Simonyan and Zisserman, 2014](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur496)); 22 layers, with filters up to 5 × 5<mml:math><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi154.png) for the Google team (Szegedy, et al., 2015). The 2015 ImageNet challenge was won by a team from Microsoft Research Asia using an architecture with 152 layers (He, et al., 2015), using tiny 3 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F00011Xsi155.png) filters combined with shortcut connections that skip over layers; they also perform pooling and decimation after multiple layers of convolution have been applied.

[Hinton and Salakhutdinov (2006)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur264) noted that it has been known since the 1980s that deep autoencoders, optimized through backpropagation, could be effective for nonlinear dimensionality reduction. The key limiting factors were the small size of the data sets used to train them, coupled with low computation speeds, plus the old problem of local minima. By 2006 data sets such as the MNIST digits and the 20 Newsgroups collection were large enough, and computers were fast enough, for Hinton and Salakhutdinov to present compelling results illustrating the advantages of deep autoencoders over principal component analysis. Their experimental work used generative pretraining to initialize weights to avoid problems with local minima.

[Graves et al. (2009)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur231) demonstrate how recurrent neural networks are particularly effective at handwriting recognition, while [Graves, Mohamed, and Hinton (2013)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur232) apply recurrent neural networks to speech. The form of gradient clipping presented in [Section 10.5](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#s0150) was proposed by [Pascanu, Mikolov, and Bengio (2013)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur428).

The vanishing gradient problem was formally identified as a key issue for learning in deep networks by Sepp Hochreiter in his diploma thesis ([Hochreiter, 1991](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur269)). The impact in terms of the difficulty of learning long-term dependencies is discussed by [Bengio, Simard, and Frasconi (1994)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur33). Further analysis of the issue is given by [Hochreiter, Bengio, Frasconi, and Schmidhuber (2001)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur270).

[Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur271) is the seminal paper on the “long short-term memory” architecture for recurrent neural networks; our explanation follows Graves and Schmidhuber’s (2005) formulation. Greff, Srivastava, Koutník, Steunebrink, and Schmidhuber’s (2015) paper “LSTM: A search space odyssey” explored a wide range of variants and found that: (1) none of them significantly outperformed the standard LSTM architecture; and (2) forget gates and the output activation function were the most critical components. Forget gates were added by [Gers, Schmidhuber, and Cummins (2000)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur212).

IRNNs were proposed by [Le, Jaitly, and Hinton (2015)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur212), while [Chung, Gulcehre, Cho, and Bengio (2014)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur100) proposed gated recurrent units and [Schuster and Paliwal (1997)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur481) proposed bidirectional recurrent neural networks. [Chen and Chaudhari (2004)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur92) used bidirectional networks for protein structure prediction, while [Graves et al. (2009)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur231) used them for handwriting recognition. [Cho et al. (2014)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur98) used encoder-decoder networks for machine translation, while [Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le (2014)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur514) proposed deep encoder-decoder networks and used them with massive quantities of data. Residual connections, proposed by [He et al. (2016)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur257), were a substantial architectural advance that eased the training of much deeper neural networks.

For further accounts of advances in deep learning and a more extensive history of the field, consult the reviews of [LeCun, Bengio, and Hinton (2015)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur357), [Bengio (2009)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur30), and [Schmidhuber (2015)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur476).

 

## 10.7 Deep Learning Software and Network Implementations

Deep learning software frameworks make it easy to develop and train deep neural network models. These frameworks typically include high-level APIs (“application programming interfaces”) that allow a model to be specified with a few lines of code; automatic differentiation features that remove the manual burden of deriving gradients, GPU support, implementations of advanced learning algorithms and deep learning architectures, and more. They generally represent the data flow in a deep neural network (or other computation) as a *computation graph*, in which the mathematical operations at each stage of the computation—and their relation to each other—are encoded as a graph. By storing the graph in advance, computations can be optimized, and backpropagation can be automatically performed with gradients flowing through the graph in the “backward pass” in the opposite direction to the original “forward pass” computations. Many of these frameworks are open source and freely available.

The most popular deep learning software platforms are currently TensorFlow and PyTorch. Historically, TensorFlow, which is developed mainly by Google, was generally viewed as better for creating deployed systems, while PyTorch, which is developed mainly by the Facebook AI Research group, was considered by many to be better for academic research due to advantages in development and debugging. The gaps between the two platforms have substantially closed, however, with both platforms addressing their perceived weaknesses vs their competition in their recent versions. Now, both platforms are highly capable for both the deployment and development phases.

 

### TensorFlow and Keras

TensorFlow is a C++ and Python-based software library for the types of numerical computation typically associated with deep learning ([Abadi et al., 2016](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur1)). It uses dataflow graphs to represent the ways in which multidimensional data arrays communicate between one another. These multidimensional arrays are referred to as “tensors.” TensorFlow also supports symbolic differentiation and execution on multiple GPUs. It was released in 2015 and is available under the Apache 2.0 license. In earlier versions building DNN models in TensorFlow involved first explicitly specifying a computation graph and then starting a session that the model is run in. Now, in TensorFlow version 2, a high-level API, Keras, is more tightly integrated into TensorFlow, allowing the developer to focus on the model rather than its underlying graph, and it now defaults to an eager execution mode, which obviates the need to deal with sessions and aids debugging.

Keras is a deep learning library that allows users to specify deep neural network models with simple Python code. Keras emphasizes its easy-to-use interface, and it requires another deep learning framework as a backend. Although Keras previously temporarily only supported TensorFlow, it currently also supports PyTorch and JAX backends.

 

### PyTorch

PyTorch is a Python ML and deep learning framework. It is based on the Torch library, an open-source ML library built using C and a high-level scripting language known as Lua ([Collobert, Kavukcuoglu, and Farabet, 2011](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur108)), but was largely rewritten in Python. Similarly to TensorFlow, it uses multidimensional array data structures, supports various basic numerical linear algebra manipulations, and has a neural network package with modules that permit the typical forward and backward methods needed for training neural networks. It also supports automatic differentiation. PyTorch uses *dynamic computation graphs*, also known as a *define-by-run* approach, in which the computation graph can change during execution. This is useful when processing data that can vary in size (e.g., text documents), and it simplifies debugging since the code is run when its corresponding line is executed, enabling more timely error messages. It also made coding in PyTorch closer to coding in native Python, making it more intuitive to code in. Historically, this was an advantage of PyTorch in terms of ease of use over TensorFlow, which traditionally used static computation graphs. However, as of version 2.0 TensorFlow has an “eager execution” mode, essentially the same as dynamic computation graphs, which mitigates this. Since this mode is optional, TensorFlow 2 users can choose whether to use it or stick to static computation graphs, which are faster.

 

### Other Packages

While TensorFlow, Keras, and PyTorch are currently the most popular deep learning frameworks, other options exist, including:

*   • The **Computational Network Toolkit (CNTK)** is a C++ library for manipulating computational networks ([Yu et al., 2014](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur583)). It was produced by Microsoft Research but has been released under a permissive license. It has been popular for speech and language processing but also supports convolutional networks of the type used for images. It supports execution on multiple machines and using multiple GPUs.
*   • **Caffe** is a C++ and Python-based BSD-licensed CNN library ([Jia et al., 2014](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur290)). It has a clean and extensible design that made it a popular alternative to the original open-source implementation of Krizhevsky et al.’s (2012) famous AlexNet, which won the 2012 ImageNet challenge. Facebook developed an extension to it called Caffe2 but it was merged into PyTorch.
*   • **Deeplearning4j** is a Java-based open-source deep learning library available under the Apache 2.0 license. It uses a multidimensional array class and provides linear algebra and matrix manipulation support similar to that provided by NumPy.
*   • **Lasagne** is a lightweight Python library built on top of Theano that simplifies the creation of neural network layers. Similarly, Keras is a Python library that runs on top of either Theano or TensorFlow ([Chollet, 2015](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur99)). It allows one to quickly define a network architecture in terms of layers and also includes functionality for image and text preprocessing.
*   • The **NVIDIA CUDA® Deep Neural Network library (cuDNN)** is a highly optimized GPU library for NVIDIA units that allows deep networks to be trained more quickly. It can dramatically accelerate the performance of a deep network and is often called by the other packages mentioned previously.
*   • **JAX** is another recent framework from Google, presently still under development and research, which can automatically differentiate native Python and NumPy functions.
*   • **Theano** was a pioneering open-source deep learning platform that is no longer under active development due to stiff competition from the platforms developed in industry, which also poached much of its development talent. A version of Theano lives on as **PyTensor**, the computational backend behind the probabilistic programming language **PyMC3**.
*   • **MXNet** was an open-source deep learning framework developed by the Apache Software Foundation but which is no longer under active development. It emphasized flexibility, speed, and scalability, and it had support for eight programming languages: Python, Scala, Julia, Clojure, Java, C++, R, and Perl.

 

## 10.8 WEKA Implementations

Deep learning can be implemented in WEKA using three methods:

*   • With the wrapper classifier for the third-party *DeepLearningForJ* package that is available in the *deepLearningForJ* package.
*   • Using the MLRClassifier from the *RPlugin* package to exploit deep learning implementations in R.
*   • By accessing Python-based deep learning libraries using the *PyScript* package.

# Chapter 11 Advanced deep learning methods

 

## Abstract

Deep learning technologies have revolutionized the fields of artificial intelligence, machine learning, computer vision, and natural language processing, and the effects are beginning to impact our daily lives. In this chapter, we overview advanced and recent deep learning methodologies, including generative deep learning (GANs, VAEs, diffusion models), and models for natural language processing beginning with word2vec and building up to transformer language models. We also discuss other important deep learning topics including adversarial examples, knowledge distillation, and deep reinforcement learning.

 

### Key Words

Deep learning; generative AI; natural language processing; word embeddings; transformer language models; BERT; GPT; knowledge distillation; deep reinforcement learning

In the machine learning (ML) community in the early 2000s, there was a running joke that “neural networks are the second-best solution to every problem.” This is no longer the case, as presently these methods, rebranded as “deep learning,” are now the best method for most ML tasks and problem domains. Moreover, deep learning methods have pushed back the boundary of what is understood to be possible for machines to do, particularly in their ability to *create* new things, a capability that was previously only associated with humans.

In this chapter, we continue our discussion of deep learning, diving into more recent and advanced techniques. We begin by discussing deep learning methods for generative AI, particularly those that can generate high-quality and compelling “AI art” works, as well as realistic images, video, audio, and more. We then shift our focus to deep learning methods for natural language processing (NLP), beginning with word embedding models and building toward modern transformer-based language models. Finally, we discuss other important advanced topics including adversarial examples, knowledge distillation, and deep reinforcement learning.

 

## 11.1 Generative AI via Deep Learning

Models that can generate artificial data are called, quite naturally, *generative models*. This term is in direct contrast to models that do not generate, but only predict, normally in a supervised fashion, which are called *discriminative models*. While there is currently a lot of excitement around generative models that are based on deep neural networks, probabilistic models can be generative too (topic models, for example. See [Chapter 14](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157), “Advanced probabilistic methods”). Here, we focus on the neural network kind of generative model. These models have impressed with their ability to generate realistic synthetic images, audio, video, text, and more. Having reached the public consciousness, the field has adopted the public’s preferred nomenclature, and these generative ML models are now called *generative AI*. The term nevertheless seems apt, since these methods now seem to *artificially* imitate creativity, a property we normally associate with *intelligence*.

 

### Generative Adversarial Networks

As we will discuss further in [Chapter 15](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169), “Moving on: applications and their consequences,” deep neural networks can now be used to generate beautiful artworks. They are already winning art contests, and generally causing artists to worry that they might be out of a job soon. They can even make many unique images that we might dream up—limited only by our imaginations—such as a chair in the shape of an avocado or a flying elephant; the sky is the limit. It really feels like we are living in the future sometimes.

*Generative Adversarial Networks* (*GANs*) are a classic and influential way to accomplish this. GANs are “adversarial” in that they are trained by playing a competitive game with themselves. Although they are no longer the only game in town when it comes to generative AI (pun intended), GANs remain a fundamental and influential approach. It is important to note that even though GANs are commonly associated with image data, there is nothing in their architecture that prevents them from being applied to other kinds of data. For example, GANs can be used to generate audio data including speech and music, as well as video and three-dimensional shapes, and even to propose candidate drug molecules.

GANs consist of two neural networks that compete with each other: the *generator* network and the *discriminator* network. The generator network tries to create realistic data that are similar to those in the training data. The discriminator network is a classifier that tries to distinguish between the real and generated data. Although the discriminator is not directly involved in the generation process, it provides the “signal” that is used to train the generator, by teaching it to produce artificial data that is indistinguishable from the real data.

The generator takes as input a randomized vector *z*<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si1.png). For example, each entry in the vector could be drawn from a standard normal distribution. This can be thought of as a point in a latent space. The generator, a deep neural network, maps the given point *z*<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si2.png) to a corresponding artificial data point *x*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si3.png), hopefully, a realistic one. The discriminator, also a deep neural network, is a probabilistic classifier that takes a data point as input and predicts class probabilities, indicating the likelihood that the data point is real (i.e., from the training data) or fake (i.e., created by the generator).

The two neural networks are trained in an iterative procedure, playing out the game in which they compete. In each iteration the two networks are updated in turn. The generator is trained to create data that “fools” the discriminator; that is, the discriminator cannot tell it apart from the real data. The discriminator is trained to detect the “forgeries” made by the generator. You can think of this as the two networks trying to defeat each other, or if you prefer a more friendly metaphor, you can think of them as “teaching” each other to do better in the next iteration, which is the practical reason why this procedure succeeds. Regardless of how you think about it, the overall training process for generator *G*<mml:math><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si4.png) and discriminator D can be formalized as a minimax game with a value function *V*(*G, D*):

$\\min\\limits\_{G}{\\max\\limits\_{D}\\mathit{V}\\mathit{G},\\mathit{D} = {E\_{x \\sim \\text{real\\ data}}\\left\\lbrack {\\log D\\left( x \\right)} \\right\\rbrack + E\_{\\overset{\\sim}{x} \\sim \\text{generator's\\ data}}\\left\\lbrack {\\log\\left( {1 - D\\left( \\overset{\\sim}{x} \\right)} \\right)} \\right\\rbrack}}.$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">G</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>max</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">V</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">G</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">D</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8764;</mml:mo><mml:mtext>real data</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>&#8764;</mml:mo><mml:mtext>generator's data</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">D</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000121si5.png)

Here, *D*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si6.png) is the discriminator’s predicted probability that data point *x*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si7.png) is a real data point from the dataset. The min player, the generator, tries to minimize this function while the discriminator tries to maximize it. In each iteration, a minibatch of data is drawn from the dataset, and a minibatch of generated data is sampled from the generator. Based on these data, the two networks are updated via minibatch stochastic gradient updates (or Adam, etc.) while holding the other network fixed. See [Fig. 11.1](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#f0010) for an illustration.

![Fig. 11.1 Generative adversarial networks. Credit: James Foulds](images/F000121f11-01-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 11.1](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#Bf0010) Generative adversarial networks. Credit: James Foulds

Although conceptually clear, GANs can be tricky to get to work well in practice as they are prone to several instability issues. One such issue is *mode collapse*, in which the generation focuses only on a small high-probability part of the space (e.g., one mode in a multimodal likelihood surface). For example, it might only generate “1” digits and not the other nine digits on the Mixed National Institute of Standards and Technology (MNIST) dataset. Another issue is *vanishing gradients* due to neuron saturation in the discriminator. An alternative GAN formulation, called the Wasserstein GAN (WGAN), can help improve the stability and reliability of GAN training. While the original GAN can be interpreted as optimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the generated and real data, the WGAN optimizes the Wasserstein divergence, also known as the earthmover distance, which has been argued to have nicer properties for optimization in this setting. The WGAN replaces the discriminator with a “*critic*,” also denoted *D*<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si8.png), which produces a real-valued score instead of a class probability, where higher scores correspond to more realistic data points. The critic aims for a big gap in its scores between the real data and the generated data. The minimax game formulation becomes:

$\\min\\limits\_{G}{\\max\\limits\_{D}{E\_{x \\sim \\text{real data}}\\left\\lbrack {D\\left( x \\right)} \\right\\rbrack - E\_{\\overset{\\sim}{x} \\sim \\text{generator's\\ data}}\\left\\lbrack \\left( {D\\left( \\overset{\\sim}{x} \\right)} \\right) \\right\\rbrack}}.$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">G</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>max</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8764;</mml:mo><mml:mtext>real&#8200;data</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">D</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>&#8764;</mml:mo><mml:mtext>generator's data</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">D</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000121si9.png)

Important and useful variations of GANs include *conditional GANs*, which generate their output conditional on some input data, and *style transfer* models, which can generate an alternate version of an image with different stylistic properties, such as being painted by a different artist, or a photo being taken in a different season, and so on.

 

### Variational Auto-Encoders

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are an alternative to GANs that are also a powerful approach to generating many types of realistic data using neural networks. While GANs try to directly learn how to generate realistic samples, VAEs do some probabilistic modeling and inference along the way. This gives us a more explicit representation of the data distribution according to the model. It may also give us more control if we want to meaningfully alter the distribution. On the other hand, an assumed probabilistic model is by definition an assumption about the data that may or may not be accurate, useful, or appropriate.

VAEs can be understood either from the perspective of neural networks, or the perspective of probabilistic models. From the neural network perspective, VAEs can be understood as having an autoencoder architecture, with an encoder network and a decoder network. The encoder maps a data point *x*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si10.png) to a latent embedding representation *z*<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si11.png), while the decoder reconstructs the data by mapping *z*<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si12.png) back to *x*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si13.png). However, rather than producing a single value for each of these quantities like ordinary autoencoders do, the encoder and decoder networks produce probability distributions *q*[*θ*](*z*,|,*x*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si14.png) over the latent representations and *p*[*ϕ*](*x*,|,*z*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#981;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si15.png), respectively. Here, *θ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si16.png) is the parameters for the encoder and *ϕ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#981;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si17.png) is the parameters for the decoder. The loss function for a VAE is:

*L*(*x*[*i*];*θ*,*ϕ*) =  − *E*[*z* ∼ *q*[*θ*](*z*|*x*[*i*])]\[log*p*[*ϕ*](*x*[*i*]|*z*)\] + *K**L*(*q*[*θ*](*z*,|,*x*[*i*])||*p*(*z*)).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">L</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#981;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8764;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">|</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#981;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mtext mathvariant="normal">|</mml:mtext><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">KL</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mtext>|</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">||</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000121si18.png)

We can interpret the first term as the negative log-likelihood or as a reconstruction loss, encouraging a good fit to the data, and the second term as a regularizer, preventing overfitting by encouraging the encoder’s distribution to be similar to the prior distribution, usually a standard normal distribution. The KL-divergence is an information theoretic quantity that measures how much information is lost (in units of nats) when using *q*<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si19.png) to represent *p*<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si20.png). It is one measure of how close *q*<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si21.png) is to *p*<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si22.png). In the case of the VAE, the encoder receives a penalty in the loss based on how different it is from a standard normal distribution. We can train this model via backpropagation, although it requires a “*reparameterization trick*” to backpropagate through random samples.

We can also alternatively interpret VAEs from a probabilistic modeling perspective. Forget for a moment our earlier interpretation of the VAE based on neural networks, including all the variables we have defined. Starting from scratch, we will reach the same place from another perspective. Suppose we want to learn a probabilistic model *P*(*x*,*z*)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si23.png), where *x*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si24.png) is the data and *z*<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si25.png) is latent variables associated with the data. We model *x*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si26.png) as being generated based on *z*<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si27.png); that is, we write *p*(*x*,*z*) = *p*(*x*|*z*)*p*(*z*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mtext>|</mml:mtext><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si28.png). This corresponds to the following assumed generative process:

*   • For each data point *x*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si29.png) 
    
    *   • Draw latent variables *z*[*i*] ∼ *p*(*z*)<mml:math><mml:mstyle displaystyle="true"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8764;</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mstyle></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si30.png)
    *   • Draw data point *x*[*i*] ∼ *p*(*x*|*z*)<mml:math><mml:mstyle displaystyle="true"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8764;</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mtext>|</mml:mtext><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mstyle></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si31.png).
    

VAEs represent these two distributions via neural networks (i.e., the encoder *q*[*θ*](*z*,|,*x*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si32.png) and the decoder *p*(*x*|*z*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mtext>|</mml:mtext><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si33.png)) and then learns them from data. It does this using *variational inference*, which refers to the general technique of solving a probabilistic inference problem by casting it as an optimization problem (see [Appendix A.2](#TableA1_617-636_B9780443158889000212.xhtml#s0050) for more information). For example, suppose wanted to find a particular target distribution of interest, *p*(*z*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si34.png). Variational inference recasts this task as “find the distribution *q*(*z*)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si35.png) that is closest to *p*(*z*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si36.png) in terms of some metric, such as KL-divergence.” If there were no additional constraints, solving this optimization problem would find the target distribution *p*(*z*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si37.png), since *p*(*z*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si38.png) is indeed the distribution that is closest to itself.

In practice, we typically cannot solve the optimization problem without approximating it by making simplifying assumptions. To make this search problem feasible, constraints or limitations are normally added to simplify the problem in some way. An approach that was popular in the past was to assume that all the variables in *z*<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si39.png) are independent random variables. This leads to tractable updates, and the approach is called *mean-field variational inference*. However, the independence assumption is often highly detrimental to performance. Instead, VAEs use a more powerful and accurate simplifying assumption instead; the distributions we want to learn can be represented by neural networks. The objective function for the VAE is equivalent to minimizing the KL-divergence between the probability of the latent variables, calculated under Bayes’ rule, and the approximation from the neural network model. This strategy is computationally practical and generally performs much better than mean field variational inference due to its more flexible modeling assumption.

 

### Diffusion Models

Currently, most of the popular AI art generation systems such as Dall-E 2 and Dall-E 3, Stable Diffusion, and Midjourney use *diffusion models*, another generative AI technique. Recall how in GANs, random noise vectors *z*<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si40.png), which are usually Gaussian generated, are transformed by a neural network into the desired synthetic data *x*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si41.png) such as images. The decoder in a VAE, which maps a latent encoding vector *z*<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si42.png) (also usually with a Gaussian prior) to a realistic data point *x*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si43.png), can also be thought of as performing a similar operation. Diffusion models envision a physical process in which real data is turned into random noise. The process of turning noise into realistic data, like GANs and VAEs do, is modeled as the reverse of this process and is estimated via deep neural networks. Inspired by statistical physics, this approach leads to a flexible yet tractable class of generative models that admit the training of very deep neural networks and have proven effective at image generation tasks.

More concretely, consider a process in which our training data points (e.g., images) are repeatedly perturbed by adding Gaussian noise to them. Eventually, the perturbed data points would be so noisy that they become completely random Gaussian noise. This type of process is called *diffusion*. In a diffusion model, the model component that does diffusion, perturbing a training sample *x*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si44.png) via *T*<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si45.png) steps *x*[1], *x*[2]…, *x*[*T*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si46.png) is called the *forward process*, and the noise transition model is denoted *q*(*x*[*t*]|*x*[*t* − 1])<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mtext>|</mml:mtext><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si47.png). This process bears some superficial resemblance to the encoder in a VAE in that it maps a data point to a Gaussian-distributed point, but it differs in that it consists of a prespecified noise distribution with no learned parameters (except perhaps, optionally, the variance of the noise) while a VAE’s encoder is a deep neural network.

Now, suppose we want to “undo” the diffusion process to recover the real data, or generate other realistic data points from the same distribution. Undoing noise is called, quite naturally, *denoising*. The denoising component in a diffusion model is called the *reverse process* since it undoes the forward process and is denoted *p*[*θ*](*x*[*t* − 1],|,*x*[*t*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si48.png). Here, *θ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si49.png) represents the parameters of the corresponding neural networks, *denoising autoencoder* models *ϵ*[*θ*](*x*[*t*],*t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si50.png), which predicts the mean *μ*[*θ*](*x*[*t*],*t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si51.png) and covariance *Σ*[*θ*](*x*[*t*],*t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si52.png) of the reverse transitions at each step *t*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si53.png) to undo the noise,

*p*[*θ*](*x*[*t* − 1]|*x*[*t*]) = *N*(*x*[*t* − 1];*μ*[*θ*](*x*[*t*],*t*),*Σ*[*θ*](*x*[*t*],*t*)).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">t</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo mathvariant="script">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">N</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">t</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000121si54.png)

The denoising autoencoders are typically either transformer models or U-Net models (a specialized convolutional neural network \[CNN\]-based architecture originally designed for image segmentation). The model can be trained by optimizing a variational lower bound via stochastic gradient descent. Finally, with the reverse process in hand, we can generate each novel data point by drawing an *x*[*T*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si55.png) from the initial noise distribution and denoising it by applying the successive transitions to sample the intermediate points until we obtain a new data point $\\widehat{x\_{0}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#710;</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si56.png) in the final step. See [Fig. 11.2](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#f0015) for an illustration of diffusion models.

![Fig. 11.2 Illustration of diffusion models. Credit: James Foulds](images/F000121f11-02-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 11.2](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#Bf0015) Illustration of diffusion models. Credit: James Foulds

Diffusion models were originally applied to generate images directly at the pixel level; however, this is extremely expensive, currently taking hundreds of graphics processing unit (GPU) days to train. A substantial advance was to apply them to points in the latent space of an autoencoder model instead of in the pixel space. This approach essentially compresses the images, reducing the size of the data that the model must work with and in turn reducing the size of the model. Such *latent diffusion models (LDMs)* require vastly reduced computational resources to produce high-resolution images. They also provide a convenient mechanism for generating images based on a textual prompt, allowing users to direct an AI art system to create the images they desire. This is accomplished by modifying the denoising autoencoder models *ϵ*[*θ*](*x*[*t*],*t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si57.png) that implement the reverse process in each step *t*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si58.png) to be *conditional denoising autoencoders* *ϵ*[*θ*](*x*[*t*],*t*,*τ*[*θ*](*y*))<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#1013;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#964;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si59.png) that include learned embeddings *τ*[*θ*](*y*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#964;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfenced open="(" close=")"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si60.png) of the prompt *y*<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000121si61.png) as inputs created via a BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers) model.

 

## 11.2 Introduction to Natural Language Processing and Large Language Models

NLP, a rich field of study with a long history, is an active application area for deep learning. As the name suggests, NLP investigates the processing of *natural language*, that is, language that is written or spoken naturally by humans. Since text is the primary medium by which humans communicate online, and since humans are good at understanding text but are expensive to employ for such tasks, NLP technologies have clear financial motivations in helping businesses understand and communicate with their (potential) customers quickly, cheaply, automatically, and at scale. The terms “*text mining*” ([Section 15.5](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#s0030)) and “*computational linguistics*” are roughly synonyms for NLP arising from the data mining and linguistics communities, respectively, differing mainly in their connotations associated with the values prioritized by those communities rather than in the technical approaches used. Text mining suggests an emphasis on the practical aspects of NLP and the goal of finding patterns in text data that inform industry applications, while computational linguistics suggests a focus on the study of language and a concordance with linguistic theories and principles.

Deep learning methods are presently the dominant methodology for most NLP tasks, but this was not always the case. Probabilistic ML techniques (see [Chapter 13](#Ch014_485-514_B9780443158889000145.xhtml#Ch014_485-514_B9780443158889000145), “Probabilistic methods: fundamentals,” and [Chapter 14](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157), “Advanced probabilistic methods”) are a powerful approach for performing NLP tasks that were popular for several decades, supplanting the earlier symbolic rule-based approaches and traditional supervised ML methodologies until deep learning methods became ascendant, particularly from 2017 onward, with the rise of transformer-based language models. As we will see in [Chapter 14](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157), “Advanced probabilistic methods,” latent semantic analysis (LSA) and latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA^b) permit exploratory topic analysis of document collections. More recently, it has been observed that neural language modeling techniques can perform significantly better than LSA for preserving relationships among words; moreover, LDA^b also has difficulty scaling to truly massive data. Word embedding models such as *word2vec* and *GloVe*, which learn to represent dictionary words with vectors that encode their semantic meaning, were a major advance in neural approaches to NLP circa 2013. These simple models, which we discuss later, use a shallow neural network architecture, but form the basis for more sophisticated and powerful deep learning methods for NLP such as transformer-based language models.

Inspired by similar successes in computer vision with deep learning models such as CNNs (e.g., AlexNet), which achieved a substantial boost in performance on ImageNet benchmark tasks in 2012 via deep learning alone, the NLP field set about developing equally successful deep learning models in their discipline. Although the benefits of deep learning came more slowly than in computer vision, the goal of revolutionizing NLP via deep learning has now been realized. Large neural networks are being applied to tasks ranging from sentiment classification and translation to dialog and question answering, to translating between languages from scratch, and beyond to startlingly realistic chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT. Transformer-based language models such as *BERT* and the *generative pretrained transformer* (*GPT*) *class of models* currently obtain state-of-the-art performance across the vast majority of NLP tasks and have been used to create chatbots such as OpenAI’s *ChatGPT* system, capable of generating fluent human-like text and answering complex questions using inputs and outputs in natural language.

A key benefit of deep learning in NLP is the ability to mine massive quantities of text data to learn as much as possible *from scratch*, replacing features that have previously been hand-engineered by ones that are learned automatically. It is difficult to overstate the significance of this point, as it has led to a complete reconfiguration of NLP research. Before deep learning, good performance in any NLP task was generally achieved via engineering problem-specific features and/or carefully designed probabilistic models; this required highly specialized domain knowledge for that particular problem. Now, general-purpose models, often based on off-the-shelf models that have been “pretrained” on massive text corpora, are successfully deployed across the spectrum of NLP tasks with little-to-no manual feature-engineering effort. Echoing insights from the computer vision research field, the power and generality of massive (yet generic) text data can be married with curated domain-specific data by “fine-tuning” large pretrained deep neural networks on the more specific datasets, frequently leading to excellent performance.

Much of the recent success in deep learning for NLP is due to advances in *language models*, which are models for computing probabilities of sequences of words. While the modeling of language is intrinsically interesting in its own right, the practical benefit of these models arises from their benefits in solving NLP tasks, frequently due to their production of latent representations (embeddings) of words, sentences, or entire documents that are created during the training process.

A *large language model* (*LLM)* is a deep learning model with many parameters that is trained on massive natural language data, generally in an unsupervised way. Word embedding models such as word2vec, discussed later, are an early example of an LLM. While not the first neural language models by any means, the simplicity of these models sped up the training process, enabling them to be trained on internet-scale data, thus revealing the benefits of doing so and beginning the push toward ever-more-powerful LLMs on ever-larger datasets. Some large language models such as the GPT series of models from OpenAI, including their ChatGPT chatbot, can be used to generate natural language text and can answer complex queries with inputs and outputs in the form of natural language. These sophisticated LLMs make use of word embeddings as a building block in their architecture, so we will begin our discussion with these models.

 

### Word Embeddings

The goal of word embedding models is to learn vector representations of each word in the dictionary, called “*word embeddings*” (a.k.a. *word vectors*). As such, these word embedding models can be understood as a type of representation learning. Word embeddings are intended to capture the semantic meanings of the words and to reveal information about the relationships between the words by way of their relative positions in the embedding space. They can be used as features for downstream NLP tasks such as classifying documents, and they also form the basis for more sophisticated deep neural network language models.

To illustrate the motivation we have just discussed, consider the following short document:

*The quick brown fox jumps over the sly lazy dog*.

Traditional NLP methods would represent each word via their indices in the dictionary. The document could be represented as:

| The || quick || brown || fox || jumps || over || the || sly || lazy || dog |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || 3 || 37 || 50 || 42 || 2 || 1 || 22 || 58 || 12 |

![Image](images/T000121tabt0020.png)

Here, words are considered to be atomic units, and so their meaning cannot be scrutinized further. If we want to have vector representations for each word instead of a document-level vector representation, the earlier example could be equivalently rewritten with “one-hot encoding” vectors for each word token, with a single one in the entry corresponding to the word’s index and zeros elsewhere ([Table 11.1](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#t0010)).

However, this representation does not contain any information about the meaning of the words or their relationships to each other. To rectify this word embedding models aim for more nuanced continuous representations. For example, the representations might look like those in [Table 11.2](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#t0015).
