Having covered the fundamentals of probabilistic methods in the previous chapter, we are now ready to go deeper into more advanced techniques. This chapter will cover general probabilistic modeling strategies, the details of more specific models such as latent Dirichlet allocation topic models, and the probabilistic inference techniques to fit those models to data.

 

## 14.1 Hidden Variable Models

We now move on to advanced learning algorithms that can infer new attributes in addition to the ones present in the data—so-called hidden (or latent) variables whose values cannot be observed. As noted in [Section 13.3](#Ch014_485-514_B9780443158889000145.xhtml#s0050), a quantity called the *marginal likelihood* can be obtained by summing (or integrating) these variables out of the model. It is important not to confuse random variables with observations or hard assignments of random variables. We write $p(x\_{i} = {\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i}) = p({\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i})$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si1.png) to denote the probability of the random variable *x*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si2.png) associated with instance *i* taking the value represented by the observation ${\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si3.png). We use *h*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si4.png) to represent a hidden discrete random variable and *z*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si5.png) to denote a hidden continuous one. mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si7.png)

where the sum is taken over all possible discrete values of *h[i]* and the integral is taken over the entire domain of *z*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si8.png). The end result of all this integrating and summing is a single number—a scalar quantity—that gives the marginal likelihood for any value of the parameters.

Maximum likelihood–based learning for hidden variable models can sometimes be done using marginal likelihood, just as when no hidden variables are present, but the additional variables usually affect the parameterization used to define the model. In fact, these additional variables are often very important—*they are used to represent precisely the things we wish to mine from our data*, be it clusters, topics in a text mining problem, or the factors that underlie variation in the data. By treating parameters as random variables and using functions that are easy to manipulate, marginal likelihoods can also be used to define sophisticated Bayesian models that involve integrating over parameters. This can create models that are less prone to overfitting.

 

### Expected Log-Likelihoods and Expected Gradients

It is not always possible to obtain a form for the marginal likelihood that is easy to optimize. An alternative is to work with another quantity, the *expected log-likelihood*. Writing the set of all observed data as $\\overset{\\sim}{X}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si9.png), the set of all discrete hidden variables as *H*, and the set of all continuous hidden variables as *Z*, the expected log-likelihood can be expressed as

$\\begin{array}{ll} {E\\left\\lbrack \\mathit{\\log}L(\\theta;\\overset{\\sim}{X},Z,H) \\right\\rbrack\_{P(H,Z|\\overset{\\sim}{X};\\theta)}} & {= \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\left\\lbrack \\int\_{z\_{i}}{\\sum\\limits\_{h\_{i}}{p(z\_{i},h\_{i}|{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i};\\theta)\\mathit{log\\ p}({\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i},z\_{i},h\_{i};\\theta)dz\_{i}}} \\right\\rbrack} \\\\ & {= E\\left\\lbrack \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{\\mathit{log\\ p}({\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i},z\_{i},h\_{i};\\theta)} \\right\\rbrack\_{p(z\_{i},h\_{i}|{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i};\\theta)}} \\\\ \\end{array}.$<mml:math><mml:mtable columnalign="left"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">log</mml:mi><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo It turns out that there is a close relationship between the log marginal likelihood and the expected log-likelihood: the *derivative* of the expected log-likelihood with respect to the parameters of the model equals the *derivative* of the log marginal likelihood. The following derivation, based on applying the chain rule from calculus and considering a single training example for simplicity, demonstrates why this is true:

$\\begin{array}{ll} {\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\theta}\\mathit{log\\ p}({\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i};\\theta)} & {= \\frac{1}{p\\left( {\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i};\\theta) \\right.}\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\theta}\\int\_{z\_{i}}{\\sum\\limits\_{h\_{i}}{p({\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i},z\_{i},h\_{i};\\theta)}}dz\_{i}} \\\\ & {= \\int\_{z\_{i}}{\\sum\\limits\_{h\_{i}}\\frac{p({\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i},z\_{i},h\_{i};\\theta)}{p({\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i};\\theta)}}\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\theta}\\mathit{log\\ However, it is also possible to establish a direct relationship between the log marginal and expected log joint probabilities. where *H*\[.\] is the entropy.

As a consequence of this analysis, to perform learning in a probability model with hidden variables, the marginal likelihood can be optimized using gradient ascent by instead computing and following the gradient of the expected log-likelihood, assuming that the posterior distribution over hidden variables can be computed. This prompts a general approach to learning in a hidden variable model based on following the expected gradient. This can be decomposed into three steps: (1) a **P-step**, which computes the posterior over hidden variables; (2) an **E-step**, which computes the expectation of the gradient given the posterior; and (3) a **G-step**, which uses gradient-based optimization to maximize the objective function with respect to the parameters.

 

### The Expectation Maximization Algorithm

Using the expected log joint probability as a key quantity for learning in a probability model with hidden variables is better known in the context of the celebrated “expectation maximization” or EM algorithm, which we encountered in the previous chapter. We discuss the general EM formulation next. [Section 14.3](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#s0055) gives a concrete example comparing and contrasting the expected gradient approach and the EM approach, using the probabilistic formulation of principal component analysis.

The EM algorithm follows the expected gradient approach. However, EM is often used with models in which the M-step can be computed *in closed form*—in other words, when exact parameter updates can be found by setting the derivative of the expected log-likelihood with respect to the parameters to 0. These updates often take the same form as the simple maximum likelihood estimates that one would use to compute the parameters of a distribution. They are essentially modified forms of the equations used for observed data that involve averages weighted over the posterior distribution in place of observed counts.

The EM algorithm consists of two steps: (1) an **E-step** that computes the expectations used in the expected log-likelihood and (2) an **M-step** in which the objective is maximized, typically using a closed-form parameter update.

In the following we assume that we have only discrete hidden variables **H**. The probability of the observed data $\\overset{\\sim}{X}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si15.png) can be maximized by maximizing the log-likelihood $\\mathit{\\log}P(\\overset{\\sim}{X};\\theta)$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">log</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mi>;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:msp1/><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si16.png) of the parameters *θ*<mml:math><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si17.png) arising from an underlying latent variable model *P*(*X*, *H**;**θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">H;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:msp1/><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si18.png) as follows. Initialize the parameters as *θ*^(*o**l**d*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">old</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si19.png) and repeat the following steps, where convergence is measured in terms of either the change to the log-likelihood or the degree of change to the parameters:

1.  1. **E-step**: Compute required expectations involving *P*(*H**|**X**;**θ*^(*o**l**d*))<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">H|X;</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">old</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si20.png)
2.  2. **M-step**: Find $\\theta^{new}{= \\textit{arg}}\\underset{\\theta}{\\mathit{\\max}}\\lbrack\\sum\\limits\_{H}{P(\\mathit{H|X;}\\theta^{old})\\mathit{\\log}P(X,\\mathit{H;}\\theta)}\\rbrack$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">new</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">arg</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">max</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">H|X;</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">old</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">log</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">H;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:msp1/><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si21.png)
3.  3. If the algorithm has not converged, set *θ*^(*o**l**d*) = *θ*^(*n**e**w*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">old</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">new</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si22.png) and return to step 1.

Note that the *M*\-step corresponds to maximizing the expected log-likelihood. Although discrete hidden variables are used, the approach generalizes to continuous ones.

For many latent variable models—Gaussian mixture, probabilistic principal component analysis (PPCA), and hidden Markov—the required posterior distributions can be computed exactly, which accounts for their popularity. However, for many other probabilistic models it is simply not possible to compute an exact posterior distribution. This can easily happen with multiple hidden random variables because the posterior needed in the E-step is the joint posterior of the hidden variables. There is a vast literature on the subject of how to compute approximations to the true posterior distribution over hidden variables in more complex models.

 

### Applying the Expectation Maximization Algorithm to Bayesian Networks

Bayesian networks capture statistical dependencies between attributes using an intuitive graphical structure, and the EM algorithm can easily be applied to such networks. Consider a Bayesian network with a number of discrete random variables, some of which are observed while others are not. Its marginal probability, in which hidden variables have been integrated out, can be maximized by maximizing the expected log joint probability over the posterior distribution of the hidden variables given the observed data—the expected log-likelihood.

For a network consisting of only discrete variables, this means that the **E-step** involves computing a distribution over hidden variables {*H*}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si23.png) given observed variables $\\{\\overset{\\sim}{X}\\}$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si24.png) or $P(\\{ H\\}|\\{\\overset{\\sim}{X}\\};\\theta^{current})$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mi>|</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mi>;</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">current</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si25.png). If the network is a tree this can be computed efficiently using the sum-product algorithm, which is explained in [Section 14.3](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#s0055). If not it can be computed efficiently using the junction tree algorithm. However, if the model is large, exact inference algorithms may be intractable, in which case a variational approximation or sampling procedure can be used to approximate the distribution.

The **M-step** seeks

$\\theta^{\\mathit{new}}{= \\textit{arg}}\\underset{\\theta}{\\mathit{\\max}}\\left\\lbrack \\sum\\limits\_{\\{ H\\}}\\left. P(\\{ H\\} \\middle| \\{\\overset{\\sim}{X}\\};\\theta^{\\mathit{old}})\\mathit{\\log}P(\\{\\overset{\\sim}{X}\\},\\{ H\\};\\theta) \\right. \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">new</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">arg</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">max</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo mathvariant="normal">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">old</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">log</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si26.png)

Recall that the log joint probability given by a Bayesian network decomposes into a sum over functions of subsets of variables. Notice also that the expression shown involves an expectation using the joint conditional distribution or posterior over hidden variables. Using the EM algorithm, taking the derivative with respect to any given parameter leaves only terms that involve the marginal expectation over the distribution of variables that participate in the function for the gradient of the relevant parameter. This means that to find the unconditional probability of an unobserved variable *A* in a network, it is necessary to determine the parameters *θ*[*A*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si27.png) of *P*(*A**;**θ*[*A*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">A;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si28.png) for which

$\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\theta\_{A}}\\left\\lbrack \\sum\\limits\_{A}{P(A \\mid \\left\\{ \\overset{\\sim}{X} \\right\\};\\theta^{\\mathit{old}})\\mathit{\\log}P(A;\\theta\_{A})} \\right\\rbrack = 0,$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8706;</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8706;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>}</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">old</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">log</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si29.png)

along with the further constraint that the probabilities in the discrete distribution sum to 1. This can be achieved using a Lagrange multiplier ([Appendix A.2](#TableA1_617-636_B9780443158889000212.xhtml#s0050) gives an example of using this technique to estimate a discrete distribution). Setting the derivative of the constrained objective to 0 gives this *closed form* result:

$\\theta\_{A = a}^{\\mathit{new}} = P(A = a) = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}{P(A\_{i} = a \\mid {\\{\\overset{\\sim}{X}\\}}\_{i};\\theta^{\\mathit{old}})}.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">new</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">old</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si30.png)

In other words, the unconditional probability distribution is estimated in the same way in which it would be computed if the variables *A[i]* had been observed but with each observation replaced by its probability. Applying this procedure to the entire data set is tantamount to replacing observed counts with expected counts under the current model settings. If many examples have the same configuration the distribution need only be computed once and multiplied by the number of times that configuration has been seen.

Estimating entries in the network’s conditional probability tables also has an intuitive form. To estimate the conditional probability of unobserved random variable *B* given unobserved random variable *A* in a Bayesian network, simply compute their joint (posterior) probability and the marginal (posterior) probability of *A* for each example. Just as when the data is observed, the update equation is

$P(B = b|A = a) = \\frac{\\sum\_{i = 1}^{N}{P(A\_{i} = a,B\_{i} = b|\\left\\{ \\overset{\\sim}{X} \\right\\}\_{i};\\theta^{\\mathit{old}})}}{\\sum\_{i = 1}^{N}{P(A\_{i} = a|\\left\\{ \\overset{\\sim}{X} \\right\\}\_{i};\\theta^{\\mathit{old}})}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">old</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">old</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si31.png)

This is simply a ratio of the expected numbers of counts. If some of the variables are fully observed the expression can be adapted by replacing the inferred probabilities by observed values, effectively assigning the observations a probability of 1. Furthermore, if variable *B* has multiple parents *A* can be replaced by the set of parents.

 

## 14.2 Bayesian Estimation and Prediction

If there is reason to believe that a certain parameter has been drawn from a particular distribution, we can adopt a more Bayesian perspective. A common strategy is to employ a hyperparameter *α* to represent that distribution. Define the *joint distribution* of data and parameters as

$p(x\_{1},x\_{2},\\ldots,\\ x\_{n},\\theta;\\alpha) = \\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{p(x\_{i} \\mid \\theta)p(\\theta;\\alpha)}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si32.png)

Bayesian-style predictions use a quantity known as the *posterior predictive distribution*, which consists of the probability model for a new observation marginalized over the posterior probability inferred for the parameters given the observations so far. Again using a notation that explicitly differentiates variables *x*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si33.png) from their observations ${\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{i}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si34.png), the posterior predictive distribution is

$p(x\_{\\mathit{new}} \\mid {\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{1},{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{2},\\ldots,{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{n};\\alpha) = \\int\_{\\theta}{p(x\_{\\mathit{new}} \\mid \\theta)p(\\theta \\mid {\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{1},{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{2},\\ldots,{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{n};\\alpha)d\\theta}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">new</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">new</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si35.png)

Given a Bayesian model that uses distributions over parameters, so-called “empirical Bayesian” methods can be employed to find a suitable value for the hyperparameter α. One such approach is obtained by maximizing the log marginal likelihood with respect to the model’s hyperparameters:

$\\alpha\_{\\mathit{MML}} = \\textit{arg}\\underset{\\alpha}{\\mathit{\\max}}\\left\\lbrack \\mathit{\\log}\\int\\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{p(x\_{i}|\\theta)p(\\theta;\\alpha)d\\theta} \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#945;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">MML</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">arg</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">max</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#945;</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8747;</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si36.png)

The remainder of this section demonstrates several techniques for creating complex structured probabilistic models.

 

### Probabilistic Inference Methods

With complex probability models—and even with some seemingly simple ones—computing quantities such as posterior distributions, marginal distributions, and the maximum probability configuration often require specialized methods to achieve results efficiently, even approximate ones. This is the field of *probabilistic inference*. Later we review some widely used probabilistic inference methods, including probability propagation, sampling and simulated annealing, and variational inference.

 

#### Probability propagation

Structured probability models like the Bayesian networks and Markov random fields discussed in [Section 14.3](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#s0055) decompose a joint probability distribution into a factorized structure consisting of products of functions over subsets of variables. Then the task of computing marginal probabilities to find a maximum-probability configuration can be computationally demanding using brute force computation. In some cases even a naïve approach is completely infeasible in practice. However, it is sometimes possible to take advantage of the model’s structure to perform inference more efficiently. When Bayesian networks and related graphical models have an underlying tree connectivity structure then *belief propagation* (also known as *probability propagation*) based on the sum-product and max-product algorithms presented in [Section 14.3](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#s0055) can be applied to compute exact marginals, hence the most probable model configuration.

 

#### Sampling, simulated annealing, and iterated conditional modes

With fully Bayesian methods that use distributions on parameters, or graphical models with cyclic structures, sampling methods are popular in both statistics and machine learning. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods are widely used to generate random samples from probability distributions that are difficult to compute. For example, as we have seen, posterior distributions are often needed for expectations required during learning but in many settings these can be difficult to compute. *Gibbs sampling* is a popular special case of the more general Metropolis–Hastings algorithm that allows one to generate samples from a joint distribution even when the true distribution is a complex continuous function. These samples can then be used to approximate expectations of interest and also to approximate marginal distributions of subsets of variables by simply ignoring parts pertaining to other variables.

Gibbs sampling is conceptually very simple. Assign an initial set of states to the random variables of interest. With *n* random variables this initial assignment or set of samples can be written *x*[1] = *x*[1]^((0)), …, *x*[*n*] = *x*[*n*]^((0))<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si37.png). We then iteratively update each variable by *sampling* from its conditional distribution given the others:

$\\begin{matrix} {\\left. x\_{1}^{(i + 1)} \\right.\\sim p(x\_{1} \\mid x\_{2}} & = & {x\_{2}^{(i)},\\ldots,x\_{n} = x\_{n}^{(i)}),} \\\\ & \\vdots & \\\\ {\\left. x\_{n}^{(i + 1)} \\right.\\sim p(x\_{n} \\mid x\_{1}} & = & {x\_{1}^{(i)},\\ldots,x\_{n - 1} = x\_{n - 1}^{(i)})} \\\\ \\end{matrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" ![Equation](images/F000157si38.png)

In practice these conditional distributions are often easy to compute. Furthermore, the idea of a “Markov blanket” introduced in [Section 13.2](#Ch014_485-514_B9780443158889000145.xhtml#s0025) can often be used to reduce the number of variables necessary because conditionals in structured models may depend on a much smaller subset of the variables.

To ensure an unbiased sample it is necessary to cycle through the data discarding samples in a process known as “burn-in.” The idea is to allow the Markov chain defined by the sampling procedure to approach its stationary distribution, and it can be shown that in the limit one will indeed obtain a sample from this distribution, and the distribution corresponds to the underlying joint probability from which we wish to sample. There is considerable theory concerning how much burn-in is required but in practice it is common to discard samples arising from the first 100–1000 cycles. Sometimes, if more than one sample configuration is desired, averages are taken over *k* additional configurations of the sampler obtained after periods of about 100 cycles. We see how this procedure is used in practice in [Section 14.3](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#s0055) under latent Dirichlet allocation.

Simulated annealing is a procedure that seeks an approximate most probable configuration or explanation. It adapts the Gibbs sampling procedure, described earlier, to include an iteration-dependent “temperature” term *t[i]*. Starting with an initial assignment *x*[1] = *x*[1]^((0)), …, *x*[*n*] = *x*[*n*]^((0))<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si39.png), subsequent samples take the form

where the temperature is decreased at each iteration: *t[i]* [+ 1] < *t[i]*. If the schedule is slow enough, this process will converge to the true global minimum. But therein lies the catch—the temperature may have to decrease very slowly. However, this is often possible, particularly with an efficient implementation of the sampler.

Another well-known algorithm is the *iterated conditional modes* procedure, consisting of iterations of the form

This can be very fast but prone to local minima. It can be useful when constructing more interesting graphical models and optimizing them quickly in an analogous, greedy way.

 

#### Variational inference

Rather than sampling from a distribution that is difficult to manipulate, the distribution can be approximated by a simpler, more tractable, function. Suppose we have a probability model with a set *H* of hidden variables and a set *X* of observed variables. Let $p = p(\\mathit{H|}\\overset{\\sim}{X};\\theta)$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">H|</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mi>;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:msp1/><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si42.png) be the exact posterior distribution of the model and $q = q(\\mathit{H|}\\overset{\\sim}{X};\\Phi)$<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">H|</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mi>;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mml:mi><mml:msp1/><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si43.png) be an approximation to it, where *Φ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si44.png) is a set of so-called “variational parameters.” Variational methods for probability models commonly involve defining a simple form for *q* that makes it easy to optimize *Φ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si45.png) in a way that brings *q* closer to *p*. The theory of variation EM optimizes latent variable models by maximizing a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood. This so-called “variational bound” is described in [Appendix A.2](#TableA1_617-636_B9780443158889000212.xhtml#s0050), where we see how the EM algorithm can be viewed through a variational analysis. This allows one to create EM algorithms using either exact or approximate posterior distributions. While statisticians often prefer sampling methods to variational ones, variational methods are popular in machine learning because they can be faster and can be combined with sampling methods.

 

## 14.3 Graphical Models and Factor Graphs

Bayesian networks give an intuitive picture of a probabilistic model that corresponds directly with how we have decided to decompose the joint probability of the random variables representing attributes into a product of conditional and unconditional probability distributions. Mixture models, such as the Gaussian mixture models of [Section 13.3](#Ch014_485-514_B9780443158889000145.xhtml#s0050), are alternative ways of approximating joint distributions. This section shows how such models can be illustrated using Bayesian networks and introduces a generalization of Bayesian networks, the so-called “plate notation,” that allows one to visualize the result of techniques that treat parameters as random quantities. A further generalization, “factor graphs,” can represent and visualize an even wider class of probabilistic graphical models. As before, we view attributes as random variables and instances as observations of them; we also represent things like the label of a cluster by a random variable in a graph.

 

### Graphical Models and Plate Notation

Consider a simple two-cluster Gaussian mixture model. It can be illustrated in the form of a Bayesian network with a binary random variable *C* for the cluster membership and a continuous random variable *x* for the real-valued attribute. In the mixture model the joint distribution P(*C*, *x*) is the product of the prior P(*C*) and the conditional probability distribution P(*x*|*C*). This structure is illustrated by the Bayesian network in [Fig. 14.1A](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0010), where for each state of *C* a different Gaussian is used for the conditional distribution of the continuous variable *x*.

![Fig. 14.1 (A) Bayesian network for a mixture model. (B) Multiple copies of the Bayesian network, one for each observation. (C) Plate notation version of (B).](images/F000157f14-01-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. 14.1 (A) Bayesian network for a mixture model. (B) Multiple copies of the Bayesian network, one for each observation. (C) Plate notation version of (B).

Multiple Bayesian networks can be used to visualize the underlying joint likelihood that results when parameter estimation is performed. The probability model for *N* observations $x\_{1} = {\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{1}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si46.png), $x\_{2} = {\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{2}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si47.png), up to $x\_{\\mathit{N}} = {\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{\\mathit{N}}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si48.png) can be conceptualized as *N* Bayesian networks, one for each variable *x[i]* observed or instantiated to the value ${\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{\\mathit{i}}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si362.png). [Fig. 14.1B](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0010) illustrates this, using shaded nodes to indicate which random variables are observed.

A “plate” is simply a box around a Bayesian network that denotes a certain number of replications of it. The plate in [Fig. 14.1C](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0010) indicates *I* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si49.png), …, *N* networks, each with an observed value for *x[i]*. Plate notation captures a model for the joint probability of the entire data with a simple picture.

Bayesian networks, and more complex models comprising plates of Bayesian networks, are known as *generative models* because the probabilistic definition of the model can be used to randomly generate data governed by the probability distribution that the model represents. Bayesian hierarchical modeling involves defining a hierarchy of levels for the *parameters* of a model and using the rules of probability arising from the application of Bayesian methods to infer the parameter values given observed data. These can be drawn with graphical models in which both random variables and parameters are treated as random quantities. The section on latent Dirichlet allocation gives an example of this technique.

 

### Probabilistic Principal Component Analysis

Principal component analysis can be viewed as the consequence of performing parameter estimation in a special type of linear Gaussian hidden variable model. This connects the traditional view of this standard technique, presented in [Chapter 6](#Ch006_209-259_B9780443158889000078.xhtml#Ch006_209-259_B9780443158889000078), “Preparation: data preprocessing and exploratory data analysis,” with the probabilistic formulation discussed here and leads to more advanced methods based on autoencoders and Boltzmann machines that are introduced in [Appendix D](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248), Technical details of deep learning, respectively. The probabilistic formulation also helps deal with missing values. The underlying idea is to represent data as being generated by a Gaussian distributed continuous hidden latent variable that is linearly transformed under a Gaussian model. As a result, the principal components of a given data set correspond to an underlying factorized covariance model for a corresponding multivariate Gaussian distribution model for the data. This factorized model becomes apparent when the hidden variables of the underlying latent variable model are integrated out.

More specifically, a set of hidden variables is used to represent the input data in a space of reduced dimensionality. Each dimension corresponds to an independent random variable drawn from a Gaussian distribution with zero mean and unit variance. Let **x** be a random variable corresponding to the *d*\-dimensional vectors of observed data and **h** be a *k*\-dimensional vector of hidden random variables; *k* is typically smaller than *d* (but need not be). Then the underlying joint probability model has this linear Gaussian form:

$\\begin{matrix} {p\\left( \\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{h} \\right) = p\\left( \\mathbf{x} \\mid \\mathbf{h} \\right)p\\left( \\mathbf{h} \\right)} \\\\ {= N\\left( \\mathbf{x};\\mathbf{Wh} + \\mathbf{\\mu},\\mathbf{D} \\right)N\\left( \\mathbf{h};0,\\mathbf{I} \\right),} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Wh</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si50.png)

where the zero vector **0** and identity matrix **I** denote the mean and covariance matrix for the Gaussian distribution used for *p*(**h**), and *p*(**x**|**h**) is Gaussian with mean **Wh**+μ and a diagonal covariance matrix **D**. (The expression for the mean is where the term “linear” in “linear Gaussian” comes from.) The mean μ is included as a parameter but it would be zero if we first mean-centered the data. [Fig. 14.2A](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0015) shows a Bayesian network for PPCA; it reveals intuitions about the probabilistic interpretation of principal component analysis based on hidden variables that will help in understanding other models discussed later.

![Fig. 14.2 (A) Bayesian network for probabilistic PCA. (B) Equal-probability contour for a Gaussian distribution along with its covariance matrix’s principal eigenvector.](images/F000157f14-02-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. 14.2 (A) Bayesian network for probabilistic PCA. (B) Equal-probability contour for a Gaussian distribution along with its covariance matrix’s principal eigenvector.

Probabilistic PCA is a form of generative model, and [Fig. 14.2A](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0015) visualizes the associated underlying generative process. Data is generated by sampling each dimension of **h** from an independent Gaussian distribution and using the matrix **W****h** + **μ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Wh</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si51.png) to project this lower dimensional representation of the data into the observed, higher dimensional representation. Noise, specified by the diagonal covariance matrix **D**, is added separately to each dimension of the higher dimensional representation.

If the noise associated with the conditional distribution of **x** given **h** is the same in each dimension (i.e., isotropic) and infinitesimally small (such that **D** = lim[*σ*² → 0]*σ*²**I**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">D</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>lim</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>&#8594;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si52.png)), a set of estimation equations can be derived that give the same principal components as those obtained by conventional principal component analysis. Restricting the covariance matrix **D** to be diagonal produces a model known as *factor analysis*). If **D** is isotropic (i.e., has the form **D** = *σ*²**I**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">D</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si53.png)), then after optimizing the model and learning σ² the columns of **W** will be scaled and rotated principal eigenvectors of the covariance matrix of the data. The contours of equal probability for a multivariate Gaussian distribution can be drawn with an ellipse whose principal axis corresponds to the principal eigenvector of the covariance matrix, as illustrated in [Fig. 14.2B](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0015).

Because of the nice properties of Gaussian distributions the marginal distributions of **x** in these models are also Gaussian, with parameters that can be computed *analytically* using simple algebraic expressions. For example, a model with **D** = *σ*²**I**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">D</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si54.png) has *p*(**x**) = *N*(**x**; **μ**, **W****W**^(**T**) + *σ*²**I**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mi>;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#956;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si55.png), which is the marginal distribution of **x** under the joint probability model, obtained by integrating out the uncertainty associated with **h** from the joint distribution *p*(**x**,**h**) defined earlier. Integrating out the hidden variables **h** from a PPCA model defines a Gaussian distribution whose covariance matrix **M** has the special form **W****W***T* + **D**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">WW</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si56.png). [Appendix A.2](#TableA1_617-636_B9780443158889000212.xhtml#s0050) relates this factorization to an eigenvector analysis of the covariance matrix, resulting in the standard matrix factorization view of principal component analysis.

 

#### Inference with PPCA

As a result of the underlying linear Gaussian formulation, various other quantities needed for making inferences and performing parameter estimation can also be obtained analytically. For example, given **M** = (**W****W**^(*T*) + *σ*²**I**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">M</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si57.png), the *posterior distribution* for **h** can be obtained from Bayes’ rule, along with some Gaussian identities given in [Appendix A.2](#TableA1_617-636_B9780443158889000212.xhtml#s0050). The posterior can be written

*p*(**h** ∣ **x**) = *N*(**h**; **M**^( − 1)**W**^(*T*)(**x** − **μ**), *σ*²**M**^( − 1)).<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mi>;</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#956;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (14.1)

![Equation](images/F000157si58.png)(14.1) 

Once the model parameters have been estimated the mean of the posterior for a new example can be calculated, which can then serve as a reduced dimensional representation for it. The mathematics (though still perhaps daunting) is greatly simplified by the fact that marginalizing, multiplying and dividing Gaussians distributions produces other Gaussian distributions that are functions of observed values, mean vectors, and covariance matrices. In fact, many more sophisticated methods and models for data analysis rely on the ease with which key quantities can be computed when the underlying model is based on linear Gaussian forms.

 

#### Marginal log-likelihood for PPCA

Given a probabilistic model with hidden variables the Bayesian philosophy is to integrate out the uncertainly associated with them. As we have just seen, linear Gaussian models make it possible to obtain the marginal probability of the data, *p*(**x**), which takes the form of a Gaussian distribution. Then the learning problem is tantamount to maximizing the probability of the given data under the model. The probability that variable **x** is observed to be $\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si59.png) is indicated by $p(\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}) = p(\\mathbf{x} = \\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}})$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si60.png). The log (marginal) likelihood of the parameters given all the observed data $\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si61.png) can be maximized using this objective function:

$L(\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}};\\theta) = \\mathit{\\log}\\left\\lbrack \\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}{P({\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i};\\theta)} \\right\\rbrack = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}{\\mathit{\\log}\\left\\lbrack N({\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i};\\mathbf{\\mu},\\mathbf{W}\\mathbf{W}^{\\mathbf{T}} + \\sigma^{2}\\mathbf{I}) \\right\\rbrack},$<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si62.png)

where the parameters *θ* = {**W**, **μ**, *σ*²}<mml:math><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#956;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si63.png), consist of a matrix, a vector, and a scalar. We will assume henceforth that the data has been mean-centered: **μ** = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#956;</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si64.png). (When creating generalizations of this approach there can be advantages to retaining the mean as an explicit parameter of the model.)

 

#### Expected log-likelihood for PPCA

[Section 14.1](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#s0010) showed that the derivative of the log marginal likelihood of a hidden variable model with respect to its parameters equals the derivative of the expected log joint likelihood, where the expectation is taken with respect to the exact posterior distribution over the model’s hidden variables. The underlying Gaussian formulation of PPCA means that an exact posterior can be computed, which provides an alternative way to optimize the model based on the expected log-likelihood. The log joint probability of all data and all hidden variables **H** under the model is

$L(\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}},\\mathbf{H};\\theta) = \\mathit{\\log}\\left\\lbrack \\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}{p({\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i},\\mathbf{h}\_{i};\\theta)} \\right\\rbrack = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}{\\mathit{\\log}\\left\\lbrack p({\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i} \\mid \\mathbf{h}\_{i};\\mathbf{W})p(\\mathbf{h}\_{i};\\sigma^{2}) \\right\\rbrack}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi ![Equation](images/F000157si65.png)

Notice that while the data $\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si66.png) is observed, the hidden variables **h***[i]* are unknown, so for a given parameter value $\\theta = \\overset{\\sim}{\\theta}$<mml:math><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si67.png) this expression does not evaluate to a scalar quantity. It can be converted into a scalar-valued function using the expected log-likelihood, which can then be optimized. As we saw in [Section 14.1](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#s0010), the expected log-likelihood of the data using the posterior distribution of each example for the expectations is given by

$E\\left\\lbrack L(\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}},\\mathbf{H};\\theta) \\right\\rbrack\_{p(\\mathbf{H}|\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}})} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}{E\\left\\lbrack \\mathit{\\log}\\left\\lbrack p({\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i},\\mathbf{h}\_{i};\\theta) \\right\\rbrack \\right\\rbrack\_{p(\\mathbf{h}\_{i}|{\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i})}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">|</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">;</mml:mi><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">|</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si68.png) 

#### Expected gradient for PPCA

Gradient descent can be used to learn the parameter matrix **W** using the expected log-likelihood as the objective, an example of the expected gradient approach was discussed in [Section 14.1](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#s0010). The gradient is a sum over examples, and a fairly lengthy derivation shows that each example contributes the following term to this sum:

$\\begin{array}{ll} {\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\mathbf{W}}E\\lbrack L(\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}},\\mathbf{h})\\rbrack} & {= E\\lbrack\\mathbf{Wh}\\mathbf{h}^{T}\\rbrack - E\\lbrack\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}\\mathbf{h}^{T}\\rbrack} \\\\ & {= \\mathbf{W}E\\lbrack\\mathbf{h}\\mathbf{h}^{T}\\rbrack - \\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}E{\\lbrack\\mathbf{h}\\rbrack}^{T},} \\\\ \\end{array}$<mml:math><mml:mtable columnalign="left"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8706;</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8706;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Wh</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd/><mml:mtd><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math> (14.2)

![Equation](images/F000157si69.png)(14.2) 

where in all cases the expectations are taken with respect to the posterior, $p(\\mathbf{h}|\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}})$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mi>|</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si70.png), using the current settings of the model parameters. This partial derivative has a natural interpretation as a difference between two expectations. The second term creates a matrix the same size as **W**, consisting of an observation and the hidden variable representation. The first term simply replaces the observation with a similar **Wh** factor, which could be thought of as the model’s prediction of the input. (We will revisit this interpretation when we examine conditional probability models in [Section 14.4](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#s0160) and restricted Boltzmann machines in [Appendix D.3](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#s0040).)

This shows that the model reconstructs the data as it ascends the gradient. If the optimization converges to a model that perfectly reconstructs the data the derivative in [(14.2)](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#eqn2) will be zero. Other probabilistic models examined show similar forms for the gradients for key parameters, consisting of differences of expectations but different types of expectation are involved.

To compute these quantities note that the expected value *E*\[**h**\] = **M**^( − 1)**W**^(*T*)(**x** − **μ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#956;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si71.png) can be obtained from the mean of the posterior distribution for each example given by [(14.1)](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#eqn1). The *E*\[**hh**^T\] term can be found using the fact that *E*\[**h****h***T*\] = *c**o**v*\[**h**\] + *E*\[**h**\]*E*\[**h**\]*T*<mml:math><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">hh</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>cov</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic" stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic" stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si72.png), where cov\[**h**\] is the posterior covariance matrix, which we also know from [(14.1)](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#eqn1) is *σ*²**M**^( − 1)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si73.png).

 

#### EM for PPCA

An alternative to gradient ascent using the expected log-likelihood is to formulate the model as an expected gradient-based learning procedure using the classical EM algorithm. The M-step update can be obtained by setting the derivative in [(14.2)](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#eqn2) to zero and solving for **W**. This can be expressed in closed form. **W** in the first term is independent of the expectation and can therefore be moved out of the expectation and terms rearranged into a closed-form M-step. In a zero mean model with **D** = *σ*²**I**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">D</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si74.png) and some small value for *σ*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si75.png), the E and M steps of the PPCA EM algorithm can be rewritten

$\\begin{array}{ll} {\\mathbf{E}\\textbf{-}\\mathbf{Step}:E\\lbrack\\mathbf{h}\_{i}\\rbrack} & {= \\mathbf{M}^{- 1}\\mathbf{W}^{T}{\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i},E\\lbrack\\mathbf{h}\_{i}\\mathbf{h}\_{i}^{T}\\rbrack = \\sigma^{2}\\mathbf{M}^{- 1} + E\\lbrack\\mathbf{h}\_{i}\\rbrack E\\lbrack\\mathbf{h}\_{i}^{T}\\rbrack,} \\\\ {\\mathbf{M}\\textbf{-}\\mathbf{Step}:\\mathbf{W}^{New}} & {= \\left\\lbrack {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}{{\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i}E{\\lbrack\\mathbf{h}\_{i}\\rbrack}^{\\mathbf{T}}}} \\right\\rbrack\\left\\lbrack {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}{E\\lbrack\\mathbf{h}\_{i}{\\mathbf{h}\_{i}}^{T}\\rbrack}} \\right\\rbrack^{- 1},} \\\\ \\end{array}$<mml:math><mml:mtable columnalign="left"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">E</mml:mi><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold">-</mml:mtext><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Step</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo
