close="\]"><mml:mrow><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si76.png)

where all expectations are taken with respect to each example’s posterior distribution, $p(\\mathbf{h}\_{i}|{\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i})$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>|</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si77.png), and, as shown, **M** = (**W****W**^(*T*) + *σ*²**I**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">M</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si78.png).

The EM algorithm can be further simplified by taking the limit as *σ*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#963;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si79.png) approaches zero. This is the *zero input noise* case, and it implies **M** = **W****W***T*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">M</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">WW</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si80.png). Define the matrix **Z** = *E*\[**H**\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si81.png), each column of which contains the expected vector from $P(\\mathbf{h}\_{i}|{\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i})$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>|</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si82.png) for one of the hidden variables **h***i*, so that *E*\[**H****H**^(*T*)\] = *E*\[**H**\]*E*\[**H**^(*T*)\] = **Z****Z**^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">H</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si83.png). This yields simple and elegant equations for the E and M steps:

$\\begin{array}{ll} {\\mathbf{E}\\textbf{-}\\mathbf{Step}:\\mathbf{Z}} & {= E\\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{H} \\right\\rbrack = \\left( \\mathbf{W}^{T}\\mathbf{W} \\right)^{- 1}\\mathbf{W}^{T}\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}},} \\\\ {\\mathbf{M}\\textbf{-}\\mathbf{Step}:\\mathbf{W}^{New}} & {= \\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}}\\mathbf{Z}^{T}\\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{Z}\\mathbf{Z}^{T} \\right\\rbrack^{- 1},} \\\\ \\end{array}$<mml:math><mml:mtable columnalign="left"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">E</mml:mi><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold">-</mml:mtext><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Step</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mml:mi></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">H</mml:mi><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">M</mml:mi><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold">-</mml:mtext><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Step</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">New</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic">=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si84.png)

where both equations operate on the entire data matrix $\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si85.png).

The probabilistic formulation of principal component analysis permits traditional likelihoods to be defined, which supports maximum likelihood–based learning and probabilistic inference. This in turn leads to natural methods for dealing with missing data. It also leads on to the other models discussed later.

 

### Latent Semantic Analysis

[Chapter 6](#Ch006_209-259_B9780443158889000078.xhtml#Ch006_209-259_B9780443158889000078), “Preparation: data preprocessing and exploratory data analysis,” introduced principal component analysis, which, as we have seen, can be viewed as a form of linear Gaussian latent variable model. We now discuss an influential early form of data driven document analysis known as “latent semantic analysis” (LSA), which uses singular value decomposition to decompose each document in a collection into *topics*. If documents and terms are projected into the topic space comparisons can be made that capture semantic structure in the documents resulting from the cooccurrence of words across the collection. Characterizing documents in this way is called “latent semantic indexing.” Probabilistic LSA (pLSA) addresses similar goals but applies a statistical model based on multinomial distributions. Latent Dirichlet allocation is a related model that uses a hierarchical Bayesian approach in which Dirichlet priors are placed on the underlying multinomial distributions.

To motivate the introduction of these techniques let us examine the relationship between the original LSA method and singular value decomposition. Imagine a term by document matrix **X**, with *t* rows and *d* columns, each element of which contains the number of times the word associated with its row occurs in the document associated with its column. LSA decomposes **X** into a product **X** = **U****S****V***T*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">USV</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si86.png), where **U** and **V** have orthogonal columns and **S** is a diagonal matrix containing the singular values, which are conventionally sorted in decreasing order. This factorization is known as the singular value decomposition, and it has the property that for every value *k* if all but the *k* largest singular values are discarded the data matrix can be reconstructed in a way that is optimal in a least squares sense. For any given approximation level *k* we can write $\\mathbf{X} \\approx \\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}} = \\mathbf{U}\_{k}\\mathbf{S}\_{k}\\mathbf{V}\_{k}^{T}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8776;</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">U</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si87.png).

[Fig. 14.3](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0020) illustrates how this works. The **U***[k]* matrix can be thought of as *k* orthogonal “topics” that are combined according to the appropriate proportions for each document, encoded in the *k* × *d*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si88.png) matrix **V**[*k*]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si89.png). The matrix **A** = **S**[*k*]**V**[*k*]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">A</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si90.png) represents the activity level of the topics associated with each document. Thus the learning phase of LSA simply performs singular value decomposition on the data matrix.

![Fig. 14.3 The singular value decomposition of a t by d matrix.](images/F000157f14-03-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 14.3](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#Bf0020) The singular value decomposition of a *t* by *d* matrix.

The dot (or scalar) product of any two columns of the approximated data matrix $\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si91.png) provides a measure of the similarity of term usage in the two documents. The dot products between all pairs of documents used to compute the singular value decomposition are

${\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}}}^{T}\\overset{\\sim}{\\mathbf{X}} = \\mathbf{V}\_{k}\\mathbf{S}\_{k}^{2}\\mathbf{V}\_{k}^{T}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si92.png)

To analyze a new document (or query) **x***[q]* that is not in the original collection used for the decomposition, it can be projected into the semantic space of topic activity defined by the model using

**a**[*q*] = **S**[*k*]^( − 1)**U**[*k*]^(*T*)**x**[*q*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">U</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math> (14.3)

![Equation](images/F000157si93.png)(14.3)  

### Using Principal Component Analysis for Dimensionality Reduction

The singular value decomposition is widely used to project data into a space of reduced dimensions, often before applying other analysis techniques. For instance, data can be projected into a lower dimensional space to effectively apply nearest neighbor techniques, which tend to break down in high dimensional spaces.

LSA is in fact a form of principal component analysis. When viewed as a probability model the projection of a document into a lower dimensional semantic space is, in effect, a *latent variable representation for the document*. The equivalent quantity in PPCA is given by the expected value of the posterior distribution over the hidden variables. This gives an intuitive view of what it means to project a document or query vector into a lower dimensional space.

For a PPCA model with no noise in the observed variables **x**, we have seen that an input vector **x** can be projected into a reduced dimensional random vector **z** by computing the mean value of the posterior for the latent variables using **z** = *E*\[**h**\] = (**W**^(*T*)**W**)^( − 1)**W**^(*T*)**x**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si94.png). [Appendix A.2](#TableA1_617-636_B9780443158889000212.xhtml#s0050) details the relationships between PCA, PPCA, the singular value decomposition, and eigendecompositions and shows that for mean-centered data the **U** matrix in [(14.3)](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#eqn3) equals the matrix of eigenvectors **Φ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si95.png) of the eigendecomposition of the corresponding covariance matrix of the data, that is, **U** = **Φ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">U</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si96.png). The diagonal matrix **S** in [(14.3)](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#eqn3) is related to the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues **Λ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si97.png) by $\\mathbf{S} = \\mathbf{\\Lambda}^{\\frac{1}{2}}$<mml:math><mml:mstyle displaystyle="false"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">S</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mstyle></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si98.png). Furthermore, the eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix implies that $\\mathbf{W} = \\mathbf{\\Phi}\\mathbf{\\Lambda}^{\\frac{1}{2}}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si99.png) in the corresponding PPCA. Thus under the probabilistic interpretation of principal component analysis with no noise for observed variables **W** = **U****S**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">US</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si100.png). Using the fact that **U** is orthogonal and **S** is diagonal this means that computing a principal component analysis of mean-centered data using the singular value decomposition and interpreting the result as a linear Gaussian hidden variable model yields the following expression for projecting results into the reduced dimensional space based on the mean of the posterior:

$\\begin{array}{ccl} \\mathbf{z} & = & {\\left( \\mathbf{W}^{T}\\mathbf{W} \\right)^{- 1}\\mathbf{W}^{T}\\mathbf{x}} \\\\ & = & {\\left( \\mathbf{S}\\mathbf{U}^{T}\\mathbf{US} \\right)^{- 1}\\mathbf{S}\\mathbf{U}^{T}\\mathbf{x}} \\\\ & = & {\\left( \\mathbf{S}^{2} \\right)^{- 1}\\mathbf{S}\\mathbf{U}^{T}\\mathbf{x}} \\\\ & = & {\\mathbf{S}^{- 1}\\mathbf{U}^{T}\\mathbf{x}.} \\\\ \\end{array}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic">=</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi ![Equation](images/F000157si101.png)

This is the same expression as the LSA projection in [(14.3)](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#eqn3) to compute **a**[q], the semantic representation of a document, and it represents a general expression for dimensionality reduction using principal component analysis. This means that principal component analysis can be performed using the singular value decomposition of the data matrix, or an eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix, the EM algorithm, or even expected gradient descent. When working with large datasets or data with missing values there are advantages and disadvantages to each method.

The input data **X** need not arise from documents; LSA is simply a concrete example of applying singular value decomposition to a real problem. Indeed the general idea of computing such projections is widely used across machine learning and data mining. Because of the relationships discussed earlier the methods are often discussed using different terminology, even when they refer to the same underlying analysis.

 

### Probabilistic LSA

PPCA is based on continuous valued representations of data and an underlying Gaussian model. In contrast the pLSA approach, also known as an “aspect model,” is based on a formulation using the multinomial distribution; it was originally applied to the cooccurrences of words and documents. The multinomial distribution is a natural distribution for modeling word occurrence counts. In the pLSA framework one considers the index of each document as being encoded using observations of discrete random variables *d[i]* for *i* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si102.png), …, *n* documents. Each variable *d[i]* has *n* states, and over the document corpus there is one observation of the variable for each state. Topics are represented with discrete variables *z[ij]*, while words are represented with random variables *w[ij]*, where *m[i]* words are associated with each document and each word is associated with a topic. There are two variants: an asymmetric and a symmetric formulation.

[Fig. 14.4A](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0025) illustrates the asymmetric formulation; the symmetric formulation reverses the arrow from *d* to *z*. *D* is a set of random variables for the document index observations, and *W* is a set of random variables for all the words observed across the documents. The asymmetric formulation corresponds to

$P(W,D) = \\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{P(d\_{i})}\\prod\\limits\_{j = 1}^{m\_{n}}{\\sum\\limits\_{z\_{\\mathit{ij}}}{P(z\_{\\mathit{ij}} \\mid d\_{i})P(w\_{\\mathit{ij}} \\mid z\_{\\mathit{ij}})}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si103.png)

![Fig. 14.4 Graphical models for (A) pLSA, (B) LDAb, and (C) smoothed LDAb.](images/F000157f14-04-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. 14.4 Graphical models for (A) pLSA, (B) LDA^b, and (C) smoothed LDA^b.

Because *d*, an index over the training documents, is a random variable in the graph, pLSA is not a generative model for new documents. However, it does correspond to a valid probabilistic model with hidden variables, so the EM algorithm can be used to estimate parameters and obtain a representation of each document in a corpus in terms of its distribution over the topic variables.

 

### Latent Dirichlet Allocation

pLSA can be extended into a hierarchical Bayesian model with three levels, known as *latent Dirichlet allocation*. We refer to this as LDA^b (“b” for Bayesian) to distinguish it from linear discriminant analysis that is commonly referred to as LDA. LDA^b was proposed in part to reduce the overfitting that has been observed with pLSA and has been extended in many ways. Extensions of LDA^b can be used to determine trends over time and identify “hot” and “cold” topics. Such analyses are particularly interesting today with the explosion of social media and the interest in analyzing it.

Latent Dirichlet allocation is a hierarchical Bayesian model that reformulates pLSA by replacing the document index variables *d[i]* with the random parameter **θ**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si104.png), a vector of multinomial parameters for the documents. The distribution of **θ**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si105.png) is influenced by a Dirichlet prior with hyperparameter **α**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#945;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si106.png), which is also a vector. ([Appendix A.2](#TableA1_617-636_B9780443158889000212.xhtml#s0050) explains Dirichlet distributions and their use as priors for the parameters of the discrete distribution.) Finally, the relationship between the discrete topic variables *z[ij]* and the words *w[ij]* is also given an explicit dependence on a hyperparameter, namely, the matrix **B**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">B</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si107.png). [Fig. 14.4B](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0025) shows the corresponding graphical model. The probability model for the set of all observed words W is

$\\begin{matrix} {P(W \\mid \\mathbf{\\alpha},\\mathbf{B})} & = & {\\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{\\int P(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i} \\mid \\mathbf{\\alpha})\\left\\lbrack \\prod\\limits\_{j = 1}^{m\_{n}}{\\sum\\limits\_{z\_{\\mathit{ij}}}{P(z\_{\\mathit{ij}} \\mid \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i})P(}w\_{\\mathit{ij}} \\mid z\_{\\mathit{ij}},\\mathbf{B})} \\right\\rbrack}d\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}} \\\\ & = & {\\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{\\int P(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i} \\mid \\mathbf{\\alpha})\\left\\lbrack \\prod\\limits\_{j = 1}^{m\_{n}}{P(w\_{\\mathit{ij}} \\mid \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i},\\mathbf{B})} \\right\\rbrack}d\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i},} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mo>=</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8747;</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd/><mml:mtd><mml:mo>=</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8747;</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si108.png)

which marginalizes out the uncertainty associated with each **θ**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si109.png) and *z[ij]*. *P*(**θ**[*i*]|**α**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>|</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#945;</mml:mi><mml:msp1/><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si110.png) is given by a *k*\-dimensional Dirichlet distribution, which also leads to *k*\-dimensional topic variables *z[ij]*. For a vocabulary of size *V*, *P*(*w*[*i**j*]|*z*[*i**j*], **B**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>|</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si111.png) encodes the probability of each word given each topic, and prior information is therefore captured by the *k* × *V*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si112.png) dimensional matrix **B**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">B</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si113.png).

The marginal log-likelihood of the model can be optimized using an empirical Bayesian method by adjusting the hyperparameters **α**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#945;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si114.png) and **B**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">B</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si115.png) via the variational EM procedure. To perform the *E*\-step of EM the posterior distribution over the unobserved random quantities is needed. For the model defined by the previous equation, with a random **θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si116.png) for each document, word observations **w**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">w</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si117.png), and hidden topic variables **z**, the posterior distribution is

$P(\\mathbf{\\theta},z \\mid \\mathbf{w},\\mathbf{\\alpha},\\mathbf{B}) = \\frac{P(\\mathbf{\\theta},z,\\mathbf{w} \\mid \\mathbf{\\alpha},\\mathbf{B})}{P(\\mathbf{w} \\mid \\mathbf{\\alpha},\\mathbf{B})}$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si118.png)

which, unfortunately, is intractable. For the *M*\-step it is necessary to update hyperparameters **α**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#945;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si119.png) and **B**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">B</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si120.png), which can be done by computing the maximum likelihood estimates using the expected sufficient statistics from the *E*\-step. The variational EM procedure amounts to computing and using a separate approximate posterior for each **θ**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si121.png) and each *z[ij]*.

A method called “collapsed Gibbs sampling” turns out to be a particularly effective alternative to variational methods for performing LDA^b. Consider first that the model in [Fig. 14.4B](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0025) can be expanded to that shown in [Fig. 14.4C](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0025), which was originally cast as the smoothed version of LDA^b. Then add another Dirichlet prior with parameters given by **Γ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#915;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si122.png) on the topic parameters of **B**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">B</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si123.png), a formulation that further reduces the effects of overfitting. Standard Gibbs sampling involves iteratively sampling the hidden random variables *z[ij]*, the **θ**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si124.png)’s and the elements of matrix **B**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">B</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si125.png). Collapsed Gibbs sampling is obtained by integrating out the θ*[i]*’s and **B**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">B</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si126.png) analytically, which deals with these distributions exactly. Consequently, conditioned by the current estimates of **Γ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#915;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si127.png), **α**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#945;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si128.png), and the observed words of a document corpus, the Gibbs sampler proceeds by simply iteratively updating each *z[ij]* to compute the required approximate posterior. Using either samples or variational approximations it is then relatively straightforward to obtain estimates for the θ*[i]*’s and **B**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">B</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si129.png).

The overall approach of using a smoothed, collapsed LDA^b model to extract topics from a document collection can be summarized as follows. First define a hierarchical Bayesian model for the joint distribution of documents and words following the structure of [Fig. 14.4C](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0025). We could think of there being a Bayesian **E-step** that performs approximate inference using Gibbs’ sampling to sample from the *joint posterior* over *all* topics for all documents in the model, or *P*(*z*[*i**j*] ∣ *w*[*i**j*], **Γ**, **α**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#915;</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#945;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si130.png), where the θ*[i]*’s and **B**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">B</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si131.png) have been integrated out. This is followed by an **M-step** that uses these samples to update the estimates of the θ*[i]*’s and **B**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">B</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si132.png), using update equations that are functions of **Γ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#915;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si133.png), **α**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#945;</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si134.png), and the samples. This procedure is performed within a hierarchical Bayesian model, so the updated parameters can be used to create a Bayesian predictive distribution over new words and new topics given the observed words.

[Table 14.1](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#t0010) shows the highest probability words from a sampling of topics mined by [Griffiths and Steyvers (2004)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur235) by applying LDA^b to 28,154 abstracts of papers published in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Science* from 1991 to 2001 and tagged by authors with subcategory information. Analyzing the distribution over these tags identifies the highest probability user tags for each topic, which are shown at the bottom of [Table 14.1](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#t0010). Note that the user tags were not used to create the topics, but we can see how well the extracted topics match with human labels.

### Factor Graphs

Bayesian networks are a special kind of probability model that factorize a joint probability distribution into the product of conditional and unconditional distributions. Factor graphs provide an even more general framework for representing general functions by factoring them into the product of local functions, each of which acts on a subset of the full argument set:

$F(x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{n}) = \\prod\\limits\_{j = 1}^{S}{f\_{j}(X\_{j})},$<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si135.png)

where *X[j]* is a subset of the original set of arguments {*x*[1], …, *x[n]*}, *f[j]*(*X[j]*) is a function of *X[j]*, and *j* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si136.png), …, *S* enumerates the argument subsets. A *factor graph* consists of variable nodes, circles, for each variable *x[k]* and factor nodes, rectangles, for each function, with edges that connect each factor node to its variables.

[Fig. 14.5A and B](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0030) shows a Bayesian network and its factor graph corresponding to the factorization

$\\begin{matrix} {F\\left( x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{5}) \\right.} & = & {f\_{A}(x\_{1})f\_{B}(x\_{2})f\_{C}(x\_{3},x\_{1})f\_{D}(x\_{4},x\_{1},x\_{2})f\_{E}(x\_{5},x\_{2})} \\\\ & = & {P(x\_{1})P(x\_{2})P(x\_{3} \\mid x\_{1})P(x\_{4} \\mid x\_{1},x\_{2})P(x\_{5} \\mid x\_{2}).} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mo>=</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" ![Equation](images/F000157si137.png)![Fig. 14.5 (A) Bayesian network. (B) Corresponding factor graph.](images/F000157f14-05-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. 14.5 (A) Bayesian network. (B) Corresponding factor graph.

Factor graphs make concepts such as the Markov blanket for a given variable in a Bayesian network easy to identify. For example, [Fig. 14.6](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0035) shows the Markov blanket for variable *x*[6] in a factor graph that corresponds to the Bayesian network in [Fig. 13.3](#Ch014_485-514_B9780443158889000145.xhtml#f0020); it consists of all nodes that are connected to it through a factor. Factor graphs are more powerful than Bayesian networks because they can represent a wider class of factorizations and models. These include Markov random fields, which we will meet shortly.

![Fig. 14.6 The Markov blanket for variable x6 in a 10-variable factor graph.](images/F000157f14-06-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 14.6](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#Bf0035) The Markov blanket for variable *x*[6] in a 10-variable factor graph.

 

#### Factor graphs, Bayesian networks, and the logistic regression model

It is instructive to compare the factor graph for a naïvely constructed Bayesian model with the factor graph for a Naïve Bayes model of the same set of variables (and, later, with the factor graph for a logistic regression formulation of the same problem). [Figs. 14.7A and B](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#f0040) show the Bayesian network and its factor graph for a network with a child node *y* that has several parents *x[i]*, *i* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si138.png), …, *n*. [Fig. 14.7B](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#f0040) involves a large conditional probability table for *P*(*y**|**x*[1], …, *x*[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">y|</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si139.png), with many parameters that must be estimated or specified, because in

$P(y,x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{n}) = P(y \\mid x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{n})\\prod\\limits\_{i - 1}^{n}{P(x\_{i})}$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si140.png)

the number of parameters increases exponentially with the number of parent variables. In contrast [Figs. 14.7C and D](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#f0040) show the Bayesian network and its factor graph for the Naïve Bayes model. Here the number of parameters is linear in the number of children because the model breaks down into the product of functions involving *y* and just one *x[i]* because the underlying factorization is

$P(y,x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{n}) = P(y)\\prod\\limits\_{i - 1}^{n}{P(x\_{i} \\mid y)}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si141.png)

![Fig. 14.7 (A) and (B) Bayesian network and corresponding factor graph. (C) and (D) Naïve Bayes model and corresponding factor graph.](images/F000157f14-07-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. 14.7 (A) and (B) Bayesian network and corresponding factor graph. (C) and (D) Naïve Bayes model and corresponding factor graph.

The factor graphs show the different complexities very clearly. The graph in [Fig. 14.7B](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#f0040) has a factor involving *n* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si142.png) variables, while the factors in [Fig. 14.7D](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#f0040) involve no more than two variables.

Factor graphs can be extended to clarify an important distinction for conditional models. The Bayesian network of [Fig. 14.8A](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#f0045) involves a large table for the conditional distribution of *y* given many *x[i]*’s but a logistic regression model could be used to reduce the number of parameters for *P*(*y**|**x*[1], …, *x*[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">y|</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si143.png) from exponential to linear, depicted in [Fig. 14.8B](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#f0045).

![Fig. 14.8 (A) Bayesian network representing the joint distribution of y and its parents. (B) Factor graph for a logistic regression for the conditional distribution of y given its parents.](images/F000157f14-08-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. 14.8 (A) Bayesian network representing the joint distribution of *y* and its parents. (B) Factor graph for a logistic regression for the conditional distribution of *y* given its parents.

Let us assume that all variables are binary. Given a separate function *f[i]*(*y,x[i]*) for each binary variable *x[i]*, the conditional distribution defined by a logistic regression model has the form

$\\begin{matrix} {P(y \\mid x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{n})} & = & {\\frac{1}{Z(x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{n})}\\exp\\left\\lbrack \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{w\_{i}f\_{i}(y,x\_{i})} \\right\\rbrack} \\\\ & = & {\\frac{1}{Z(x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{n})}\\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}{\\phi\_{i}(x\_{i},y)},} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mo>=</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>exp</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd /><mml:mtd><mml:mo>=</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#981;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si144.png)

where the denominator *Z* is a data-dependent normalization term that makes the conditional distribution sum to 1, and *ϕ*[*i*](*x*[*i*], *y*) = exp (*w*[*i*]*f*[*i*](*y*, *x*[*i*]))<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#981;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>exp</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si145.png). This corresponds to a factor graph that resembles the Naïve Bayes model but with the factorized conditional distribution shown in [Fig. 14.8B](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#f0045). Here curved rectangles represent variables that are not explicitly defined as random variables. This graph represents the conditional probability function *P*(*y**|**x*[1], …, *x*[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">y|</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si146.png), and the number of parameters scales linearly because each function is connected to just a pair of variables.

 

### Markov Random Fields

Markov random fields define another factorized model for a set of random variables *X* where these variables are divided into so-called “cliques” *X[c]* and a factor Ψ*[c]*(*X[c]*) is defined for each clique:

$P\\left( X \\right) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\prod\\limits\_{c = 1}^{C}{\\Psi\_{c}\\left( X\_{c} \\right)}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#936;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si147.png)

A clique is a group of nodes in an undirected graph that all connect to every other node in the clique. *Z*, known as the partition function, normalizes the model to ensure that it is a probability distribution and consists of a sum over all possible values for all variables in the model. It could be written

$Z = \\sum\\limits\_{x \\in X}{\\prod\\limits\_{c = 1}^{C}{\\Psi\_{c}\\left( X\_{c} \\right)}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#936;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si148.png)

[Fig. 14.9A and B](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#f0050) shows an undirected graph corresponding to a Markov random field and its factor graph. Again the factor graph makes explicit the nature of the underlying functions used to create the model. For example, it shows that functions are associated with each node, which is not clear from the undirected graph notation. The Markov random field structure in [Fig. 14.9](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#f0050) has been widely used for images; this general structure is typically repeated over an entire image, with each node representing a property of a pixel (e.g., a label or its depth).

![Fig. 14.9 (A) Undirected graph representing a Markov random field structure. (B) Corresponding factor graph.](images/F000157f14-09-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. 14.9 (A) Undirected graph representing a Markov random field structure. (B) Corresponding factor graph.

[Fig. 14.9](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_a.xhtml#f0050) factorizes the joint probability for four variables as follows:

$\\begin{matrix} {P(x\_{1},x\_{2},x\_{3},x\_{4})} & = & where *ϕ*[*u*](*X*[*u*]) = *ϕ*[*u*](*x*[*i*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#981;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#981;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si150.png) represents a set of unary functions of just one variable while *Ψ*[*v*](*X*[*v*]) = *Ψ*[*v*](*x*[*i*], *x*[*j*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#936;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">&#936;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si151.png) represents a set of pairwise functions of two variables. Subscripts *u* and *v* index both the functions and the sets of single variables *X*[*u*] = {*x*[*i*]}[*u*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si152.png) and variable pairs *X*[*v*] = {*x*[*i*], *x*[*j*]}[*v*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si153.png) that serve as their arguments.

This representation can equivalently be expressed using an energy function *F*(*X*) of this form:

$F\\left( X \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{u = 1}^{U}{U\\left( X\_{u} \\right)} + \\sum\\limits\_{v = 1}^{V}{V\\left( X\_{v} \\right)}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>U</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si154.png)

Then a Markov random field can be written

$P\\left( X \\right) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\exp( - F\\left( X \\right)) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\exp\\left( - \\sum\\limits\_{u = 1}^{U}{U\\left( X\_{u} \\right)} - \\sum\\limits\_{v = 1}^{V}{V\\left( X\_{v} \\right)} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>exp</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>U</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si155.png)

Since *Z* is constant for any assignment of the variables *X* the negative log probability under the model can be written

$\\begin{matrix} {- \\mathit{\\log}P(x\_{1},x\_{2},x\_{3},x\_{4}) = - \\mathit{\\log}\\left\\lbrack \\prod\\limits\_{u = 1}^{U}{\\phi\_{u}\\left( X\_{u} \\right)\\prod\\limits\_{V = 1}^{V}{\\psi\_{V}\\left( X\_{V} \\right)}} \\right\\rbrack - \\mathit{\\log}Z} \\\\ {\\alpha\\sum\\limits\_{u = 1}^{U}{U\\left( X\_{u} \\right) +}\\sum\\limits\_{V = 1}^{V}{V\\left( X\_{V} \\right),}} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable width="336pt"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">log</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>U</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#981;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#968;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">log</mml:mi><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>&#945;</mml:mi><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>U</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si156.png)

This leads to the commonly used strategy of minimizing an energy function in this form to perform tasks such as image segmentation and entity resolution in text documents. When such minimization tasks are “submodular,” a term that denotes a particular category of optimization problems, an exact minimum can be found using algorithms based on graph-cuts; otherwise methods such as tree-reweighted message passing are used.

 

### Computing Using the Sum-Product and Max-Product Algorithms

Key quantities of interest for any probability model are the marginal probabilities and the most probable explanation of the model. For tree-structured graphical models, exact solutions for these can be found efficiently by the sum-product and max-product algorithms. When applied to the hidden Markov models discussed in [Section 14.5](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157_b.xhtml#s0215), these are known as the *forwards-backwards* and *Viterbi* algorithms, respectively. We begin with some simple examples for motivation and then present the algorithms themselves.

 

#### Marginal probabilities

With a Bayesian network an initial step is to determine the marginal probability of each node given no observations whatsoever. These *single node marginals* differ from the conditional and unconditional probabilities that were used to specify the network. Indeed, software packages for manipulating Bayesian networks often take the definition of a network in terms of the underlying conditional and unconditional probabilities and show the user the single node marginals for each node in a visual interface. The marginal for variable *x[i]* is

$P(x\_{i}) = \\sum\\limits\_{x\_{j \\neq i}}{P(x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{n})},$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8800;</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8230;</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si157.png)

where the sum is over the states of all variables *x*[*j*] ≠ *x*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8800;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si158.png) and can be computed by the sum-product algorithm. In fact, the same algorithm serves in many other situations, such as when some variables are observed and we wish to compute the belief of others, as well as for finding the posterior distributions needed for learning (e.g., using the EM algorithm).

Consider the task of computing the marginal probability of variable *x*[3] given the observation $x\_{4} = {\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000157si159.png) from the Bayesian network in [Fig. 14.5A](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#f0030). Since we are conditioning on a variable, we need to compute a marginal *conditional* probability. This corresponds to the practical notion of posing a query, where the model is used to infer an updated belief about *x*[3] given the state of variable *x*[4].

Since other variables in the graph have not been observed, they should be integrated out of the graphical model to obtain the desired result:

$P(x\_{3} \\mid {\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4}) = \\frac{P(x\_{3},{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4})}{P({\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4})} = \\frac{P(x\_{3},{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4})}{\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{3}}{(x\_{3},{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4})}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="normal">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">~</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000157si160.png)

Here the key probability of interest is

$\\begin{array}{ll} {P(x\_{3},{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4})} & {= \\sum\\limits\_{x\_{1}}{\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{2}}{\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{5}}{P(x\_{1},x\_{2},x\_{3},{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4},x\_{5})}}}} \\\\ & {= \\sum\\limits\_{x\_{1}}{\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{2}}{\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{5}}{P(x\_{1})P(x\_{2})P(x\_{3} \\mid x\_{1})P({\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4} \\mid x\_{1},x\_{2})P(x\_{5} \\mid x\_{2}).}}}} \\\\ \\end{array}$<mml:math><mml:mtable columnalign="left"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo However, this sum involves a large data structure containing the joint probability, composed of the products over the individual probabilities. The *sum-product algorithm* refers to a much better solution—simply *push the sums as far as possible to the right* before computing products of probabilities. Here the required marginalization can be computed by

$\\begin{matrix} {P(x\_{3},{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4})} & = & {\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{1}}{P(x\_{3} \\mid x\_{1})P(x\_{1})}\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{2}}{P({\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4} \\mid x\_{1},x\_{2})P(x\_{2})}\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{5}}{P(x\_{5} \\mid x\_{2})}} \\\\ & = & {\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{1}}{P(x\_{3} \\mid x\_{1})P(x\_{1})P({\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4} \\mid x\_{1})}} \\\\ & = & {\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{1}}{P(x\_{1},x\_{3},{\\overset{\\sim}{x}}\_{4})}.} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover
