The probability of taking any particular link is smaller if there are many outlinks, which is exactly the behavior we want from PageRank. It turns out that the PageRank of a given page is proportional to the probability that the random surfer lands on that page.

Now the problem raised by a page with no outlinks becomes apparent; it’s a PageRank sink because when surfers come in they cannot get out. More generally a set of pages might link to each other but not to anywhere else. This incestuous group is also a PageRank sink—the random surfer gets stuck in a trap. And a page with no inlinks? Random surfers never reach it. In fact, they never reach any group of pages that has no inlinks from the rest of the Web, even though it may have internal links and outlinks to the Web at large.

These two problems mean that the iterative calculation described earlier does not converge, as we earlier claimed it would. But the solution is simple: *teleportation*. With a certain small probability make the surfer arrive at a randomly chosen page instead of following a link from the one they are on. That solves both problems. If surfers are stuck at **G** they will eventually teleport out of it. And if they can’t reach **H** by surfing they will eventually teleport into it.

The teleport probability has a strong influence on the rate of convergence of the iterative algorithm and on the accuracy of its results. At the extreme, if it were equal to 1, meaning that the surfer always teleported, the link structure would have no effect on PageRank, and no iteration would be necessary. If it were 0 and the surfer never teleported, the calculation would not converge at all. Early published experiments used a teleportation probability of 0.15; some speculate that search engines increase it a little to hasten convergence.

Instead of teleporting to a randomly chosen page you could choose a predetermined probability for each page, and—once you had decided to teleport—use that probability to determine where to land. This does not affect the calculation but it does affect the result. If a page was discriminated against by receiving a smaller probability than the others it would end up with a smaller PageRank than it deserves. This gives search engine operators an opportunity to influence the results of the calculation—an opportunity that they probably use to discriminate against certain sites (e.g., ones they believe are trying to gain an unfair advantage by exploiting the PageRank system). This is the stuff of which lawsuits are made.

 

## 15.7 Images and Speech

Until recently images and speech signals received less attention from data mining researchers. However, the deep learning renaissance has changed all that. Signal processing in general is an area where massive amounts of data are easily available, and it seems to be well suited to the kind of automatic extraction of low-level features that are built up into successively higher levels that deep networks do so well. The world abounds with signal data but it is generally unlabeled. The production of large collections of *labeled* data is stimulating practitioners to apply deep learning techniques to many signal-processing tasks, principally image recognition and face verification and recognition.

 

### Images

[Chapter 10](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X), “Deep learning: fundamentals,” discussed how deep learning techniques have revolutionized aspects of the field of computer vision. This impact has only been possible because academic groups and technology companies made substantial investments in mining and labeling data on a large scale. The availability of carefully curated datasets enables high-capacity supervised or discriminative deep learning techniques to push recognition performance into the realm of usability for many applications. In addition to the examples highlighted later, convolutional neural network architectures have been used on tasks ranging from segmenting brain tumors to computing the depth in a scene from stereo cameras; the *Further Reading* section gives pointers to specific examples.

Deep convolutional neural network techniques have transformed the field of object category recognition. On large-scale visual recognition challenges such as ImageNet they can outperform people in terms of agreement with human judgments. ImageNet imagery was mined from the Internet and labeled in a large-scale academic project. Google has prepared a dataset of digits obtained by mining and labeling house numbers in their massive collection of Street View images. Again, deep convolutional networks outperform people in terms of agreement with human judgments.

There is an important distinction between recognizing object categories and identifying particular objects; identifying *your car* in a photograph is quite different from recognizing that *a car* is present. Here also deep learning–based methods are continually improving recognition performance. An alternative approach, “SIFT descriptors,” which are based on the scale-invariant feature transform, are already deployed in systems that recognize specific objects. These descriptors are computed from “interest points” that are found in an image—things like corners, which are easy to find and localize in images of the same object from different viewpoints. Once these points have been found a descriptor inspired by the human visual system is computed based on a trick that helps select an appropriate scale and orientation. This involves cutting out a patch with a certain orientation and rotation, and then creating a histogram of image gradients using the patch. While SIFT descriptors find their greatest application in 3D reconstruction, panoramic image creation, and robotic mapping, they are also widely used for identifying and tracking specific instances of objects.

Face recognition, an important special case of object recognition, has been the subject of intense research for decades, and deep convolutional networks have transformed the field. Better-than-human performance has been achieved on the task of face verification, using databases such as the “Labeled faces in the wild” data collected by the University of Massachusetts. In face verification one is given two photographs of faces and asked whether they belong to the same person or not. Good results are achieved using a special “Siamese network” architecture that takes two images as input and compares them using the internal representation of the convolutional neural network. The images are generally preprocessed to center the faces, crop them, and register them on a common coordinate system. Facial keypoint or landmark detection methods are used to help with the registration and warping process or to localize key zones to be used as input.

It is worth noting, given the discussion of data mining and ethics in [Chapter 1](#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029.xhtml#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029), “What’s it all about?,” [Chapter 7](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X), “Ethics: what are the impacts of what’s been learned?,” and [Sections 15.10](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#s0085) and [15.11](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#s0115) in this chapter, that face verification and face recognition raise difficult ethical issues. Federal governments deploy the technology in the fight against international terrorism; airports use it to reduce lineups at immigration. Its potential application in widespread video surveillance has a profound effect on the balance between security and privacy and other civil liberties. At the individual level stalkers would welcome end-user web services for face recognition.

 

### Speech

Speech recognition is rapidly becoming a widely used technology. Major companies use large datasets to render their systems robust to different speakers and noise sources. The classical architecture uses a signal processing front end to compute features inspired by the human auditory system from a spectral analysis of the audio input and passes them to a large system of hidden Markov models that have Gaussian mixture models for their observation likelihoods. Sophisticated language models are used to help disambiguate what words are present in the audio. Here again deep learning methods have been having substantial impact, and many large industrial groups are replacing elements of the classic speech recognition pipeline with deep learning techniques such as recurrent neural networks.

 

## 15.8 Adversarial Situations

A prime application of machine learning is junk email filtering. When we wrote the second edition of this book (late 2004) the scourge of unwanted email was a burning issue; by the writing of the third edition of this book (early 2010) the problem had abated despite the continual growth of spam email (by some estimates it accounts for 95% of all emails). This is largely due to the widespread use of spam filtering, which often uses learning techniques. At first blush junk email filtering appears to present a standard problem of document classification—divide documents into “ham” and “spam” on the basis of the text they contain, guided by training data, of which there are copious amounts. But it differs from ordinary document classification because it involves an adversarial aspect. The documents that are being classified are not chosen at random from an unimaginably huge set of all possible documents; they contain emails that are carefully crafted to evade the filtering process, designed specifically to beat the system.

Early spam filters simply discarded messages containing “spammy” words that connote such things as sex, lucre, and quackery. Of course, much legitimate correspondence concerns gender, money, and medicine; a balance must be struck. So filter designers recruited Bayesian text classification schemes that learned to strike an appropriate balance during the training process. Spammers quickly adjusted with techniques that concealed the spammy words by misspelling them; overwhelmed them with legitimate text, perhaps printed in white on a white background so that only the filter saw it; or simply put the spam text elsewhere, in an image or a URL that most mail readers download automatically.

The problem is complicated by the fact that it is hard to compare spam detection algorithms objectively. Although training data abounds, privacy issues preclude publishing large public corpora of representative email. And there are strong temporal effects. Spam changes character rapidly, invalidating sensitive statistical tests such as cross-validation. Finally, the bad guys can also use machine learning. For example, if they could get hold of examples of what your filter blocks and what it lets through they could use this as training data to learn how to evade it.

There are, unfortunately, many other examples of adversarial learning situations in our world today. Closely related to junk email is search engine spam—sites that attempt to deceive Internet search engines into placing them prominently in lists of search results. Highly ranked pages yield direct financial benefits to their owners because they present opportunities for advertising, providing strong motivation for profit seekers. Then there are the computer virus wars, in which designers of viruses and virus-protection software react to one another’s innovations. Here the motivation tends to be general disruption and denial of service rather than monetary gain.

Computer network security is a continually escalating battle. Protectors harden networks, operating systems, and applications, and attackers find vulnerabilities in all three areas. Intrusion detection systems sniff out unusual patterns of activity that might be caused by a hacker’s reconnaissance activity. Attackers realize this and try to obfuscate their trails, perhaps by working indirectly or by spreading their activities over a long time—or, conversely, by striking very quickly. Machine learning is being applied to this problem in an attempt to discover semantic connections among attacker traces in computer network data that intrusion detection systems miss. This is a large-scale problem; audit logs used to monitor computer network security can amount to gigabytes a day even in medium-sized organizations.

Many automated threat detection systems are based on matching current data to known attack types. The US Federal Aviation Administration developed the *Computer Assisted Passenger Pre-Screening System* (CAPPS), which screens airline passengers on the basis of their flight records and flags individuals for additional checked baggage screening. Although the exact details are unpublished, CAPPS is thought to assign higher threat scores to cash payments. However, this approach can only spot known or anticipated threats. Researchers are using unsupervised approaches such as anomaly and outlier detection in an attempt to detect suspicious activity. As well as flagging potential threats, anomaly detection systems can be applied to the detection of illegal activities such as financial fraud and money laundering.

Data mining is being used today to sift through huge volumes of data in the name of homeland defense. Heterogeneous information such as financial transactions, health care records, and network traffic is being mined to create profiles, construct social network models, and detect terrorist communications. This activity raises serious privacy concerns and has resulted in the development of privacy-preserving data mining techniques. These algorithms try to discern patterns in the data without accessing the original data directly, typically by distorting it with random values. To preserve privacy, they must guarantee that the mining process does not receive enough information to reconstruct the original data. This is easier said than done.

On a lighter note, not all adversarial data mining is aimed at combating nefarious activity. Multiagent systems in complex, noisy real-time domains involve autonomous agents that must both collaborate in a team and compete against antagonists. If you are having trouble visualizing this, think soccer. Robo-soccer is a rich and popular domain for exploring how machine learning can be applied to such difficult problems, primarily using reinforcement learning techniques, which are beyond the scope of this book. Players must not only hone low-level skills but must also learn to work together and adapt to the behavior patterns of different opponents.

Finally, machine learning has been used to solve an actual historical literary mystery by unmasking a prolific author who had attempted to conceal his identity. Ben Ish Chai was the leading rabbinic scholar in Baghdad in the late 19th century. Among his vast literary legacy are two separate collections of about 500 Hebrew-Aramaic letters written in response to legal queries. He is known to have written one collection. Although he claims to have found the other in an archive, historians suspect that he wrote it, too, but attempted to disguise his authorship by deliberately altering his style. The problem this case presents to machine learning is that there is no corpus of work to ascribe to the mystery author. There were a few known candidates but the letters could equally well have been written by anyone else. A new technique appropriately called *unmasking* was developed that creates a model to distinguish the known author’s work A from the unknown author’s work X, iteratively removes those features that are most useful for distinguishing the two, and examines the speed with which cross-validation accuracy degrades as more features are removed. The hypothesis is that if work X is written by work A’s author, who is trying to conceal his identity, whatever differences there are between work X and work A will be reflected in only a relatively small number of features compared with the differences between work X and the works of a completely different author, say the author of work B. In other words, when work X is compared with works A and B the accuracy curve as features are removed will decline much faster for work A than it does for work B. It was concluded that Ben Ish Chai did indeed write the mystery letters. This technique is a striking example of original and creative use of machine learning in an adversarial situation.

 

## 15.9 Ubiquitous Data Mining

We began this book by pointing out that we are overwhelmed with data. Nowhere does this impact the lives of ordinary people more than on the World Wide Web. No one can keep pace with the information explosion. Whereas data mining originated in the corporate world because that’s where the databases are, text and web mining are moving machine learning technology out of the companies and into the home. Whenever we are overwhelmed by data on the Web mining techniques promise tools to tame it. Applications are legion. Finding friends and contacting them, maintaining financial portfolios, shopping for bargains in an electronic world, using data detectors of any kind—all of these could be accomplished automatically without explicit programming. Already mining techniques are being used to predict what link you’re going to click next, to organize documents for you, sort your mail, and prioritize your search results. In a world where information is overwhelming, disorganized, and anarchic, text and web mining may be the solution we so desperately need.

Many believe that the Web is but the harbinger of an even greater paradigm shift: *ubiquitous computing*. Small portable devices are everywhere—mobile phones, personal digital assistants, personal stereo and video players, digital cameras, mobile Web access. Already some devices integrate all these functions. They know our location in physical time and space, help us communicate in social space, organize our personal planning space, recall our past, and envelop us in global information space. It is easy to find scores of processors in a middle-class home in the United States today, and they often communicate with one another and with the global information infrastructure. Thus the potential for data mining will soar.

Take consumer music. Popular music leads the vanguard of technological advance. Sony’s original Walkman paved the way to today’s ubiquitous portable electronics. Apple’s iPod pioneered large-scale portable storage. Napster’s network technology spurred the development of peer-to-peer protocols. Recommender systems such as Firefly brought computing to social networks. Content-aware music services are migrating to portable devices. Applications for data mining in networked communities of people are legion—discovering musical trends, tracking preferences and tastes, and analyzing listening behaviors.

Ubiquitous computing weaves digital space closely into real-world activities. To many, extrapolating their own computer experiences of extreme frustration, arcane technology, perceived personal inadequacy, and machine failure, this sounds like a nightmare. But proponents point out that it can’t be like that because, if it is, it won’t work. Today’s visionaries foresee a world of “calm” computing in which hidden machines silently cooperate behind the scenes to make our lives richer and easier. They’ll reach beyond the big problems of corporate finance and school homework to the little annoyances such as where are the car keys, can I get a parking place, and is that shirt I saw last week at Macy’s still on the rack? Clocks will find the correct time after a power failure, the microwave will download new recipes from the Internet, kids’ toys will refresh themselves with new games and new vocabularies. Clothes labels will track washing, coffee cups will alert cleaning staff to mold, light switches will save energy if no one is in the room, and pencils will digitize everything we draw. Where will data mining be in this new world? Everywhere!

It’s hard to point to examples of a future that does not yet exist. But advances in user interface technology are suggestive. Many repetitive tasks in direct-manipulation computer interfaces cannot be automated with standard application tools, forcing users to perform the same interface actions over and over again. This typifies the frustrations alluded to previously—who’s in charge, me or it? Experienced programmers might write a script to carry out such tasks on their behalf but as operating systems accrue layer upon layer of complexity the power of programmers to command the machine is eroded and vanishes altogether when complex functionality is embedded in appliances rather than in general-purpose computers.

Research in *programming by demonstration* enables ordinary users to automate predictable tasks without requiring any programming knowledge at all. The user need only know how to perform the task in the usual way to be able to communicate it to the computer. One system, called *Familiar*, helps users automate iterative tasks involving existing applications on Macintosh computers. It works across applications and can work with completely new ones never before encountered. It does this by using Apple’s scripting language to glean information from each application and exploiting that information to make predictions. The agent tolerates noise. It generates explanations to inform the user about its predictions and incorporates feedback. It’s adaptive; it learns specialized tasks for individual users. Furthermore, it is sensitive to each user’s style. If two people were teaching a task and happened to give identical demonstrations, Familiar would not necessarily infer identical programs—it’s tuned to their habits because it learns from their interaction history.

Familiar employs standard machine learning techniques to infer the user’s intent. Rules are used to evaluate predictions so that the best one can be presented to the user at each point. These rules are conditional so that users can teach classification tasks such as sorting files based on their type and assigning labels based on their size. They are learned incrementally. The agent adapts to individual users by recording their interaction history.

Many difficulties arise. One is scarcity of data. Users are loath to demonstrate several iterations of a task; they think the agent should immediately catch on to what they are doing. Whereas a data miner would consider a 100-instance dataset miniscule, users bridle at the prospect of demonstrating a task even half a dozen times. A second difficulty is the plethora of attributes. The computer desktop environment has hundreds of features that any given action might depend upon. This means that small datasets are overwhelmingly likely to contain attributes that are apparently highly predictive but nevertheless irrelevant, and specialized statistical tests are needed to compare alternative hypotheses. A third is that the iterative, improvement-driven development style that characterizes data mining applications fails. It is impossible *in principle* to create a fixed training and testing corpus for an interactive problem such as programming by demonstration because each improvement in the agent alters the test data by affecting how users react to it. A fourth is that existing application programs provide limited access to application and user data; often the raw material on which successful operation depends is inaccessible, buried deep within the application program.

Machine learning is already widely used at work. Text and Web mining is bringing the techniques in this book into our own lives as we read our email and surf the Web. As for the future, it will be stranger than we can imagine. The spreading computing infrastructure will offer untold opportunities for learning. Machine learning will be in there, behind the scenes, playing a role that will turn out to be foundational.

 

## 15.10 Machine Learning Technologies and Applications of Concern

In [Chapter 7](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X), “Ethics: what are the impacts of what’s been learned?,” we discussed concerns around applications of machine learning in hiring, criminal justice, credit scoring, and facial recognition, mostly revolving around fairness and bias issues. Here we’ll consider several other applications and technologies in which different ethical issues arise.

 

### Deepfakes

Generative deep learning technologies have now made it possible to generate or manipulate photos, video, audio, and text in a realistic manner, as we discussed in [Chapter 11](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121), “Advanced deep learning methods.” These technologies are rapidly improving, and they will have a profound impact on our society. A *deepfake* is an artificially created or altered piece of media that is achieved via deep learning technology. These technologies have many benefits such as creating beautiful artworks, enhancing educational content or films, or even making funny memes to share on the internet. They may be able to help people with some forms of paralysis such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) to speak again in a close approximation of their own voice. However, the potential harms of these technologies are severe. This is not merely hypothetical, as some of these harms have already occurred. In 2019 a deepfake app called DeepNude was released that modified images of women to “undress” them, creating realistic nude images. After widespread public outrage the app’s creators took it down. In a tweet the creators of the app wrote “The world is not yet ready for DeepNude.”

In the wake of the 2018 school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, Emma González, a student survivor, posted a compelling video in which she ripped up a sheet of paper with a bullseye target on it. To counter her activism as a proponent of gun-control, deepfake images and videos were made that fraudulently showed her instead ripping up the constitution of the United States. Despite the low quality of the images and video, many people were fooled into thinking that they were real. While fake or misleading content is not a new problem, generative AI has made the production of such content cheaper, faster, more scalable, and more realistic.

Experts have cited many potential harms to individuals, organizations, and society from deepfakes, including:

*   • Identity theft
*   • Blackmail
*   • Pornography (cf., the DeepNude example)
*   • Reputational sabotage to scuttle employment or romantic opportunities of rivals
*   • Political reputational sabotage to discredit opponents
*   • Falsifying politically inflammatory acts such as police violence or terrorism to stoke anger, violence, or panic, stoke social divisions, or even start a war (cf., the Parkland shooting example)
*   • Creating “fake news”
*   • Manipulating elections
*   • Damaging trust in institutions
*   • Undermining diplomatic relations between nations
*   • Disinformation and cyber-espionage
*   • Discrediting journalists and news outlets
*   • Obfuscating the truth by claiming that legitimate videos are deepfakes.

An example of a deepfake is shown in [Fig. 15.2](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#f0015).

For example, the prompt “A real photo of Barack Obama eating a taco, grayscale” produces a similar image of the former US president. We encourage you to try this prompt yourself. ### AI Art

The capability of generative deep learning models such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) and diffusion models to create artistic works has opened up both exciting possibilities and ethical dilemmas (see [Section 11.1](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#s0010) for more information on these models). These “*AI art*” models can create realistic and artistically impressive synthetic artworks resembling paintings, drawings, photographs, and more. The systems can be directed via natural language prompts describing the desired image. *Style transfer* models such as *CycleGAN* can automatically convert artworks into the artistic style of another artist, change the season where a scene takes place, or produce a drawing based on a photograph. Commercial AI art software such as Dall-E, CrAIyon, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion has put the power of AI art into the hands of consumers.

However, the impact on human artists and their livelihoods looms large. In 2022 an AI-generated artwork won first place at the Colorado State Fair Fine Arts Competition, in the “digital arts/digitally-manipulated photograph” category, raising the ire of some artists. The piece, developed by digital artist Jason M. Allen using Midjourney and titled “Théâtre D’opéra Spatial” (“Space Opera Theater” in French), combined Victorian and futuristic imagery ([Fig. 15.3](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#f0020)). The use of Midjourney was declared in the submission. One of the judges said that he had missed this fact when judging it but he stood by the result, calling it a “beautiful piece.” On the other side of the debate one Twitter user wrote “This sucks for the exact same reason we don’t let robots participate in the Olympics.”

Mr. Allen asked us to include the following text: Théâtre D’opéra Spatial “© 2022 Jason M Allen.” However, at the time of writing, the US copyright office has not registered this work. Mr. Allen has worked to advocate for legal ownership rights for artists who use generative AI. For more information on his advocacy, see https://artincarnate.com/. Courtesy Jason M. Allen, via Midjourney.](images/F000169f15-03-9780443158889.jpg)

[Fig. 15.3](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#Bf0020) Théâtre D’opéra Spatial, an AI-generated artwork that won first place at the 2022 Colorado State Fair Fine Arts Competition, created by Jason M. Allen via the Midjourney AI art system, reproduced with permission. Mr. Allen has worked to advocate for legal ownership rights for artists who use generative AI. For more information on his advocacy, see [https://artincarnate.com/](https://artincarnate.com/). Courtesy Jason M. Allen, via Midjourney.

Some of the concerns around AI art have been framed as copyright infringement issues. AI art models are typically trained on billions of images scraped from the Internet, often without consent of the original artists or compensation for the use of their work. As of 2023 there were at least two copyright infringement lawsuits against AI art companies including Stability AI (who created Stable Diffusion), DeviantArt (who created DreamUp based on Stable Diffusion and art submitted to their platform), and Midjourney. In a blog post announcing one of the lawsuits lawyer Matthew Butterick said that “because all the visual information in the system is derived from the copyrighted training images, the images produced—regardless of outward appearance—are necessarily works derived from those training images.” He also voiced concerns that AI art will make it difficult for artists to compete. According to Butterick, “At minimum, Stable Diffusion’s ability to flood the market with an essentially unlimited number of infringing images will inflict permanent damage on the market for art and artists.”

Not all artists are against AI art, however, and some digital artists who use generative AI in their work are fighting their own battle regarding copyright. In most countries and legal jurisdictions copyright protection is only granted to works that are authored by a human, which excludes work created by AI. The US Copyright Office clarified its position in a 2023 policy document, stating that “In the Office’s view, it is well-established that copyright can protect only material that is the product of human creativity. Most fundamentally, the term ‘author,’ which is used in both the Constitution and the Copyright Act, excludes non-humans.”

Jason M. Allen requested copyright protection for Théâtre D’opéra Spatial but was declined, as the US Copyright Office refused to grant copyright to the AI-generated portions of the work, and Allen refused to restrict his claim to only the postprocessing work he performed on top of the original AI-generated image. Allen has subsequently worked to advocate for copyright protection for digital art created with the assistance of generative AI technologies, founding an organization called Art Incarnate to champion AI art. In a mission statement on Art Incarnate’s website Allen said “With your support, together we can create the momentum needed to bring to bear the necessary arguments to rightly recognize creative users of any tool, regardless of how advanced, as the rightful authors of the works they actively choose to create.”

 

### Large Language Models

As we covered in [Chapter 11](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121), “Advanced deep learning methods,” *language models* are natural language processing (NLP) models that compute probabilities of sequences of words. When described this way they sound boring and not particularly useful. This belies the fact that *large language models* (*LLMs*)—language models with many parameters that have been trained on massive datasets—have tipped the NLP field on its head and are poised to do the same thing quite possibly to our entire society. Some LLMs, such as *Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers* (*BERT*), are designed to be useful for learning latent representations of text that can solve many (or even most!) NLP tasks with state-of-the-art performance. Other LLMs, such as *Generative Pre-trained Transformer* (*GPT*) models, are designed to generate realistic human-like text and respond to queries or prompts. These models have burst into the public consciousness with the release of US company OpenAI’s ChatGPT system, a chatbot based on GPT language models. ChatGPT has proved startlingly successful at not only producing coherent and stylistically cogent language in response to user-given prompts but at solving novel and challenging tasks across a variety of domains, from mathematics to medicine, to law, and beyond. It can write code, write poetry, and create graphics. Some researchers have claimed that the generality of the capabilities of the most recent OpenAI GPT model, GPT-4, suggests that it already reaches the beginning stages of an *artificial general intelligence* (*AGI*) system. ChatGPT and similar LLM technologies are expected to bring benefits to areas such as customer service, marketing, banking and financial services, tourism, and hospitality. In the academic sector they will help students learn with personalized tutoring.

Both the strengths and weaknesses of LLMs bring potential ethical challenges. In terms of weaknesses, while LLMs can often produce correct answers to difficult questions they can also produce fluent, plausible-sounding responses that are completely incorrect. They “*hallucinate*” false statements as readily as they produce facts, and it is not always easy for a human to identify these hallucinations. The fluency and apparent coherency of the generated text may increase the chance of *automation bias*, that is, inappropriate trust in an AI system.

LLMs can replicate or even amplify *discriminatory biases* by echoing stereotypes that may be harmful or offensive, potentially leading to representational or allocative harm. They may produce *hate speech* if not adequately filtered to prevent this (and such filters can sometimes be circumvented with clever prompts in a process known as “*jailbreaking*”). At best, they typically reflect the dominant hegemonic worldview that pervades their training data. They may reveal personally identifiable information (PII). Their training data may not be sufficiently diverse or representative of marginalized populations. If not frequently retrained based on recent data they may reflect outdated social norms. LLMs are generally not transparent or explainable so their behavior cannot easily be scrutinized. Errors in machine translation via LLMs can lead to harmful misunderstandings, such as the Palestinian man who was arrested by Israeli police when his Facebook post that said “good morning” in Arabic was incorrectly translated to “hurt them” in English and “attack them” in Hebrew.^(<a aria-label="noteref" href="#fn5" id="Cfn5">5</a>5)

According to the perspective advanced by computational linguist Emily Bender and colleagues, since the “knowledge” encoded in LLMs is gleaned from statistical patterns in text without grounding that knowledge in experience of the real world the systems cannot truly “understand” the meaning of this knowledge. With text data as their only input LLMs have access to “*form*,” such as observable realizations of language, but they do not have access to “*meaning*,” that is, the relation between form and the external world beyond language. Nor do they have access to the communicative intent of the authors that would be required to ground their “understanding” in relation to the real world. In this perspective LLMs are only “*stochastic parrots*”—they randomly stitch together linguistic forms based on the patterns found in their training data without reference to meaning. Therefore, the argument goes, when LLM systems are asked to reason about things beyond their input data that require true understanding of the external world they would be expected to fail.

Not everyone is convinced by this argument, or at least, that its practical implications are severe. The opposing school of thought, championed by computational linguist Christopher Manning, embodies the *distributional hypothesis*, the principle that motivated word embedding models. The distributional hypothesis, as stated by linguist J.R. Firth in the 1950s, is that “a word is characterized by the company it keeps.” More concretely, meaning can be estimated based on the contexts in which a word appears (without reference to external phenomena). Manning coined the term *distributional semantics* for the research field that seeks to quantify and implement the distributional hypothesis, including word embeddings and related models.

The strengths of LLMs bring their own ethical concerns. Most of the previously mentioned concerns around deepfakes apply to the misuse and abuse of LLMs, including identity theft, fraud, romantic and financial scams, disinformation and election interference, cyber-warfare, spam, and so on. Cheating in academic assessments using ChatGPT is already endemic, as it can answer many assessed tasks automatically with no thought or effort on the part of the student. LLMs may make some jobs obsolete, putting people out of work. (Of course, AI and LLMs will create some new jobs as well.) Some scholars believe that the rapid progress in LLM technologies may soon produce *artificial superintelligence* (*ASI*), which could represent an existential threat to life on Earth, although this view is not presently the majority opinion among experts. Citing these types of concerns, a 2023 petition by the Future of Life Institute called for all AI labs to pause the training of all AI systems more powerful than GPT-4 for at least 6 months. The petition has so far received more than 33,000 signatures, including high-profile technologists such as deep learning expert Yoshua Bengio, AI expert Stuart Russell, Apple Co-founder Steve Wozniak, and tech CEO/entrepreneur Elon Musk. Not everyone thinks this is a good idea. For example, in an opinion published by Bloomberg Tyler Cowen, economics professor at George Mason University, argued that a pause would simply shift the development of the technologies to countries that did not agree to the pause (and which might be even less responsible), harming US national security and hampering potentially beneficial innovation (such as AI for curing cancer, or better-aligned AI systems created by small businesses) while accomplishing very little to improve the situation.

The environmental and climate impacts of LLMs are also an issue. In 2022 training GPT-3 consumed the equivalent annual energy of approximately 200 Germans while producing nearly 500 metric tons of CO[2]. Since this does not include postdeployment energy costs, the actual amount of energy consumed is likely much higher. There are also ethical concerns around OpenAI’s practice of the use of cheap labor, primarily from African countries, to manually flag problematic content for training their system to avoid generating it.

 

### Self-Driving Cars

*Autonomous vehicles* (*AVs*), better known as *self-driving cars*, are vehicles that can drive on their own without human input ([Fig. 15.4](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#f0025)). In 2023 the California Public Utilities Commission’s (CPUC) approved two commercial AV companies, Cruise and Waymo, to operate commercial “*robotaxi*” vehicles autonomously across San Francisco, with paid fares, at any time of day. Both companies had previously operated robotaxi services subject to restrictions on factors including the hours of operation and number of vehicles, and they were not allowed to charge a fare unless there was a “backup” human operator present. Prior to that vehicles that had some automation capabilities—though not fully autonomous—had been on the road for some time, including Tesla’s “Autopilot” feature and AI-based features from many automobile manufacturers for collision prevention, automatic parking, and so on.

The model has since been retired but the design of the Firefly, similar to the one shown in this image, remains in the public consciousness when we think of self-driving cars. From Shutterstock, contributed by user Andrush, Stock Vector ID: 529387732](images/F000169f15-04-9780443158889.jpg)

The model has since been retired but the design of the Firefly, similar to the one shown in this image, remains in the public consciousness when we think of self-driving cars. From Shutterstock, contributed by user Andrush, Stock Vector ID: 529387732

Although self-driving cars have the potential to be safer than human drivers, the safety concerns around them are a thorny ethical issue. The aforementioned CPUC approval met with a lot of public comment both for and against the resolution. On behalf of city transit and planning officials, San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu formally requested that that state regulators temporarily halt the approved expansion of robotaxi services and redo the hearing approving it. “AV technology has a place in San Francisco, but we’re concerned it is not yet capable of safely operating in our complex transportation environment,” Chiu said in a statement. “These vehicles may be able to drive themselves, but they can’t regulate themselves. The CPUC must do that to protect passenger and public safety. Since the CPUC’s decision to allow unfettered expansion of AVs for commercial passenger service in San Francisco, AVs have continued to present safety risks and interfere with first responders.”

While Waymo and Cruise robotaxis had not caused any (human) deaths as of the time of the hearing, they had malfunctioned and stopped, causing traffic flow issues. A Waymo self-driving car killed a dog in San Francisco early in 2023. Shortly after the hearing a Cruise vehicle was involved in a crash with the fire truck in which a passenger sustained minor injuries. Later in 2023 a Cruise AV ran over a pedestrian, dragged her 20 feet while attempting to pull over, and stopped with its rear tire on top of her leg until first responders could extricate her with the jaws of life. The incident occurred after a human-driven vehicle hit the pedestrian and knocked her into the AV’s path. The CPUC alleged that Cruise misled them and the public by withholding the fact that their AV had dragged the passenger. In the wake of this incident and others the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) suspended Cruise’s AV permits, Cruise voluntarily suspended its robotaxi operations across the United States, and the company’s CEO, Kyle Vogt, resigned. At the time of writing the situation is in flux and the long-term implications of these events are unclear.

The safety record of self-driving cars has been mixed. According to watchdog website tesladeaths.com, as of August 2023 there have been 41 deaths from crashes involving a vehicle where Tesla Autopilot was engaged at least 30 seconds earlier, across 36 separate incidents. As is standard for recording automobile death statistics, this figure includes cases where Tesla was deemed not at fault. On the other hand, a 2017 report from the US National Transportation Safety Board, which was investigating an earlier Tesla Autopilot-related death, concluded that for Tesla cars the crash rate dropped by 40% after Autopilot was installed.

Since self-driving cars travel at high speeds among other vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists, it may not ever be possible to make them perfectly safe. In cases where an accident is unavoidable the AI system may need to make decisions that determine who is likely to be harmed or killed between its passengers and other road users. In such a case should the AI prioritize the safety of its own passengers or aim to minimize the number of deaths overall? This situation is sometimes likened to the *trolley problem* from moral philosophy and psychology. The trolley problem is a thought experiment in which a runaway tram will hit and kill one or more people if left to continue on its railway track but an operator could decide to switch it to a different track, where it would hit and kill a different set of people. While some philosophers have emphasized the similarity between accident avoidance in self-driving cars and the trolley problem, others have pointed out substantial differences including:

*   • The role of moral and legal responsibility. With real-world self-driving cars one needs to consider *who* is responsible for making these life or death decisions and what their legal and moral responsibilities are, while this is abstracted out of the trolley problem.
*   • There may be potentially unlimited set of considerations factoring into the decision, instead of a small, predefined list of considerations in the trolley problem (e.g., age, whether the person is a war criminal).
*   • Temporal aspects differ. The accident management algorithm is designed in advance then later executed in real time.
*   • With self-driving cars there is the necessity of risk estimation and reasoning under uncertainty that is not present in the traditional trolley problem.

Whether or not we view such decisions as instances of the trolley problem, solutions are far from easy. Self-interest plays a complicating role. A 2016 study performed on the Mechanical Turk crowdsourcing platform by economist Jean-François Bonnefon and colleagues found that although participants in principle preferred AVs to implement *utilitarian ethics* that prioritized minimizing deaths, even at the expense of their passengers, and would like others to buy such systems, they themselves preferred to ride in AVs that prioritize protecting their passengers at all costs. They were overall against regulation enforcing the utilitarian approach and would be less likely to buy such a vehicle. The study’s authors concluded that enforcing the utilitarian approach could slow the adoption of self-driving cars, which might ironically increase the overall number of vehicular deaths, supposing that the self-driving vehicles are safer than human-driven ones.

Other ethical concerns around self-driving cars include:

*   • *Cybersecurity*. A hacker could take control of a self-driving car and use it as a weapon.
*   • *Privacy*. The destinations visited and in-vehicle video or audio data would likely need to be recorded. Since AVs are internet connected, this information could be hacked.
*   • *Liability*. Who is at fault when a self-driving car crashes?
*   • *Loss of jobs for professional drivers*. This would impact professions such as taxi drivers, truck drivers, chauffeurs, and postal workers.

 

### Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems

*Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems* (*LAWS*) are weapons that can locate, select, and kill human targets without human supervision. These systems already exist. Israel’s Harop missile is a “loitering munition” with a 10-foot wingspan and a 50-pound warhead. It searches for up to 6 hours for a target that meets a particular set of criteria (e.g., “looks like a tank”). The Kargu quadcopter, made by Turkish manufacturer STM, can carry up to 1.5 kg of explosives and is capable of selecting and tracking targets based on images using facial recognition. Not all *automated* systems are *autonomous*. Drones that are remotely piloted by human operators, such as General Atomics’ Reaper and Predator drones used by the US military, are not autonomous weapons systems although they could potentially be made autonomous in the near future.

Killer robots that roam on two or four legs, akin to those seen in the Terminator movies, can be built using existing technology. US company Boston Dynamics builds bipedal and quadrupedal robots and has received US military funding, although it states in its ethical principles documents that it will not authorize or partner with those who wish to weaponize its robots. Turning its robots into weapons, however, is as simple as taping a gun to one of them. In 2021 a US art installation by art collective MSCHF, titled “Spot’s Rampage,” attached a paintball gun to Boston Dynamics’ four-legged “Spot” robot and allowed exhibit visitors to remotely control the robot. Boston Dynamics was naturally unimpressed with the project, calling it “provocative” in a statement released on Twitter and threatening to void the robot’s warranty if the exhibition went ahead.

There is a growing movement to ban LAWS. The International Committee for Robot Arms Control (ICRAC), a Non-Government Organization (NGO), called for a discussion on the prohibition of LAWS as early as 2009. In a 2023 United Nations policy brief titled “A New Agenda for Peace” UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for a legally binding prohibition on LAWS that function without human control or oversight, with regulation on all other autonomous weapons system, to be instituted by 2026.

 

## 15.11 AI and Society

Since AI, machine learning, and data mining technologies are rapidly revolutionizing and disrupting many aspects of daily life, it seems inevitable that these technologies will have lasting impacts on society at large, both positive and negative. Some of these impacts have already occurred, and we have seen many examples of this in this chapter. Here we focus on some of the impacts of AI that are at the societal scale. The discussion only scratches the surface of these impacts, and undoubtedly there will be many more that are currently unforeseen.

 

### Power and Control in the Workplace

The workplace is a front line for the impact of AI on our society. We discussed in [Chapter 7](#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X.xhtml#Ch007_261-315_B978044315888900008X), “Ethics: what are the impacts of what’s been learned?” that even after hiring AI can, and frequently does, contribute to exacerbating the power differential between employers and employees. The AI systems used by businesses are almost always designed to prioritize the business owner’s interests, such as profit, rather than employee welfare considerations. For example, shift scheduling systems, most often used by companies with low-wage employees including McDonald’s, Walmart, and Starbucks, produce wildly unpredictable schedules, with relatively short notice given to the employees. Since increasing their availability could increase their hours, it is not easy for employees to carve out time for furthering their education (a key to obtaining a higher-wage job) or spending time with their families. Gig economy workers, including ride-share and food delivery drivers as well as online labor marketplace workers on platforms such as TaskRabbit, are at the mercy of the AI algorithms that match them with jobs, set their wages, and make automated decisions that could boot them from the platforms, in many cases removing their source of income without human intervention or adequate recourse.

The problems of algorithmic management systems extend beyond gig work. In 2019 it was reported by the Verge, a US news firm, that Amazon uses AI to set a rigidly enforced performance and productivity threshold, called “the rate,” on its warehouse employees. Warnings and termination decisions were generated automatically by the system without input from human supervisors (although the supervisors were able to override the decisions). According to the report, Amazon used the system to fire at least 300 employees at a Baltimore facility, more than 10 % of the staff at that location, between August 2017 and September 2018. The practice has led to unlawful discrimination and terminations and an injury rate well above the industry average, according to a 2023 blog post by US law firm JD Supra. In response to these issues, in 2022 the California state senate passed the Warehouse Workers Protection Act, which requires companies to disclose productivity quotas to state regulators and prohibits unsafe and unrealistic quotas. Similar legislation is appearing across the United States. In the AI Now Institute’s 2023 annual report researchers highlighted how such AI-based algorithmic management systems increase the devaluation of work, unequally distribute benefits and risks, hamper collective action efforts, and surveil workers at the cost of their right to privacy. They call for increased legislation to restrict these systems and restore the balance of power between employers and employees,

 

### The Future of Work

There are also concerns around the impact of AI technologies on the *future of work*. Self-driving cars are poised to replace human drivers in the taxi/rideshare and trucking industries. Ever since the Industrial Revolution, automation has been a big part of manufacturing, and advances in robotics will likely see this increase, possibly at the cost of jobs for human employees. Large language models and closely related chatbot and personal assistant technologies may automate clerical and administrative work, medical decision making, etc. (IBM’s Watson AI was an early, failed attempt at this).

At least initially, low-wage workers are most at risk of being displaced by AI, with the impacts expected to disproportionately impact minoritized populations.

In the short-to-medium term workers in many fields will need to reskill to keep pace with the rapidly changing environment due to AI. In the longer term, as AI will increasingly do many of the jobs that humans currently do, at minimal cost, we as a society may need to rethink our relationship with work and decide what a future without work should look like and how a positive version of this future could be achieved. Similarly, there are concerns that AI and data mining technologies, which are most readily exploited by those who are well-resourced, are already concentrating power in the hands of large technology companies, the wealthy, and governments.

 

### Surveillance Capitalism

In this chapter we’ve discussed a number of ethical concerns around the use of data mining and machine learning technologies, particularly in their use by Big Tech companies to profit from data about people. We’ve also described techniques that can mitigate some of these issues, such as privacy-preserving machine learning via differentially private algorithms, or fair machine learning methods. A few of the scarier issues aside, our tacit assumption has generally been that if the Big Tech companies could simply be persuaded to take ethical and responsible AI issues seriously and make the appropriate changes everything would be fine.

In her 2018 book *The Age of Surveillance Capitalism: The Fight for a Human Future at the New Frontier of Power* Soshana Zuboff, Emeritus Professor of Harvard Business School and former Faculty Associate at the Berkman Center for Internet and Society, advanced a much more pointed critique of the business models and practices of certain Big Tech companies, which she calls *surveillance capitalism*. From this perspective the economic logic that drives such tech firms is fundamentally problematic and is a threat to human rights, autonomy, and democracy. As such, the problems may run deeper than the band-aid of responsible AI technologies and practices can realistically salve or solve. Like *Big Brother* from George Orwell’s *Nineteen Eighty-Four*, the problems of surveillance capitalism come down to mass surveillance, power, and control. While Big Brother is emblematic of totalitarian control by the state by perpetrating mass surveillance, Zuboff analogously considers mass surveillance and control performed by the Big Tech industry (and startups that follow the same model), which she names “*Big Other*.”

The key points in the definition of surveillance capitalism are:

*   • It is a new kind of capitalism, heralding a new economic order.
*   • It is based on an exploitative process that takes human experience as its raw material, extracts data, makes predictions, and increases sales.
*   • Beyond simply predicting surveillance capitalism aims at control and manipulation via rewards, punishments, digital rules, nudges, and so on.

In short, surveillance capitalism is the economic logic that seeks to profit from extracting data from human experience, predicting human behavior, and ultimately controlling human behavior. According to traditional Marxist theory, power comes from controlling the *means of production*. In contrast, in the theory of surveillance capitalism power arises from controlling the “*means of behavior modification*.” The notion of surveillance capitalism is a critique of the business practices of some tech companies, with Google being the main progenitor, followed by Facebook, Microsoft, and numerous startups. It however is not a critique of the AI technologies themselves, or the use of AI/data mining to improve products and services, or of traditional industrial-era capitalist practices.

To illustrate the rise of surveillance capitalism, Zuboff contrasts an early vision of the smart home and ubiquitous computing with the current state of affairs in those areas. The Aware Home was a research project begun in 2000 at Georgia Tech, which envisioned a symbiosis of humans and home via context-aware sensors. Crucially, the researchers made the working assumption that *the data and knowledge arising from the system would belong entirely to the people who live in the house*. As such, the home would keep its ancient role as a private sanctuary, protected from outside observation or influence. In the year 2000 this assumption was in line with most people’s expectations and was considered uncontroversial. Fast-forward to 2018, when Nest, a subsidiary of Alphabet, was merged with Google. Like the Aware home the Nest Thermostat uses sensors in the home to learn about its environment and the home’s inhabitants. But unlike the Aware Home data and knowledge acquired from the system are *uploaded to Google’s servers and hence shared with third parties for analytics*. Since Nest takes little responsibility for the use of the data by those third parties, users would need to read many other privacy policies and license agreements to understand what might happen to their data. A study from the University of London found that a user of a single Nest Thermostat would need to read almost 1000 contracts to understand how their data are being used! So what went wrong between the year 2000 and 2018? You guessed it—the rise of surveillance capitalism.

Zuboff dissects surveillance capitalism with reference to observations from Google’s Chief Economist, Hal Varian. She repurposes Varian’s ideas on the uses of computer-mediated transactions to change and improve the economy in the Internet era, and which presumably underpin Google’s business model, as a framework for explaining the main elements of surveillance capitalism. These elements include:

*   • **Data Extraction and Analysis:** As we know well by now, “Big Other” harvests data from many sources including online transactions, a growing array of sensors including drones, wearable devices, smart homes, smart phones, and so on, as well as government and corporate databases, and surveillance cameras. Further, everyday actions are increasingly digitized and hence recorded and stored. Your every click, social media post, email, text message, search query, and more can be captured to learn about you. This data stream is sometimes called the *digital exhaust*.  
    As the saying goes, “If it’s free, you are the product.” For example, Google’s users are not its customers. Rather, its customers are advertisers, to whom it sells ads via the Google AdWords platform, which performs an algorithmic auction process. Since well-targeted ads are more valuable, Google is motivated to store every scrap of information it can on its users to improve ad targeting and thus increase profits. This also incentivizes aggressive data collection strategies—whenever there is a legal gray area on whether data collection is allowed, Big Other companies will take data first, ask permission later, and when the protests and finally lawsuits inevitably come, pay the resulting fines or settlements at a small fraction of the resulting profits. This brings to mind Facebook’s former internal motto, attributed to Mark Zuckerberg: “Move fast and break things.” For instance, not only do Google Street View’s vans take photos of peoples’ homes without asking for permission but they also had scanners that were scraping data from private Wi-Fi networks, including those of residential Internet users. A lawsuit from 38 US states resulted in a $7 million settlement and forced Google to police its employees over privacy issues. At the time of writing overseas lawsuits are ongoing.  
    As you are now well familiar with, after collecting all this data machine learning is then brought to bear to analyze the data, particularly to predict behavior, which Zuboff calls a “*behavioral futures market*.” Ubiquitous data collection for behavioral prediction, feeding into a surveillance capitalism business model, has become the default model for Silicon Valley startups.
*   • **Monitoring and Contracts:** The increasing computer mediation and digitization of all aspects of life enables Big Other to increase their control by imposing contracts in a more fine-grained and constraining manner and monitor and enforce them digitally. If someone misses a car payment the vehicle can cease to operate and report its location for pickup. Auto insurance companies can monitor their customers’ driving to determine whether to pay out claims. Smartphone location tracking data can be used to check whether gig economy workers have completed their assigned tasks and automatically refuse payment for the work.  
    Contracts, which are essentially promises and obligations, are central to the functioning of our society. If contracts are enforced automatically, it removes the necessity to, or possibility of, developing trust.  
    Zuboff has concerns that Big Other is removing contracts from the social sphere and turning them into automated processes. Surveillance capitalists have stepped into the role of contract enforcer, occupying a power typically held by the state, which in a democratic society was legitimately chosen by the people to wield that power. According to Zuboff, Big Other has seized that power unilaterally, without legitimate authority to do so, and mechanically enforced it, without oversight and in many cases without detection. She sees the enforcement of rewards and punishments by Big Other as “a new kind of invisible hand” that overthrows the rule of law and could even be understood as a “coup des gens” (overthrow of the people).  
    Zuboff compares the automatic monitoring and enforcement of contracts to the *panopticon*, a theoretical prison design proposed by philosopher Jeremy Bentham in the late 1700 s that is frequently used as metaphor for modern-day surveillance in the workplace. The use as a metaphor is associated with philosopher Michel Foucault. In the panopticon there is a central guard tower, with cells around the periphery and blinds that prevent prisoners from observing the guards ([Fig. 15.5](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#f0030)). The design makes it so that the guards can watch any or all of the prisoners, and the prisoners cannot tell whether or not they are being watched at any given moment. Hence the prisoners must behave as if they are always watched. This behavior modification, called “*anticipatory conformity*,” is the main goal of the system. Zuboff sees the automaticity that surveillance capitalism strives for as even worse than the panopticon, in which the prisoners at least had a choice on whether to conform. With continual monitoring and automatic enforcement of contracts, even the option not to conform is removed.
*   • **Personalization and Communication:** Personalization has become a key part of the surveillance capitalism business model. To receive personalized search results, personalized product and movie recommendations, personalized assistance from personal digital assistants, and yes, personalized advertising, we as users must submit to giving our data to Big Other. Varian, Google’s Chief Economist, sees this as a fair and reasonable trade, like giving your private information to your doctor, lawyer, or accountant. Zuboff instead sees this as exploitative. For Zuboff, rather than a reciprocal exchange the products and services become the “hooks” that lure people into a bad deal. It has become difficult to entirely opt out of the surveillance economy since those products have become integral to our society and necessary to compete in the rat race with our peers. We have become desensitized and numb to the proposition of giving up our private data to Big Other. To Zuboff this is like a Faustian pact, also known as a deal with the Devil. In making a Faustian pact we are tricked, cheated, and even though we may initially think we got a bargain we will ultimately lose out.
*   • **Continuous Experiments:** Since big data is continually harvested as it becomes available, it is generally *observational data*, that is, data that is not constructed via a rigorous causal experiment design. As such it is generally difficult to determine causality from generic big data. This motivates the pervasive use of more deliberate causal experiments to identify causal patterns by trying out different website layouts or machine learning models, etc., on different subsets of the users and measuring how this impacts metrics such as click-through rates. At Google this practice is called *A/B testing*, and it is done routinely.  
    Concerns arise when the experiments aim to study not only the design of a system but how it can be used to control user behavior. The infamous 2014 “Facebook mood study” by Adam Kramer et al., for example, demonstrated that it was possible to alter users’ moods by modifying the amount of emotional content in their Facebook feeds, leading to a public outcry. (To be fair, the study aimed to investigate the psychological phenomenon of emotional contagion on a social network and did not explicitly seek to develop methods of influence and control.)  
    Far worse, Pokémon Go, an augmented reality game created by a subsidiary of Google called Niantic in which users hunt Pokémon that virtually appear on their devices at real-world locations, demonstrated that it is possible to herd users to visit real-world locations and profit from this digitally influenced behavior via local advertising. Zuboff calls this a “surveillance capitalist’s dream come true” since it facilitates collecting real-world user behavior data, the control of user behavior in physical spaces, and the experimental study of how to control users’ behavior and profit because of this control.

![Fig. 15.5 The panopticon is a conceptual design for a prison from the late 1700 s that has been used as a metaphor for systems of social control. This diagram shows the panopticon from a birds-eye view. The prison is circular with cells around the circumference and a guard tower in the center. The guard tower has windows that the guards can see out of but the prisoners cannot see into. This would have been achieved using blinds, or more recently, one-way mirrors. Since the prisoners cannot see when they are being watched, they must behave as if they are being always watched. Thus the prisoners are made compliant (“anticipatory conformity”). The goal of the system is not simply monitoring but control. Surveillance and monitoring in schools, hospitals, factories, offices, and public spaces have been compared to the panopticon.
