[Fig. 15.5](#Ch016_571-615_B9780443158889000169.xhtml#Bf0030) The panopticon is a conceptual design for a prison from the late 1700 s that has been used as a metaphor for systems of social control. This diagram shows the panopticon from a birds-eye view. The prison is circular with cells around the circumference and a guard tower in the center. The guard tower has windows that the guards can see out of but the prisoners cannot see into. This would have been achieved using blinds, or more recently, one-way mirrors. Since the prisoners cannot see when they are being watched, they must behave as if they are being always watched. Thus the prisoners are made compliant (“anticipatory conformity”). The goal of the system is not simply monitoring but control.  
Surveillance and monitoring in schools, hospitals, factories, offices, and public spaces have been compared to the panopticon. Zuboff argues that surveillance capitalism goes beyond the panopticon in achieving control since digital monitoring is total and compliance with contracts can be automated, removing all possibility of freedom of choice.

  

## 15.12 Further Reading and Bibliographic Notes

The paper on the “illusion of progress” in classification is by [Hand (2006)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur248), and he found that a very simple method achieves more than 90% of the classification improvement yielded by the most sophisticated scheme.

There is a substantial volume of literature that treats the topic of massive datasets, and we can only point to a few references here. [Fayyad and Smyth (1995)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur165) describe the application of data mining to voluminous data from scientific experiments. [Shafer, Agrawal, and Metha (1996)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur487) describe a parallel version of a top-down decision tree inducer. A sequential decision tree algorithm for massive disk-resident datasets has been developed by [Mehta, Agrawal, and Rissanen (1996)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur387). The technique of applying any algorithm to a large dataset by splitting it into smaller chunks and bagging or boosting the result is described by [Breiman (1999)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur65); [Frank, Holmes, Kirkby, and Hall (2002)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur181) explain the related pruning and selection scheme.

Early work on incremental work on decision trees is reported by [Utgoff (1989)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur537) and [Utgoff, Berkman, and Clouse (1997)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur538). The Hoeffding tree was introduced by [Domingos and Hulten (2000)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur139). Our description of it, including extensions and improvement, closely follows Kirkby’s (2007) PhD thesis. The MOA system is described by [Bifet, Holmes, Kirkby, and Pfahringer (2010)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur41).

Despite its importance, comparatively little seems to have been written about the general problem of incorporating metadata into practical data mining. A scheme for encoding domain knowledge into propositional rules and its use for both deduction and induction has been investigated by [Giraud-Carrier (1998)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur219). The related area of inductive logic programming, which deals with knowledge represented by first-order logic rules, is covered by [Bergadano and Gunetti (1996)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur34). Probabilistic logic learning is covered by [de Raedt (2008)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur124).

Text mining is a broad area, and there are few comprehensive surveys of the area as a whole; [Witten (2004)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur569) provides one. Numerous feature selection and machine learning techniques have been applied to text categorization ([Sebastiani, 2002](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur482)). [Martin (1995)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur379) describes applications of document clustering to information retrieval. [Cavnar and Trenkle (1994)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur85) show how to use *n*\-gram profiles to ascertain with high accuracy the language in which a document is written. The use of support vector machines for authorship ascription is described by [Diederich, Kindermann, Leopold, and Paass (2003)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur132); the same technology was used by [Dumais, Platt, Heckerman, and Sahami (1998)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur150) to assign key phrases from a controlled vocabulary to documents on the basis of a large number of training documents. The use of machine learning to extract key phrases from the document text has been investigated by [Turney (1999)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur535), [Frank, Paynter, Witten, Gutwin, and Nevill-Manning (1999)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur183), and [Medelyan and Witten (2008)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur386).

Appelt (1999) describes many problems of information extraction. Many authors have applied machine learning to seek rules that extract slot-fillers for templates, including [Soderland, Fisher, Aseltine, and Lehnert (1995)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur501), [Huffman (1996)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur280), and [Freitag (2002)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur189). [Califf and Mooney (1999)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur82) and [Nahm and Mooney (2000)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur410) investigated the problem of extracting information from job ads posted on Internet newsgroups. An approach to finding information in running text based on compression techniques has been reported by Witten, Bray, Mahoui, and Teahan (1999a). [Mann (1993)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur375) notes the plethora of variations of *Muammar Qaddafi* on documents received by the Library of Congress.

[Chakrabarti (2003)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur88) has written an excellent and comprehensive book on techniques of Web mining. [Kushmerick, Weld, and Doorenbos (1997)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur339) developed techniques of wrapper induction. The founders of Google wrote an early paper that introduced the PageRank algorithm ([Brin and Page, 1998](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur70)). At the same time [Kleinberg (1998)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur315) described a system called HITS (for hypertext-induced topic selection) that has some superficial similarities but produces strikingly different results.

The first paper on junk email filtering was written by [Sahami, Dumais, Heckerman, and Horvitz (1998)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur468). Our material on computer network security is culled from [Yurcik et al. (2003)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur584). The information on the CAPPS system comes from the [US House of Representatives Subcommittee on Aviation (2002)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur536), and the use of unsupervised learning for threat detection is described by [Bay and Schwabacher (2003)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur26). Issues with privacy-preserving data mining techniques are discussed by [Datta, Kargupta, and Sivakumar (2003)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur122). [Stone and Veloso (2000)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur509) surveyed multiagent systems of the kind that are used for playing robo-soccer from a machine learning perspective. The fascinating story of Ben Ish Chai and the technique used to unmask him is from [Koppel and Schler (2004)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur329).

A popular early framework for neural probabilistic language models was proposed by [Bengio, Ducharme, Vincent, and Janvin (2003)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur32); a key element of the approach is to project words into a continuous vector representation. Extending the general idea, [Collobert and Weston (2008)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur110) present a large unified neural network architecture for performing many natural language processing tasks using the same underlying network and shared word representations and showed that its performance is competitive across many common tasks. The influential *word2vec* technique was proposed by [Mikolov, Chen, Corrado, and Dean, (2013a](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur392), [2013b)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur393), while [Morin and Bengio (2005)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur405) explored the hierarchical softmax technique for language modeling.

Russakovsky et al. (2015) reviews the ImageNet challenge and the rise of convolutional neural networks to prominence in object category recognition. The Google Street View house numbers are described by [Netzer et al. (2011)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur414), who estimate human performance at 98% accuracy—and now many experiments with convolutional neural networks described in the literature exceed this figure. David Lowe invented SIFT descriptors. [Lowe (2004)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur370) gives details of their implementation and applications. They work well and have been patented.

Facebook’s “DeepFace” Siamese architecture for face verification uses a facial keypoint detector followed by a sophisticated 3D warping procedure to frontalize faces ([Taigman, Yang, Ranzato, and Wolf, 2014](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur522)). Of course, Facebook has access to a huge labeled database—4.4 million labeled faces from 4000 people (about 1000 each, on average). Siamese neural architectures were proposed by [Bromley, Guyon, LeCun, Säckinger, and Shah (1994)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur72). The first system to produce face verification that rivaled human performance was Sun, Chen, Wang, and Tang’s (2014) convolutional neural network, which used a 200,000-image database of faces of 10,000 celebrities. This system uses fewer facial landmarks and crops patches out of images centered on the key points; ensembles of many models produced the best performance.

Among many other applications, [Havaei et al. (2016)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur255) used deep convolutional neural networks for brain tumor segmentation; [Zbontar and LeCun (2015)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur588) present impressive results for stereo vision.

The vision of calm computing, as well as the examples we have mentioned, is from [Weiser (1996)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur559) and [Weiser and Brown (1997)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur560). More information on different methods of programming by demonstration can be found in compendia by [Cypher (1993)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur118) and [Lieberman (2001)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur362). [Mitchell, Caruana, Freitag, McDermott, and Zabowski (1994)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur398) report some experience with learning apprentices. Familiar is described by [Paynter (2000)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur429). Permutation tests ([Good, 1994](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur225)) are statistical tests that are suitable for small sample problems. [Frank (2000)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur178) describes their application in machine learning.

[Citron and Chesney (2019)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur104) highlighted the many concerns around the rise of deepfake technologies, while [Dwivedi et al. (2023)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur151) consolidated diverse opinions on LLMs such as ChatGPT from a large number of scholars across a variety of disciplines. For information on advocacy for copyright protection for artists who use generative AI, see the website of the Art Incarnate organization led by J.M. Allen.^(<a aria-label="noteref" href="#fn6" id="Cfn6">6</a>6) [Bonnefon et al. (2016)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur52) found that the opinions of Mechanical Turk participants on self-driving cars lead to an ethical dilemma, while [Nyholm and Smids (2016)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur422) pointed to the limitations of the trolley problem as a metaphor for moral dilemmas in life-and-death decisions made automatically by self-driving cars. [Asaro (2012)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur16) makes a compelling case for the banning of LAWS.

For a discussion on current and potentially worsening problems on our society from AI, [Baecker and Grudin (2024)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur21) is recommended reading. The previously mentioned AI Now Report provides an up-to-date discussion on these issues annually ([Crawford, 2019](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur114); [Kak and Myers West, 2023](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur300)). The theory of surveillance capitalism is due to [Zuboff (2015)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur601), with her textbook providing a more comprehensive treatment ([Zuboff, 2019](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur602)).

## 15.14 Exercises

 

*   15.1 Identify and explain a strategy for scaling up machine learning algorithms to massive datasets. Describe a concrete example of the approach you identified.
*   15.2 Explain, in your own words, the importance of incorporating domain knowledge into machine learning and data mining methods and discuss how this can be accomplished.
*   15.3 In [Chapter 1](#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029.xhtml#Ch001_3-42_B9780443158889000029), “What’s it all about?” we defined data mining as the extraction of information from data that is (1) implicit, (2) previously unknown, and (3) potentially useful. How many of these properties apply to text mining?  
    1.  A. 0
    2.  B. 1
    3.  C. 2
    4.  D. 3
*   15.4 Compare and contrast text mining to standard data mining by listing their similarities and differences.
*   15.5 Identify and explain a real-world application of machine learning for computer vision. What role does deep learning play in your chosen application? What ethical concerns arise in this application, if any?
*   15.6 What are the possible ethical concerns and considerations regarding OpenAI’s ChatGPT system? Identify as many as you can and explain why these issues could be harmful.
*   15.7 In your opinion, should self-driving cars be allowed to operate as “robotaxis” on our roads? Explain why, or why not, and justify your answer.
*   15.8 In your opinion, should LAWS be banned? Explain why, or why not, and justify your answer.
*   15.9 In your opinion, are the services provided by large technology companies such as Google a fair and reciprocal exchange for your data and privacy rights? Or are they the “hooks” that exploit you into giving up data and privacy? Explain and justify your answer.
*   15.10 Do you feel that in today’s society a typical person could reasonably choose to opt out of all products and services that facilitate surveillance capitalism? Explain and justify your answer.
*   15.11 Identify companies other than Google that practice surveillance  
    capitalism and explain why they can be characterized as such.
*   15.12 Compare and contrast the panopticon and surveillance capitalism.

# Appendix A: Theoretical foundations

Abstract

This appendix covers the theoretical and mathematical background necessary to understand the details of the chapters on deep learning and probabilistic methods, including matrix algebra and multivariate calculus, and the fundamentals of probabilistic methods.

Keywords

Matrix algebra; probabilistic methods; covariance matrices; singular value decomposition; Bayesian statistics; variational methods

 

## A.1 Matrix Algebra

 

### Basic Manipulations and Properties

A column vector **x** with *d* dimensions can be written

$\\mathbf{x} \\equiv \\begin{bmatrix} x\_{1} \\\\ x\_{2} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ x\_{d} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\begin{bmatrix} x\_{1} & x\_{2} & \\cdots & x\_{d} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}^{T},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8801;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mo>&#8942;</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mo>&#8943;</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000212si1.png)

where the *transpose* operator, superscript *T*, allows it to be written as a transposed row vector, which is useful when defining vectors in running text. In this book vectors are assumed to be row vectors.

The transpose **A***^T* of a matrix **A** involves copying all the rows of the original matrix **A** into the columns of **A***^T*. Thus a matrix with *m* rows and *n* columns becomes a matrix with *n* rows and *m* columns:

$\\begin{matrix} {\\mathbf{A} \\equiv \\begin{bmatrix} a\_{11} & a\_{12} & \\cdots & a\_{1n} \\\\ a\_{21} & a\_{21} & \\cdots & a\_{2n} \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ a\_{m1} & a\_{m2} & \\cdots & a\_{mn} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}} & \\Rightarrow & {\\mathbf{A}^{T} = \\begin{bmatrix} a\_{11} & a\_{21} & \\cdots & a\_{m1} \\\\ a\_{12} & a\_{21} & \\cdots & a\_{m2} \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ a\_{1n} & a\_{2n} & \\cdots & a\_{nm} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}} \\\\ \\end{matrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi ![Equation](images/F000212si2.png)

The *dot product* or *inner product* between vector **x** and vector **y** of the same dimensionality yields a scalar quantity,

$\\mathbf{x} \\cdot \\mathbf{y} = \\left\\langle {\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}} \\right\\rangle = \\mathbf{x}^{T}\\mathbf{y} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{D}x\_{i}y\_{i}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#183;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">&#9001;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">&#9002;</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000212si3.png)

For example, the Euclidean norm can be written as the square root of the dot product of a vector **x** with itself, $|{|\\mathbf{x}|}|\_{2} = \\sqrt{\\mathbf{x}^{T}\\mathbf{x}}$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000212si4.png).

The *tensor product* or *outer product* ⊗ between an *m*\-dimensional vector **x** and an *n*\-dimensional vector **y** yields a matrix,

$\\mathbf{x} \\otimes \\mathbf{y} \\equiv \\mathbf{x}\\mathbf{y}^{T} = \\begin{bmatrix} x\_{1} \\\\ x\_{2} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ x\_{m} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}\\left. \\lbrack{\\begin{matrix} y\_{1} & y\_{2} & \\cdots & y\_{n} \\\\ \\end{matrix}{\\rbrack =}\\lbrack\\begin{matrix} {x\_{1}y\_{1}} & {x\_{1}y\_{2}} & \\cdots & {x\_{1}y\_{n}} \\\\ {x\_{2}y\_{1}} & {x\_{2}y\_{2}} & \\cdots & {x\_{2}y\_{n}} \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ {x\_{m}y\_{1}} & {x\_{m}y\_{2}} & \\cdots & {x\_{m}y\_{n}} \\\\ \\end{matrix}} \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8855;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8801;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:msup><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo Given an *N* row and *K* column matrix **A**, and a *K* row and *M* column matrix **B**, if we write each row of **A** as **a**[*n*]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000212si6.png) and each column of **B** as **b***[m]* the matrix product **AB** (i.e., matrix multiplication) can be written

$\\mathbf{A}\\mathbf{B} = \\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{a}\_{1}^{T} \\\\ \\mathbf{a}\_{2}^{T} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ \\mathbf{a}\_{N}^{T} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}\\left. \\lbrack{\\begin{matrix} \\mathbf{b}\_{1} & \\mathbf{b}\_{2} & \\cdots & \\mathbf{b}\_{M} \\\\ \\end{matrix}{\\rbrack =}\\lbrack\\begin{matrix} {\\mathbf{a}\_{1}^{T}\\mathbf{b}\_{1}} & {\\mathbf{a}\_{1}^{T}\\mathbf{b}\_{2}} & \\cdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ {\\mathbf{a}\_{N}^{T}\\mathbf{b}\_{1}} & {\\mathbf{a}\_{N}^{T}\\mathbf{b}\_{2}} & \\cdots & {\\mathbf{a}\_{N}^{T}\\mathbf{b}\_{M}} \\\\ \\end{matrix}} \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">A</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">B</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo If we write each column of **A** as **a***[k]* and each row of **B** as **b**[*k*]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000212si8.png) the matrix product **AB** can also be written in terms of tensor products

$\\mathbf{A}\\mathbf{B} = \\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{a}\_{1} & \\mathbf{a}\_{2} & \\cdots & \\mathbf{a}\_{K} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{b}\_{1}^{T} \\\\ \\mathbf{b}\_{2}^{T} \\\\ The *elementwise product* or *Hadamard product* of two matrices that are of the same size is

$\\begin{matrix} {\\mathbf{A} \\circ \\mathbf{B}} & {= \\left\\lbrack {\\begin{matrix} a\_{11} & a\_{12} & \\cdots & a\_{1n} \\\\ a\_{21} & a\_{21} & \\cdots & a\_{2n} \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ b\_{m1} & b\_{m2} & \\cdots & b\_{mn} \\\\ \\end{matrix}} \\right\\rbrack} \\\\ & {= \\begin{bmatrix} {a\_{11}b\_{11}} & {a\_{12}b\_{12}} & \\cdots & {a\_{1n}b\_{1n}} \\\\ {a\_{211}b\_{21}} & {b\_{21}b\_{21}} & \\cdots & {a\_{2n}b\_{2n}} \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ {a\_{m1}b\_{m1}} & {a\_{m2}b\_{m2}} & \\cdots & {a\_{mn}b\_{mn}} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">A</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8728;</mml:mo><mml:mi l:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mo>&#8943;</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000212si10.png)

A square matrix **A** with *n* rows and *n* columns is *invertible* if there exists a square matrix **B** = **A** − 1<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000212si11.png) such that **A****B** = **B****A** = **I**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">AB</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">BA</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000212si12.png), where **I** is the identity matrix consisting of all zeros except that all diagonal elements are one. Square matrices that are not invertible are called *singular*. A square matrix **A** is singular if and only if its determinant, det(**A**) is zero. The following equation for the inverse shows why a zero determinant implies that a matrix is not invertible:

$\\mathbf{A}^{- 1} = \\frac{1}{\\det\\left( \\mathbf{A} \\right)}\\mathbf{C}^{T},$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">det</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">A</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000212si13.png)

where det(**A**) is the determinant of **A** and **C** is another matrix known as the cofactor matrix. Finally, if a matrix **A** is orthogonal, then **A** − 1 = **A**^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000212si14.png).

 

### Derivatives of Vector and Scalar Functions

Given a scalar function *y* of an *m*\-dimensional column vector **x**,

$\\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial\\mathbf{x}} \\equiv \\begin{bmatrix} \\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x\_{1}} \\\\ \\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x\_{2}} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ \\frac{\\partial y\_{1}}{\\partial x\_{m}} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\mathbf{g}.$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>&#8801;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mo>&#8942;</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">g</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000212si15.png)

This quantity is known as the *gradient*, **g**. We have defined it here as a column vector but it is sometimes defined as a row vector. Defining the gradient as a column vector implies certain orientations for the other quantities defined later, so keep in mind that the derivatives that follow are sometimes defined as the transposes of those given here. Using the definition and orientation noted earlier we can write the types of parameter updates frequently used in algorithms like gradient descent in vector form with expressions such as **θ**^(*n**e**w*) = **θ**^(*o**l**d*) − **g**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">new</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">old</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">g</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000212si16.png), where θ is a parameter (column) vector.

Given a scalar *x* and *n*\-dimensional vector function **y**,

$\\frac{\\partial\\mathbf{y}}{\\partial x} \\equiv \\begin{bmatrix} \\frac{\\partial y\_{1}}{\\partial x} & \\frac{\\partial y\_{2}}{\\partial x} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial y\_{n}}{\\partial x} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>&#8801;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mo>&#8943;</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000212si17.png)

For an *m*\-dimensional vector **x** and an *n*\-dimensional vector **y**, the *Jacobian matrix* is given by

$\\frac{\\partial\\mathbf{y}}{\\partial\\mathbf{x}} \\equiv \\begin{bmatrix} \\frac{\\partial y\_{1}}{\\partial x\_{1}} & \\frac{\\partial y\_{2}}{\\partial x\_{1}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial y\_{n}}{\\partial x\_{1}} \\\\ \\frac{\\partial y\_{1}}{\\partial x\_{2}} & \\frac{\\partial y\_{2}}{\\partial x\_{2}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial y\_{n}}{\\partial x\_{2}} \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ \\frac{\\partial y\_{1}}{\\partial x\_{m}} & \\frac{\\partial y\_{2}}{\\partial x\_{m}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial y\_{n}}{\\partial x\_{m}} \\\\ The Jacobian is sometimes defined as the transpose of this quantity even given the other definitions noted. Watch out for the implications. The derivative of a scalar function *y* = *f*(**X**)<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000212si19.png) with respect to an *m* × *n*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#215;</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000212si20.png) dimensional matrix **X** is known as a *gradient matrix* and is given by

$\\frac{\\partial f}{\\partial\\mathbf{X}} \\equiv \\begin{bmatrix} \\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x\_{11}} & \\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x\_{12}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x\_{1n}} \\\\ \\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x\_{21}} & \\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x\_{22}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x\_{2n}} \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ \\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x\_{m1}} & \\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x\_{m2}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x\_{mn}} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\mathbf{G}.$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi Our choice for the orientations of these quantities means that the gradient matrix has the same layout as the original matrix, so updates to a parameter *matrix* **X** take the form **X**^(*n**e**w*) = **X**^(*o**l**d*) − **G**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">new</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">old</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">G</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000212si22.png).

While many quantities can be expressed as scalars, vectors, or matrices, there are many that cannot. ### The Chain Rule

The chain rule for a function *z*, which is a function of *y*, which is a function of *x*, all of which are scalars, is

$\\frac{\\partial z}{\\partial x} = \\frac{\\partial z}{\\partial y}\\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x},$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000212si23.png)

where the two terms could be reversed because multiplication is commutative. Now, given an *m*\-dimensional vector **x**, an *n*\-dimensional vector **y**, and an *o*\-dimensional vector **z**, if **z** = **z**(**y**(**x**))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000212si24.png), then

$\\frac{\\partial\\mathbf{z}}{\\partial\\mathbf{x}} \\equiv \\begin{bmatrix} \\frac{\\partial z\_{1}}{\\partial x\_{1}} & \\frac{\\partial z\_{2}}{\\partial x\_{1}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial z\_{o}}{\\partial x\_{1}} \\\\ \\frac{\\partial z\_{1}}{\\partial x\_{2}} & \\frac{\\partial z\_{2}}{\\partial x\_{2}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial z\_{o}}{\\partial x\_{2}} \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ \\frac{\\partial z\_{1}}{\\partial x\_{m}} & \\frac{\\partial z\_{2}}{\\partial x\_{m}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial z\_{o}}{\\partial x\_{m}} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>&#8801;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo $\\begin{matrix} \\frac{\\partial\\mathbf{z}}{\\partial\\mathbf{x}} & {= \\begin{bmatrix} \\frac{\\partial y\_{1}}{\\partial x\_{1}} & \\frac{\\partial y\_{2}}{\\partial x\_{1}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial y\_{n}}{\\partial x\_{1}} \\\\ \\frac{\\partial y\_{1}}{\\partial x\_{2}} & \\frac{\\partial y\_{2}}{\\partial x\_{2}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial y\_{n}}{\\partial x\_{2}} \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ \\frac{\\partial y\_{1}}{\\partial x\_{m}} & \\frac{\\partial y\_{2}}{\\partial x\_{m}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial y\_{n}}{\\partial x\_{m}} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix} \\frac{\\partial z\_{1}}{\\partial y\_{1}} & \\frac{\\partial z\_{2}}{\\partial y\_{1}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial z\_{o}}{\\partial y\_{1}} \\\\ \\frac{\\partial z\_{1}}{\\partial y\_{2}} & \\frac{\\partial z\_{2}}{\\partial y\_{2}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial z\_{o}}{\\partial y\_{2}} \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ \\frac{\\partial z\_{1}}{\\partial y\_{n}} & \\frac{\\partial z\_{2}}{\\partial y\_{n}} & \\cdots & \\frac{\\partial z\_{o}}{\\partial y\_{n}} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}} \\\\ \\frac{\\partial\\mathbf{z}}{\\partial\\mathbf{x}} & {= \\frac{\\partial\\mathbf{y}}{\\partial\\mathbf{x}}\\frac{\\partial\\mathbf{z}}{\\partial\\mathbf{y}},} \\\\ which yields the chain rule for vectors, where chains extend toward the left as opposed to the right as is often done with the scalar version. For the special case when the final function evaluates to a scalar, which is frequently encountered when optimizing a loss function, we have

$\\begin{matrix} \\frac{\\partial z}{\\partial x\_{j}} & {= \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}\\frac{\\partial y\_{k}}{\\partial x\_{j}}\\frac{\\partial z}{\\partial y\_{k}},} \\\\ \\frac{\\partial \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:munderover><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi The rule generalizes so if there were yet another vector function **w** that is a function of **x**, through **z**, then

$\\frac{\\partial\\mathbf{w}}{\\partial\\mathbf{x}} = \\frac{\\partial\\mathbf{y}}{\\partial\\mathbf{x}}\\frac{\\partial\\mathbf{z}}{\\partial\\mathbf{y}}\\frac{\\partial\\mathbf{w}}{\\partial\\mathbf{z}}.$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000212si30.png)

To find the derivative of a matrix that is the function of another matrix the chain rule generalizes. For example, for a matrix **X** if matrix **Y** = *f*(**X**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000212si31.png), the derivative of a function *g*(**Y**) is

### Derivatives of Functions of Vectors and Matrices

Here are some useful derivatives for functions of vectors and matrices. [Petersen and Pedersen (2012)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur433) gives an even larger list.

$\\begin{matrix} {\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\mathbf{x}}\\mathbf{Ax} = \\mathbf{A}^{T}} \\\\ {\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\mathbf{x}}\\mathbf{x}^{T}\\mathbf{x} = 2\\mathbf{x}} \\\\ {\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\mathbf{x}}\\mathbf{x}^{T}\\mathbf{A}\\mathbf{x} = \\mathbf{A}\\mathbf{x} + \\mathbf{A}^{T}\\mathbf{x}} \\\\ ### Vector Taylor Series Expansion, Second-Order Methods, and Learning Rates

The method of gradient descent, the interpretation of learning rates, and more sophisticated second-order methods can be viewed through the lens of the Taylor series expansion of a function. The approach presented next is also known as Newton’s method.

The Taylor expansion of a function near point *x[o]* can be written

$f\\left( x \\right) = f\\left( x\_{o} \\right) + \\frac{f\\prime\\left( x\_{o} \\right)}{1!}\\left( {x - x\_{o}} \\right) + \\frac{f''\\left( x\_{o} \\right)}{2!}\\left( {x - x\_{o}} \\right)^{2} + \\frac{f^{(3)}\\left( x\_{o} \\right)}{3!}\\left( {x - x\_{o}} \\right)^{3} + \\cdots.$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mo $\\begin{matrix} & {\\frac{df{(\\mathbf{\\theta})}}{d\\mathbf{\\theta}} = 0 = \\mathbf{g}\_{o} + \\mathbf{H}\_{o}{({\\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}})},\\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta} \\equiv
