stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8727;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000248si66.png)

where **D**[*i*] = *d**L*/∂**A**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>/</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si67.png) is a matrix containing the partial derivative of the elementwise act() function’s input with respect to its preactivation value for the *i*th feature type, organized according to spatial positions given by row *j* and column *k*. Intuitively, the result is a sum of the convolution of each of the (zero padded) filters **W***[i]* with an image-like matrix of derivatives **D***[i]*. The partial derivatives of the hidden layer output are

$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial\\mathbf{W}\_{i}} = \\sum\\limits\_{j}\\sum\\limits\_{k}\\frac{\\partial a\_{ijk}}{\\partial\\mathbf{W}\_{i}}\\frac{\\partial\\mathbf{H}\_{i}}{\\partial a\_{ijk}}\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial\\mathbf{H}\_{i}} = \\left\\lbrack {\\mathbf{X}^{\\dagger} \\ast \\mathbf{D}\_{i}} \\right\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:munder><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8224;</mml:mo></mml:msup><mml:mo>&#8727;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

where **X**^†<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8224;</mml:mo></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si69.png) is the row- and column-flipped version of the input **X** (if the convolution is written as a linear matrix operation this will involve only a matrix transpose).

 

### Pooling and Subsampling Layers and Gradients

Consider applying a pooling operation to a spatially organized feature map. The input consists of matrices **H***[i]* for each feature map with elements *h[ijk]*. The max pooled and average pooled feature maps are matrices **P***[i]* with elements *p[ijk]* given by

$\\begin{matrix} {p\_{i,j,k} = \\max\\limits\_{\\substack{r \\in R\_{j,k}, \\\\ c \\in C\_{j,k}}}h\_{i,r,c},} & {p\_{i,j,k} = \\frac{1}{m}\\sum\\limits\_{\\underset{c \\in C\_{j,k}}{r \\in R\_{j,k},}}h\_{i,r,c},} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:msp1/><mml:mrow><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mfrac><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msp1/><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000248si70.png)

respectively, where *R[j,k]* and *C[j,k]* are sets of indices that encode the pooling regions for each location *j*, *k*, and *m* is the number of elements in the pooling region. Although these pooling operations do not include a subsampling step, they typically account for boundary effects either by creating a matrix **P***[i]* that is slightly smaller than the input matrix **H***[i]*, or by padding with zeros. The subsampling step either samples every *n*th output or avoids needless computation by only evaluating every *n*th pooling computation.

What are the consequences of backpropagating gradients through layers consisting of max or average pooling? In the former case the units that are responsible for the maximum within each zone *j*, *k*—the “winning units”—are given by

$\\left\\{ {r\*,c\*} \\right\\}\_{j,k} = \\underset{r \\in R\_{j,k},c \\in C\_{j,k}}{\\arg\\max}h\_{i,r,c}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>\*</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>\*</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:msp1/><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000248si71.png)

For nonoverlapping zones the gradient is propagated back from the pooled layer P*[i]* to the original spatial feature layer **H***[i]*, flowing from each *p[ijk]* to just the winning unit in each zone. This can be written

$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial h\_{i,r\_{j},c\_{k}}} = \\left\\{ \\begin{matrix} 0 & {r\_{j} \\neq r\_{j}^{\\ast},c\_{k} \\neq c\_{k}^{\\ast}} \\\\ \\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial p\_{i,j,k}} & {r\_{j} = r\_{j}^{\\ast},c\_{k} = c\_{k}^{\\ast}} \\\\ \\end{matrix}. \\right.$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8800;</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8270;</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8800;</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8270;</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mtd><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8270;</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8270;</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000248si72.png)

In the latter case average pooling, the averaging operation, is a special type of convolution with a fixed kernel that computes the (possibly weighted) average of pixels in a zone so the required gradients are computed using the result previously shown. These various pieces are the building blocks that allow for the implementation of a CNN according to a given architecture.

 

## D.3 Stochastic Deep Networks

The networks considered in [Chapter 10](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X), “Deep learning: fundamentals,” and [Chapter 11](#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121.xhtml#Ch012_433-471_B9780443158889000121), “Advanced deep learning methods,” are constructed from deterministic components. We now look at stochastic networks, beginning with a model for unsupervised learning known as a Boltzmann machine. This stochastic neural network model is a type of Markov random field ([Section 14.3](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#s0055)). Unlike the units of a feedforward neural network the units in Boltzmann machines correspond to random variables, such as are used in Bayesian networks. Older variants of Boltzmann machines were defined using exclusively binary variables but models with continuous and discrete variables are also possible. They became popular prior to the impressive results of CNNs on the ImageNet challenge but have since waned in popularity because they are more difficult to work with. However, stochastic methods have certain advantages such as the ability to capture multimodal distributions.

 

### Pretraining Deep Autoencoders with RBMs

Deep autoencoders, discussed in [Section 10.4](#Ch011_391-432_B978044315888900011X.xhtml#s0140), are an effective framework for nonlinear dimensionality reduction that formed an important use case of stochastic networks, particularly when used as part of an unsupervised pretraining strategy. Once such a network has been built the top-most layer of the encoder, the code layer **h***[c]*, can be input to a supervised classification procedure. If a neural network classifier is used, the entire deep autoencoder network can be discriminatively fine-tuned using gradient descent. In effect the autoencoder approach is used to pretrain a neural network classifier.

However, it is difficult to optimize autoencoders with multiple hidden layers in both encoder and decoder. It is well known that initializing any deep neural network with weights that are too large leads to poor local minima, while initialization with weights that are too small can lead to small gradients that make learning slow. One approach is to be very careful about the choices of activation function and initialization. However, this has been found difficult in practice.

Another approach is based on pretraining by stacking two-layered restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs). “RBMs are a generalized form of probabilistic principal component analysis (PPCA), which we discussed in [Section 14.3](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#s0055), binary hidden variables and binary or continuous observed variables that can perform unsupervised learning; they are discussed further later. To use them for pretraining start by learning a two-layer RBM from the data, project the data into its hidden-layer representation, use that to train another RBM, and repeat the process until the encoding layer is reached. The parameters of each two-layer network are then used to initialize the parameters of an autoencoder with a similar structure that has nonstochastic sigmoid hidden units. Next we discuss RBMs, Boltzmann machines that they are based on, and various modeling and learning strategies based on them that were prominent in the 2000s–2010s. These models have largely fallen into disuse but remain important for historical reasons.

 

### Boltzmann Machines

To create a Boltzmann machine we begin by partitioning variables into ones that are visible, defined by a *D*\-dimensional binary vector **v** ∈ {0,1}^(*D*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0,1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si73.png), and ones that are hidden, defined by a *K*\-dimensional binary vector **h** ∈ {0,1}^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8712;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0,1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si74.png). Then a Boltzmann machine is a joint probability model of the form

$\\begin{matrix} {p\\left( {\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h};\\theta} \\right) = \\frac{1}{Z\\left( \\theta \\right)}\\exp\\left( {- E\\left( {\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h};\\theta} \\right)} \\right),} \\\\ {Z\\left( \\theta \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{v}}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{h}}\\exp\\left( {- E\\left( {\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h};\\theta} \\right)} \\right),} \\\\ {E\\left( {\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h};\\theta} \\right) = - \\frac{1}{2}\\mathbf{v}^{T}\\mathbf{A}\\mathbf{v} - \\frac{1}{2}\\mathbf{h}^{T}\\mathbf{B}\\mathbf{h} - \\mathbf{v}^{T}\\mathbf{W}\\mathbf{h} - \\mathbf{a}^{T}\\mathbf{v} - \\mathbf{b}^{T}\\mathbf{h},} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mi ![Equation](images/F000248si75.png)

where *E*(**v**,**h**;*θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si76.png) is the energy function; *Z*(*θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si77.png) normalizes *E* so that it defines a valid joint probability; the matrices **A**, **B**, and **W** encode the visible-to-visible, hidden-to-hidden, and visible-to-hidden variable interactions, respectively; and vectors **a** and **b** encode the biases associated with each variable. Matrices **A** and **B** are symmetric, and their diagonal elements are 0. This structure is effectively a binary Markov random field with pairwise connections between all variables, illustrated in [Fig. D.4A](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#f0025).

![Fig. D.4 Boltzmann machines. (A) Fully connected. (B) Restricted. (C) More general form of (B). Credit: Christopher J. Pal.](images/F000248bm04-9780443158889.jpg)

Fig. D.4 Boltzmann machines. (A) Fully connected. (B) Restricted. (C) More general form of (B). Credit: Christopher J. Pal.

A key feature of Boltzmann machines (and binary Markov random fields in general) is that the conditional distribution of one variable given the others is a sigmoid function whose argument is a weighted linear combination of the states of the other variables:

$\\begin{matrix} {p(h\_{j} = 1 \\mid \\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h}\_{\\neg j};\\theta) = {sigmoid}\\left( {\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{D}W\_{ij}v\_{i} + \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}B\_{jk}h\_{k} + b\_{j}} \\right),} \\\\ {p(v\_{i} = 1 \\mid \\mathbf{h},\\mathbf{v}\_{\\neg i};\\theta) = {sigmoid}\\left( {\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{K}W\_{ij}h\_{j} + \\sum\\limits\_{d = 1}^{D}A\_{id}v\_{d} + c\_{i}} \\right),} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#172;</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sigmoid</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo ![Equation](images/F000248si78.png)

where the notation ¬*i*<mml:math><mml:mo>&#172;</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si79.png) indicates all elements with subscript other than *i*. The diagonal elements of *A* and *B* are zero so there is no need for the sum to skip terms involving *h*[*k* = *j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si80.png) and *v*[*d* = *i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si81.png) since they are zero anyway. The fact that these equations are separate sigmoid functions for each variable makes it easy to construct a Gibbs’ sampler ([Section 14.2](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#s0030)), which can be used to compute approximations to the conditional probability $p(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}})$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#732;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si82.png) and the joint probability *p*(**h**,**v**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si83.png).

Define the loss as the negative log-likelihood of the marginal probability for a single example $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#732;</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si84.png) under the Boltzmann machine model: $L = - \\log p{({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}};\\theta})} = - \\log\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{h}} p{({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}},\\mspace{270mu}\\mathbf{h};\\theta})}$<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mspace width=".25em"/><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#732;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mspace width=".25em"/><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mspace width=".25em"/><mml:munder><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1px"/><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#732;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1.5pt"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si85.png). Then, based on some calculus, the partial derivatives can be shown to be

$\\begin{array}{l} {\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial\\mathbf{W}} = - \\left\\lbrack {E\\left\\lbrack {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}}\\mathbf{h}^{T}} \\right\\rbrack\_{P(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}})} - E\\left\\lbrack {\\mathbf{v}\\mathbf{h}^{T}} \\right\\rbrack\_{P{({\\mathbf{h},\\mathbf{v}})}}} \\right\\rbrack,} \\\\ {\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial\\mathbf{A}} = - \\left\\lbrack {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}}}^{T} - E\\left\\lbrack {\\mathbf{v}\\mathbf{v}^{T}} \\right\\rbrack\_{P{({\\mathbf{h},\\mathbf{v}})}}} \\right\\rbrack,} \\\\ {\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial\\mathbf{B}} = - \\left\\lbrack {E\\left\\lbrack {\\mathbf{h}\\mathbf{h}^{T}} \\right\\rbrack\_{P(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}})} - E\\left\\lbrack {\\mathbf{h}\\mathbf{h}^{T}} \\right\\rbrack\_{P{({\\mathbf{h},\\mathbf{v}})}}} \\right\\rbrack,} \\\\ {\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial\\mathbf{a}} = - \\left\\lbrack {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}} - E\\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{v} \\right\\rbrack\_{P{({\\mathbf{h},\\mathbf{v}})}}} \\right\\rbrack,} \\\\ {\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial\\mathbf{b}} = - \\left\\lbrack {E\\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{h} \\right\\rbrack\_{P(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}})} - E\\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{h} \\right\\rbrack\_{P{({\\mathbf{h},\\mathbf{v}})}}} \\right\\rbrack.} \\\\ \\end{array}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi columnalign="left"><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#732;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi columnalign="left"><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>&#8706;</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#732;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000248si86.png)

The distributions $p(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}})$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#732;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si87.png) and *p*(**h**,**v**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si88.png) needed to compute the expectations in these derivatives are not available in analytic form but samples approximating them can be used instead. To compute the gradient of the negative log-likelihood over an entire training set with *N* examples the sum of the terms is *N* times a single expectation using the empirical distribution of the data $P\_{data}\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}} \\right)$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">data</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#732;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si89.png), or the distribution obtained by placing a delta function on each example and dividing by *N*. A sum over a training set involving expectations of the form $p(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}})$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#732;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si90.png) is sometimes written as a single expectation and referred to as the *data-dependent expectation*, whereas the expectations involving *p*(**h**,**v**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si91.png) do not depend on the data and are referred to as the *model’s expectation*.

Using these equations and approximations for the distributions one can implement optimization via gradient descent. Gradients in probabilistic models often come down to computing differences of expectations, as in models such as logistic regression, conditional random fields, and even probabilistic principal component analysis, as we saw in [Chapter 14](#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157.xhtml#Ch015_516-570_B9780443158889000157), “Advanced probabilistic methods.”

 

### Restricted Boltzmann Machines

Eliminating connections between hidden variables and visible variables yields an RBM with the same distribution *p*(**v**,**h**;*θ*) = *Z*^( − 1)(*θ*)exp (−*E*(**v**,**h**;*θ*))<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi>exp</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si92.png) but this energy function:

*E*(**v**,**h**;*θ*) =  − **v**^(*T*)**W****h** − **a**^(*T*)**v** − **b**^(*T*)**h**.<mml:math><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Wh</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000248si93.png)

[Fig. D.4B](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#f0025) shows the result of this transformation on [Fig. D.4A](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#f0025); while [Fig. D.4C](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#f0025) shows a more general form.

Eliminating the coupling matrices **A** and **B** means that the exact inference step for **h**, the entire vector of hidden variables, can be performed in one shot. *p*(**h**|**v**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si94.png) becomes the product of a different sigmoid for each dimension, each sigmoid depending only on the observed input vector **v**. *p*(**v**|**h**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si95.png) has a similar form.

$\\begin{matrix} {p(\\mathbf{h} \\mid \\mathbf{v}) = \\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}p(h\_{k} \\mid \\mathbf{v}) = \\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}{Bern}{({h\_{k};{sigmoid}{({b\_{k} + \\mathbf{W}\_{\\cdot k}^{T}\\mathbf{v}})}})},} \\\\ {p(\\mathbf{v} \\mid \\mathbf{h}) = \\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{D}p(v\_{i} \\mid \\mathbf{h}) = \\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{D}{Bern}{({v\_{i};{sigmoid}{({a\_{i} + \\mathbf{W}\_{i \\cdot}\\mathbf{h}})}})},} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:munderover><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Bern</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sigmoid</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8901;</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:munderover><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#8739;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Bern</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sigmoid</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8901;</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000248si96.png)

where **W**[ ⋅ *k*]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8901;</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si97.png) is a vector consisting of the transpose of the *k*th column of the weight matrix **W**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si98.png), while **W**[*i*⋅]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8901;</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si99.png) is the *i*th row of **W**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">W</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si100.png). These are conditional distributions that are derived from the underlying joint model and the equations can be used to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to **W**, **a**, and **b**. The expectations needed for learning are easier to compute than for an unrestricted model; an exact expression can be obtained for $p(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}})$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#732;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si101.png), but *p*(**h**,**v**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si102.png) remains intractable and must be approximated.

 

### Contrastive Divergence

Running a Gibbs sampler for a Boltzmann machine often requires many iterations, and a technique called “contrastive divergence” is a popular alternative that initializes the sampler to the observed data instead of randomly and performs a limited number of Gibbs updates. In an RBM a sample ${\\overset{\\hat{}}{\\mathbf{h}}}^{(0)}$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:msp1/><mml:mi>&#710;</mml:mi></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si103.png) can be generated from the distribution $p(\\mathbf{h}|{\\overset{\\hat{}}{\\mathbf{v}}}^{(0)} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{v}})$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">v</mml:mi><mml:msp1/><mml:mi>&#710;</mml:mi></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">&#732;</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si104.png) followed by a sample for ${\\overset{\\hat{}}{\\mathbf{v}}}^{(1)}$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">v</mml:mi><mml:msp1/><mml:mi>&#710;</mml:mi></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si105.png) from $p(\\mathbf{v}|{\\overset{\\hat{}}{\\mathbf{h}}}^{(1)})$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi><mml:msp1/><mml:mi>&#710;</mml:mi></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si106.png). This single step often works well in practice, although the process of alternating the sampling of hidden and visible units can be continued for multiple steps.

 

### Categorical and Continuous Variables

The RBMs discussed so far have been composed of binary variables. However, they can be extended to categorical or continuous attributes by encoding *r* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si107.png), …, *R* visible categorical variables using one-hot vectors **v**[(*r*)]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si108.png) and defining hidden binary variables **h** with the following energy function

$E\\left( {\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h};\\theta} \\right) = - \\sum\\limits\_{r = 1}^{R}\\left\\lbrack {\\mathbf{v}\_{(r)}^{T}\\mathbf{W}\_{(r)}\\mathbf{h} + \\mathbf{a}\_{(r)}^{T}\\mathbf{v}\_{(r)}} \\right\\rbrack - \\mathbf{b}^{T}\\mathbf{h}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8721;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000248si109.png)

The joint distribution defined by this model is complex but as for binary RBMs the conditional distributions under the model for one layer given the other have simple forms:

$\\begin{matrix} {p(\\mathbf{h} \\mid \\mathbf{v}\_{({r = 1,\\ldots,R})}) = \\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}{Bern}\\left( {h\_{k};{sigmoid}\\left( {b\_{k} + \\sum\\limits\_{r = 1}^{R}\\mathbf{W}\_{{(r)} \\cdot k}^{T}\\mathbf{v}\_{(r)}} \\right)} \\right),} \\\\ {p(\\mathbf{v}\_{({r = 1,\\ldots,R})} \\mid \\mathbf{h}) = \\prod\\limits\_{r = 1}^{R}{Cat}{({\\mathbf{v}\_{(r)};{softmax}{({\\mathbf{a}\_{(r)} + \\mathbf{W}\_{{(r)} \\cdot}\\mathbf{h}})}})},} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:munderover><mml:mi stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo A model with a layer of continuous observed variables **v** and a layer of hidden binary variables **h** can be constructed using this energy function:

$E\\left( {\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h};\\theta} \\right) = - \\mathbf{v}^{T}\\mathbf{Wh} - \\frac{1}{2}\\left( {\\mathbf{v} - \\mathbf{a}} \\right)^{2} - \\mathbf{b}^{T}\\mathbf{h}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>&#952;</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Wh</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:msup><mml:mo>&#8722;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/F000248si111.png)

The conditional distributions are

$\\begin{matrix} {p(\\mathbf{h} \\mid \\mathbf{v}) = \\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}{Bern}{({h\_{k};{sigmoid}{({b\_{k} + \\mathbf{W}\_{\\cdot k}^{T}\\mathbf{v}})}})},} \\\\ {p(\\mathbf{v} \\mid \\mathbf{h}) = \\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{D}N{({v\_{i};a\_{i} + \\mathbf{W}\_{i \\cdot}\\mathbf{h},1})} = N\\left( {v;a + Wh,I} \\right),} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo mathvariant="normal">Bern</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo>&#8719;</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:munderover><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo ![Equation](images/F000248si112.png)

where the conditional distribution of the observed variables given the hidden is a Gaussian whose mean depends on a bias term plus a linear transformation of the binary hidden variable. This Gaussian has an identity covariance matrix and can therefore be written as a product of independent Gaussians for each dimension.

 

### Deep Boltzmann Machines

Deep Boltzmann machines involve coupling layers of random variables using RBM connectivity, as illustrated in [Fig. D.5A](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#f0030). Assuming Bernoulli random variables the energy function is

$\\begin{matrix} & {{E{({\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h}^{(1)},\\ldots,\\mathbf{h}^{(L)};\\theta})}}{= - \\mathbf{v}^{T}\\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\\mathbf{h}^{(1)} - \\mathbf{a}^{T}\\mathbf{v} - \\mathbf{b}^{{(1)}T}\\mathbf{h}^{(1)}}} \\\\ & {- \\left\\lbrack {\\sum\\limits\_{l = 2}^{L}\\left\\lbrack {\\mathbf{h}^{{({l - 1})}T}\\mathbf{W}^{(l)}\\mathbf{h}^{(l)} + \\mathbf{b}^{{(l)}T}\\mathbf{h}^{(l)}} \\right\\rbrack} \\right\\rbrack,} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$<mml:math><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd/><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo ![Equation](images/F000248si118.png)

This enables all variables in a layer to be updated in parallel using a method known as “block Gibbs sampling.” This is quicker than standard Gibbs sampling yet yields samples of sufficient quality for fast learning.

The overall learning procedure in deep Boltzmann machines using sampling or variational methods can be slow and consequently greedy; incremental approaches are often used to initialize weights prior to learning. Deep Boltzmann machines can be trained incrementally by stacking two-layer Boltzmann machines and learning the two-layer models using gradient descent and the contrastive divergence-based sampling procedure.

When training a deep RBM incrementally by stacking, to deal with the lack of top-down connections in the model, one can double the input variables of the lower-level model and constrain the associated matrix to be the same as the original; double the output variables of the higher-level model and constrain its matrix in the same way. Once the first Boltzmann machine has been learned the next can be learned using either a sample from independent Bernoulli distributions for the dimensions of *p*(**h**^((1))|**v**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si119.png) based on the sigmoid models of the rewritten Boltzmann machine or using the value of the sigmoid activations. In both cases a fast approximate inference upward pass can be performed using a doubled weight matrix to compensate for the fact that the top-down influence of the model is not captured. When generating a sampler or sigmoid activity for the final layer it is not necessary to double the weights. Subsequent levels can be learned similarly.

 

### Deep Belief Networks

While any deep Bayesian network is technically a deep belief network, the term “deep belief network” has become strongly associated with a particular type of deep architecture that can be constructed by training RBMs incrementally. The procedure is based on converting the lower part of a growing model into a Bayesian belief network, adding an RBM for the upper part of the model then continuing the training, conversion, and stacking process. As we saw earlier, an RBM is a two-layer joint model for which we can use some algebra to write conditional models of observed given hidden or hidden given observed layers that are consistent with the underlying joint distribution. It therefore follows that a deep belief network can be obtained through a procedure of learning a joint RBM model for two layers, converting the model into its conditional formulation for the layer below given the layer above, then adding a new layer on top to the model, parameterizing the top two layers as a new joint RBM model then learning the new parameters. [Fig. D.5B](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#f0030) illustrates the general form, which can be written

$P{({\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h}^{(1)},\\ldots,\\mathbf{h}^{(L)};\\theta})} = P(\\mathbf{v} \\mid \\mathbf{h}^{(1)})\\left\\lbrack \\prod\\limits\_{l = 1}^{L - 2}P(\\mathbf{h}^{(l)} \\mid \\mathbf{h}^{({l + 1})}) \\right\\rbrack P{({\\mathbf{h}^{({L - 1})},\\mathbf{h}^{(L)}})},$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi where, as before, the model is defined in terms of a visible layer **v**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si121.png) and *l* = *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si122.png), …, *L* hidden layers **h**^((*l*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si123.png). The conditional distributions are all products of Bernoulli distributions with sigmoidal parameterizations.

The top *two* layers are parameterized as an RBM. If they have directed rather than undirected connections they can be decomposed into the form *P*(**h**^((*L* − 1)), **h**^((*L*))) = *P*(**h**^((*L* − 1))|**h**^((*L*)))*P*(**h**^((*L*)))<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo *P*(**h**^((*L*)))<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo The result is known as a deep sigmoidal belief network.

The network shown in [Fig. D.5B](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#f0030) can be constructed and trained in a layer-by-layer manner. To see this consider an RBM with visible variables **v**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si127.png) and two layers of hidden variables **h**^((1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si128.png) followed by **h**^((2))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si129.png) on top. A joint model for *P*(**v**, **h**^((1)), **h**^((2)))<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si130.png) can be defined as either a three-layer Boltzmann machine or, by restructuring the parameterization of the lower two layers, as a belief network with an RBM at the top using

stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/F000248si140.png).

Such networks can be trained as follows: first train a two-layer Boltzmann machine using the observed data. Then add a layer on top and initialize its weights to the transpose of the weights learned in the layer below. To train the next layer compute the conditional distribution for the layer above given the layer below and either generate a sample or use the activation of the sigmoid function to transform each example of the training data into the first hidden layer representation. The properties of an RBM can be further exploited to obtain the conditional distribution of the lower layer given the upper layer, and the parameters of the conditional model in this direction can be fixed. Once the second Boltzmann machine has been trained the model has the form ([Eq. D.1](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#eqn1)) and the process of transforming the data, transforming the top-level Boltzmann machine into a conditional model, adding a layer, and training a top layer Boltzmann machine can be repeated as desired.

If the layer above has a different number of units the transpose of the matrix below cannot be used for initialization and certain theoretical guarantees no longer apply. However, in practice the procedure is known to work well with random initialization.

 

## D.4 Further Reading and Bibliographic Notes

Many neural network books ([Haykin, 1994](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur256); [Bishop, 1995](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur43); [Ripley, 1996](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur457)) do not formulate backpropagation in vector-matrix terms. However, recent online courses (e.g., by Hugo Larochelle) and Rojas’ (1996) text do adopt this formulation, as we have done in this Appendix.

[Bourlard and Kamp (1988)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur58) provide a deep analysis of the relationships between autoencoders and principal component analysis. [Vincent, Larochelle, Lajoie, Bengio, and Manzagol (2010)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur547) proposed stacked denoising autoencoders and found that they outperform both stacked standard autoencoders and models based on stacking RBMs. [Cho and Chen (2014)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur97) produced state-of-the-art results on motion capture sequences by training deep autoencoders with rectified linear units using hybrid unsupervised and supervised learning.

The history of Markov random fields has roots in statistical physics in the 1920s with so-called “Ising models” of ferromagnetism. Our presentation of Boltzmann machines follows [Hinton and Sejnowski (1983)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur265) but we use matrix-vector notation and our exposition more closely resembles formulations such as that of [Salakhutdinov and Hinton (2009)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur470). Harmonium networks proposed in [Smolensky (1986)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur499) are essentially equivalent to what are now commonly referred to as RBMs.

Contrastive divergence was proposed by [Hinton (2002)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur263). The idea of using unsupervised pretraining to initialize deep networks using stacks of RBMs was popularized by [Hinton and Salakhutdinov (2006)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur264); [Salakhutdinov and Hinton (2009)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur470) give further details on the use of deep Boltzmann machines and training procedures for deep belief networks, including the variable doubling procedure and other nuances discussed earlier for greedy training of deep restricted Boltzmann machines. [Neal (1992)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur411) introduced sigmoidal belief networks. [Welling, Rosen-Zvi, and Hinton (2004)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur562) showed how to extend Boltzmann machines to categorical and continuous variables using exponential-family models. The greedy layerwise training procedure for deep Boltzmann machines in [Section D.3](#FigD1_687-703_B9780443158889000248.xhtml#s0040) is based on a procedure proposed by [Hinton and Salakhutdinov (2006)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur264) and refined by [Murphy (2012)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur407).

Hybrid supervised and unsupervised learning procedures for restricted Boltzmann machines were proposed by [McCallum, Pal, Druck, and Wang (2006)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur382) and further explored by [Larochelle and Bengio (2008)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur349). [Vincent et al. (2010)](#References_705-736_B978044315888900025X.xhtml#fur547) proposed the autoencoder approach to unsupervised pretraining; they also explored various layerwise stacking and training strategies and compared stacked RBMs with stacked autoencoders.
